• Synonymous variants. These result in a change in the codon that doesn’t alter the amino acid. This is particularly common when the third base of a codon is changed. For example, AAG and AAA both encode the amino acid lysine, as illustrated in Figure 3.4 and Figure 3.7A.

• Non-synonymous (also known as a missense) variant. These result in a change in the codon and the encoded amino acid. An example would be a change from AAG to CAG, changing the amino acid from lysine (Fig. 3.7A) to glutamine (Fig. 3.7C).

• Insertion and deletion (indel) variants. These variants occur when one or more nucleotides are inserted or lost in a DNA sequence. If an indel change affects one or two nucleotides within the ORF of a protein-coding gene, this can have serious consequences because the triplet nucleotide sequence of the codons is totally disrupted, resulting in a frameshift variant. The effect of such a variant is typi-cally severe because the amino acid sequence is totally disrupted, as shown in Box 3.1 and Figure 3.7D. However, if a multiple of three nucleotides is involved, this is ‘in frame’ and does not disturb the triplet nucleotide sequence, meaning that the next codon can be read as normal. The effect of these variants on the gene may there-fore be minor.

• Stop-gain (or nonsense) variant. These variants introduce a prema-ture stop codon, resulting in truncation of the protein. An example would be AAG to TAG changing a lysine (Fig. 3.7A) to a stop codon (Fig. 3.7E). These variants may not only cause an abnormal trun-cated protein but also result in nonsense mediated RNA decay (NMD), resulting in haploinsufficiency due to degradation of the abnormal allele. This is a common mechanism of disease in type I osteogenesis imperfecta (Ch. 25).

• Splice-site variants. These variants occur at the junction between exons and introns and can affect either the splice donor site or the splice acceptor site. In almost all cases the splice donor site at the start of an intron is a GT sequence and the acceptor site at the end of an intron is an AG sequence, as illustrated in Figure 3.8. Pathogenic var-iants affecting either the splice donor or splice acceptor site can stop the introns being removed and the exons being joined together nor-mally. This can lead to exons being completely removed (exon skipping) or to an abnormal or a truncated protein being produced, as shown in Figure 3.8B. In some instances where a premature stop codon is introduced as the result of a splice-site variant, the nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) pathway may be activated and the abnormal RNA degraded to prevent production of an abnormal and potentially harmful protein, as described for stop gain (or nonsense) variants in exons.
Simple tandem repeat variants

Variations in the length of simple tandem repeats of DNA are thought to arise as the result of slippage of DNA during meiosis. These are termed microsatellite (small) or minisatellite (larger) repeats. These repeats are unstable and can expand or contract in different generations. This instability is proportional to the size of the original repeat, in that longer repeats tend to be more unstable. Many microsatellites and minisatellites occur in introns or in chromosomal regions between genes and have no obvious adverse effects. However, some genetic diseases are caused by microsatellite repeats that result in duplication of amino acids within the affected gene product or affect gene expression (Box 3.2).
Copy number variations

Variation in the number of copies of an individual segment of the genome from the usual diploid (two copies) content can be categorised by the size of the segment involved. Rarely, individuals may gain or lose a whole chromosome, which is called aneuploidy. Having only one of a particu-lar chromosome is called monosomy and having an extra one is called trisomy. Such numerical chromosome anomalies most commonly occur by a process known as non-disjunction, where pairs of homologous chromosomes do not separate at meiosis II (p. 38). Common trisomies include Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13). Monosomy of the autosomes (present in all the cells, as opposed to in a mosaic distribution) is not compatible with life, but Turner syndrome, in which there is monosomy for the X chromosome, affects approximately 1 in 2500 live births (Box 3.3). Large insertions or deletions of chromosomal DNA also occur and are usually associated with a learning disability and/or congenital malforma-tions. Such structural chromosomal anomalies usually arise as the result of one of two different processes, explained below:
• non-homologous end-joining
• non-allelic homologous recombination.

Random double-stranded breaks in DNA are a necessary process in meiotic recombination and also occur during mitosis at a predictable rate. The rate of these breaks is dramatically increased by exposure to ionising radiation. When such breaks take place, they are usually repaired accu-rately by DNA repair mechanisms within the cell. However, in a propor-tion of breaks, segments of DNA that are not normally contiguous will be joined (‘non-homologous end-joining’). If the joined fragments are from different chromosomes, this results in a translocation. If they are from the same chromosome, this will result in inversion, duplication or dele-tion of a chromosomal fragment (Fig. 3.9). Large insertions and deletions may be cytogenetically visible as chromosomal deletions or duplications. If the anomalies are too small to be detected by microscopy (smaller than around 5 million base pairs), they are termed microdeletions and microduplications. Many microdeletion syndromes have been described and most result from ‘non-allelic homologous recombination’ between repeats of highly similar DNA sequences. This means that recurrent chro-mosome anomalies – and clinical syndromes – occur in unrelated individ-uals (see Fig. 3.9 and Box 3.3).

The consequence of an individual genomic variant depends on many factors, including the variant type, the nature of the gene product and the position of the variant in the protein. Variants can have profound or subtle effects on gene and cell function. Variants that have profound effects are responsible for ‘classical’ genetic diseases, whereas those with subtle effects may contribute to the pathogenesis of common disease where there is a genetic component, such as diabetes.
• Neutral variants have no effect on quality or type of protein produced.

• Loss-of-function variants result in loss or reduction in the normal protein function. Whole-gene deletions are the archetypal loss-of-function variants but stop-gain or indel variants (early in the ORF), missense variants affecting a critical domain and splice-site variants can also result in loss of protein function.

• Gain-of-function variants result in a gain of protein function. They are typically non-synonymous variants that alter the protein structure, leading to activation/alteration of its normal function either by caus-ing it to interact with a novel substrate or by changing its normal function.

• Dominant negative variants are the result of non-synonymous substitutions or in-frame deletions/duplications but may also be caused by triplet repeat expansions. Dominant negative variants are heterozygous (present on one allele) changes that result in the production of an abnormal protein that interferes with the function of the normal protein.

We each have 3–5 million variants in our genome, occurring approxi-mately every 300 bases. These variants are mostly polymorphisms, aris-ing in more than 1% of the population; they have no or subtle effects on gene and cell function and are not associated with an increased risk of disease. Polymorphisms can occur within exons, introns or the intergenic regions that comprise 98%–99% of the human genome. The most frequent variants are single nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNP (pronounced ‘snip’), describing the substitution of a single base. When considering human genetic variation, it is also important to bear in mind that the human genome is present in two copies in our germline cells. An allele is one of the two copies of DNA sequence at a given genomic loca-tion. Genetic variations can therefore be present on one or both alleles.
Polygenic inheritance

Polygenic inheritance refers to the situation whereby susceptibility to a disease is caused by the combined action of multiple individual genetic variants, each with a small effect on disease susceptibility as compared to a monogenic or familial disease that is caused by a pathogenic variant in a single gene. This is discussed in more detail later in the chapter.
Evolutionary selection

Genetic variants play an important role in evolutionary selection, with advantageous variants resulting in positive selection via improved repro-ductive fitness, and variations that decrease reproductive fitness becom-ing excluded through evolution. Given this simple paradigm, it would be tempting to assume that common variants are all advantageous and all rare variants are deleterious. Unfortunately, it is often difficult to classify any single common variant as either advantageous or deleterious – or, indeed, neutral. Variants that are advantageous in early life and thus enhance reproductive fitness may be deleterious in later life. There may be variants that are advantageous for survival in particular conditions (for example famine or pandemic) that may be disadvantageous in more benign circumstances by causing a predisposition to obesity or autoim-mune disorders.

Familial genetic disease, also known as monogenic disease, is caused by constitutional variants which are inherited through the germline. It has been estimated that about 1% of the human population carries constitu-tional variants that are pathogenic and can directly cause disease or play a major role in the pathogenesis of disease. It should be noted that different pathogenic variants can have differ-ent consequences, depending on the genetic mechanism underlying the disease. The variants that cause familial genetic disease can also vary in penetrance. Penetrance is defined as the proportion of individuals that carry a specific variant who develop the disease phenotype. A variant is said to be fully penetrant if all individuals who inherit that variant develop the disease. Inherited variants may show differences in expressivity. Expressivity describes the level of severity of each aspect of the disease phenotype. Both penetrance and expressivity can influence the number of affected individuals and the clinical manifestations of disease in each generation. Huntington disease is an example of a condition that is fully penetrant since everyone with a pathogenic expansion in the HTT gene will go on to develop the condition, if they live long enough. By contrast, pathogenic variants in the BRCA2 gene tend not to be fully penetrant, such that some variants only cause tumours in about 50% of people. An example of variable expressivity is Marfan syndrome, caused by variants in the FBN1 gene. Some people with pathogenic FBN1 variants may have mild expression, such as being tall with long, slender fingers, while others who may carry the same variant can develop life-threatening aortopathy. This is thought to be due to an interaction with environmental factors or the effects of modifying genetic variants that influence the phenotype. An example of variable penetrance and expressivity of the autosomal codominant disease is α1-antitrypsin deficiency caused by loss-of-func-tion variants in SERPINA1 (Box 3.4). The severity of the disease is worse in homozygotes for the Z variant where α1-antitrypsin levels are much reduced as compared with compound heterozygotes for the Z/S variant. Another example of a difference in penetrance resulting from different pathogenic variants in the same gene is provided by Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) and Becker muscular dystrophy (BMD), both of which are X-linked recessive disorders. Originally these were considered to be different diseases, but they are actually allelic disorders caused by differ-ent variants in the same gene, which encodes the dystrophin protein. In DMD, virtually no functional dystrophin is produced, resulting in progres-sive muscle weakness and early loss of ambulation, whereas in BMD, reduced levels of a truncated dystrophin protein are produced, which retains function, causing a much milder disorder (Box 3.5).
Constructing a family tree

The family tree – or pedigree – is a fundamental tool of the clinical geneticist, who will routinely take a three-generation family history, on both sides of the family, enquiring about details of all medical conditions in family members, consanguinity (literally ‘with blood’ meaning relatedness of parents), dates of birth and death, and any history of pregnancy loss or infant death.
3.4 Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
Inheritance pattern
• Autosomal co-dominant
Genetic cause
• Two common variants in the SERPINA1 gene: p.Glu342Lys and p.Glu264Val
Prevalence
• 1 in 1500–3000 of European ancestry
Clinical presentation
• Variable presentation from neonatal period through to adulthood
• Neonatal period: prolonged jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia or (rarely) liver disease
• Adulthood: pulmonary emphysema and/or cirrhosis. Rarely, the skin disease, panniculitis, develops
Disease mechanism

• SERPINA1 encodes α1-antitrypsin, which protects the body from the effects of neutrophil elastase. The symptoms of α1-antitrypsin deficiency result from the effects of this enzyme attacking normal tissue
Disease variants
• M variant: if an individual has normal SERPINA1 genes and produces normal levels of α1-antitrypsin, they are said to have an M variant
• S variant: p.Glu264Val variant results in α1-antitrypsin levels reduced to about 40% of normal
• Z variant: p.Glu342Lys variant results in α1-antitrypsin levels reduced to about 10% of normal
• PiZZ: individuals who are homozygous for the p.Glu342Lys variant are likely to have α1-antitrypsin deficiency and the associated symptoms

• PiZS: individuals who are compound heterozygous for p.Glu342Lys and p.Glu264Val are likely to be affected, especially if they smoke, but usually to a milder degree 3.5 Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies
Inheritance pattern
• X-linked recessive
Genetic cause
• Pathogenic variants which disrupt the ORF of the dystrophin gene located at Xp21, resulting in a truncated protein that lacks the cysteine rich and C-terminal domains
Prevalence
• 1 in 3000–4000 live male births
Clinical presentation
• Delayed motor milestones
• Speech delay
• Grossly elevated creatine kinase levels (in the thousands)
• Ambulation is usually lost between the ages of 7 and 13 years
• Lifespan is reduced, with a mean age of death, usually from respiratory failure, in the mid-twenties
• Cardiomyopathy affects almost all boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy and some female carriers
Disease mechanism
• DMD encodes dystrophin, a major structural component of muscle
• Dystrophin links the internal cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix
Disease variants

• Becker muscular dystrophy is also caused by pathogenic variants in DMD, but these are in-frame deletions that result in production of a truncated dystrophin, which retains function but is expressed at lower and more variable levels than full-length dystrophin
Patterns of disease inheritance

The basic symbols and nomenclature used in drawing a pedigree are shown in Figure 3.10A. Examples of pedigrees with autosomal domi-nant, autosomal recessive and X-linked recessive and mitochondrial pat-terns of inheritance are illustrated in Figure 3.10B–E. Examples of human diseases with all these types of inheritance discussed in more detail else-where in this book are shown in Box 3.6.
Autosomal dominant inheritance

An example of autosomal inheritance is shown in Figure 3.10B. Here, the disease is inherited through four generations with affected individuals in each generation. Both males and females are affected in approximately equal numbers and the risk of passing the disease from an affected indi-vidual in one generation to offspring in the next generation is 50% inde-pendent of gender.
Autosomal recessive inheritance

In this case, both copies (alleles) of a gene must be mutated before the disease is manifest in an individual. An example of autosomal recessive inheritance is shown in Figure 3.10C. An affected individual inherits one mutant allele from each of their parents, who are unaffected carriers for the condition. Approximately 25% of children born to carriers of an auto-somal recessive condition will be affected. The chances of an unaffected child who is not a carrier is 50% and the chances of a child who is a carrier is 25%. An autosomal recessive condition should be suspected in a family with the following features:
• Males and females are affected in roughly equal proportions.
• Parents are consanguineous. Where there is consanguinity, the variants are usually homozygous, meaning the same mutant allele is inherited from both parents.
• More than one sibling born to healthy parents is affected and so the condition may appear to have arisen ‘out of the blue’.

The pattern of autosomal codominant inheritance is similar to auto-somal recessive inheritance. Autosomal codominant inheritance is the term used to describe the situation whereby two different alleles of a gene are expressed, but each version makes a different pro-tein. The combination of both alleles influences the characteristics of the genetic condition. A good example of autosomal codominance is in α1-antitrysin deficiency, where the Z and S protein variants may be inherited, resulting in different degrees of disease severity (see Box 3.4).
X-linked inheritance

An example of X-linked recessive inheritance is shown in Figure 3.10D. Here the disease only occurs in males but is transmitted from the mother, who is an unaffected carrier. Affected males cannot transmit the condition to their sons (but all their daughters are carriers). The chance of a female carrier having an affected child is 25% or half of her male offspring. This is because with each conception, she has a 50% chance of passing on the pathogenic variant but only males are affected. This type of inheritance occurs because males have only one X chromosome, whereas females have two (see Fig. 3.1). Note that female carriers may occasionally exhibit signs and symptoms of an X-linked disease due to a phenomenon called skewed X-inactivation. All female embryos, at about 100 cells in size, stably inactivate one of their two X chromosomes in each cell. Where this inactivation is ran-dom, approximately 50% of the cells will express the genes from one X chromosome and 50% of cells will express genes from the other. Where there is a pathogenic variant, there is often skewing away from the affected X chromosome, resulting in an unaffected female carrier. However, if, by chance, there is a disproportionate inactivation of the 3.6 Patterns of inheritance for selected familial genetic normal X chromosome with skewing towards the mutant allele, then an affected female carrier may be clinically affected (albeit more mildly than males). An example of this is in DMD, where cardiomyopathy may be observed in some female carriers (see Box 3.5).
Mitochondrial inheritance

An example of mitochondrial inheritance is shown in Figure 3.10E. In this case the disease is transmitted only by females, but males and females are generally equally affected. Unlike the inheritance pat-terns mentioned above, mitochondrial inheritance has nothing to do with meiosis but reflects the fact that mitochondrial DNA is transmit-ted by oocytes: sperm do not contribute mitochondria to the zygote. Mitochondrial disorders tend to be variable in penetrance and expres-sivity within families, and this is mostly accounted for by the fact that only a proportion of multiple mtDNA molecules within mitochondria contain the pathogenic variant (the degree of mtDNA heteroplasmy). Some examples of mitochondrial disease are shown in Box 3.7. As mitochondria are most numerous in cells with high metabolic demands, such as muscle, retina and the basal ganglia, these tissues tend to be the ones most severely affected in mitochondrial diseases. It is important to remember that a mitochondrial pattern of inheritance only applies when the pathogenic variant directly affects the mitochondrial genome. Some mitochondrial diseases are due to pathogenic variants in nuclear genes like RRM2B, where the gene product is transported into the mitochondrion to maintain mtDNA. In such cases the disease may be inherited in an autosomal manner.
Imprinting

In several chromosomal regions (loci), gene expression is dependent on the parent of origin. These are called imprinted loci. Within these loci, the paternally inherited allele may be active while the mater-nally inherited allele may be silenced, or vice versa. Variants within imprinted loci lead to an unusual pattern of inheritance where the phe-notype is manifest only if inherited from the parent who contributes the transcriptionally active allele. Examples of imprinting disorders are given in Box 3.8.

Somatic variants are not inherited but instead occur during post-zygotic mitotic cell divisions at any point from embryonic development to late adult life. An example of this phenomenon is polyostotic fibrous dys-plasia (McCune–Albright syndrome), in which somatic gain-of-function variants in the GNAS gene in embryonic development cause constitutive activation of G protein signalling. This influences hormone regulation and many other cell functions, resulting in focal lesions in the skeleton and endocrine dysfunction. The most important example of human disease caused by somatic variants is cancer (Ch. 8). Here, ‘driver mutations’ occur within genes that are involved in regulating cell division or apoptosis, resulting in abnormal cell growth and tumour formation. The two general cat-egories of cancer-causing variants are gain-of-function variants in growth-promoting genes (oncogenes) and loss-of-function variants in growth-suppressing genes (tumour suppressor genes). Whichever mechanism is operative, most tumours require an initiating variant in a single cell that can then escape from normal growth controls. This cell replicates more frequently or fails to undergo programmed death, resulting in clonal expansion. As the size of the clone increases, one or more cells may acquire additional variants that confer a further growth advantage, leading to proliferation of these subclones, which may ultimately result in aggressive metastatic cancer. The cell’s com-plex self-regulating machinery means that more than one variant is usually required to produce a malignant tumour (see Fig. 8.3). For example, if a variant results in activation of a growth factor gene or receptor, then that cell will replicate more frequently due to autocrine stimulation. However, this mutant cell will still be subject to nor-mal cell-cycle checkpoints to promote DNA integrity in its progeny.

If additional variants in the same cell result in defective cell-cycle checkpoints, however, it will rapidly accumulate further genomic var-iants, which may allow completely unregulated growth and/or sepa-ration from its matrix and cellular attachments and/or resistance to apoptosis. As cell growth becomes increasingly dysregulated, cells de-differentiate, lose their response to normal tissue environment and cease to ensure appropriate mitotic chromosomal segregation. These processes combine to generate the classical malignant character-istics of disorganised growth, variable levels of differentiation and numerical and structural chromosome abnormalities. An increase in somatic variant rate can occur from exposure to external mutagens, such as ultraviolet light or cigarette smoke, or if the cell has defects in DNA repair systems. Accordingly, cancer is a disease that affects the fundamental processes of molecular and cell biology.

For decades, the analysis of metaphase chromosomes by light micros-copy was the mainstay of clinical cytogenetic analysis, the aim being to detect gains or losses of whole chromosomes (aneuploidy) or large chromosomal segments (> 4 million bp). More recently, genome-wide microarrays (array comparative genomic hybridisation or array CGH and SNP arrays) have replaced chromosome analysis, allowing rapid and precise detection of segmental gain or loss of DNA throughout the genome (see Box 3.3). Microarrays consist of grids of multiple wells containing short DNA sequences (reference DNA) that are complemen-tary to known sequences in the genome. In array CGH, patient and reference DNA are each labelled with a coloured fluorescent dye (gen-erally, patient DNA is labelled with a green fluorescent dye and refer-ence DNA with a red fluorescent dye) and added to the microarray grid. Where there is an equal quantity of patient and reference DNA bound to the spot, this results in yellow fluorescence. Where there is too much patient DNA (representing a duplication of a chromosome region), the spot will be greener; it will be more red (appears orange) where there is 2:1 ratio of the control to patient DNA (representing heterozygous deletion of a chromosome region (Fig. 3.11). Array CGH and other array-based approaches can detect small chromosomal deletions and duplications. They are also generally more sensitive than conventional karyotyping at detecting mosaicism (where there are two or more populations of cells, derived from a single fertil-ised egg, with different genotypes). However, array-based approaches will not detect balanced chromosome rearrangements where there is no loss or gain of genes/chromosome material, such as balanced reciprocal translocations, or a global increase in copy number, such as triploidy (where there are three copies of each chromosome rather than two). The widespread use of array-based approaches has brought a num-ber of challenges for clinical interpretation, including the identification of copy number variants (CNVs) of uncertain clinical significance, CNVs of variable penetrance and incidental findings. A CNV of uncertain clinical significance describes a loss or gain of chromosome material where there are insufficient data to conclude whether or not it is associated with a learning disability and/or medical problems. While this uncertainty can be difficult to prepare families for, and can be associated with consider-able anxiety, it is likely that there will be greater clarity in the future as we generate larger CNV datasets. A CNV of variable penetrance, also known as a neurosusceptibility locus, describes a chromosome deletion or duplication associated with a lower threshold for manifesting a learning disability or autistic spectrum disorder. These CNVs of variable penetrance are therefore identified at greater frequencies among individuals with a learning disability and/or
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: CGH autistic spectrum disorder than in the general population. The current understanding is that additional genetic and environmental modifying factors must influence the phenotypic expression of these neurosuscep-tibility loci. Finally, an incidental CNV finding describes a deletion or duplication encompassing a gene or genes that are causative of a phenotype or risk unrelated to the presenting complaint. For instance, if, through the array CGH investigation for an intellectual disability, a deletion encompassing the BRCA1 gene were identified, this would be considered an incidental finding.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Gene amplification: polymerase chain reaction
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a fundamental laboratory tech-nique that amplifies targeted sections of the human genome for further analysis – most commonly, DNA sequencing. The method uses thermal cycling: repeated cycles of heating and cooling allow the initial separation of double-stranded DNA into two single strands (known as denaturation) followed by DNA amplification, using DNA polymerase (under cooled conditions). Since DNA polymerase is only able to add a nucleotide to an existing 3′OH group, specially designed primers (short segments of nucleotides) are used to anneal to the DNA template and target the region for amplification. This cycle of heating/cooling and denaturation/ replication is repeated many times, resulting in the exponential amplifica-tion of DNA between primer sites (Fig. 3.12).
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Gene sequencing
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: In the mid-1970s, a scientist called Fred Sanger pioneered a DNA sequencing technique (Sanger sequencing) that could determine the precise order and nucleotide type (thymine, cytosine, adenine and gua-nine) in a particular molecule of DNA. Modern Sanger sequencing uses fluorescently labelled, chain-terminating nucleotides that are sequentially incorporated into the newly synthesised DNA, thus generating multiple DNA chains of different lengths. Capillary electrophoresis then sepa-rates these DNA chains, allowing the fragments to be ‘read’ by a laser and producing a sequence chromatogram that corresponds to the tar-get sequence (Fig. 3.13). Although transformative, Sanger sequencing was difficult and costly to scale, as exemplified by the Human Genome Project, which used this technology, taking 12 years to sequence the entire human genome at a cost approaching US$3 billion. Recently, DNA sequencing has been transformed again by a group of technologies col-lectively known as ‘next-generation sequencing’ (NGS; Fig. 3.14). This refers to a family of post-Sanger sequencing technologies that use the same five basic principles:
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: • Library preparation: DNA samples are fragmented (by enzyme cleavage or ultrasound) and then modified with a custom adapter sequence.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: • Amplification: the library fragment is amplified to produce DNA clus-ters, each originating from a single DNA fragment. Each cluster will act as a single sequencing reaction.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: • Capture: if an entire genome is being sequenced, this step will not be included. The capture step is required if targeted resequencing is necessary, such as for a panel gene test or an exome (Box 3.9).
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: • Sequencing: each DNA cluster is simultaneously sequenced and the data from each captured; this is known as a ‘read’ and is usu-ally between 50 and 300 bases long. See Box 3.10 for a detailed description of the three most commonly used sequencing methods: synthesis, ligation and ion semiconductor sequencing.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: • Alignment and variant identification: specialised software analyses read sequences and compares the data to a reference template. This is known as alignment or mapping and, although there are approximately 3 billion bases in the human genome, allows the remarkably accurate determination of the genomic origin where a read consists of 25 nucleotides or more. Variants are identified as differences between the read and the reference genome (this is called variant calling). For instance, if there is a different nucleotide in half the reads at a given position compared to the reference genome, this is likely to represent a heterozygous base substitution. The number of reads that align at a given point is called the depth or coverage. The higher the read depth, the more accurate the variant call. However, in general, a depth of 30 or more reads is generally accepted as producing diagnostic-grade results.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Rather than sequencing only one small section of DNA at a time, NGS allows the analysis of many hundreds of thousands of DNA strands in a single experiment and so is also commonly referred to as multiple parallel sequencing technology. Today’s NGS machines can sequence the entire human genome in a single day at a cost of less than US$1000.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Next-generation sequencing capture
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Although we now have the capability to sequence the entire genome in a single experiment, whole-genome sequencing is not always the optimal use of NGS. NGS capture refers to the ‘pull-down’ of targeted regions of the genome and may constitute several to several hundred genes associated with a given phenotype (a gene panel), the exons of all known coding genes (an exome), or the exons of all coding genes known to be associated with disease (a clinical exome). Each of these targeted resequencing approaches is associated with a number of advantages and disadvantages (see Box 3.9). In order for NGS to be used for opti-mal patient benefit, it is essential for the clinician to have a good under-standing of which test is the best one to request in any given clinical presentation.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Challenges of next-generation sequencing technologies
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Genomic technologies are transforming the way that we practise med-icine, and ever faster and cheaper DNA sequencing offers increasing opportunities to prevent, diagnose and treat disease. However, genomic technologies are not without their challenges: for instance, storing the enormous quantities of data generated by NGS. While the A, C, T and G of our genomic code could be stored on the memory of a smartphone, huge computers, able to store several petabytes of data (where 1 peta-byte is 1 million gigabytes of data), are required to store the information needed to generate each individual’s genome. Even if we can store and handle these huge datasets successfully, we then need to be able to sift through the millions of normal variants to identify the single (or, rarely, several) pathogenic, disease-causing variant. While this can, to an extent, be achieved through the application of com-plex algorithms, these take time and considerable expertise to develop and are not infallible. Furthermore, even after these data have been sifted by bioinformati-cians, it is highly likely that clinicians will be left with some variants for which there are insufficient data to enable their definitive categorisation as either pathogenic or benign. This may be because we simply do not know enough about the gene: because the particular variant has not previously been reported and/or it is identified in an unaffected parent. These variants must be interpreted with caution and, more usually, their interpretation will require input from a genetics expert in the context of the clinical presenta-tion, where an ‘innocent until proven guilty’ approach should be adopted. Finally, if the entire genome or even the exome is interrogated, it is foreseeable that we will routinely identify incidental or secondary findings – in other words, findings not related to the initial diagnostic question. Whether or not to report these incidental findings is a topic of much debate, although there is general agreement that clinicians should feed back incidental findings where there is an intervention that could slow or halt development/progress of the associated disease. Some argue that any clinically relevant pathogenic variants should be fed back to patients, even when no intervention is possible and that to withhold any such information is paternalistic. However, such an approach is problem-atic since, even if patients consent to receiving incidental findings, the breadth of possible outcomes means that meaningful consent is likely to be impossible to achieve. Where children are having testing, returning such findings may violate their right to autonomy and an open future. It is also much harder to interpret variants where there is no associated phe-notype, so seemingly pathogenic novel variants may not actually cause a condition in a particular individual or family (see the end of this chapter for more discussion of ethical considerations in genomics).
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Uses of next-generation sequencing
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Next-generation sequencing is frequently used within diagnostic lab-oratories to identify base substitutions and indels (although the latter were initially problematic). Previously NGS could not reliably detect large deletions or duplications spanning several hundreds or thousands of bases. Similarly, copy number variants, or triplet repeat disorders such as those that cause Huntington disease, myotonic dystrophy and fragile X syndrome (see Box 3.2), were previously difficult to detect by NGS. Increasingly, however, disorders caused by both copy number variants and triplet repeat expansions are being diagnosed with NGS using sophisticated computational methods. Additional potential uses of NGS include detection of balanced and unbalanced translocations and mosaicism: NGS has proved remarkably sensitive at detecting the latter when there is high read coverage for a given region. Of note, however, NGS is still not able to interrogate the epigenome and so will not iden-tify conditions caused by a disruption of imprinting, such as Beckwith– Wiedemann, Silver–Russell, Angelman and Prader–Willi syndromes (see Boxes 3.8 and 3.2).
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Long read sequencing
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Increasingly, long read sequencing, also called third-generation, or sin-gle-molecule sequencing, is entering the diagnostic arena. As with NGS, a number of different platforms are commercially available. One of the most successful is SMRT technology (single-molecule sequencing in real time). This system uses a single-stranded DNA molecule (as compared to the amplified clusters used in NGS), which acts as a template for the sequential incorporation of fluorescently labelled nucleotides. As each complementary nucleotide is added, the fluorescence (and therefore the identity of the nucleotide) is recorded in real time before it is removed and another nucleotide added. A key advantage of third-generation sequencing is the long length of the read it generates. Whereas NGS cannot exceed read lengths of 1 kilobase pairs, long read sequencing technologies typically use read lengths between 10 kilobase pairs and 100 kilobase pairs. This makes it much easier, quicker and cheaper to assemble full genomes; it can also detect structural variation and copy number variation. As well as this, it is better for sequencing repetitive DNA (for example, with respect to the triplet repeat disorders). With NGS, since smaller reads need to be reassembled using bioinformatics software, repeats may be overlooked or duplicated. Another advantage is in analysis of epigenetic changes. Because this technology targets native unamplified templates, the DNA and RNA molecules retain base modifications, allowing epigenomic changes to be detected. Given these inherent advantages, long read sequencing is likely to supersede NGS in the near future. Given the many terms used for NGS and long read sequencing, these technologies are increasingly referred to collectively as ‘massively parallel sequencing’.
section_path: Interrogating the genome: the changing landscape of genomic technologies

text: Genomics in rare neurodevelopmental disorders

Although, by definition, the diagnosis of a rare disorder is made infre-quently, rare diseases collectively affect about 3 million (1 in 17) peo-ple in the UK, the majority of whom are children. NGS has transformed the ability to diagnose individuals affected by a rare disease. Whereas previously, when we were restricted to the sequential analysis of single genes, a clinician would need to make a clinical diagnosis in order to target testing, NGS instead allows the interrogation of multiple genes in a single experiment. This might be done through a gene panel, a clinical exome or whole exome/genome sequencing (see Box 3.9 and p. 50), and has increased the diagnostic yield in neurodevelopmental disorders to 35%–50%. Not only does the identification of the genetic cause of a rare disorder potentially provide families with answers, prognostic infor-mation, the opportunity to meet and derive support from other affected families, and in some cases, access to targeted treatments, it can pro-vide valuable information for those couples planning more children and wishing to consider prenatal testing in the future.
Polygenic diseases

Most common disorders are determined by interactions between a num-ber of genes and the environment. In this situation, the genetic contribu-tion to disease is termed polygenic. Until recently, very little progress had been made in identifying the genetic variants that predispose to common disorders, but this has been changed by the advent of genome-wide association studies (GWAS). A GWAS typically involves genotyping many (> 500 000) genetic markers (SNPs) spread across the genome in a large group of individuals with the disease and in controls. By comparing the SNP genotypes in cases and controls, it is possible to identify regions of the genome, and therefore genes, more strongly associated with a given SNP profile and therefore more likely to contribute to the disease under study. Increasingly there is a move to develop disease-specific polygenic risk scores (PRS) in order to stratify individual risk and determine person-alised management strategies. Whilst not yet in mainstream practice, it is likely that PRS will be integrated into clinical management in the next few years.
Genomics and obstetrics

Prenatal genetic testing may be performed where a pregnancy is consid-ered at increased risk of being affected with a genetic condition, either because of the ultrasound/biochemical screening results or because of the family history. While invasive tests, such as amniocentesis and chorionic villus sampling, have been the mainstay of prenatal diagno-sis for many years, they are increasingly being superseded by non-in-vasive testing of cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA), originating from placental 3.10 Next-generation sequencing methods
Sequencing by synthesis
• The most frequently used NGS method, as illustrated in Figure 3.14
• Used in Illumina systems (commonly used in diagnostic laboratories)
• Uses fluorescently labelled, terminator nucleotides that are sequentially incorporated into a growing DNA chain
• Library DNA samples (fragmented DNA flanked by DNA adapter sequences) are anchored to a flow cell by hybridisation of the DNA adapter sequence to probes on the flow-cell surface
• Amplification occurs by washing the flow cell in a mixture containing all four fluorescently labelled terminator nucleotides: A, C, T and G
• Once the nucleotide, complementary to the first base of the DNA template, is incorporated, no further nucleotides can be added until the mixture is washed away
• The nucleotide terminator is shed and the newly incorporated nucleotide reverts to a regular, non-fluorescent nucleotide that can be extended
• The process is then repeated with the incorporation of a second base etc.

• Sequencing by synthesis is therefore space- and time-dependent: a sensor will detect the order of fluorescent emissions for each spot on the plate (representing the cluster) and determine the sequence for that read
Sequencing by ligation
• Used in SOLiD systems
• Uses DNA ligase rather than DNA polymerase (as is used in sequencing by synthesis) and short oligonucleotides (as opposed to single nucleotides)
• Library DNA samples are washed in a mixture containing oligonucleotide probes representing 4–16 dinucleotide sequences. Only one nucleotide in the probe is fluorescently labelled
• The complementary oligo probes will hybridise, using DNA ligase, to the target sequence, initially at a primer annealed to the anchor site and then progressively along the DNA strand
• After incorporation of each probe, fluorescence is measured and the dye is cleaved off
• Eventually, a new strand is synthesised (composed of a series of the oligo probes)
• A new strand is then synthesised but is offset by one nucleotide
• The process is repeated a number of times (5 rounds in the SOLiD system), providing overlapping templates that are analysed and a composite of the target sequence determined
Ion semiconductor sequencing

• When a nucleotide is incorporated into a growing DNA strand, a hydrogen ion is released that can be detected by an alteration in the pH of the solution. This hydrogen ion release forms the basis of ion semiconductor sequencing
• Each amplified DNA cluster is located above a semiconductor transistor, capable of detecting differences in the pH of the solution
• The DNA cluster is washed in a mixture containing only one type of nucleotide
• If the correct nucleotide, complementary to the next base on the DNA template, is in the mixture and incorporated, a hydrogen ion is released and detected

• If a homopolymer (sequence of two or more identical nucleotides) is present, this will be detected as a decrease in pH proportionate to the number of identical nucleotides in the sequence trophoblasts and detectable in the maternal circulation from 4–5 weeks’ gestation; it is present in sufficient quantities for testing by 9 weeks.

• Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). This refers to the sequencing and quantification, using NGS, of cffDNA chromosome-specific DNA sequences to identify trisomy 13, 18 or 21. The accuracy of NIPT in detecting pregnancy-specific aneuploidy approaches 98%. A false-negative result can occur when there is too little cffDNA (possibly due to early gestation or high maternal body mass index) or when aneuploidy has arisen later in development and is confined to the embryo and not represented in the placenta. False positives can occur with confined placental mosaicism (describing aneuploidy in the placenta, not the fetus) or with an alternative cause of aneu-ploidy in the maternal circulation, such as cell-free tumour DNA.

• Non-invasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD). This refers to the identifi-cation of a fetal single-gene defect that either has been paternally inherited or has arisen de novo and so is not identifiable in the maternal genome. Examples of conditions that are currently amena-ble to NIPD include achondroplasia and the craniosynostoses. Increasingly, however, NIPD is being used for autosomal recessive conditions such as cystic fibrosis, where parents are carriers for dif-ferent gene variants. Research is underway to perform more agnos-tic fetal gene sequencing through whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing on cffDNA.

Where a genetic diagnosis is known in a family, a couple may opt to undertake pre-implantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M, previously known as PGD or pre-implantation genetic diagno-sis). PGT-M is used as an adjunct to in vitro fertilisation and involves the genetic testing of a single cell from a developing embryo in very early life, prior to transfer to the uterus.
Genomics and oncology

Until recently, individuals were stratified to genetic testing if they pre-sented with a personal and/or family history suggestive of an inherited cancer predisposition syndrome (Box 3.11). Relevant clinical information included the age of cancer diagnosis and number/type of tumours. For example, the diagnosis of bilateral breast cancer in a woman in her thir-ties with a mother who had ovarian cancer in her forties is suggestive of BRCA1/2-associated familial breast/ovarian cancer. In many familial cancer syndromes, somatic gene variants act together with an inherited variant to cause specific cancers (p. 47). Familial cancer syndromes may be due to germline loss-of-function variants in tumour suppressor genes encoding DNA repair enzymes or gain-of-function variants in proto-on-cogenes, which have important roles in cell growth and survival. Some variants can cause constitutive activation, transforming a proto-onco-gene into an oncogene, and allowing cells to grow inappropriately. At the cellular level, loss of one copy of a tumour suppressor gene does not have any functional consequences, as the cell is protected by the remaining normal copy. However, a somatic variant affecting the nor-mal allele is likely to occur in one cell at some point during life, resulting in complete loss of tumour suppressor activity and a tumour develop-ing by clonal expansion of that cell. This two-hit mechanism (one inher-ited, one somatic) for cancer development is known as the Knudson, or two-hit hypothesis. It explains why tumours may not develop for many years (or ever) in some members of these cancer-prone families. In DNA repair diseases, the inherited variants increase the somatic mutation rate. Autosomal dominant variants in genes encoding components of specific DNA repair systems are relatively common causes of familial colon can-cer and breast cancer. Increasingly, genetics is moving into the mainstream, becoming inte-grated into routine care as new gene-specific treatments are introduced. Diagnostic testing for a genetic predisposition to cancer in patients who have already developed a tumour has therefore largely moved from the domain of clinical genetics to oncology, where it is often informing their immediate management. This is exemplified by BRCA1 and BRCA2 (BRCA1/2)-related breast cancer. Previously, women with a pathogenic variant in either the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene would have received similar first-line chemotherapy to women with a sporadic breast cancer with-out a known genetic association. More recently, it has been shown that BRCA1/2 mutation-positive tumours are sensitive to poly ADP ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors which block the single-strand break-repair pathway. In a BRCA1/2 mutation-positive tumour – with compromised double-strand break repair – the additional loss of the single-strand break-repair pathway will drive the cell towards apoptosis. Indeed, PARP inhibitors have been shown to be so effective at destroying BRCA1/2 mutation-positive tumour cells, that BRCA1/2 gene testing is increasingly determining patient management. It is likely, with a growing understand-ing of the genomic architecture of tumours, increasing accessibility of NGS and an expanding portfolio of gene-directed therapies, that testing for many of the other inherited cancer susceptibility genes will, in time, move into the mainstream. Pre-symptomatic testing for unaffected rel-atives remains in the sphere of clinical genetics, where it informs cas-cade screening of wider family members and surveillance/prophylactic management.
Genomics in infectious disease

Genomic technologies are also transforming infectious disease. Given that a microbial genome can be sequenced within a single day at a current cost of under US$100, microbiologists are able to identify a causative microorganism and target effective treatment rapidly and accu-rately. Moreover, microbial genome sequencing enables the effective surveillance of infections to reduce and prevent transmission. Finally, an understanding of the microbial genome will drive the development of vaccines and antibiotics, essential in an era characterised by increasing microbial resistance to established antibiotic agents. This was exempli-fied during the COVID-19 pandemic, when rapid sequencing of the virus enabled the development of fast-tracked vaccines.
Pharmacogenomics

Pharmacogenomics is the science of dissecting the genetic determi-nants of drug kinetics and effects using information from the human genome. For more than 50 years it has been appreciated that polymor-phic variants within genes can affect individual responses to some drugs. For example, loss-of-function variants in a gene called CYP2D6 pres-ent in 3% of the population cause hypersensitivity to debrisoquine, an adrenergic-blocking medication formerly used for the treatment of hyper-tension. This gene is part of a large family of highly polymorphic genes encoding cytochrome P450 proteins, mostly expressed in the liver, which determine the metabolism of a host of specific drugs. Polymorphisms in the CYP2D6 gene also determine codeine activation, while those in the CYP2C9 gene affect warfarin inactivation. Polymorphisms in these and other drug metabolic genes determine the persistence of drugs and, therefore, should provide information about dosages and toxic-ity. With the increasing use of NGS, genetic testing for assessment of drug response is beginning to be employed routinely, and it is becoming more and more possible to predict the best specific drugs and dosages for individual patients based on genetic profiling: so-called ‘personal-ised medicine’. An example is the enzyme thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT), which catabolises azathioprine, a drug that is used in the treat-ment of autoimmune diseases and in cancer chemotherapy. Genetic screening for polymorphic variants of TPMT can be useful in identifying patients who have increased sensitivity to the effects of azathioprine and who can be treated with lower doses than normal.
Gene therapy and genome editing

Replacing or repairing mutated genes (gene therapy) is challenging in humans, but in recent years significant strides have been made in the treatment of genetic disorders. The most exciting development in genetics for a generation has been the discovery of accurate, efficient and specific techniques to enable editing of the genome in cells and organisms. This technology is known as CRISPR/Cas9 (clustered reg-ularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and CRISPR-associated protein 9) genome editing. Ex vivo gene therapy approaches can be used for conditions that affect tissues that are straightforward to remove and replace into the body, such as the blood. For example, in a one-off gene therapy named exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), blood stem cells are removed from the body of patients with haemoglobinopathies beta-thalassaemia and sickle-cell disorder. The stem cells are edited in a laboratory using CRISPR technology, and the treated cells are then returned to the patient via an infusion. In vivo correction is also avail-able via certain groundbreaking drugs, such as voretigene neparvovec (Luxturna), which treats RPE65-related retinal dystrophy via a retinal injection; and onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma), which treats spinal muscular atrophy type 1, a muscle-wasting disorder that usually results in death in the first year of life. In vivo gene therapies are required when the affected tissue cannot be removed. For in vivo therapies, the new genetic material or genome-ed-iting molecules need to be packaged inside a delivery vehicle (called a vector), often a virus, that can deliver them into a cell. Downsides of virally delivered gene therapy have been oncogenic integration of the exogenous DNA into the genome and severe immune response to the virus. Alternative vectors such as plasmid DNA (small, extrachromosomal DNA molecules which replicate independently) are in use but they may also result in immunogenicity. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) show much promise in the treat-ment of genetic disorders and, at the time of writing, are already used in licensed treatments for spinal muscular atrophy and SOD1-amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (also known as motor neuron disease), a fatal degenera-tive disorder of nerve cells in the brain and spinal cord. ASOs are single strands of DNA or RNA that are complementary to a specific sequence of mRNA. They work by binding to a targeted region of RNA and block-ing the translation of certain proteins, thereby altering gene expression. ASOs’ small size means they can easily penetrate cell membranes and target both nuclear- and cytoplasmic-located RNAs. Downsides of ASOs include off-target effects, where they bind to unintended RNA sequences and cause unwanted biological effects.

Other therapies for genetic disease include PTC124, a compound that can ‘force’ cells to read through a stop-gain variant that results in a premature termination codon in an ORF with the aim of producing a near-normal protein product. This therapeutic approach could potentially be applied to any genetic disease caused by stop-gain variants.
Induced pluripotent stem cells and regenerative medicine

Adult stem cell therapy has been in wide use for decades in the form of bone marrow transplantation. The identification of adult stem cells for other tissues, coupled with the ability to purify and maintain such cells in vitro, now offers exciting therapeutic potential for other diseases. It was recently discovered that many different adult cell types can be trans-dif-ferentiated to form cells (induced pluripotent stem cells or iPS cells) with almost all the characteristics of embryonal stem cells derived from the early blastocyst. In mammalian model species, such cells can be taken and used to regenerate differentiated tissue cells, such as in heart and brain. They have great potential both for the development of tissue mod-els of human disease and for regenerative medicine.
Pathway medicine

The ability to manipulate pathways that have been altered in genetic dis-ease has tremendous therapeutic potential for Mendelian disease, but this requires a firm understanding of both disease pathogenesis and drug action at a biochemical level. One example is the development of drugs that can interact with the abnormal CFTR proteins in cystic fibrosis and partially restore their function either by opening the chloride channel or allowing the abnormal protein to reach the cell surface. Another exam-ple is the use of burosumab, a monoclonal antibody to FGF23 which is a highly effective treatment for X-linked hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH). While XLH is caused by pathogenic variants in the PHEX gene, raised levels of FGF23 are responsible for the hypophosphataemia. Accordingly, burosumab works by targeting the pathways that are disrupted by PHEX rather than targeting the gene itself (Ch. 25).

As genomic technology is increasingly moving into mainstream clinical practice, it is essential for clinicians from all specialties to appreciate the complexities of genetic testing and consider whether genetic testing is the right thing to do in a given clinical scenario. To exemplify the ethical considerations associated with genetic testing, it may be helpful to think about them in the context of a clinical scenario. As you read the scenario, try to think what counselling/ethical issues might arise: A 32-year-old woman is referred to discuss BRCA2 testing; she is currently pregnant with her second child (she already has a 2-year-old daughter) and has an identical twin sister. Her mother, a healthy 65-year-old with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, participated in direct-to-consumer (DTC) testing for ‘a bit of fun’ and a BRCA2 gene variant – common in the Ashkenazi Jewish population – was identified. There is no significant cancer family history of note. Consider the following issues:

• Pre-symptomatic/predictive testing. Although predictive testing could be considered for the unaffected patient, in the current sce-nario, any testing would also have implications for her identical twin sister. This needs to be fully explored with the patient and her sister prior to testing. There is also the potential issue of predictive testing in the patient’s first child. A fundamental tenet in clinical genetics is that predictive genetic testing should be avoided in childhood for adult-onset conditions. This is because, if no benefit to the patient is accrued through childhood testing, it is better to retain the child’s right to decide for herself, when she is old enough, whether she wishes to participate in genetic testing or not.

• Prenatal testing. The principles behind predictive genetic test-ing in childhood can be extended to prenatal testing. That is, if a pregnancy is being continued, a baby should not be tested for an adult-onset condition that cannot be prevented or treated in child-hood. However, prenatal testing itself is hugely controversial and there is much debate as to how severe a condition should be to justify prenatal diagnosis, which would determine ongoing preg-nancy decisions.

• Direct-to-consumer testing. While direct-to-consumer (DTC) test-ing can be interesting and empowering for individuals wishing to find out more about their genetic backgrounds, it also has several drawbacks. Perhaps the main one is that, unlike face-to-face genetic counselling (which usually precedes any genetic testing), DCT may uncover abnormalities which have serious implications for the individual and their family, such as pathogenic variants in BRCA1/2. Also, DTC testing is undertaken in isolation with no direct access to professional support. Furthermore, in addition to some (common) single-gene variants, such as the founder BRCA1/2 variants frequently identified in the Ashkenazi Jewish population and discussed in this example, current DTC packages use a series of SNPs to determine an overall risk profile; they eval-uate the number of detrimental and protective SNPs for a given disease. However, given that only a minority of the risk SNPs have so far been characterised, this is often inaccurate. Individuals may be falsely reassured that they are not at increased risk of a genetic condition despite a family history suggesting otherwise, resulting in inadequate surveillance and/or treatment.

The ethical considerations listed in this clinical scenario give just a fla-vour of some of the issues frequently encountered in clinical genetics. They are not meant to be an exhaustive summary and whole textbooks and meetings are devoted to the discussion of hugely complex ethical issues in genetics. However, a guiding principle is that, although each counselling situation will be unique with specific communication and eth-ical challenges, a genetic result is permanent and has implications for the whole family, not just the individual. Where possible, therefore, an informed decision regarding genetic testing should be taken by a com-petent adult following counselling by an experienced and appropriately trained clinician.
