text: Anti-cancer therapy may be used with either curative or palliative intent, and this distinction influences the approach to management of individual patients. The goal of treatment should be recorded in the medical notes.

• Curative therapy is given with the aim of achieving complete remis-sion. Surgery to remove all macroscopic disease is most frequently the primary curative intervention. However, in some circumstances radiotherapy, systemic anti-cancer therapy or a combination of these may be used with curative, or radical, intent.

• Adjuvant therapy is additional therapy given after the primary curative intervention to lower the risk of disease recurrence. Radiotherapy and/or systemic anti-cancer therapy may be given after surgery with the intention of eradicating any micrometastatic disease that remains.

• Neoadjuvant therapy is additional therapy given prior to the primary curative intervention. Systemic anti-cancer therapy may be admin-istered prior to planned surgery. The principal aim is to lower the risk of disease recurrence. Any reduction in the volume of disease, or ‘downstaging’, may also allow less extensive surgery, increase the likelihood of successful debulking and improve subsequent surgical morbidity. Direct evaluation of the surgical specimen allows assessment of the effectiveness of neoadjuvant therapies, guiding subsequent management and lending this approach to translational research.

• Palliative therapy is primarily used to treat patients with metastatic disease, or where curative treatment is not possible. The goal is to control cancer, with the aim of improving or maintaining quality of life, treating and preventing symptoms and improving survival. The choice of therapy depends on the clinical situation and a careful evaluation of the risks and benefits of the intervention.

Surgery has a pivotal role in the management of cancer. It is the main curative management of most solid cancers. In early localised cases of colorectal, breast and lung cancer, cure rates are high with surgery. There is evidence that outcome is related to surgical expertise, and most multidisciplinary teams include surgeons experienced in the management of a particular cancer. There are some cancers for which surgery is one of two or more options for primary management, and the role of the MDT is to recommend appropriate treatment for an individual patient. Examples include prostate and transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder, in which radiotherapy and surgery may be equally effective. Specialised surgical or interventional radiol-ogy techniques may also be employed with curative intent. Radiofrequency ablation, microwave ablation or cryotherapy may be used to treat small renal cell carcinomas or hepatocellular carcinomas. Surgery has less of a role in lymphoma, high-grade neuroendocrine tumours or small-cell cancer, where systemic anti-cancer therapy is the main treatment used. Surgical procedures are often the quickest and most effective way of palliating symptoms in patients with metastatic disease. Examples include the treatment of faecal incontinence with a defunctioning colos-tomy; fixation of pathological fractures; decompression of spinal cord compression; and the treatment of fungating skin lesions by ‘toilet’ sur-gery. Debulking cytoreductive surgery may improve survival in some can-cers, including renal cell carcinoma and ovarian cancer. In very selected cases, such as patients with oligometastatic disease, resection of metas-tases may improve survival and reduce the need for other therapies.

Radiotherapy (radiation therapy) involves treating cancers with ionising radiation such as X-rays, gamma rays, electrons or charged atoms. Ionising radiation kills cancer cells by two mechanisms: directly damag-ing cancer DNA or indirectly by triggering the formation of very reactive molecules (free radicals) that also damage cancer DNA. Radiotherapy can be given alongside systemic therapy and some anti-cancer thera-pies act as radiosensitisers, which can make cancer cells more sensitive to radiation and allow reduced radiation doses. There are several types of radiation therapy including external beam radiotherapy, stereotactic radiotherapy (a precisely targeted form of high-dose external beam radiotherapy), proton beam therapy, brachytherapy (internal or locally applied radiotherapy) and radioisotope therapy (sys-temically delivered radiotherapy).
External beam radiotherapy

External beam radiotherapy is most commonly delivered by a linear accelerator, which produces electron or photon beams. As normal tis-sues can also be damaged by radiotherapy, treatments are planned to ensure maximum exposure of the tumour and minimal exposure of sur-rounding normal tissues (Fig. 8.10). Improved localisation of the target volume, or tumour, can be achieved by the use of surgical clips at the site of resection and fusion of radiotherapy planning CT scans with diagnos-tic MRI or PET-CT scans. Treatment-planning software controls the size and shape of the beam. Intensity-modulated radiotherapy (which allows for more homogeneous dose distribution) and volumetric radiotherapy (in which the shape of the radiation beam is designed to closely fit the tumour) have largely replaced conventional methods that use a limited number of square or rectangular beams. Biological differences between normal and tumour tissues are exploited to obtain therapeutic benefit. Fundamental to this is fractionation, which entails delivering the radiation as a number of small doses on a daily basis. This allows normal cells to recover from radiation damage, while recovery occurs to a lesser degree in malignant cells. Fractionation regimens vary depending on the tumour being treated, the total radiation dose to be delivered and the intent of treatment. Curative, or radical, treatments typically deliver a higher over-all dose in 20–35 fractions over 4–7 weeks. For palliative treatments a smaller dose given over 1–10 fractions is usually adequate. Malignant tissues vary widely in their sensitivity to radiotherapy. Germ cell tumours and lymphomas are extremely radiosensitive, and relatively low doses are adequate for cure. However, most other cancers require higher doses. Normal tissue also varies in its radiosensitivity, with the central nervous system, small bowel and lung being among the most sensitive.
Stereotactic radiotherapy

Stereotactic radiotherapy is a highly targeted method of external beam radi-otherapy, which delivers a high dose of radiation in a small number of treat-ments. It uses advanced imaging techniques to focus radiation beams from many different angles so that they converge precisely on the tumour with minimal damage to surrounding healthy tissues. This is commonly used to treat early-stage lung cancers or oligometastatic cancer sites.
Proton beam radiotherapy

Proton beam radiotherapy uses a cyclotron to produce beams of high-en-ergy protons, which release their energy at a specific depth within the tumour, thereby delivering a high dose of radiation directly to cancer deposits while sparing surrounding healthy tissues. It can be used when treating sensitive areas like the brain or in treating cancers that are difficult to reach with other forms of radiotherapy.
Brachytherapy

Brachytherapy, or internal radiation therapy, involves the direct applica-tion of a radioactive source onto or into a tumour. This allows the delivery of a high, localised dose of radiation. Brachytherapy is a common treat-ment for cancers of the prostate, uterus and cervix. Most commonly, an applicator device is used to deliver a radioactive source directly to the tumour for a set time, typically 10–20 minutes. In other cases, such as in prostate cancer, small radioactive seeds may be permanently placed into the organ, releasing radiation slowly over several months.
Radioisotope therapy

Radioisotope therapy is a precise way to deliver systemic, targeted radi-ation therapy to certain cancers using radioactive substances, which are either ingested or injected into the bloodstream. Radioactive iodine (131 I) may be administered orally and is absorbed by thyroid cells (both normal and malignant). Radioactive iodine emits predominantly beta particles. It is used as an adjuvant therapy in differentiated thyroid cancer (following thyroidectomy), in the treatment of metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer (see p. 708) and to treat benign thyroid disease (such as Graves disease, see p. 704). Other therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals include radium-223 (223 Ra), strontium-89 (89 Sr) and samarium-153 (153 Sm), which are used to treat bone pain from prostate cancer metastases. These are administered by intravenous injection and are taken up by bony tissue due to their sim-ilarity to calcium or affinity to bone tissue with a high turnover. 223 Ra emits alpha particles, while 89 Sr and 153 Sm emit beta particles, to deliver high doses of radiation directly to cancer cells in the bone. Lutetium-177 (177 Lu)-DOTATATE and 131 I-MIBG are intravenous radiopharmaceuticals used to treat metastatic neuroendocrine tumours (p. 732) and advanced malignant phaeochromocytoma/paraganglioma (p. 730).
Side-effects of radiotherapy

The side-effects of radiotherapy depend on the site being treated, the tissue’s radiosensitivity and the dose delivered. For example, skin reactions are common with high-dose radical head and neck cancer treatments, or proctitis and cystitis with treatment to the bladder or prostate. These acute reactions typically settle within a few weeks after treatment. Late effects of radiotherapy develop more than 6 weeks after treatment and occur in 5%–10% of patients. Examples include brachial nerve damage or lymphoedema after breast cancer treatment and fibrosis leading to bladder, bowel and sexual problems after pelvic radiotherapy. There is also a risk of inducing new cancers after radiotherapy, which varies depending on the site treated and on whether the patient has had other treatment such as cytotoxic chemotherapy. Systemic radioisotope therapies can cause bone mar-row and renal toxicity.

Systemic anti-cancer therapy (SACT) is a collective term to describe the growing number of differing drug therapies used to treat cancer. These drugs reach throughout the body to treat cancer cells wherever they may be. Increasingly, treatment is tailored to a patient’s particular cancer and its molecular profile, allowing more personalised therapy. Whilst most anti-cancer therapies cause some side-effects, most of these can be managed with supportive medicines at home. Some patients will develop severe toxicities and an acute assessment will be needed. Examination of the patient on anti-cancer treatment should consider the type of anti-cancer treatment, duration since the last treat-ment and other concurrent toxicities. Patients on anti-cancer therapy can deteriorate quickly and prompt assessment and management is required. There may be specific management protocols to help man-age treatment-related toxicities and advice should be sought from the patient’s cancer centre or acute oncology team.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy

Cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs work by interfering with the processes involved in cell division. They are sub-classified by their mode of action (Fig. 8.11). Cytotoxic chemotherapies have their greatest activity in proliferating cells and this provides the rationale for their use in the treatment of cancer. However, they are not specific for cancer cells and the side-effects of treatment are largely a result of their antiproliferative actions in normal tissues such as the bone marrow, skin and gut (p. 159). Other organs, such as the heart, kidney and peripheral nervous system, may also be affected by some cytotoxic drugs. The choice of cytotoxic chemotherapy agent, or combination of treatments, is determined by the cancer type. The dosing schedule is determined by the choice of treatments and recovery of normal tissues, usually the bone marrow. For most common cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens the treatment is administered in cycles. A course of treatment may constitute a pre-defined number of cycles, or may continue indefi-nitely until evidence of disease progression or until limiting side-effects.
Side-effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy

Supportive therapy is used to enable patients to tolerate therapy and achieve benefit. Nausea and vomiting are common, but with modern antiemetics, regimens such as the combination of dexamethasone and highly selective 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT 3, serotonin) receptor antago-nists such as ondansetron, most patients now receive cytotoxic chemo-therapy without any significant problems. Myelosuppression is common to almost all cytotoxics and this not only limits the dose of drug but also can cause life-threatening complications. The risk of neutropenia can be reduced with the use of specific growth factors that accelerate the repopulation of myeloid precursor cells. The most commonly employed is granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G–CSF; see p. 944), which is widely used with prophylactic intent with cytotoxic chemotherapy regi-mens that induce a high rate of neutropenia.
Neutropenic fever

Neutropenia is a common complication of malignancy. It is usually sec-ondary to cytotoxic chemotherapy but may occur with radiotherapy, if large amounts of bone marrow are irradiated, and some targeted therapy agents. It may also be a component of pancytopenia due to malignant infiltration of the bone marrow. After cytotoxic chemotherapy neutropenic fever is most commonly defined as a single oral temperature of ≥ 38.3°C or a temperature of ≥ 38°C sustained for over 1 hour in a patient with a neutrophil count of < 0.5 × 10 9 /L (or < 1.0 × 10 9 /L if the nadir is antici-pated to drop to < 0.5 × 10 9 /L in the next 48 hours). The risk of sepsis is greater with profound neutropenia (neutrophil count < 0.1 × 10 9 /L), prolonged neutropenia (< 0.5 neutrophils for ≥ 7 days) or a rapid rate of decline in neutrophils as well as the presence of other risk factors, such as intravenous cannulae or urinary catheters. Neutropenic fever is an emergency in cancer patients as, if left untreated, it can result in sepsis with a high mortality rate.
Clinical features

The typical presentation is with high fever, and affected patients may feel non-specifically unwell. If patients have been taking paracetamol or glucocorticoids then fever or symptoms may be masked. Examination is usually unhelpful in defining a primary source of the infection. Hypotension is an adverse prognostic feature and may progress to systemic circula-tory shutdown and organ failure.
Investigations and management

An infection screen should be performed, including blood cultures (both peripheral and from central lines), urine culture, chest X-ray and swabs for culture (throat, central line, wound). High-dose intravenous antibiotics should be commenced (ideally within 1 hour of admission) for all febrile patients on systemic anti-cancer therapy, without await-ing test results. The standard approach is to commence empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics according to local hospital policies agreed with microbiologists and based on local antibiotic resistance patterns. Depending on the patient’s MASCC risk index score (Box 8.18) and likely organisms, this may be either monotherapy (e.g. piperacillin– tazobactam or meropenem) or combination therapy (e.g. with the addition of gentamicin if high risk on MASCC score, metronidazole if anaerobic infection is suspected, or vancomycin/teicoplanin where gram-positive infection is suspected). Antibiotics should be adjusted according to culture results, although these are often negative. If there is no clinical improvement after 36–48 hours, antibiotics should be reviewed with microbiological advice, and antifungal cover should be considered (e.g. fluconazole or liposomal amphotericin B). G–CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) can be used to hasten neutro-phil recovery in some patients with febrile neutropenia, in line with local guidelines. Other supportive therapy, including intravenous fluids, oxy-gen, inotrope therapy, ventilation or haemofiltration, may be required (see p. 235).
Tumour lysis syndrome

The acute destruction of a large number of cells can be associated with metabolic sequelae and is called tumour lysis syndrome. It is usu-ally related to bulky, cytotoxic chemosensitive disease, including lym-phoma, leukaemia and germ cell tumours. More rarely, it can occur spontaneously. Pre-treatment serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) cor-relates with tumour bulk and may indicate increased risk.
Clinical features

Cellular destruction results in the release of potassium, phosphate, nucleic acids and purines that can cause transient hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hyperuricaemia and hyperkalaemia. This can lead to acute impairment of renal function and the precipitation of uric acid crystals in the renal tubular system. These can manifest with symptoms associated with multiple underlying electrolyte abnormalities, including fatigue, nausea, vomiting, cardiac arrhythmia, heart failure, syncope, tet-any, seizures and sudden death.
Investigations and management

Prophylaxis with allopurinol and hydration for 24 hours should be con-sidered for high-risk patients. In patients with bulky disease, when rapid tumour shrinkage is anticipated, recombinant urate oxidase (rasburicase) should also be given before the start of treatment. Serum biochemistry should be monitored regularly for 48–72 hours after treatment in patients at risk. Elevated serum potassium may be the earliest biochemical marker. In the treatment of tumour lysis syndrome, adequate hydration is vital, as it has a dilution effect on the extracellular fluid, improving elec-trolyte imbalance, and increases circulating volume, improving filtration in the kidneys. Rasburicase can be used to reduce uric acid levels when other treatments fail, and if these are not effective at correcting the prob-lems, haemodialysis should be considered at an early stage to prevent progression to irreversibility.
Hormone therapy

Hormones are important cell-signalling molecules and, in some cancers, may be key drivers of tumour growth. Blocking hormonal signalling path-ways in these cancers may be a very effective treatment strategy. Approximately 80% of breast tumours are positive for expression of the oestrogen receptor (ER). Assessment of ER status is now standard in the diagnostic workup of breast cancer. Drugs that reduce oestrogen levels or block the effects of oestrogen on the receptor are widely used in the management of ER-positive breast cancer. Adjuvant hormone ther-apy may reduce the risk of relapse and death at least as much as cyto-toxic chemotherapy and in advanced cases can induce stable disease and remissions that may last months to years, with acceptable toxicity. Hormonal manipulation may be effective in other cancers. In prostate cancer, hormonal therapy (e.g. luteinising hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues such as goserelin and/or anti-androgens such as bicalutamide) aimed at reducing androgen levels can provide good long-term control of advanced disease. The side-effects of hormone therapies are linked to their hormonal targets.
Targeted therapies

Advances in knowledge about the molecular basis of cancer have resulted in the development of treatments to target specific genes and proteins that are involved in the growth and survival of cancer cells (Box 8.19). These signalling pathways may have broad importance to a range of cancer types or be specific to certain cancers. They may not be impor-tant in all tumours of the same cancer type, requiring specific molecular testing to predict whether the patient may benefit. Targeted therapies are broadly divided into two groups: monoclonal antibodies (-mab) and small molecule inhibitors (-ib). The -mab family are typically utilised for targets that are overexpressed on the outside of the cancer cell. The -ib family typically target processes within the cell, such as the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, and are designed to be small enough to enter the cell. A wide range of targeted therapies are now used routinely in oncolog-ical practice. Some of these are described below, linked to the hallmark of cancer growth being targeted (see Box 8.19 and p. 160). The side-ef-fects of targeted therapies are determined by the molecular pathway being targeted (p. 159).
EGFR, BRAF and HER2 inhibitors to target sustained proliferative signalling

Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is an important transmem-brane signalling protein. Mutations in the EGFR gene lead to overexpres-sion of the EGFR protein or constitutive activation of the cell-signalling pathway, leading to uncontrolled cell division, in several cancer types. Approximately 15% of lung adenocarcinomas have activating mutations of EGFR, which may be targeted with drugs such as gefitinib, erlotinib or osimertinib. The latter of these agents has been designed to overcome a particular mutation (i.e. T790M) responsible for 50% of resistance to older EGFR inhibitors. In colorectal cancer, drugs such as cetuximab and panitumumab are only active against those cancers that do not have mutations in the RAS/BRAF family of genes (as these infer drug resistance). Colon cancers harbouring a BRAF V600E mutation do not respond to BRAF inhibitors alone due to EGFR reactivation of the BRAF signalling pathway. This reactivation can be overcome by using BRAF inhibitors such as encorafenib at the same time as EGFR inhibitors, such as cetux-imab, to inhibit the EGFR pathways. HER2 is a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor family. Amplification or over-expression of HER2 is found in breast, gastric, pan-creatic, lung and some uterine cancers. Approximately 20% of breast cancers are HER2-positive, where it is associated with increased risk of recurrence and poor prognosis. Several agents have been developed to target HER2, including trastuzumab and pertuzumab. Antibody–drug conjugates are targeted therapies that deliver cytotoxic chemotherapy directly to cancer cells via a linker attached to a mono-clonal antibody (see also Box 24.21). An advantage of this approach is the more precise delivery of cytotoxic chemotherapy to a cancer cell, potentially increasing its efficacy and reducing damage to other cells. The agent trastuzumab emtansine is an antibody–drug conjugate con-sisting of trastuzumab covalently linked to the cytotoxic chemotherapy agent emtansine, which is delivered specifically to HER2-positive breast cancer cells.
CDK4/6 inhibitors to target evasion of growth suppressors

Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors prevent the phos-phorylation of the tumour suppressor retinoblastoma protein, thereby reducing DNA synthesis, cell cycle progression and reducing breast can-cer cell proliferation. CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib, ribociclib and abemaciclib are commonly used in combination with hormone therapies to treat breast cancer.
Telomerase inhibitors to target replicative immortality

The enzyme telomerase helps cancer cells to divide indefinitely and is often overactive in cancer cells. Telomerase inhibitors cause progressive shortening of telomeres, which cause cancer cells to lose their ability to divide so that they eventually undergo apoptosis. The telomerase inhibitor imetelstat has been used in myelodysplastic syndromes to treat refractory anaemia (p. 993).
c-MET/HGF inhibitors to target activation of invasion and metastases

The c-MET receptor is a tyrosine kinase that is activated by its ligand, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), to trigger downstream signalling path-ways, like PI3K/AKT, to promote cell proliferation, invasion and metas-tases. The small molecule c-MET inhibitor crizotinib is used to treat non-small-cell lung cancers that harbour mutations of the ALK or ROS1 genes.
Anti-inflammatory agents to target tumour promoting inflammation

Inflammatory cells release cytokines and growth factors that help pro-mote cancer growth and create an environment enabling tumour pro-gression. The COX-2 enzyme is often overexpressed in cancers and helps them proliferate and evade the immune system. Selective non-ste-roidal anti-inflammatory agents like the COX-2 inhibitor celecoxib may help the cancer immune response and is being investigated alongside immunotherapy. Glucocorticoids, like dexamethasone or prednisolone, are often used in combination with other anti-cancer therapies, for exam-ple as part of lymphoma and myeloma regimens, to improve responses (Ch. 24).
VEGF inhibitors to target the induction of angiogenesis

Activation of members of the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) family play an important role in tumour angiogen-esis and continued cancer growth. VEGFR small molecule inhibitors such as sunitinib, pazopanib and cabozantinib are pillars of renal cell carcinoma treatment and are used in the management of hepato-cellular carcinoma and thyroid cancer. Bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody therapy targeted at VEGF-A, is active in a number of can-cers, including ovarian, colorectal and breast, when used alongside chemotherapy.
PARP inhibitors to target genome instability

Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) is involved in repairing DNA dam-age in cells. Some cancer cells, especially those with mutations of the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes, have a faulty DNA repair system. PARP inhib-itors specifically target these compromised cancer cells so that they are not able to repair DNA damage to effectively proliferate. PARP inhibitors including olaparib are used to treat ovarian and breast cancers. Some cancers have deficiency in mismatch repair genes, which are responsible for correcting mistakes during DNA replication. This deficiency results in microsatellite instability (MSI) and this can be a target for immunotherapy treatments such as checkpoint inhibitor therapy.
BCL-2 inhibitors as a target to resist cell death

The BCL-2 protein helps cancer cells avoid apoptosis and thereby allows ongoing proliferation of cancer growth. Venetoclax is a BCL-2 inhibitor that triggers apoptosis and is used to treat some patients with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and acute myeloid leukaemia (Ch. 24).
IDH1 and IDH2 inhibitors to target the deregulation of cellular energetics and metabolism

Isocitrate dehydrogenases 1 and 2 (IDH1 and IDH2) are some of the most frequently mutated metabolic genes in human cancers. Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 lead to the production of an oncometabolite, which disrupts normal cellular metabolism and contributes to cancer develop-ment and growth. IDH inhibitors, such as vorasidenib for glioma harbour-ing IDH1 or IDH2 mutations, help to restore normal cellular metabolism and help slow tumour progression.
Side-effects of targeted therapies

Fatigue, nausea/vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and hepatic dysfunction are frequent side-effects of targeted therapies. However, the side-effect pro-files of targeted therapy vary dependent on the class of targeted therapy used (p. 159). For example, EGFR inhibitors are commonly associated with adverse dermatological reactions, most frequently consisting of an acneiform rash, but also xerosis, pruritus, palmar plantar erythema, fis-sures or hair changes. Hypertension, proteinuria and bleeding are impor-tant side-effects to monitor for in patients treated with VEGFR inhibitors. The increased risk of significant cardiotoxicity warrants on-treatment monitoring of left ventricular ejection fraction for patients being treated with HER2 targeted therapies. The management of targeted therapy tox-icity usually involves the use of supportive medications to help patients tolerate treatment. More severe toxicity may necessitate targeted ther-apy treatment breaks and/or dose reductions to enable treatment to continue safely.
Immunotherapy

The term immunotherapy encompasses a range of anti-cancer thera-pies that work by harnessing the immune system to attack cancer cells. Cytokines, such as interferon-alfa and interleukin-2, have been used with some success in melanoma and renal cell carcinoma. However, in recent years the development of other immunotherapy treatments has revolu-tionised the management of several cancer types. Immune checkpoints are key regulators of the immune system which work to prevent the immune response from attacking normal healthy cells. Cancers may co-opt this mechanism to evade immune destruction. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are targeted therapies that inhibit these checkpoint molecules (CTLA4, PD-1) or their ligands (PD-L1) (see p. 84; Fig. 4.14). Their use has rapidly expanded and they are now licensed in the management of many cancers, including melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, lung, bladder, head and neck, and, more broadly, any cancers demonstrat-ing microsatellite instability. ICIs may be used alone, or in combination with other ICIs, targeted therapies or cytotoxic chemotherapy. Adoptive cell therapy, also known as cellular immunotherapy, is increas-ingly being used, particularly in haematological malignancies. Immune cells isolated from either the patient’s tumour or bloodstream may be activated and expanded, before being infused back into the patient to attack cancer cells (i.e. tumour infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy). The immune cells may also be genetically modified to improve the likelihood that they identify the cancer cells (i.e. engineered T-cell (TCR) therapy, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy; see pp. 85 and 967). Immunotherapy treatment is likely to become more prevalent in the future for many types of cancers and indications. In patients with advanced or metastatic disease, a key observation has been the poten-tial for durable treatment responses. For example, average survival for patients with metastatic melanoma has improved from 6–8 months in the pre-immunotherapy era to over 5 years with the use of combination anti-CTLA4 and anti-PD-1 ICIs in clinical trials. However, many patients do not respond and others are affected by potentially life-threatening immune-related adverse events.
Side-effects of immunotherapy

Side-effects of ICIs occur when the immune system is stimulated to attack healthy cells and tissues in the body. These immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are increasingly being recognised as oncological emergencies as they have the potential to result in severe, life-threaten-ing or life-long complications. They require prompt recognition, manage-ment and monitoring.
Clinical features

Almost any organ system may be affected, but inflammation of the colon, endocrine organs (thyroid, adrenal and pituitary glands), lungs, liver, kid-ney, skin and nervous system are more frequently seen (see p. 159). irAEs may occur at any point in a patient’s treatment, or even after they have stopped receiving the checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy agent. Multiple irAEs may occur in the same patient.
Investigations and management

Investigation and management of irAEs requires a multidisciplinary approach including oncologists and relevant system specialists. Specialist investiga-tions may be required depending on the body system affected. The focus of treatment is on dampening the over-active immune response, often using high-dose glucocorticoids. Additional immunosuppressant therapies are sometimes required in steroid refractory or persistent cases. In patients who experience severe irAEs, ICI treatment will usually be permanently discon-tinued. In other cases it may be possible to reintroduce ICI treatment once glucocorticoids are weaned down. The investigation and management of several irAEs are summarised below.
Colitis

Immune-related colitis is the most common gastrointestinal irAE, affecting up to 15% of those treated with anti-CTL4 therapy. The hallmark symp-toms of immune-related colitis (ir-colitis) are diarrhoea and abdominal pain. Severe colitis can lead to dehydration, toxic megacolon, colonic perforation or death, especially in cases of diagnostic delay. Persistent diarrhoea or an increase ≥ 4 stools/day over baseline should prompt further investigations and management while immunotherapy is withheld. Specialist gastroen-terology review should be considered. An infective screen and review of renal function and electrolytes should be conducted. Faecal calprotectin is a sensitive and specific non-invasive biomarker of gastrointestinal inflam-mation. Early endoscopic evaluation with biopsy is recommended. The mainstay of ir-colitis treatment is glucocorticoid therapy, given either orally or intravenously dependent on the severity, once bowel perforation has been excluded. A proportion of patients will experience glucocorticoid-re-fractory ir-colitis, in whom second-line immunosuppressants such as inflix-imab or vedolizumab should be considered.
Hepatitis

Hepatitis occurs in 5%–10% of patients treated with monotherapy and 25%–30% treated with immune checkpoint inhibitor combination therapy. Serum transaminases, alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin should be monitored during treatment. Many patients will be asymptomatic, but fever, malaise, abdominal discomfort, jaundice or anorexia may be present. An increase of liver transaminases ≥ 3 times above the upper limit of the normal range (ULN) should prompt further investigations and management whilst immunotherapy is withheld. Specialist hepatology review should be considered. Liver function tests, a coagulation screen and albumin should be measured regularly. A hepatitis screen including infective and autoimmune markers should be performed. Radiological imaging of the liver should be performed to evaluate the liver parenchyma and rule out metastases or thromboembolic events. In severe cases a liver biopsy should be considered. The mainstay of ir-hepatitis treatment is glucocorticoid treatment given either orally or intravenously depend-ent on the severity. Potentially hepatotoxic drugs should be withheld. Additional immunosuppressive agents such as mycophenolate mofetil should be considered in patients with no response to glucocorticoids within 2–3 days. In patients with poor response to initial glucocorti-coids or liver transaminases ≥ 5× ULN, further ICI therapy will usually be discontinued.
Endocrinopathies

Immune-related endocrinopathies are relatively frequent. Any of the endocrine organs may be affected. Symptoms may be non-specific and hormone testing, particularly cortisol, should always be considered at an early stage. Ir-primary hypothyroidism is the most common ir-en-docrinopathy, affecting approximately 10% of patients treated with ICI. Hypophysitis, primary adrenal insufficiency and type 1 diabetes mellitus are also common. The management of ir-endocrinopathies differs from other irAEs in several ways. ICI-therapy may continue, high-dose gluco-corticoids are rarely required and endocrine deficiency usually persists, necessitating life-long hormone replacement. Specialist endocrinology review should be considered. Investigations and treatment depend on the endocrine organ involved. In cases of ir-hypophysitis, a full pituitary axis screen should be performed, with initiation of appropriate hormone replacement therapy and consideration of glucocorticoid therapy follow-ing consultation with a specialist endocrinologist. Visual field assessment and MRI pituitary should be performed to identify any inflammatory mass in the pituitary (and associated impingement on the optic nerves/chiasm) and to exclude metastatic disease as a cause of hypopituitarism.
Neurological

Neurological irAEs are relatively rare, affecting only 1%–5% of patients, but some are associated with a significant risk of mortality. Central nervous system irAEs may include encephalitis or aseptic meningitis. Approximately two-thirds affect the peripheral nervous system, most commonly presenting as polyradiculoneuropathy or cranial neuropa-thies. A common presentation is of a myopathy, which can be associ-ated with neuromuscular junction involvement. A particularly concerning ICI-related complication is a myasthenia gravis–like syndrome (irMG). Typical symptoms include exercise-dependent fluctuating weakness of the proximal extremities or bulbar muscle groups, and ocular symp-toms such as ptosis and diplopia. Early recognition and involvement of neurological specialists is necessary, along with consideration of early referral to intensive care specialists. Urgent assessment of respiratory function should be undertaken. It is also vital to assess for myocardial involvement, as ir-myopathies are frequently associated with myocarditis and the combination of respiratory and cardiac failure is life-threaten-ing. Discontinuation of ICIs, glucocorticoids and pyridostigmine consti-tute first-line management of irMG-like syndrome, with consideration of intravenous immunoglobulins or plasmapheresis for severe cases. Other immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive drugs may also be required.
Evolving cancer therapies

Oncology is an ever-changing clinical specialty, driven by ongoing advances in our understanding of cancer. Every year, research leads to new treatments and tools being developed that improve patient outcomes. At the forefront of development is the expanding use of immunotherapy treatments, both in combination with other systemic therapies and also now as individualised mRNA cancer vaccines. These vaccines are synthesised following an analysis of an individual’s tumour, to identify the most immunogenic tumour-associated antigens or neoan-tigens. mRNA sequences that encode these antigens are designed and encapsulated (e.g. into lipid nanoparticles) and injected into the individual to stimulate an immune response against the cancer cells. Precision-oncology is also rapidly developing. Detailed profiling of tumour DNA by next-generation sequencing (NGS) is increasingly direct-ing targeted treatments in both routine clinical practice and in clinical trials. Analyses of circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) and/or circulating tumour cells (CTC) may be helpful for detecting cancer earlier, decid-ing who needs post-operative treatment, or for tracking the evolution of resistance pathways in an individual’s cancer over time. This may allow treatments to be tailored to retain treatment-sensitive cells and inhibit the growth of drug-resistant cells. These adaptive therapy strategies are currently being explored in clinical trials.

In advanced or metastatic cancer, the evaluation of treatment is an ongoing process and includes assessments of treatment response, toxicity and quality of life. Clinical evaluation, patient-reported outcome measures, biochemical monitoring (including sequential tumour marker analysis), and radiological evaluation are commonly used to determine whether a treatment is being effective. Uniform criteria have been estab-lished to measure these, primarily measuring morphologic criteria using the response evaluation criteria in solid tumours (RECIST; Box 8.20), or iRECIST for immunotherapy treatments. Measurement of metabolic criteria using positron emission tomography (PET) response criteria in solid tumours (PERCIST) can be used to assess metabolic response depending on sequential 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET activity in tumours on treatment. It can be useful to detect metabolic changes in cancers, even if their size remains unchanged, or if there is residual tumour after treatment; however, consistent imaging protocols must be used. Side-effects of treatment are recorded using common toxicity criteria (e.g. common terminology criteria for adverse events (CTCAE)). This allows clinicians to inform patients accurately about the prognosis, effectiveness and toxicity of systemic anti-cancer therapy and empowers patients to take an active role in treatment decisions.

The late toxicities of treatment for cancer are particularly important for patients where multimodality therapy is given with curative intent, where the patient is young and as more patients are living longer. This can cause considerable morbidity: for example, radiotherapy can retard bone and cartilage growth, impair intellect and cognitive function, and cause dysfunction of the hypothalamus, pituitary and thyroid glands. Late con-sequences of cytotoxic chemotherapy include heart failure due to cardi-otoxicity, pulmonary fibrosis, nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity. Premature gonadal failure can result from cytotoxic chemotherapy or radiotherapy and leave a patient subfertile. Patients should be made aware of this before treatment is initiated, as it may be possible to store sperm for male patients before treatment starts; this should always be offered, if practical. Egg storage or embryo banking after in vitro fertil-isation may be an option for young women. Sterility develops at higher radiotherapy doses, but erectile dysfunction is seen in patients receiving high radiotherapy doses to the pelvis, as in prostate cancer. Additional social or psychological support may be required to address these issues. Infertility and pubertal delay are potential late effects of therapy in chil-dren, especially boys. Second malignancies may be induced by cancer treatment and occur at greatest frequency following chemoradiation. Secondary acute leu-kaemia (mostly AML) can occur 1–2 years after treatment with topo-isomerase II inhibitors, or 2–5 years after treatment with alkylating agents. The most common second malignancy within a radiation field is osteosarcoma, but others include soft tissue sarcoma and leukaemia.

Cancer clinical trials are embedded within routine practice in oncol-ogy. Close collaboration with laboratory scientists, active recruitment of cancer patients into clinical trials and robust translational research have led to many new cancer treatments, personalised therapies and a transformation of cancer management over the last 20 years. As many anti-cancer drugs are expected to have toxicities, which may ultimately limit the deliverable dose, clinical trials in cancer differ from trials of other medicines.

• Phase I cancer clinical trials take treatments of interest from labo-ratory studies and test them in patients with advanced cancer for whom no other standard anti-cancer treatment exists. Phase I trials assess the safety of a treatment and identify an optimal dose and dosing schedule. Initial doses are very low and each sequential cohort of patients receives a higher dose. Doses are escalated in controlled cohorts of 1–6 patients, according to toxicities, pharma-cokinetics and pharmacodynamics, until the maximum tolerated dose, or optimum biological dose, is reached.

• Phase II cancer clinical trials treat patients with specific cancers of interest with the trial drug, using the dose established in phase I trials. Phase II trials may be randomised or non-randomised but will recruit enough patients to further assess the safety of the treatment and whether it results in enough anti-cancer activity in a specific cancer to develop the drug further by way of phase III trials.

• Phase III cancer trials are large, multi-centre randomised controlled trials to compare the new treatment of interest with the current established therapy for this indication. Cancer response, toxicity, quality of life and survival data will usually be assessed. Phase III trials may also compare current standard treatment with a different treatment, either looking for improved outcome or improved quality of life with non-inferior outcome. If a treatment is deemed to be safe and effective it will be licensed for clinical use.

• Phase IV trials involve the continuing safety surveillance of a treat-ment after it receives a licence for clinical use. This can be particu-larly useful to detect any rare or long-term adverse effects in a much larger population and longer time period than was possible during phase I–III trials.

As cancer management becomes more complex and personalised, and incorporates multi-modality treatment approaches, oncology teams are increasingly subspecialised and work as part of tumour-specific multidis-ciplinary teams. The diagnosis and management of specific cancers are discussed in more detail elsewhere in the book (Box 8.21). Here we dis-cuss the pathogenesis, clinical features, investigation and management of some common tumours that are not covered elsewhere.

Globally, the incidence of breast cancer is second only to that of lung cancer, and the disease represents the leading cause of cancer-related deaths among women. Invasive ductal carcinoma with or without ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common histology, accounting for 70%, whilst invasive lobular carcinoma accounts for most of the remain-ing cases. DCIS constitutes 20% of breast cancers detected by mam-mography screening. It is multifocal in one-third of women and has a high risk of becoming invasive (10% at 5 years following excision only). Pure DCIS does not cause lymph node metastases, although these are found in 2% of cases where nodes are examined, owing to undetected invasive cancer. Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) is a predisposing risk factor for developing cancer in either breast (7% at 10 years). The survival for breast cancer by stage is outlined in Box 8.22.
Pathogenesis

Both genetic and hormonal factors play a role: about 5%–10% of breast cancers are hereditary and occur in patients with pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2, AT or TP53 genes. Prolonged oestrogen exposure associated with early menarche, late menopause and use of hormone replacement therapy (HRT) has been associated with an increased risk. Other risk factors include obesity, alcohol intake, nulliparity and late first pregnancy. There is no definite evidence linking use of the contraceptive pill to breast cancer.
Clinical features

Breast cancer usually presents as a result of mammographic screen-ing or as a palpable mass, with nipple discharge in 10% and pain in 7% of patients. Less common presentations include inflammatory car-cinoma with diffuse induration of the skin of the breast, and this confers an adverse prognosis. Around 40% of patients will have axillary nodal disease, with likelihood correlating with increasing size of the primary tumour. Distant metastases are infrequently present at diagnosis and the most common sites of spread are bone (70%), lung (60%), liver (55%), pleura (40%), adrenals (35%), skin (30%) and brain (10%–20%).
Investigations

Following clinical examination, patients should undergo imaging with mammography or ultrasound evaluation, and a biopsy using fine needle aspiration for cytology or core biopsy for histology. Histological assess-ment should be carried out to assess tumour type and to determine oestrogen and progesterone receptor (ER/PR) status and HER2 status. If distant spread is suspected, CT of the thorax and abdomen and an isotope bone scan are required. Molecular subtyping is being used to classify tumours into four major subtypes: luminal A (ER+ and/or PR+, HER2−), luminal B (ER+ and/or PR+, HER2+), HER2 type (ER− and PR−, HER2+) and basal-like (often called ‘triple negative’, i.e. ER−, PR− and HER2−). Germline BRCA mutation is performed in high-risk patients, such as those with a family history. This information may allow more targeted selection of therapies.
Management

Surgery is the mainstay of curative treatment. This can range from a lumpectomy, where only the tumour is removed, to mastectomy, where the whole breast is removed. Breast-conserving surgery is as effective as mastectomy if complete excision with negative margins can be achieved. Lymph node sampling is performed at the time of surgery. There is significant evidence to support the use of additional ther-apies to reduce the risk of breast cancer recurrence. Adjuvant radio-therapy is given to reduce the risk of local recurrence. In those patients considered at high risk of recurrence (i.e. tumour of > 1 cm, ER-negative disease or the presence of involved axillary lymph nodes), cytotoxic chemotherapy may be offered. In patients with HER2-positive breast cancer, adjuvant trastuzumab, a humanised monoclonal antibody to HER2, may be used alongside standard cytotoxic chemotherapy. ICI therapy may also be used in patients with triple-negative breast cancer or those with BRCA pathogenic variants. These treatments are increas-ingly being used in the neoadjuvant setting, with the aim of achiev-ing a complete pathological response when the cancer is resected, often with a more organ-preserving surgical procedure. In patients with ER-positive tumours, adjuvant hormonal therapy may gain additional disease-free and overall survival benefits. Patients at low risk of recur-rence (i.e. small, ER-positive disease) may require only adjuvant hor-monal therapy. In post-menopausal women, adjuvant bisphosphonate therapy may also be used. The treatment of metastatic breast cancer is complex. Radiotherapy may be used to palliate painful bone metastases. Systemic anti-cancer therapy decisions are made with consideration of ER status, HER2 sta-tus, PD-L1 status, the distribution of metastatic disease and previous neoadjuvant treatment, alongside assessments of performance status (PS) and comorbidities. For example, in a post-menopausal patient with ER-positive, HER2-negative bone-only metastatic disease who is PS 0, hormonal therapy (i.e. an aromatase inhibitor) in combination with a CDK4/6 targeted therapy (i.e. palbociclib, abemaciclib or ribociclib) may be used as first-line treatment. In a similar patient with additional symp-tomatic liver metastases, cytotoxic chemotherapy may be more appro-priate. The addition of HER2 targeted therapy for HER2-positive breast cancer or ICI therapy for triple-negative breast cancer provides additional benefit.

Most ovarian cancers are epithelial in origin (90%), and up to 7% of women with ovarian cancer have a positive family history. Patients often present late in ovarian cancer with vague abdominal discomfort, low back pain, bloating, altered bowel habit and weight loss. Occasionally, peritoneal deposits are palpable as an omental ‘cake’ and nodules in the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph nodules).
Pathogenesis

Genetic and environmental factors play a role. The risk of ovarian cancer is increased in patients with pathogenic variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2, and Lynch type II families (a subtype of hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer, HNPCC) can have ovarian, endometrial, colorectal and gastric tumours due to mutations of mismatch repair enzymes (p. 848 and Box 3.11). Advanced age, nulliparity, ovarian stimulation and European descent all increase the risk of ovarian cancer, while suppressed ovu-lation appears to protect, so pregnancy, prolonged breastfeeding and the contraceptive pill have all been shown to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer.
Investigations

Initial workup for patients with suspected ovarian cancer includes imag-ing in the form of ultrasound and CT. Serum levels of the tumour marker CA-125 are often measured. Surgery plays a key role in the diagnosis, staging and treatment of ovarian cancer, and in early cases, palpation of viscera, peritoneal washings and biopsies are generally performed to define disease extent.
Management

In early disease, surgery followed by adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy with carboplatin, or carboplatin plus paclitaxel, is the treatment of choice. Surgery should include removal of the tumour along with total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and omentectomy. Even in advanced disease, surgery is undertaken to maximally debulk the tumour and is followed by cytotoxic chemotherapy, typically using carbo-platin and paclitaxel. Bevacizumab, a targeted therapy against VEGFR, is indicated for patients with high-grade tumours that are suboptimally debulked or those with a more aggressive biological pattern. Subsequent treatment decisions are made with consideration of response to first-line cytotoxic chemotherapy and germline BRCA mutation status. Options include further platinum/paclitaxel combination, liposomal doxorubicin or targeted therapy against poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP, e.g. olaparib, niraparib or rucaparib). The serum tumour marker CA 125 and clinical examination may be used to monitor treatment response in ovarian cancer, with CT imaging for those with suspected progressive disease.

Endometrial cancer primarily affects post-menopausal women, with a peak incidence at 65–75 years of age. Mortality from endometrial cancer is currently falling; however, 25% of patients will not survive for 5 years or more. The most common presentation is with post-menopausal bleed-ing, which often results in early detection of the disease before distant spread has occurred.
Pathogenesis

Oestrogen plays an important role in the pathogenesis of endometrial cancer, and factors that increase the duration of oestrogen exposure, such as nulliparity, early menarche, late menopause and unopposed HRT, increase the risk. Endometrial cancer is 10 times more common in obese women and this is thought to be due to elevated levels of oestrogens.
Investigations
The diagnosis is confirmed by endometrial biopsy. MRI scans are used to assess the primary tumour and pelvic lymph nodes, and CT scans assess for metastatic spread.
Management

Surgery is the treatment of choice for early-stage endometrial cancer and is used for staging. A hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy are performed with peritoneal cytology and, in selected cases, lymph node dissection. Adjuvant therapy may be considered and is dependent on the extent of myometrial invasion, grade, presence of lymphovascular invasion and molecular subtypes as classified by the Cancer Genome Atlas. Treatment may include vaginal vault brachytherapy, external beam radio-therapy and systemic anti-cancer therapy, either alone or in combination, dependent on the risk of recurrence. Locally advanced, metastatic or recurrent disease may be treated palliatively with radiotherapy and/or systemic anti-cancer therapy. Immunotherapy alone, or in combination with chemotherapy or other targeted therapies, is used increasingly in this patient group.

Cervical cancer is the leading cause of death from gynaecological can-cer worldwide. The incidence is decreasing in high-income countries as a result of HPV vaccination and screening programmes, but continues to rise in low- and middle-income nations. Early-stage cervical cancer may not cause symptoms. In the UK the most common presentation of these cancers is with an abnormal smear test through the cervical cancer screening programme. Patients may also present with abnormal uterine bleeding, heavy menstrual or unexpected bleeding, including post-men-opausal bleeding. New vaginal discharge, pelvic discomfort or dyspare-unia may also occur. Locally advanced cervical cancer may cause renal impairment, bladder or rectal symptoms due to involvement of adjacent structures. Occasionally, patients present with distant metastases to bone and lung.
Pathogenesis

Almost all cases of cervical cancer are linked to high-risk human papil-lomaviruses (HPV), transmitted through sexual contact. This has under-pinned the introduction of programmes to immunise adolescents against HPV in an effort to prevent up to 90% of cervical cancer.
Investigations

If cervical cancer is suspected, patients will be referred for colpos-copy to examine the cervix and perform a biopsy. Further examination may require cystoscopy and flexible sigmoidoscopy if there are symp-toms referable to the bladder, colon or rectum. Radiological investiga-tions, including CT of the chest and abdomen and MRI of the pelvis, are performed to stage cervical cancer. In some cases PET is also required.
Management

This depends on the stage of disease. For patients with very early cer-vical cancer, a large loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or a cone biopsy may be employed, which may be the only treatment required. These treatments are most frequently used in women with abnormal cells picked up through cervical screening. For small, localised disease, radical surgery is performed. For bulky or locally advanced dis-ease that has spread to tissue around the cervix or regional lymph nodes, chemoradiotherapy is most frequently recommended. Some women may also receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy or a ‘boost’ of brachyther-apy, dependent on the extent of their disease. In the metastatic set-ting, palliative platinum-based cytotoxic chemotherapy, with or without bevacizumab, may be offered. In patients with PD-L1 positive disease, concurrent pembrolizumab may also be used.

Head and neck cancers are typically squamous tumours that arise in the nasopharynx, hypopharynx and larynx. They are most common in older adult males, but oropharyngeal cancers now occur with increasing frequency in a younger cohort of patients, including in women. The rising incidence of oropharyngeal cancers, especially in high-income countries, is thought to be secondary to HPV infection. Presentation depends on the location of the primary tumour and the extent of disease. For exam-ple, early laryngeal cancers may present with hoarseness, while more extensive local disease may present with pain due to invasion of local structures or with a lump in the neck. Patients who present late often have pulmonary symptoms, as this is the most common site of distant metastases (Box 8.23).
Pathogenesis

The tumours are strongly associated with a history of smoking and excess alcohol intake, but other recognised risk factors include Epstein– Barr virus for nasopharyngeal cancer and HPV infection for oropharyn-geal tumours.
Investigations

Careful inspection of the primary site is required as part of the stag-ing process, and most patients will require endoscopic evaluation and examination under anaesthesia. Tissue biopsies should be taken from the most accessible site. CT of the primary site and the thorax is the investigation of choice for visualising the tumour, while MRI may be useful in certain cases.
Management

In general, the majority of patients with early or locally advanced disease are treated with curative intent. In localised disease where there is no involvement of the lymph nodes, long-term remission can be achieved in up to 90% of patients with surgery or radiotherapy. The choice of surgery versus radiotherapy often depends on patient preference, as surgical treatment can be mutilating with an adverse cosmetic outcome. Patients with lymph node involvement are treated with a combination of surgery and radiotherapy (often with a radiosensitising agent such as cisplatin or cetuximab), and this produces long-term remission in approximately 60%–70% of patients. Recurrent or metastatic tumours may be palli-ated with further surgery or radiotherapy to aid local control, or systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy or immunotherapy may be used. Second malig-nancies are common (3% per year) following successful treatment for pri-mary disease, and all patients should be encouraged to give up smoking and drinking alcohol to lower their risk.

Advances in cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment mean that more people are surviving cancer. Cancer survival has doubled in the last 40 years in the UK. There are an estimated 2 million people living with, or beyond, cancer in the UK today and 50% of those diagnosed with can-cer will survive their disease for 10 years or more. Cancer survivorship has at least two common meanings:
• completing treatment for cancer and having no signs of cancer after finishing treatment
• living with, through and beyond cancer, thus including people who receive curative treatment and people who receive intermittent anti-cancer treatment to control their cancer over a longer time.

Many people feel that life is never the same after a cancer diagnosis. There are often long-lasting physical, social and emotional consequences of both cancer and its treatment. These start at diagnosis and last through first treatment (acute survivorship), continue through and beyond cancer treatments (extended survivorship) and can be long-lasting, even when risk of cancer recurrence is low (permanent survivorship). An increas-ing awareness of survivorship, the impact of a cancer diagnosis and its wide-ranging effects on patients has highlighted the need for holistic and patient-centred care, support and services throughout and after cancer treatment.

Multiple Choice Questions 8.1. A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a fever and a sore throat. She has recently been diagnosed with left-sided breast cancer and associated axillary lymph node disease. Twelve days ago she received her first cycle of neoadjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, epirubicin and cyclophosphamide). On clinical examination her temperature is 38.3°C, she appears dehydrated and there is evidence of oral candidiasis. An intravenous catheter is placed and bloods, including blood cultures, taken. What is the most appropriate next step in this patient’s care?
A. B. C. D.

Start oral fluconazole Await blood test results to inform further management Start intravenous fluids Perform a chest X-ray, collect a urine sample and throat swab to complete the infection screen E. Start high-dose broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic therapy immediately
Answer: E.

The clinical features here are of fever in a patient at high risk of neutropenia. This is an oncological emergency. Patients are at risk of neutropenia at any point during their systemic anti-cancer therapy treat-ment cycle, with the highest risk typically 10–14 days after a treatment. In patients with potential neutropenic sepsis, high-dose broad-spec-trum intravenous antibiotics should be commenced, ideally within 1 hour of admission, without awaiting test results. In this patient flu-conazole (A) for oral candidiasis, intravenous fluids (C) and further tests (D) are also appropriate, but should not delay the first dose of antibiotic therapy. Test results may later inform changes to antimicrobial therapy and its duration.

8.2. A 61-year-old man recently diagnosed with sigmoid colon cancer with peritoneal, liver and lung metastases is seen in the oncology clinic. He is keen to talk about treatment for his cancer. His ECOG performance status is 1 and he has no significant comorbidities. He has some mild abdominal discomfort and 5 kg weight loss. His routine bloods demonstrate anaemia (Hb 105 g/L) and mild elevations in his liver enzymes. A biopsy of his tumour has shown a moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma which is KRAS/NRAS/BRAF wild type and microsatellite stable. What is the most appropriate treatment option for this patient?

A. Cytotoxic chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, folinic acid and oxaliplatin) alone B. Surgery to all cancer sites C. Cytotoxic chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil, folinic acid and oxaliplatin) with an EGFR inhibitor (cetuximab) D. BRAF inhibitor (encorafenib) alone E. Refer to palliative care
Answer: C.

This man wishes to pursue anti-cancer therapy and, from the information provided, appears fit to do so. In patients with metastatic disease affecting several organs, systemic anti-cancer therapies are most often used. As the tumour is KRAS, NRAS and BRAF wild type, cytotoxic chemotherapy combined with an EGFR inhibitor, such as cetuximab, would be an appropriate option here. BRAF inhibitors, such as encorafenib, are only used in combination with EGFR inhibitors in colon cancers with BRAF mutations.

8.3. A 59-year-old woman is seen in the emergency department with a 2-day history of severe diarrhoea. She has had 10 loose stools today, the most recent of which have been bloody and associated with crampy abdominal pain. Her past medical history includes metastatic melanoma and she had her fourth cycle of ipilimumab and nivolumab therapy 20 days ago. At the time of her treatment she was constipated and the outpatient systemic anti-cancer therapy unit doctor prescribed her a macrogol laxative. She notes that the evening prior to the diarrhoea starting she had reheated some leftover rice for her supper. What is the most important likely diagnosis?
A. B. C. D. E.
Bacillus cereus-associated food poisoning Overflow diarrhea Laxative overuse Immunotherapy-related colitis Clostridioides difficile infection
Answer: D.

Immune-related adverse events should be considered in all patients who present acutely unwell following immunotherapy treatments for cancer. Although the other options are on the differential diagnosis list, severe irAEs are oncological emergencies and prompt recognition and management are vital. This is a grade 3 colitis and should be treated with IV methylprednisolone in the first instance. Investigations such as bloods, stool sample, radiological imaging and flexible sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy are also appropriate.

8.4. A 58-year-old man is seen in clinic with a diagnosis of metastatic lung cancer. He is coping well at home, where he lives alone. However, he has taken early retirement as a brick-layer as he feels unable to work due to increasing fatigue. He awakes early each morning and goes to the shops to collect his newspaper, but has taken to napping for an hour in the afternoon. What is this man’s ECOG performance status?
A. B. C. D. E.
Answer: B.

This man is ambulatory and capable of self-care, but unable to under-take strenuous activity. He is up for more than 50% of waking hours. Performance status is a key assessment tool in patients with cancer.

8.5. You have been asked to see a 70-year-old man on a medical ward. He was admitted 2 weeks ago following a fall. On admission he had abnormal liver function tests and an elevated CRP. He has been treated for a urinary tract infection. A CT scan has demonstrated multiple liver, lung and bone metastases, but no obvious primary cancer. The ward nurses tell you he remains mildly confused at times, sleeps for most of the day and does not wish to engage with physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate management for this man?
A. Refer to the hepatobiliary pancreatic cancer multidisciplinary team B. Ultrasound-guided liver biopsy C. Colonoscopy D. Palliative care E. Cytotoxic chemotherapy
Answer: D.

This man has a new diagnosis of metastatic cancer of undefined primary origin (MUO). His ECOG performance status (3), requirement for hospital admission, multi-organ metastatic disease, end-organ dys-function and raised inflammatory markers are poor prognostic features. Further investigations may not be warranted and honest conversations about the likely diagnosis, palliative care and end-of-life care, taking into account the patient’s wishes, are often preferable.

8.6. A 56-year-old woman is seen in oncology clinic following surgery to remove a localised clear cell renal cell carcinoma. She is eligible for a phase III clinical trial comparing adjuvant immunotherapy to the current clinical standard of observation. Patients will be randomised to receive either the immunotherapy treatment or a placebo every 4 weeks for 1 year. Neither the patient nor the investigator will know what treatment she is receiving. Which of the following statements regarding randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is true?
A. Patients may choose which treatment they receive B. RCTs are always ‘double-blinded’

C. RCTs are considered to be the ‘gold standard’ for determining efficacy and safety in clinical research D. RCTs always have a control arm that uses placebo E. RCTs always equally divide patients between each treatment
Answer: C.

Phase III RCTs are often used to determine whether a treatment should be licensed for clinical use. Patients are randomised to each arm, sometimes with stratification to ensure equal allocation of patient sub-groups. RCTs may be double-blinded, as is the case here, single-blinded or ‘open-label’. The control arm should be the current clinical standard treatment. In this example a placebo is used in the place of observation only to ensure blinding and avoid potential bias of results. Patients may be divided in alternative ratios. This is sometimes the case when earlier studies suggest large differences between the investigational and current treatment.
neuropathy

Pain is an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with, or resembling that associated with, actual or potential tissue damage (World Health Organization). The evolutionary purpose of pain is based on protection and healing, but the pain experience is one of the most common sources of distress in medicine. Pain was originally considered a purely physical experience (‘specificity theory of pain’), whereby tissue damage triggered pain receptors to send one-way signals to the brain, where they were realised (Fig. 9.1). It is now understood that higher brain activity is involved in the modification of incoming pain signals, shaping the individual pain experience (the ‘biopsychosocial model’). Factors that influence that pain experience include the individual’s biology, physiology, life experiences and sociocultural landscape (Fig. 9.2).
There are several ways to classify pain, but two broad themes are duration (acute or chronic) and underlying mechanism (neuropathic or nociceptive).

Pain can be broadly classified as acute or chronic. However, there are many subtypes of pain that fall under these headings (Fig. 9.3). Although the classification of pain is helpful to guide management, in practice patients often present with varying combinations of acute and chronic pain. Acute pain occurs as a result of impending or actual tissue damage to skin, bone, muscle and visceral structures secondary to trauma, surgery, burns, infection or physiological states, such as labour pains. It protects against sustaining further damage at the time of injury and during heal-ing. Pain improves as tissue damage recovers, and the expected out-come is that pain resolves within 3 months.

Chronic pain does not appear to serve any evolutionary purpose and persists beyond three months despite tissue healing. Chronic pain is broadly classified as primary or secondary, although patients often pre sent with a combination of both in practice. Primary chronic pain occurs in one or more anatomical regions asso-ciated with significant levels of emotional distress and produces varying ­ levels of functional disability. The pain cannot be better explained by another chronic condition, e.g. fibromyalgia. Secondary chronic pain results from an injury or underlying disease process and is diagnosed when the pain lasts beyond three months and becomes a problem requiring management in its own right. Pain may be related to progressive tissue damage or may continue to evolve after the initial damage has resolved.

Neuropathic pain is caused by a lesion or disease of the somatosensory nervous system. Pain arises from damage to the peripheral nerves (see Box 27.96) or central nervous system (CNS), when it is termed central pain. Neuropathic pain may be acute, such as in sciatica, but is most debilitating when it becomes chronic, impacting on quality of life and function. The clinical features of neuropathic pain are detailed in Box 9.1. Nociceptive pain is caused by noxious stimuli to body tissues, such as extreme temperatures, chemicals and mechanical force, causing activa-tion of several receptors called nociceptors. This can be further classified as somatic (arising from the skin, bone etc.) or visceral (from organs, peritoneum etc.).

The functional anatomy of the somatosensory system is shown in Figures 27.3 and 27.11. Nociceptors utilise specific ion channel transducers which trigger pain signal action potentials once stimuli exceed a given threshold (Fig. 9.4). The signals generated by nociceptors are relayed to the dorsal column of the spinal cord via sensory afferent neurons. Anatomical features of the afferent pain pathway are illustrated in Figure 9.5. Nociceptive signals from cutaneous and musculoskeletal tissues travel in myelinated Aδ fibres (fast), producing somatic pain (sharp in nature and easily localised), while signals from internal organs and body structures travel in C fibres (slow) alongside autonomic nerves, producing visceral pain (diffuse and poorly localised).

Sensory neurons terminate in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where they synapse with secondary order ascending neurons. Considerable modulation of pain messages occurs at this level by other incoming sen-sory fibres and descending neural pathways from the brain, as depicted in Figures 9.5 and 27.11. Several excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmit-ters are involved in pain processing at this level. Pharmacological mod-ulation of these neurotransmitters and their target receptors underlie the mode of action of many analgesic medications. Referred pain may occur when incoming visceral pain fibres associate closely with somatic pain fibres in the same segment of the spinal cord.
Pain is interpreted as arising from the superficial dermatome served by the somatic fibres rather than the original visceral source (Fig. 9.6; see Fig. 27.10).

Pain signals from the spinal cord travel to the sensory cortex via the thalamus. Individual experience of pain is then influenced by complex multidirectional interactions between a range of structures in the CNS, called the pain neuromatrix (see Fig. 9.5). It is here that sensory, cogni-tive, memory and emotional aspects of pain are integrated. Descending pain inhibition from the brainstem reduces input from peripheral stimuli via serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways.

The peripheral and central nervous systems adapt to the presence of pain, especially in response to sustained tissue damage, a process called neuronal plasticity. In chronic pain this produces prolonged changes in the pathways involved in detecting and processing nocicep tive stimuli. Peripheral sensitisation occurs secondary to inflammation with the release of cytokines and mediators, including bradykinin, sub-stance P and prostaglandins, which activate nociceptor to ion channel transducers (see Fig. 9.4). If these pain-provoking mediators persist, ion channel transducers are upregulated and their threshold for activa-tion falls. In neuropathic pain this results in pain signalling in response to innocuous stimuli (allodynia) or spontaneous pain signalling. Central sensitisation occurs at the level of the spinal cord. Activation of microglial cells in the region of nociceptive synapses triggers release of pro-inflammatory mediators and decreases re-uptake of excitatory neu-rotransmitters such as glutamate. Prolonged glutamate release causes prolonged activation of the N-methyl- d -aspartate (NMDA) receptor, ­ causing over-amplification of afferent pain signals (hyperalgesia) and increasing amplitude of pain signals with repeated stimuli (pain wind-up) and continued neuronal firing after noxious stimuli have stopped.

Pain can be difficult for patients to describe. Acute pain can cause com-plete cognitive distraction, while chronic pain carries biopsychosocial elements that are hard to verbalise. Common medical descriptors (e.g. sharp, dull) or short phrases (e.g. radiating to the back) can oversimplify the person’s pain experience. It is important to allow adequate time for patients to tell their pain story. Establishing a general rapport with the patient and taking a more general medical history before focusing on their pain can give valuable insight into the patient’s understanding of their pain and treatments. In general, the site, severity, nature, exacerbating/relieving factors and associated features should be documented for each individual pain the patient describes. These focused prompts are particularly useful for patients with acute pain, but they do not cover the emotional, psy-chological and functional impacts of pain. Aim to determine the extent to which pain is interfering with normal daily activities, such as work, leisure pursuits and sleep. Disruption of activities that give a person enjoyment and purpose in life can exacerbate an individual’s perception of pain. All current and previously tried medications should be covered, whether these have been effective and any associated side-effects. Ask about over-the-counter medicines (including cannabinoid prod-ucts), alternative medicines and previous or current substance mis-use, all of which must be considered for safe and effective prescribing. Explore the patient’s beliefs around what is causing their pain, as well as their expectations of treatment; unless these are addressed, man-agement may be less effective. Social circumstances, support network and cultural background should be discussed, including employment status and their support network. If evidence of low mood is detected, a suicide risk assessment should be considered (see Fig. 29.1).

A wide range of tools have been developed to assess pain (Box 9.2). Unidimensional tools are used to grade the severity of pain and can be carried out verbally using the Numerical Rating Scale, which grades pain from 0 to 10, or by asking a patient to indicate their score on a Visual Analogue Scale from 0 to 10. Multidimensional tools include the severity, distribution, character and psychological/functional impacts of pain. Verbal self-reporting of pain is seen as the gold standard, but not all patients will manage this. Assessing pain in some people with cognitive impairment or learning difficulties relies on using observational skills and working closely with their family or carers. Observational pain tools such as Doloplus-2 or the Abbey Pain Scale are used to assess pain in those with difficulties in communication. Documenting changes in pain scores over time helps assess treatment benefits, reducing the time taken to achieve accept-able level pain control.

Patients experiencing pain may appear pale and develop sweating due to autonomic activity. This can also be reflected by tachycardia, tachypnoea and changes in blood pressure. Severe acute pain can produce vasovagal events and vomiting. Facial expressions such as grimacing, tightly closed eyes and lacrimation are common, as are vocalisations such as groaning. The patient’s position and actions can give an indication of the severity, location and cause of pain. Patients may massage, hold or guard the pain-ful area or indicate pain by rocking/inability to stay still. Shallow breathing or trying to remain still may indicate peritoneal or pleural pain. Pain may precipitate delirium or present as behavioural change in those with cogni-tive impairment, when it may present as emotional distress or aggression due to fear of pain during movement by carers or family. Palpation may reveal superficial or deep tenderness. Deep inspiration or joint movement may elicit pain. A focused neurological examination using a simple set of tools helps identify neuropathic elements of pain. Lightly touching the skin with cotton-wool tests for reduced fine touch and allodynia. Response to pin-prick can identify mechanical hyperalge-sia and central wind-up. Touching the patient’s skin with warm and cool thermal rollers (or cool swab) tests for abnormalities of thermal sensation. An unaffected area of skin should be tested first, to establish normal sensation, before testing the affected area.

Blood tests may help identify the underlying cause, e.g. in patients with peripheral neuropathy (see Box 27.98). Biochemical evidence of liver and/ or renal failure can help guide prescribing of opioids and other analgesics.

Plain X-ray or CT scanning can identify pathological fractures and bone metastases (Fig. 9.7). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used to assess patients with suspected malignant spinal cord compression, disc prolapses, or pain that follows a nerve root distribution.
