Nerve conduction studies can be helpful in demonstrating and quan-tifying a definitive nerve lesion. They can be used to help differentiate between central and peripheral neuropathic pain, but do not effectively examine small nerve fibre function.

Performing a nerve block with infiltration of a local anaesthetic, such as 1% lidocaine, can be useful in assessing whether pain is due to involve-ment of a specific nerve or nerve root. Nerve blockade can also be used to assess whether more definitive therapies, such as nerve ablation, might be helpful in controlling pain.

The management of acute pain is broadly similar regardless of the underlying pathology and focuses on identifying and treating the primary cause, providing adequate analgesia to allow rehabilitation and gradual reduction in analgesia as pain resolves. Undertreatment of acute pain can lead to prolonged hospital admission, musculoskeletal decondition-ing and is a risk factor for developing chronic pain.

The underlying condition causing the pain should be treated whenever possible. Pain relief can be provided through immobilisation of the painful area using slings, braces and splints or by positioning the patient appro-priately. Painful wounds can be dressed and the application of heat or cold can provide relief. Early physiotherapy input can help maintain func-tion and promote functional recovery.

The choice of initial medication is based on clinical assessment and the severity of the pain. A simple numerical rating scale can be used to assess severity, dividing pain into mild (score 1–3), moderate (score 4–6) and severe (score 7–10). Mild pain can usually be managed using non-opioids, while moderate and severe pain may require the short-term use of opioid medications. A multimodal approach is recommended for acute pain; combining paracetamol with a non-steroidal anti-inflamma-tory drug (NSAID) or opioid can produce increased benefit while reducing individual drug dosage requirement. Regular re-assessment of response to drug treatment is vital.

Paracetamol is recommended for the treatment of mild to moderate pain. Its mechanism of action is incompletely understood, but it is believed to inhibit cyclooxygenase enzyme activity, enhance the endocannabinoid system and promote spinal serotonergic inhibition of pain. It is generally well-tolerated with few side-effects, but the dose must be reduced in people with low body weight (< 50 kg). Acute liver failure is a well-recog-nised complication of paracetamol overdose.

NSAIDs are widely used in the treatment of inflammatory pain, but can be used as a general analgesic for mild to moderate pain. These drugs can be given systemically or locally and are discussed in more detail in Chapter 25. They are also useful in the management of pain in cancer patients, as discussed later in this chapter.

The term ‘opioids’ covers a group of drugs that act on opioid recep-tors to produce pain relief. Morphine was originally obtained from the resin of the opium poppy (Papaver somniferum) and remains the most commonly prescribed opioid. A number of semi-synthetic opi-oids derived from morphine and fully synthetic opioids are available. The characteristics of commonly prescribed opioids are shown in Box 9.3. Opioids are traditionally divided into subclasses of weak opioids (e.g. codeine, dihydrocodeine and tramadol) and strong opi-oids (e.g. morphine). Weak opioids have a lower affinity for opioid receptors and have a ‘ceiling dose’ above which side-effects predom-inate over pain relief. Strong opioids bind more effectively to opioid receptors and are less limited by this ceiling of analgesia effect so they produce much more potent pain relief. All opioids carry the same inherent risks and side-effects. Opioid effects are mediated through activation of a number of G-protein-coupled receptors. The most prevalent are μ, κ and δ receptors, with the μ receptor being the primary mediator of opi-oid-related analgesia. There is considerable inter-individual variability in response to opioids. There are many reasons for this, including genetic variations in the enzymes that metabolise drugs. For example, codeine is metabolised to morphine via the liver cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2D6. Inherited differences in CYP2D6 expression results in varying morphine production when different individuals are given identical doses of codeine. While most people metabolise around 10% of a codeine dose to morphine, those who are rapid metabo-lisers (high CYP2D6 activity) produce more morphine and gain better pain relief, while poor metabolisers (low CYP2D6 activity) will experi-ence minimal analgesia.

Opioids are used to manage moderate to severe acute pain in com-bination with non-opioids. Weak opioids are used for moderate pain, with oral preparations combining paracetamol or an NSAID (with codeine commonly used). Strong opioids are reserved for severe pain or moderate pain that is refractory to a combination of weak opioid and non-opioid therapy. Opioids used for severe pain can be administered orally or via bolus injection using an intravenous, intra-muscular or subcutaneous route. The onset of pain relief is faster when opioids are given via injection. Typical opioid doses used in acute pain are presented in Box 9.4. The lowest effective dose should be used for as short a time as possible. If opioid doses are not reduced in parallel with reducing pain severity, then patients can develop opioid toxicity or respiratory depression as their sympa-thetic arousal produced in response to pain reduces. A clear plan for discontinuing opioids should form part of the management plan for all patients with acute pain.

Opioids such as morphine and oxycodone can be delivered intrave-nously using a computerised pump that is set up to deliver a bolus dose of the drug in response to the patient pressing a handheld button. When the patient develops worsening pain, they press the button. The bolus dose of drug, minimum interval between doses (lock out) and maximum number of doses in a fixed period, are all pre-set by a pain specialist. PCA is often used post-operatively and is usually delivered in a hospital setting to allow close monitoring and ongoing changes to the pump regimen.
Entonox is a gaseous mixture of 50% oxygen and 50% nitrous oxide, which is used for the short-term relief of moderate to severe acute pain.

The patient activates the flow of the gas by inhaling through a mouth-piece; pain relief both occurs and wears off within minutes. Inhalation of methoxyflurane (Penthrox) via a handheld device is used for short-term relief of moderate to severe pain associated with traumatic injury. Inhaled therapies are used as bridging measures until more definitive manage-ment can be undertaken.

The targeted injection of local anaesthetic around a nerve sheath can produce temporary relief of pain while awaiting more definitive interven-tion, e.g. femoral nerve block in a patient awaiting surgery for a fractured neck of femur. Use of a peripheral nerve stimulator or ultrasound can help identify the target nerve. The duration of pain relief varies but can last up to 36 hours. The use of a peripheral nerve catheter attached to a pump, which infuses local anaesthetic into the tissues around a target nerve, can provide pain relief for up to 4 days.

Injection of a small volume of local anaesthetic +/− opioid into the sub arachnoid space is known as spinal anaesthesia. This technique produces several hours of pain relief, absent sensation and loss of motor function. Spinal anaesthesia is used to manage pain associated with lower abdom-inal, pelvic and lower limb surgery (caesarean section, hip replacement). Spinal infusions called intrathecal infusions are used to manage chronic intractable cancer pain. The continuous infusion of local anaesthetic and/ or opioids via a catheter into the epidural space is known as epidural anaesthesia, which can be used to manage pain associated with surgery, trauma, labour and some chronic conditions such as cancer. Epidurals can be used for pain in the thorax, and infusions can be adjusted allowing some sparing of motor function. Both techniques involve selecting a level of the spinal cord above that which innervates the painful area. Bladder function can be affected by both techniques, requiring urethral catheteri-sation, and close monitoring of the highest anatomical level of anaesthetic block is vital as extension into cervical spinal segments can lead to respira-tory failure, hypotension and bradycardia.

It is important to recognise that the approaches above cover the general management of acute pain. Treating the underlying cause is important, and there are many conditions where pain can be relieved using specific approaches such as glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray to relieve angina or triptans to treat migraine.

When a definitive underlying disease has not been identified, the manage-ment of chronic pain focuses on supporting the patient with the psycho-logical, emotional and functional impacts to improve quality of life. In 2021 the UK National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) published guidance on managing primary chronic pain, which recommends multidisci-plinary non-pharmacological interventions as the mainstay of treatment. The only pharmacological agents recommended are antidepressants (amitrip-tyline, duloxetine, citalopram, sertraline or paroxetine), which may improve pain and sleep. The guidelines advise against initiating any other drug ther-apy, including paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, gabapentin and pregabalin. For those already taking these medications, it is recommended that a review of benefit versus harms is carried out. For patients obtaining benefit from any of these medications and not experiencing harmful effects, a shared care plan for ongoing use and review should be agreed upon with the patient.

The principles of managing chronic primary pain largely apply to second-ary chronic pain. Treatment of the underlying disease or injury, when pos-sible, is recommended, and non-pharmacological approaches remain the foundations of management. NICE has also produced guidance spe-cific to several chronic painful diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, endometriosis and osteoarthritis.
NICE guidelines recommend that a trial of amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregab-alin or gabapentin can be considered for the patient with neuropathic pain.

Further information on these drugs is presented in Box 9.5. Combinations of these drugs may be required in some patients. Prescribing of opioids is not recommended for neuropathic pain. Duloxetine is licensed for the management of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, while the pain of trigeminal neuralgia may respond to the anti-convulsant carbamazepine. Outcomes are often disappointing for patients, so it is vital when trialling medications to set realistic expectations of reducing pain rather than eradicating pain completely. Nerve blocks and neuraxial techniques (see above) may be required in carefully selected patients.

Physiotherapy has a key role in the multidisciplinary approach to chronic pain, especially in the prevention of muscle spasm, contractures, reduced mobility and lymphoedema. Rehabilitation based on patient-led goal setting and the use of focused exercise has been shown to improve outcomes and reduce medication use.

Individual and group-based approaches aim to train patients to use coping strategies and behavioural techniques to manage pain and its impacts. Cognitive behavioural therapy can help change behavioural responses that may be exacerbating the patient’s pain experience. Support can also be provided to manage anxiety and depression as well as the impacts of underlying chronic diseases.

Acupuncture and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) are low-risk therapies that may be useful in some patients. Acupuncture has been used successfully in Eastern medicine for centuries. The mech-anisms are incompletely understood, although endorphin release may play a role. Acupuncture is particularly effective in pain related to muscle spasm, with some evidence of short-term benefit for patients with low back pain. Similar mechanisms probably apply to TENS, which is worth considering in many types of chronic pain.

Complementary techniques, such as herbal medicines, vitamins, home-opathy and reflexology, have been used for the treatment of chronic pain but lack robust evidence of efficacy. It is important that patients are encouraged to discuss any alternative medicines they are considering, given the potential interactions with prescribed therapies.

Pain can be the initial presenting symptom or can occur at any time throughout a wide spectrum of cancer disease (Box 9.6). Cancer is universally feared by patients and the term cancer is commonly asso-ciated with pain, suffering and shortening of life expectancy, which can add an additional existential component to pain. Worsening pain is often interpreted by patients as the cancer returning or progressing, while dying in pain is the most common fear of people with advanced cancer.

Acute cancer pain is generally somatic or visceral nociceptive pain and occurs in the context of investigations or surgical intervention. The assessment and management is broadly similar to acute pain arising from other causes. Concern over impending diagnostic biopsy and scan results can increase the distress related to acute pain.

It is estimated that about two-thirds of patients with cancer experi-ence moderate or severe chronic pain, and a quarter have three or more different sites of pain. Chronic cancer pain is most commonly of mixed aetiology with a combination of nociceptive and neuropathic elements. Pain may be persistent and unremitting as the result of advancing malignant tissue destruction; minimal healing occurs, and the patient usually has a short prognosis. Alternatively, pain may evolve as a separate problem when malignant processes are con-trolled or cured by systemic anti-cancer treatments. Patients com-monly experience both courses of chronic cancer pain throughout the course of their cancer.

The assessment of cancer pain should follow the general principles described earlier in this chapter. Improved control of cancer-asso-ciated pain has been demonstrated with use of the Edinburgh Pain Assessment and management Tool (EPAT), which uses a simple screening question about worst pain on a scale of 0–10 in the last 24 hours, followed by questions to identify specific pain(s) in addition to exploring distress. The identified pains are linked to management algorithms. Continuing review of pain and any opioid side-effects is key (see ‘Further information’).

Pharmacological treatments are the mainstay of management; however, they must be underpinned by regular holistic assessment of pain and associated symptoms. Non-pharmacological and oncological treatments should run in parallel with each stage of prescribing for pain control. The non-pharmacological approaches described earlier in this chapter (p. 197) should be explored for all patients with chronic cancer pain.

The World Health Organization (WHO) analgesic three-step ladder formed the basis of managing cancer pain after its introduction in 1986. This remains a useful educational tool, but is not a strict protocol for management of cancer pain. The subsequent addition of a fourth step is now incorporated, which recognises the important role of interventional cancer pain management in patients who have ongoing pain despite pharmacological intervention, as shown in Figure 9.8. Using the WHO ladder approach, the initial analgesic regimen pre-scribed is determined by the severity of pain reported. Those with mild pain are started on a non-opioid analgesic drug (step 1). If the patient fails to respond adequately or develops moderate pain, a weak opioid, such as codeine or tramadol, is added (step 2). If pain relief is still not achieved or the patient develops severe pain, a strong opioid is substi-tuted for the weak opioid (step 3). If cancer pain is severe at the outset, a jump straight to prescribing step 3 strong opioids can be undertaken and titrated according to the patient’s response. There is increasing evidence that the use of a low dose of a step 3 opioid like morphine rather than a traditional step 2 opioid such as codeine is safe and effective. This approach is also cheaper, which is of great importance in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where step 2 drugs are usually much more expensive than morphine. The ladder should be viewed as bidirectional, and regular review of pain can identify patients who can attempt a step-down if their pain has improved.

A number of other medications, termed adjuvants, can be introduced alongside the primary medication of each analgesic ladder step. An adju-vant analgesic is a drug that has a primary indication other than pain, but which provides benefit in some painful conditions and may enhance the effect of other analgesics. Adjuvant analgesics used in the manage-ment of chronic cancer pain are summarised in Box 9.7. It is important to monitor for the specific side-effects of adjuvant drugs. The use of adjuvant analgesic can enhance the sedative effects of opioids as pain arousal falls, meaning opioid dose reductions may be required soon after commencing adjuvants.

Cancer pain responds more effectively to opioids than chronic pain secondary to non-cancer causes. Oral administration is effective, and morphine should be first choice whenever possible, although there is no good evidence that one opioid is superior to others for managing cancer pain. Oral morphine comes in immediate-release and modified-release preparations. Immediate-release morphine takes around 30–45 min-utes to produce pain relief, which peaks around 1 hour and lasts for up to 4 hours. Modified-release preparations have a slower onset of 1–2 hours for pain relief for up to 8–12 hours. Patients with chronic cancer pain can be initiated on regular morphine using either type of preparation, depending on the pattern of pain and patient pref-erences. Typical initial morphine dosing regimens are shown in Box 9.8. This regular use of morphine provides relief from background pain over each 24-hour period. Additional doses of immediate-re-lease morphine should be prescribed as required for the treatment of pain that is not controlled by the regular background administration. Such transient severe increases in pain are called breakthrough pain. As a general rule, opioid breakthrough doses are one-sixth of the total 24-hour background dose of opioid, although this is sometimes adjusted on an individual basis. The time interval between doses and maximum number of daily breakthrough doses should be clearly pre-scribed. The patient or carer should note the timing of any break-through doses and the reason for them. This should be reviewed daily when first initiating morphine. It is normal for patients to still 9.8 Approaches to starting oral morphine for treating cancer pain
• Usual adult dosing: commence 5 mg every 4 hours plus 5 mg up to every 2 hours for breakthrough pain
• If elderly or frail: commence 2 mg every 4 hours plus 2 mg up to every 2 hours for breakthrough pain
• Usual adult dosing: commence 10–15 mg every 12 hours plus 5 mg immediate-release morphine up to every 2 hours for breakthrough pain

• If elderly or frail: commence 5 mg every 12 hours plus 2 mg immediate-release morphine up to every 2 hours for breakthrough pain. Use immediate-release preparations for initiation when possible require 1–2 breakthrough doses on average each day, even when pain is well managed. When pain remains problematic, and morphine is well tolerated, the total of the breakthrough doses required over the previous 24 hours is calculated and regular background dose increased accordingly. Patients initially commenced on immediate-re-lease morphine for background pain will usually have this converted to 12-hourly modified-release morphine once pain is well controlled. This approach of adjusting opioids based on requirement is known as opioid titration. Short-acting opioid analgesia used to treat move-ment-related pain, known as incident pain, is generally not included in background opioid dose titration, as this can lead to overdosing and opioid-related side-effects.

Renal failure Systemic clearance of active morphine metabolites occurs mostly via renal excretion (> 90%). Renal impairment can lead to accu-mulation of these active compounds, which eventually produces wors-ening side-effects and opioid toxicity. Oxycodone and hydromorphone clearance relies less on renal excretion, but accumulation can occur with repeated use. A reduction in the dose and frequency of administration for all three of these drugs is recommended in mild to moderate renal impairment (estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) 30–59 mL/min). Use in severe (eGFR 15–29 mL/min) or end-stage renal failure (eGFR < 15 mL/min) is not recommended, and an alternative opioid should be used when possible. Fentanyl, alfentanil, buprenorphine and methadone are less likely to accumulate in renal failure, although the prescribing of each of these drugs should only be undertaken by a cancer pain specialist.

Liver failure The risk of accumulation increases with most opioids in patients with severe hepatic impairment. Reduced first pass metabo-lism increases opioid oral bioavailability (fraction of opioid dose ingested that reaches the circulation); with morphine this increases from around 40% to nearly 100%. Reduced inactivation of opioids such as alfentanil and oxycodone via cytochrome P450 enzymes can significantly increase their effects. Fentanyl is considered the opioid of choice in liver failure, although low-dose immediate-release oral morphine is commonly used in practice.

The oral route is first choice for opioid administration whenever possi-ble. Alternative routes are required for patients unable to swallow due to dysphagia, vomiting or reduced consciousness and those who have significant issues with drug absorption. Transdermal patches, which provide controlled release of fentanyl or buprenorphine, can be used to manage pain in people who have sta-ble chronic cancer pain (Box 9.9). These preparations are not suitable for people who have pain that is poorly controlled, as changes in the patch dosage can take days to take effect. Specialist advice is required when starting transdermal opioid patches especially in those who are not already established on another regular strong opioid (opioid naïve). Delivery of several opioids via mucosal surfaces (transmucosal absorption) is also possible. Transmucosal fentanyl products are avail-able, which can be administered sublingually, buccally or transnasally. These rapidly acting opioid preparations produce pain relief faster than oral immediate-release morphine and should only be prescribed by a specialist.

Patients with advanced cancer and those near the end of life are com-monly administered opioid via subcutaneous injection or continuous infu-sion. Compared with intravenous administration, this route requires less training to use, is less painful and can be used in the community. A con-tinuous subcutaneous infusion over 24 hours of opioid using a syringe driver can provide highly effective background pain relief, mimicking pain control produced by taking modified-release opioid. Breakthrough pain is then managed using bolus subcutaneous opioid injections, which work faster than oral immediate-release opioid.
Opioid switching

The practice of substituting one opioid for another is known as opioid switching and is commonly used in palliative medicine when the current opioid is ineffective or causing opioid toxicity. When performing a switch, an approximate starting dose of the new opioid is calculated using opioid equivalency formulae as presented in Figure 9.9. The new opioid dose regimen is usually reduced by 20%–30% to introduce an additional ele-ment of safety. Opioid switching can involve changing the route of administration, as opioids such as diamorphine and alfentanil are normally given only via injection. Compared with oral opioids, approximately twice as much drug reaches the bloodstream when given via subcutaneous routes. The oral opioid dose is therefore halved to calculate an approximate subcutane-ous dose, e.g. oral morphine 10 mg = subcutaneous morphine 5 mg.

Adverse effects are a common problem with opioids. The most common side-effects are nausea, drowsiness, constipation and dry mouth, as summarised in Box 9.10. Nausea, vomiting and drowsiness can occur at opioid initiation and dose increase. These usually settle within 7 days as tolerance to opioid effects develop in the affected neural areas. Tolerance does not develop in the salivary glands or colon, meaning dry mouth and constipation do not decrease with continued use. Opioid-related constipation is a significant cause of suffering. Dietary measures and hydration may offer little benefit unlike other causes of constipation. In those who do not respond to first-line laxatives such as macrogol, consideration should be given to the use of a peripherally acting μ-opioid receptor antagonist (PAMORA), e.g. naldemedine. These drugs block opioid receptors on the bowel, but do not reduce pain relief in the CNS as they do not cross the blood–brain barrier.

Neurotoxicity occurs when opioids or their active metabolites reach a high enough level in the CNS. This presents as persisting drowsiness, visual hallucinations (often a sense of movement at the periphery of vision), delirium and myoclonic jerks. Pin-point pupils (miosis) are not a reliable sign of opioid toxicity. Opioid toxicity requires urgent assess-ment because if it is not managed, the patient may develop seizures, respiratory depression or coma. If pain is well controlled, then the current opioid dose should be reduced; if pain is not controlled, then an opioid switch is required. Good practice includes excluding renal impairment causing opioid accumulation or hypercalcaemia, which can mimic opioid toxicity. Respiratory depression can occur with acute dosing, but is rare in patients on regular opioids or those starting on small, regular doses with appropriate titration. Opioid reversal using naloxone in patients with can-cer pain needs careful assessment and should only be considered in life-threatening situations, as unnecessary use of naloxone will unmask cancer pain and cause acute opioid withdrawal.

Some patients may have concerns about using opioids, and it is vital this is explored. Fear of addiction is common, and patients should be reassured that psychological dependence is rare when opioids are used for cancer pain. Media coverage of the opioid epidemic crisis in USA and Canada has increased fear and stigma worldwide. Unfamiliarity and concerns around prescribing opioids also exist among some health-care professionals. An opioid shortage crisis also exists. Many parts of the world have limited or no access to morphine for cancer pain relief. In 2018 the International Narcotics Control Board reported that 87% of the total amount of morphine used for pain relief is used in countries with only 21% of the world’s population (mainly Europe, America, Australia and New Zealand). Cancer patients from many LMICs still suffer inade-quate pain control due to restrictive government policies and a reliance on expensive opioids from step 2 of the WHO analgesic ladder.

The presenting features and assessment of bone metastases are covered in Chapter 8. Vertebrae, pelvic and long bones are the most commonly affected sites. Primary bone tumours such as osteosarcoma can also cause significant pain. CIBP occurs in response to mediators released by cancer cells, which lead to local changes in bone architecture via stimulation of osteoclasts and osteoblasts, increased nerve growth and the production of highly acidic local environment. Weakening of bone may lead to pathological fractures (see Fig. 9.7), which can precipitate pain due to compression of peripheral nerves, cauda equina or spinal cord. The risk of long bone fracture due to a can-cer deposit can be assessed using Mirel’s criteria, and those at increased risk should be considered for prophylactic orthopaedic fixation or joint replacement (Box 9.11). CIBP has both nociceptive and neuropathic elements. Opioids are normally required but pain relief is often unsatisfactory even with high doses. NSAIDs or dexamethasone are helpful in some individuals, but in general there is a lack of evidence to support the use of most adjuvant analgesics in CIBP. Immediate-release morphine or transmucosal fenta-nyl taken around 30 minutes before movement may offer some relief of activity-related pain. Radiotherapy is the gold standard for managing CIBP with 60%–80% experiencing significant pain relief and 30% gaining complete relief. A single treatment (fraction) or short course of daily treatments is used. An initial pain flare can occur in the 24–48 hours after radiotherapy, which is managed using a short course of glucocorticoids. 50% of patients have a response within 2 weeks, but pain relief usually evolves over 4–6 weeks. An overview of managing CIBP is presented in Box 9.12.

Nerve damage can result from cancer infiltration, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Addressing the underlying cause whenever possible should be the first goal of management. This can be difficult for patients with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), where the cause may simultaneously offer survival benefit. Pharmacological man-agement follows the same principles as for chronic neuropathic pain sec-ondary to other causes (see Box 9.5). It is important to remember that most cancer pain is mixed (nociceptive and neuropathic), and a trial of opioid will often provide pain relief in this group of patients. Duloxetine is recommended first line for managing CIPN, and the use of 5% menthol in aqueous cream topically may provide some local relief. Topical lidocaine 5% patches can also be helpful in focal neuropathic pain. Methadone and ketamine may produce benefit in a subset of patients who have evidence of allodynia and hyperalgesia; both require specialist supervision for initiation and monitoring.

The use of systemic analgesics to manage cancer pain can fail to bring sufficient relief for some patients, and many struggle with the impact of side-effects. Therapeutic techniques that block or reduce pain signals can be carried out by anaesthetists. If these are being considered, they should form part of a multidisciplinary management plan.

Local anaesthetic injections or infusions via nerve catheters can be used to provide temporary relief of cancer pain, which may allow other treatments to be undertaken, such as physiotherapy or lymphoedema care. The use of radiofrequency ablation, cryoablation or the injection of chemicals (phenol or alcohol) to cause targeted destruction of nerves (neurolysis) may be considered in selected patients, usually those with a short prognosis due to the potential for worsening pain as nerves regrow. Coeliac plexus neurolysis (CPN) can be helpful for visceral pain asso-ciated with pancreatic or upper gastrointestinal cancers. CPN can be performed under CT guidance, but is increasingly performed using transoesophageal ultrasound guidance during endoscopy. Up to 80% of patients will gain pain relief from CPN, although pain often recurs after several months, which may lead to discussion about repeating the procedure. Lateral cordotomy involves CT-guided radiofrequency ablation of one side of the spinothalamic tract at the level of the cervical spinal cord. This results in unilateral pain relief on the contralateral side of the body below the dermatomal level of C5. Cordotomy is commonly used to manage unilateral chest wall pain in patients with mesothelioma.

The delivery of local anaesthetic, opioid and clonidine via the intrathecal route (see spinal anaesthesia above) is preferred to the epidural route in patients experiencing intractable cancer pain who have a longer progno-sis. Intrathecal drug infusion is initially trialled using an external pump to achieve an acceptable balance between analgesia and lower limb motor function. If successful, then the pump is implanted into an abdominal subcutaneous pocket, with the drug delivery lines tunnelled internally to the spine. Intrathecal drug delivery can be used for months to years, with scheduled pump drug refills taking place every few weeks via an injection port accessed superficially through the skin.

Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for CIBP but can also be considered to reduce involvement at other sites. Chemotherapy and other systemic anti-cancer drugs that reduce cancer size will often reduce pain by relieving existing pressure on nerves, bones and other structures.

The fundamentals of managing cancer pain were largely developed during the early hospice movement at a time when patient prog-noses were frequently short (weeks to a short number of months). Although there was recognition of immediate and short-term opioid side-effects, the impacts of opioid-related harms from prolonged use were not factored into emerging practice. The traditional palliative care management of cancer pain typically involved upward titration of opioid doses with the addition of other analgesic medications as reflected in the original 1986 WHO analgesic ladder model, which was unidirectional. In general, those with unremitting progressive can-cer pain are managed by palliative care teams. The management of chronic cancer pain in people with longer prognoses is not as clearly defined. Advances in surgical and oncology treatments over the past two decades have improved the prognosis for an ever-growing pop-ulation of patients.
section_path: The evolution of managing cancer pain

text: Many patients are now living longer with incurable but treatable cancer. There is also an increasing cohort of people who have survived cancer (survivorship). These patients can experience chronic pain that is not due to progressive or persistent tissue destruction, and many will already be taking opioids as well as other analgesics. Traditional palliative care pre-scribing and the WHO analgesic ladder cannot be universally transposed to manage such patients with complex cancer pain, who often have a prognosis of many years. Longer-term use of opioids and adjuvant anal-gesics in this patient population requires careful assessment and regular, long-term follow-up. Monitoring is vital for medication-related harm, such as iatrogenic addiction and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, which compound the psy-chological and emotional distress typical of chronic pain. Multidisciplinary assessment for the potential role of cancer pain interventions needs to be considered, but availability of these services is variable. In the UK many of these patients are currently cared for by a combination of gen-eral practice, oncology, chronic pain and palliative care teams, who may not have the specific training or resources to fully meet their needs. The specialty of supportive oncology is growing in response to the evolving need to optimise management for such patients. These special-ist doctors and nurses provide integrated care alongside oncology teams to manage symptoms resulting from cancer and its treatments, including long-term sequelae like chemotherapy-induced neuropathy and other chronic pains.

The WHO defines palliative care as an approach that improves the quality of life of patients and their families who are facing problems associated with life-threatening illness. It prevents and relieves suffering through the early identification, holistic assessment and treatment of pain and other problems, whether physical, psychosocial, or spiritual. As the beneficial effects from medical treatment diminish in advanced disease, there should be a gradual transition to focusing on optimising symptom control and quality of life. The second part of this chapter covers a selection of pres-entations common in palliative care settings, including caring for the dying patient.

Cachexia is a multifaceted syndrome characterised by severe malnu-trition, muscle wasting and weight loss, commonly associated with chronic illnesses such as heart failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and cancer. The presence of malnutrition in these chronic conditions significantly impacts patients, their families and their overall quality of life.

Cachexia is a condition where terminology can be confusing and often mis-used; therefore, defining key terms is important and the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria are recommended here:

• Sarcopenia is a condition characterised by loss of skeletal mus-cle quantity and therefore strength. It usually affects older adults due to ageing but can occur at any age due to other factors, including physical inactivity or acute illness. Set criteria can be used to define sarcopenia based on skeletal muscle index (quan-tity of muscle) and skeletal muscle density (quality of muscle). In the clinic, sarcopenia is not routinely assessed, but this is chang-ing as it can be measured using computer-based body composi-tion via a CT scan.
• Malnutrition is characterised by reduced dietary intake leading to weight loss. The GLIM criteria state that for malnutrition to be pres-ent, certain criteria need to be present (Fig. 9.10).

• Cachexia. When sarcopenia and malnutrition coexist with systemic inflammation, this is termed cachexia. This syndrome is prevalent in many chronic diseases, particularly in cancer, with its occurrence varying widely across different types. For example, it affects up to 80% of patients with certain cancers, being more frequent in lung and gastrointestinal cancers and less so in breast and prostate cancers.

The pathophysiology of cachexia is intricate and involves a dynamic interaction between the disease and the patient (host). This inter-action triggers a cascade of metabolic changes primarily driven by the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines. These cytokines induce a state of bioamplification through hepatic mediation, affecting both central (appetite and energy centres in the brain) and peripheral (muscle, liver, heart, gastrointestinal system) systems. The result-ing metabolic disturbances lead to the clinical manifestations of cachexia (Fig. 9.11).

Clinically, cachexia manifests as significant weight loss, predominantly of muscle mass, with or without accompanying fat loss, reduced appetite, and diminished physical activity. Weight loss is often the most noticeable clinical feature, but the underlying biological changes begin much earlier. Cachexia can be present even before noticeable weight loss, a stage referred to as pre-cachexia (see Fig. 9.11).
Cachexia is not a static condition but progresses through various stages:
• Pre-cachexia: Early metabolic disturbances without significant weight loss
• Cachexia: Noticeable weight loss and muscle wasting
• Refractory cachexia: Advanced stage where interventions become less effective

Historically, treatment has often been delayed until the later stages of cachexia, particularly refractory cachexia. However, this approach is increasingly recognised as inadequate. Early identification and interven-tion are crucial, with the goal of preventing or delaying the progression of cachexia.

Modern medical practice emphasises the importance of recognising cachexia in its early stages, even before significant weight loss occurs. By identifying metabolic disturbances early, health-care providers can implement strategies to mitigate the progression of cachexia. These strategies may include nutritional support, anti-inflammatory treatments, and physical rehabilitation programs aimed at preserving muscle mass and overall functionality.

The European Society for Clinical Nutrition and Metabolism (ESPEN) guidelines on clinical nutrition in cancer highlight several key areas for consideration, including regular dietary intake, exercise and the use of nutritional supplements (Fig. 9.12).
Basic cachexia care
Effective management of cachexia targets its complex pathophysiology through a multifaceted approach:
• Optimising nutrition
• Encourage energy-dense (high-calorie, small-volume) foods.
• Recommend frequent small meals throughout the day rather than large meals, aiming for 25–30 kcal/kg/day.
• Consider oral nutritional supplements if regular dietary intake is insufficient.
• Preventing sarcopenia and building muscle
• Engage patients in aerobic and resistance exercises (30 minutes, three to four times a week) to improve muscle mass and physical function.
• Addressing inflammation
• Although inflammation is a key component of cancer cachexia, there is insufficient evidence to recommend non-steroidal anti-in-flammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for treatment.

The MENAC (Multimodal Exercise/Nutrition/Anti-inflammatory treatment for Cachexia) trial demonstrated that combining exercise, nutrition and anti-inflammatory treatments is more effective than standard care in sta-bilising weight and improving outcomes in patients with lung or pancre-atic cancer receiving palliative therapy.
• Olanzapine: Low-dose olanzapine (2.5 mg daily) can be used to improve appetite and reduce weight loss in patients with cancer cachexia.

• Glucocorticoids: These can be used to increase appetite in ano-rectic cancer patients with advanced disease for a restricted period (1–3 weeks). However, they come with side-effects such as muscle wasting, insulin resistance and increased risk of infections.
• Progestins: These can be considered to increase appetite in ano-rectic cancer patients with advanced disease but have potentially serious side-effects, including thromboembolism.
Several novel therapies are currently under investigation:
• Cannabinoids: Being studied for their potential to stimulate appetite and reduce weight loss.
• Anti-growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) antibodies: Targeting specific pathways involved in cachexia.
• S-pindolol: Under investigation for its potential benefits in treating cancer cachexia.

Delirium is common, especially in palliative care settings. The point prev-alence of delirium during the first palliative community visit is between 4% and 12%. In hospitals, the prevalence on the first palliative service review increases to 25%. Upon admission to inpatient palliative care units (IPCU), the prevalence is 32%, and the period prevalence in IPCU prior to death reaches 75%. Importantly, up to 50% of delirium cases may be reversible. Hypoactive delirium is the most common subtype in palliative care settings. This subtype carries an increased risk of being missed or misdiagnosed as fatigue, depression, dementia or impending death. It is crucial to recognise and appropriately manage delirium to mitigate its impact on the quality of life for patients and the emotional well-being of their families. Various factors can contribute to the onset of delirium and these are discussed, along with investigation and management, in Chapter 32. Cancer treatments such as cranial radiotherapy, along with the direct effects of cancer such as brain metastases and indirect effects like para-neoplastic syndromes, are additional factors to consider in patients with malignancy (Fig. 9.13).

Nausea and vomiting (emesis) are common in patients with cancer and can be caused by a variety of factors related to the disease itself, its treatment and other associated conditions. Nausea may occur without vomiting, while someone with small bowel obstruction may have severe vomiting with only transient nausea. Nausea is ranked as a more debili-tating experience than pain by many patients. There are multiple causes, as detailed below, which can frequently co-exist:
• Cancer treatment

• Chemotherapy: Many chemotherapy drugs trigger nausea and vomiting by directly stimulating the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) in the brainstem or indirectly by causing release of medi-ators from damaged cells, e.g. serotonin from enterochromaffin cells in the gastrointestinal tract (see Fig. 9.14).
• Radiation therapy: Radiation, especially to the abdomen, chest, or brain, can irritate tissues and lead to nausea.
• Immunotherapy: Some immunotherapy treatments can cause end-organ inflammation or other side-effects that result in nausea.
• Surgery: Postoperative nausea is common after cancer surger-ies, often due to anaesthesia, ileus or pain medications.
Cancer
• Tumour location: Tumours in the gastrointestinal tract, liver or brain can directly cause nausea due to obstruction, pressure or increased intracranial pressure.
• Metabolic changes: Advanced cancer can lead to metabolic imbal-ances (e.g. hypercalcaemia, uraemia) that produce nausea via CTZ.
Medications
• Pain medications: Opioids, NSAIDs and antidepressants used for cancer pain commonly cause nausea as a side-effect.
• Other drugs: Antibiotics, bisphosphonates, hormone therapies and many other medications taken during cancer treatment can produce nausea as a side-effect.
Psychological factors
• Anxiety and anticipation: The psychological stress of a cancer diagnosis and treatment can cause or exacerbate nausea. Anticipatory nausea is common in patients undergoing repeated chemotherapy.
Infections
• Infections: Cancer patients are often immunocompromised, making them more susceptible to infections and sepsis with associated nausea.
Gastrointestinal issues

• Gastrointestinal obstruction: Tumours or scar tissue in the gas-trointestinal tract can obstruct normal digestion, leading to nau-sea and different patterns of vomiting depending on the level of obstruction.
• Gastroparesis: Delayed gastric emptying due to autonomic neu-ropathy, tumour encroachment or opioids cause nausea, which is typically relieved after vomiting.
Nutritional deficiencies
• Malnutrition: Cancer and its treatment can lead to malabsorption and nutritional deficiencies such as hypomagnesaemia, which can result in nausea.
• Cancer
• Medications
• Psychological factors
• Infections
• Gastrointestinal issues
• Nutritional deficiencies

Effectively managing nausea in cancer patients requires a thorough understanding of its underlying causes, as treatment strategies must be tailored to address the specific factors contributing to the symptom (Fig. 9.14). Below is a detailed approach to managing nausea based on various potential causes.

Abnormal levels of electrolytes, such as sodium, potassium, calcium or urea, can significantly contribute to nausea. It is essential to regularly monitor these levels in cancer patients, particularly those undergoing intensive treatments. Correction of these imbalances through appropri-ate supplementation or medication adjustments is crucial. For example, hypercalcaemia is often treated with intravenous fluids, bisphosphonates or denosumab, while hyponatraemia may require fluid restriction or saline administration.

A comprehensive review of the patient’s medication regimen is essential. If a particular drug is identified as the cause, options include dose reduc-tion, switching to an alternative medication or discontinuing the drug if possible. Opioid analgesics, for example, often cause nausea when first initiated, but this side-effect usually subsides within 1–2 weeks. If persistent, antiemetics or alternative pain management strategies may be necessary. Around 10% of patients may continue to experience opi-oid-induced nausea in the long term, requiring ongoing management.

Constipation, even if distal, can lead to symptoms such as abdominal fullness, bloating and nausea. This is particularly common in cancer patients due to factors like reduced mobility, dietary changes and opioid use. Effective management includes the proactive use of laxatives, stool softeners or enemas to maintain regular bowel movements. Ensuring adequate hydration and encouraging physical activity, where possible, can also help alleviate constipation-related nausea. A PAMORA should be considered in those with opioid-related constipation.

Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), often resulting from brain metasta-ses, can cause significant nausea and vomiting. Management typically includes the use of glucocorticoids, such as dexamethasone, to reduce inflammation and oedema. In some cases, radiotherapy may be indi-cated to shrink metastatic lesions and further alleviate pressure. Early intervention is critical to prevent worsening symptoms and improve the patient’s quality of life.

Gastric irritation, which can occur due to direct effects of the cancer or as a side-effect of treatment, often leads to nausea. Proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs), such as omeprazole or pantoprazole, can be effec-tive in reducing gastric acid production and irritation. This treatment is particularly important in patients receiving medications known to irritate the stomach lining, such as NSAIDs or certain chemotherapy agents.
Effective pharmacological management of nausea, particularly in cancer patients, often requires a stepwise approach based on the level of evi-dence supporting the use of different medications.
• Metoclopramide is widely regarded as a first-line treatment for nau-sea, particularly when associated with gastrointestinal dysmotility.
• Haloperidol, traditionally used as an antipsychotic, has been found to be effective in treating nausea, particularly when other treatments are ineffective or contraindicated.
• Methotrimeprazine, also known as levomepromazine, is considered a second-line treatment option.
• Olanzapine, an atypical antipsychotic, has shown promise in treat-ing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) and other refractory cases.

Bowel obstruction is a significant and distressing complication in patients with advanced disease, particularly in the presence of autonomic neu-ropathy or intra-abdominal carcinomatosis. The obstruction may be par-tial or complete, with clinical manifestations varying depending on the level, type and duration of the obstruction.

Partial obstruction presents with reduced bowel sounds and often no colic. Symptoms include constipation, faecal incontinence, intermittent nausea and vomiting (which may provide some relief). As the obstruction progresses, intermittent colicky pain and nausea worsen, while vomiting can become feculent due to the colonisation of small bowel contents by colonic bacteria. Abdominal distension is common, though it may be absent in cases of gastroduodenal obstruction or extensive peritoneal involvement.

Complete obstruction is characterised by the absence of flatus per rectum. Patients often experience continuous pain, which may be due to tumour or nerve infiltration, along with colic and altered bowel sounds.

The management of bowel obstruction requires a multidisciplinary approach involving surgical, oncological and palliative care teams. Treatment decisions should be guided by the patient’s clinical con-dition, the likely benefits and risks of intervention, and patient preferences.

Exclude faecal impaction, which can complicate or mimic bowel obstruc-tion. For localised obstructions, surgical intervention may be considered, though other interventional palliative treatments like stenting (for gastric outlet, proximal small bowel or colon) or laser therapy may be appropri-ate. In cases of gastroduodenal or jejunal obstruction, a venting gastros-tomy can provide relief.

In the acute phase (2–3 days), conservative management may include resting the bowel, keeping the patient nil by mouth (NBM), and possibly using a nasogastric (NG) tube. Encourage a low-fibre diet and consider additional hydration via subcutaneous or intravenous routes. Given that oral absorption is often unreliable, most patients will require subcutane-ous infusion of medications.

The use of prokinetic agents such as metoclopramide may relieve partial obstruction, often temporarily. This is usually given in con-junction with subcutaneous dexamethasone 8 mg/day for 4–7 days, which can reduce gut wall oedema. If colicky abdominal pain occurs while using metoclopramide, this should be stopped, as this indicates progression towards complete obstruction. Other symptomatic inter-ventions include:
• Pain management: Use opioids to control pain.
• Colic: Hyoscine butylbromide (Buscopan) can be effective.
• Nausea: First-line treatment includes cyclizine or hyoscine butylbro-mide, with levomepromazine as a second-line option.
• Vomiting: Hyoscine butylbromide or octreotide may be used; the latter is particularly effective in reducing the volume of vomit.

Frequent mouth care is essential, especially as patients may be NBM. Hyoscine butylbromide and opioids both cause dry mouth. Ensure ongo-ing communication with the patient and family, addressing concerns and preferences as part of a comprehensive care plan. Overall, the manage-ment of bowel obstruction in advanced disease is complex and should be tailored to the individual patient’s needs, focusing on symptom control and quality of life.

Breathlessness, also known as dyspnoea, is a common and distress-ing symptom in patients with advanced malignancies, affecting between 29% and 74% of these individuals. It is particularly prevalent in those with lung cancer, where breathlessness can occur in the presence of normal oxygen saturations due to abnormal stimulation of airway and chest wall mechanoreceptors.
Breathlessness in patients with advanced disease can arise from various causes:
• Direct tumour effects:
• Pleural effusion: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, reduc-ing lung capacity.
• Bronchial obstruction: Tumour growth can obstruct airways, leading to reduced airflow and lobar collapse.
• Lung replacement by tumour: Tumour infiltration reduces effec-tive gas exchange.
• Lymphangitis carcinomatosis: Spread of cancer through the lymphatic system in the lungs.
• Superior vena cava obstruction: Compression or invasion of the superior vena cava, leading to venous congestion, reduced car-diac pre-load and bronchial/tracheal compression.
• Pericardial effusion: Fluid accumulation around the heart, com-promising cardiac function.
• Massive ascites and abdominal distension: Increased intra-ab-dominal pressure affecting diaphragmatic movement.
• Treatment-induced causes:
• Surgical procedures: Pneumonectomy or lobectomy will reduce lung capacity.
• Radiation therapy: Can lead to fibrosis and reduced lung compliance.
• Chemotherapy: Drugs such as doxorubicin and bleomycin can cause pulmonary toxicity.
• Debility-related causes:
• Anaemia: Reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.
• Atelectasis: Collapse of lung tissue, reducing ventilation.
• Pulmonary embolism: Obstruction of pulmonary arteries, reduc-ing blood flow to the lungs.
• Pneumonia and empyema: Infection and pus accumulation in the pleural space, compromising lung function.
• Concurrent diseases:
• Asthma
• COPD
• Congestive cardiac failure
• Interstitial lung disease.
Effective management of breathlessness requires a comprehensive approach that includes both non-pharmacological and pharmacological strategies.

Reassurance and clear explanations of the disease process help reduce anxiety; relaxation techniques may be beneficial. Physiotherapy can assist with positioning and techniques to control hyperventilation. Creating a stream of cool air onto the nose and mouth with a fan or open window can provide relief. Practical aids and adaptations for daily living can improve the patient’s quality of life.

Oxygen (provided in cylinders or via a concentrator device) can reverse hypoxia and give symptomatic relief to some patients (although some of the perceived benefit may be a placebo effect). It can also provide important reassurance to the patient and their family. However, it can lead to dependence, tying the patient to an oxygen source. It also can cause dry mouth and difficulties with communication. Oxygen therapy is expensive if used in the long term and cannot be given to patients who smoke (or where there is another smoker in the accommodation).

• Opioids: Low-dose oral opioids may effectively reduce the sensa-tion of breathlessness, although strong evidence to support this is lacking. Starting with morphine 2 mg every 4 hours, doses can be titrated up as needed. If the patient is already on opioids, the dose may be increased by 33%–50%. There is no strong evidence supporting the use of nebulised opioids, which can actually cause bronchospasm.
• Bronchodilators: These are useful in patients with reversible airway obstruction, such as those with asthma or COPD.

• Pleural effusion: Management includes draining the effusion, con-sidering surgical pleurodesis, or placing a pleuro-peritoneal shunt. Indwelling pleural catheters, which can be used to drain fluid regu-larly, are a suitable option for some with recurrent effusions.
• Endobronchial obstruction: High-dose glucocorticoids, radiotherapy, CO 2 laser bronchoscopy or the placement of bronchial stents may be effective in relieving obstruction and improving airflow.
• Blood transfusion to treat anaemia may be appropriate in some situations.

Coughing is a vital protective mechanism designed to clear foreign mate-rials and excess mucus from the bronchial tree, helping to maintain air-way patency and respiratory health. Cough management depends on whether the cough is dry (non-pro-ductive) or wet (productive).
The primary approach is to treat the underlying cause, whether it be infection, reflux or another condition. Symptomatic interventions include:
• Demulcents, such as simple linctus, soothe the throat and reduce irritation.
• Cough suppressants: Codeine or pholcodine linctus can be used to reduce the frequency of coughing.

• Opioids: Morphine liquid can be prescribed, with the dose increased if the patient is already on regular opioid therapy. Methadone linctus is another option. It is important to note that there is no strong evi-dence supporting the use of nebulised agents for dry cough, except for saline and bronchodilators.
The goal is to encourage the expulsion of mucus and to treat the under-lying cause, such as infection or chronic lung disease.
• Expectoration: Encouraging patients to cough effectively can help clear the mucus from their airways.
• Physiotherapy: Techniques such as chest percussion or postural drainage can be beneficial.
• Nebulised saline: Helps to thin mucus, making it easier to cough up.
• Mucolytics: Medications like carbocisteine can reduce the viscosity of mucus, aiding in its clearance from the lungs.

Medical treatments have advanced significantly even in the past dec-ade. Despite these advances, the inescapable fact remains that every-one will die at some time. Radiological investigations, invasive medical treatments and hospital admissions remain high in the last year of peo-ple’s lives. For many people with advanced illness, hospital admission or dying in hospital is completely appropriate. However, when death is foreseeable, a hospital admission can cause undue distress, with an increasing number of people expressing a wish to die at home. Hospice admission is another option, but may be limited by the small number of inpatient units available. Dying at home can often be well supported, but gaps in health and social care exist, which can make optimal symptom control and family support challenging. It is impor-tant to have an honest discussion with people about the support available in their local area. The Supportive and Palliative Care Indicators Tool (SPICT) can help identify people with advancing illness that would benefit from a process known as future care planning (also known as advance care planning), which involves discussions between health-care professionals, the patient and their family or legal proxy. Through open, honest exchanges of information over time, the patient is assisted to have their preferences around medical care documented in advance of changes in their health. This process is dynamic, and patient views on interventions frequently change over time. It is important to distinguish between interventions that will not provide clinical benefit (a medical decision) and those that may not confer suffi-cient benefit to be worthwhile (a decision that can only be made with the patient’s involvement).

The Australia-modified Karnofsky Performance Status (AKPS) is routinely used to guide patient prognosis in palliative care (Box 9.13). The rate at which performance status falls can give an indication of how long they have to live, e.g. someone with a score of 50% falling steadily week by week to 20% may have a short number of weeks to live. When patients with cancer or other conditions become bed-bound, semi-comatose, are unable to take tablets and only able to take sips of water, with no reversible cause (AKPS 10%), they are likely to be in their last few days of life. Signs that someone is close to death include skin mottling, movement of the jaw with breathing, audible respiratory secretions and changes in breathing such as Cheyne–Stokes respiration. It is important for health-care professionals to make the assessment that someone is dying as a multidisciplinary team.

For most people, dying is a gentle and peaceful process that needs very minimal medical input. It is vital that patients who do develop dis-tressing symptoms at end of life have these managed promptly and effectively. Oral medications can often be used until close to end of life, but it is important to carry out a regular medication review with the patient. Drugs such as statins, vitamins, bisphosphonates and antihy-pertensives can usually be stopped in the last weeks of life to reduce the burden of taking pills.
section_path: Management of symptoms at end of life

text: A continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) of medication can be used to provide symptom control for people near end of life who can no longer swal-low medications. Opioids may be required for pain or breathlessness, mida-zolam can be used to manage agitation or seizures, hyoscine butylbromide (anti-cholinergic) is used to reduce respiratory secretions and haloperidol or levomepromazine is used to manage both nausea and agitation. Anti-epileptics, NSAIDs, tranexamic acid and a range of other drugs can also be given via this route. Some of these drugs can be mixed together in the same syringe; guidance is available on compatible mixtures.

It is good practice to have a selection of ‘as required’ symptom con-trol medications prescribed for patients who are approaching end of life. These medications are usually administered as subcutaneous injections but can be given via transmucosal routes if appropriate. Should a patient develop symptoms, then pre-prescribed medication can be given by nursing staff without delay, e.g. waiting for a doctor to come and prescribe. A similar supply of injectable medication can also be stored in a patient’s house or care home to be administered by district nurses or trained informal carers. The medication dose, indication, minimum dose interval and maximum 24-hour dose should be clear on the prescription. The common medications prescribed (UK) are as follows:
• an opioid medication for managing pain or breathlessness, e.g. morphine sulphate injection 2 mg up to 1 hourly – max 6 doses in 24 hours
• a benzodiazepine for managing breathlessness or agitation, e.g. midazolam injection 2 mg up to 1 hourly – max 6 doses in 24 hours
• an antiemetic for managing nausea, e.g. levomepromazine 2.5 mg up to 8 hourly – max 3 doses in 24 hours
• an anti-secretory medication to reduce audible respiratory secre-tions, e.g. hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg up to 2 hourly – max 6 doses in 24 hours
For those at risk of seizures, bleeding or airway compromise, a higher dose of midazolam may be prescribed to use only in an emergency.
The following elements of care are essential in the care of the dying person:

• Mouth care: Dry mouth, ulcers and candidiasis can all cause pain. Oral fluids should be provided to relieve thirst while the patient is able to drink. Small sips of fluid or a water spray may still be soothing near end of life. A soft toothbrush can be used to cleanse the teeth and tongue. Foam mouth swabs or sponges should be avoided due to the risk of choking.
• Skin care: Pressure area protection using positional changes and pressure-relieving mattresses.
• Bowel care: Constipation can cause agitation. Use of suppositories may be needed.
• Bladder care: Urinary retention due to opioids or hyoscine can occur. Urethral catheterisation can help preserve skin integrity, save energy and produce dignity for the patient.

Communication with the patient and family should occur with all aspects of care. Explaining what medication or nursing care is being given and why is important. Involvement of family in the practical care of their loved ones should be explored, remembering that family are usually the main carers when people are dying at home.

This patient has clear signs of opioid-induced constipation (OIC) that has not responded to a first-line laxative (senna). When a patient with OIC fails to respond to conventional laxatives, current guidelines rec-ommend initiating a PAMORA such as naloxegol, methylnaltrexone, or naldemedine. These agents target the underlying mechanism by antago-nising opioid receptors in the gut without affecting analgesia. Increasing senna or adding docusate is unlikely to resolve refractory OIC, and die-tary measures alone are inadequate in this context. Manual disimpaction is only indicated in cases of faecal impaction, which is not evident here.
Answer: C.

There is good evidence that increasing physical activity is an effective way to manage chronic pain, but it is acknowledged that there may be a number of barriers preventing people who live with chronic pain from doing this successfully. These can include fear avoidance, not pacing activities well, depression, financial problems or other commit-ments that prevent their ability to attend appointments or go to a leisure centre. Advice alone is not enough and personal preference/previous experience will impact on patient engagement. There is no one type of exercise that will work for everyone. Opioids are not recommended for long-term use in chronic pain, and combining these with other seda-tive drugs may be harmful. Ongoing review of the benefits versus risks of continuing co-codamol at the current dose should be undertaken. Review for potential opioid side-effects such as somnolence or consti-pation from her current co-codamol therapy is important to make sure these are not impacting her quality of life. There is no good evidence that benzodiazepines are helpful in chronic low back pain. Continued investigation in the absence of specific concerns is not recommended.
Answer: D.

This patient has uncontrolled cancer-related bone pain. Radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for improving pain and will be effective in around 50% of people in the first 2 weeks. An increase in pain can occur in the first 24–48 hours after radiotherapy for bone metastases, known as a pain flare; the risk of this can be reduced by prescribing dexamethasone 4–6 mg/day, which this patient is already taking. This patient requires an immediate increase in her morphine to manage her current pain levels. Morphine has been giving some analgesic benefit and has been well tolerated so far, meaning there is no indication to switch to oxycodone. An increase from 5 mg to 10 mg per morphine dose would be appropri-ate in the first instance, with ongoing review over the day. She may also require a further dose adjustment in the coming days should her pain flare with radiotherapy. It will be important to subsequently reduce her opioid dose should she experience good pain relief from her radiotherapy over the coming weeks. Failure to adjust doses in this reactive man-ner could result in distressing pain acutely and opioid toxicity over time. Using regular and as-required immediate-release (short-acting) morphine to provide this flexibility in the first few days will allow more refined dose adjustment. The option to have immediate-release morphine as required up to 1 hourly rather than 4 hourly will reduce the chance of the patient waiting for analgesia while in pain and allow recognition of acutely wors-ening pain. Introducing modified-release morphine would be a potential option once the 24-hour morphine dose requirement becomes clearer in due course. Although using a continuous infusion of morphine may give some flexibility to adjust the dose over the coming days, the patient can currently take oral medications, so this is not indicated. Consideration of an adjuvant such as pregabalin is not currently indicated and may complicate opioid titration due to side-effects from the combination. The combination of NSAID and dexamethasone can increase the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding; analgesic benefit is unlikely to be superior to opioids in this scenario.

Which of the following did John’s doctor suggest?
Answer: A.

Pain affects, and is affected by, many other symptoms and aspects of daily living. Time spent on the initial detailed assessment of all aspects of the patient is key to successful management. For John, rapid proposed solutions to his myriad of problems would only lead to therapeutic chaos. The key decision is what is the greatest driver of the symptoms and how does this potentially interact with other symptoms and distress. Our patient had very severe pain with a strong neuropathic com-ponent, as would be expected from pressure on and/or invasion of the brachial plexus by the tumour. It is not surprising that he was not sleeping because of this extremely severe pain, and felt thoroughly miserable and hopeless. His poor appetite and weight loss could be a result of the uncontrolled pain; however, it could also be the result of the cancer process via a cachexia mechanism. It is important to recognise that neuropathic pain is particularly associated with mood disturbances.

When assessing complexities, it is important to ground decisions on information obtained directly from the patient. John was able to give a clear history that a codeine and paracetamol combination worked within 40 minutes but lasted for just an hour, and the clue here is that his pain was at least partially opioid responsive. It is critical not to move sideways on an analgesic ladder, and if maximum dose of codeine is not effective, the patient should move to a strong opioid, such as morphine. The usual starting dose in this situation of normal renal function and such severe pain should be 5 mg of normal release morphine orally 6 times daily. If starting modified-release morphine, the dose is 10–15 mg 2 times daily. For breakthrough analgesia, the dose is usually 1/6 of the total 24-hour dose, so 5 mg in this case. The patient should be advised that if breakthrough pain relief is required, it will take 30 minutes to start having an effect. The patient should be instructed to take a careful note of duration onset and duration of effect of the regular dose, and frequency of onset and duration and effect of the breakthrough dose.
What did John’s doctor decide to do next?
Answer: B.

There is a strong ongoing neuropathic element to John’s pain. He likely has mixed cancer pain (somatic and neuropathic) with a partial response evident to adequately titrated morphine. There does not appear to be much benefit in further increasing his morphine given the last dose incre-ment offered no subjective benefit for John. There is no evidence to sup-port that oxycodone is any better for management of neuropathic cancer pain than morphine. At this point it would be acceptable to try adding an adjuvant analgesic to his established morphine regimen. It is impor-tant when considering an adjuvant analgesic to consider the potential side-effects of the drug itself and how it might interact with currently prescribed medications. Although adding dexamethasone may produce some analgesic benefit if there is nerve compression, it can interfere with people’s ability to sleep and may exacerbate John’s anxiety and racing thoughts. Ketamine is usually only considered for neuropathic pain once more commonly used adjuvants have been tried. Pregabalin has been shown to improve neuropathic pain in some individuals and also has anx-iolytic calming properties which would potentially offer some relief from John’s distress overnight. The combination of pregabalin and morphine can increase the risk of daytime somnolence, confusion and falls, so patient counselling, careful dose titration and review is essential.

dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for 3 days with her last cycle of chemotherapy to reduce the risks of nausea and vomiting. She has also been taking ondansetron 4 mg three times daily for the past 2 weeks. She developed severe nausea and vomiting after her first cycle, which resolved fully after 72 hours. She found this very distressing and required IV fluids to manage dehydration. When attending the oncology ward for pre-chemotherapy bloods this week, she became acutely nauseous on arrival but reports this settled once she got home. She has phoned the oncology department today to say she is nervous about coming to the hospital tomorrow and has developed worsening nausea again today. She has taken her prescribed ondansetron and a pre-chemo dose of dexamethasone 4 mg this morning. Her chemotherapy regimen for her upcoming 2nd cycle has been altered by her consultant to reduce the risk of nausea and vomiting.
What action did the oncology doctor take?
Answer: D.

The most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms is anticipatory nausea and vomiting. Her first chemotherapy session led to severe nausea and vomiting, which caused her significant distress. That experience has led to a learned association between being in the hospital ward and feeling nauseous. This was evident when she attended for her blood tests and became nauseous, which has further reinforced this anxiety response to the location. She is now feeling nauseous even when thinking about attending the ward, which is closely tied in with her anxieties about fur-ther treatment. Anticipatory nausea and vomiting is mediated primarily by the neurotransmitter GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid), and therefore using a benzodiazepine such as lorazepam may offer relief of symptoms.

Hospital medicine is becoming ever-more specialised and people are living longer while accruing increasing numbers of chronic disease diag -noses. Rather than diminishing the role of the generalist, these factors paradoxically create a need for experts in the undifferentiated presenta -tion. In the UK such physicians are known as ‘general physicians’, while in the United States they are referred to as ‘hospitalists’. Acute illness can present in a large variety of ways, depending on the nature of the illness, the underlying health of the individual, and their cul -tural and religious background. The skills of prompt diagnosis formation and provision of appropriate treatment rely on the integration of infor -mation from all the available sources, along with careful consideration of underlying chronic health problems. Patients who deteriorate while in hospital make up a small but impor-tant cohort. If they are well managed, in-hospital cardiac arrest rates will be low. This can be achieved through the combined effects of prompt resuscitation and appropriate end-of-life decision-making. Early recog-nition of deterioration by ward teams and initial management by health-care professionals operating within a functioning rapid response system are the central tenets of any system designed to improve the outcomes of deteriorating ward patients. Intensive care medicine has developed into a prominent specialty, central to the safe functioning of a modern acute hospital. Scientific endeavour has resulted in a much better understanding of the molecu-lar pathophysiology of processes such as sepsis and acute respiratory distress syndrome, which account for much premature death worldwide.

Acute medicine is the part of general medicine that is concerned with the immediate and early management of medical patients who require urgent care. As a specialty, it is closely aligned with emergency medicine and intensive care medicine, but is firmly rooted within general medicine. Acute physicians manage the adult medical take and lead the develop-ment of acute care pathways that aim to reduce variability, improve care and cut down hospital admissions. In order to achieve these aims, acute physicians must use their knowledge, combined with high-level clinical reasoning and decision-making skills, to minimise both diagnostic error and the risks of over-investigation. These concepts are explained more fully in Chapter 1.

Every patient presenting to hospital should be assessed by a clinician who is able to determine whether or not admission is required. The requirement for admission is determined by many factors, including the severity of illness, the patient’s physiological reserve, the need for urgent investigations, the nature of proposed treatments and the patient’s social circumstances. In many cases, it is clear early in the assessment pro-cess that a patient requires admission. In such cases, a move into a medical receiving unit – often termed a medical admissions unit (MAU) or acute medical unit (AMU) – should be facilitated as soon as the initial assessment has been completed and urgent investigations and/or treat-ments have been instigated. In hospitals where such units do not exist, patients will need to be moved to a downstream ward once treatment has been commenced and they have been deemed sufficiently stable. In suspected cases of airborne-transmissible infectious diseases, patients should be isolated initially and may require cohorting in specific areas of the hospital once diagnoses have been confirmed. Following the ini-tial assessment, it may be possible to discharge stable patients home with a plan for early follow-up (such as a rapid-access specialist clinic appointment).
