Hormones are chemical messengers critical for maintaining homeosta-sis, regulating responses to environmental challenges, controlling growth and reproduction. Endocrinology concerns the synthesis, secretion and action of hormones. Endocrine disease may result directly from pathol-ogy within endocrine glands, and indirectly from disrupted hormone signalling. This chapter describes the principles of endocrinology before discussing the physiology and pathology of each gland in turn.

Most endocrine glands are controlled by hormones released from the anterior pituitary gland, although some, such as the parathyroid glands and pancreas, respond directly to metabolic signals. Hormone secretion from the anterior pituitary is controlled in turn by messengers produced in the hypothalamus and released into the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system, which drains directly down the pituitary stalk (Fig. 20.1). Posterior pituitary hormones are synthesised in the hypothalamus and transported down nerve axons, to be released from the posterior pitu-itary. Hormone release in the hypothalamus and pituitary is regulated by numerous neuropeptides and by feedback control by hormones produced by the target glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads). These integrated endocrine systems are called ‘axes’ and are listed in Figure 20.2. A wide variety of molecules can act as hormones. Small peptides such as insulin, glycoproteins such as thyroid-stimulating hormone, and amines such as noradrenaline (norepinephrine) bind to specific receptors on the membrane of their target cells. Activation of these receptors trig-gers a cascade of intracellular signalling to affect cell function. Steroid (for example cortisol) and thyroid hormones cross the cell membrane and exert their effects predominantly by binding to intracellular receptors forming complexes that affect the transcriptional activity of target genes. The classical model of endocrine function involves hormones syn-thesised in endocrine glands, which are released into the circula-tion and act at distal sites (as in Fig. 20.1). Hormone activity is also regulated by a number of ‘fine-tuning’ physiological processes: (1) hormones may be activated or deactivated locally at their target organ (local deiodinases activate and deactivate thyroid hormones); (2) circulat-ing peptide hormones, such as insulin, have a short half-life due to deg-radation by peptidases thereby limiting the risk of hormone activity when it is no longer required; (3) hormones may be rendered inactive by bind-ing to large proteins circulating in the bloodstream, leaving a small pool of circulating active ‘free’ hormone (thyroid hormone is almost entirely bound to carrier proteins). Some hormones can act in a paracrine fashion to affect adjacent cells, or act in an autocrine way to affect behaviour of the cell that produced the hormone.

For each endocrine axis or major gland, diseases can be classified as shown in Box 20.1. Pathology arising within the gland is often called ‘primary’ disease (e.g. primary hypothyroidism resulting from Hashimoto thyroiditis), while abnormal stimulation of the gland is often called ‘sec-ondary’ disease (e.g. secondary hypothyroidism due to thyroid-stim-ulating hormone deficiency in patients with pituitary tumours). Some pathological processes can affect multiple endocrine glands; these may have a genetic basis (such as the multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes) or be a consequence of therapy for another disease (such as following systemic anti-cancer treatment and/or radiotherapy).

As chemical messengers, most hormones can be measured in samples of bodily fluids, commonly in blood, urine and saliva. Physiological hor-mone secretion can be highly variable and thus the timing and context of a sample may impact significantly on the interpretation of results; for example, a low cortisol value may be normal at 2300 hrs, but indicate adrenal insufficiency if assessed at 0800 hrs. Furthermore, some hor-mones are labile and have specific requirements for sample processing (for example, collection into particular tubes, transport on ice, rapid pro-cessing). Local protocols for hormone measurement should be followed carefully. For some hormones, dynamic tests may be required to identify dis-rupted secretion; suppression tests are used to assess for hypersecre-tion (for example, dexamethasone suppression testing for excessive cortisol secretion); and stimulation tests are required where there is concern about insufficiency (for example, ACTH stimulation testing [also known as short Synacthen, corticotrophin, cosyntropin or tetracosactide stimulation test] for adrenal insufficiency). The choice of stimulus can help to determine the level of the endocrine axis affected; whilst the ACTH stimulation test will assess primarily adrenal responsiveness, an insulin tolerance test (inducing hypoglycaemia) will assess appropriate hypo-thalamus, pituitary and adrenal response to stress. Intra- and inter-indi-vidual variation in hormone levels means that some tests may have poor sensitivity and specificity; an understanding of the accuracy of the test being interpreted is thus important. The context in which a hormone has been measured will affect its concentration, with important implications for interpretation of results. For example, parathyroid hormone levels may be reported within the reference range for a patient with hypercalcaemia; in this context one would expect suppressed parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels; thus, levels are ‘inappropriately normal’ and suggestive of hyperparathyroidism. The principles of investigation are shown in Box 20.2. The choice of test is often pragmatic, taking local access to reliable sampling facilities and laboratory measurements into account.

Endocrine diseases present in many ways to clinicians in different dis-ciplines. The classical syndromes associated with disorders of individ-ual glands are described in the following sections. However, patients often present with non-specific symptoms (Box 20.3) or are seemingly asymptomatic with only biochemical abnormalities. Endocrine diseases are also encountered within the differential diagnosis of common pres-entations discussed in other chapters of this book, including electrolyte 20.2 Principles of endocrine investigation
Timing of measurement
• Release of many hormones is rhythmical (pulsatile, circadian or monthly), random measurement may be invalid and specifically timed, sequential or dynamic tests may be required
Choice of dynamic biochemical test
• If hormone deficiency is suspected, choose a stimulation test
• If hormone excess is suspected, choose a suppression test
• The more tests there are to choose from, the less likely it is that any single test is infallible, so avoid interpreting one result in isolation
Imaging
• ‘Functional’ as well as conventional ‘structural’ imaging can be performed as secretory endocrine cells often take up labelled substrates, e.g. radio-labelled iodine or octreotide
• Most endocrine glands have a high prevalence of ‘incidentalomas’, so do not scan unless the biochemistry confirms endocrine dysfunction or the primary problem is a tumour
Biopsy

• Many endocrine tumours are difficult to classify histologically (e.g. adrenal carcinoma and adenoma) abnormalities (Ch. 19), hypertension (Ch. 16), obesity (Ch. 5) and osteo-porosis (Ch. 25). The non-specific presentation of some endocrine dis-orders means diagnosis relies on astute clinical observation and so it is important to be familiar with their key features.

Thyroid disease has an incidence of 2.6 cases per 1000 per year in European populations with the rate 5 times higher in females than males. The incidence is twice as high in populations deficient in iodine. Diseases of the thyroid are summarised in Box 20.4. Thyroid hormones regulate cellular differentiation and metabolism in virtually all nucleated cells, meaning disorders of thyroid function have diverse manifestations. Structural disease of the thyroid gland, such as goitre or thyroid nodules, may not necessarily affect thyroid function.

Thyroid physiology is illustrated in Figure 20.3. Parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin, which reduces plasma calcium but is seemingly redundant in humans. Follicular cells synthesise thyroid hormones; they secrete thyroglobulin (Tg), a scaffold protein, and transport iodide into the thyroid colloid. Here, thyroid peroxidase catalyses the iodination of tyrosine residues, forming triiodothyronine (T3) and the prohormone thy-roxine (T4). Iodide is essential for thyroid hormone synthesis. The thyroid secretes predominantly T4 and a small amount of T3; approximately 85% of T3 is produced peripherally from T4 by deiodinase enzymes that regulate localised thyroid hormone activity. T4 has a much longer half-life in blood than T3 (approximately 1 week compared with approximately 18 hours). T3 and T4 circulate in plasma almost entirely (>99%) protein-bound, predominantly to thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) but also to albumin and transthyretin. Only unbound or free hormones are transported into cells to activate the thyroid receptor. Historically, laboratories used assays that measured total T4 and T3; however, it is now common to measure free T4 and free T3. The advantage of free hormone measurements is that they are not influenced by changes in the concentration of binding proteins. For example, TBG levels are increased by oestrogen (such as in the combined oral contraceptive pill), which results in raised total T3 and T4, whilst free thyroid hormone levels remain normal. Production of T3 and T4 in the thyroid gland is stimulated by thy-roid-stimulating hormone (TSH). TSH is a glycoprotein released from the thyrotroph cells of the anterior pituitary primarily in response to the hypo-thalamic tripeptide, thyrotrophin-releasing hormone (TRH). A circadian rhythm of TSH secretion can be demonstrated with a peak at about midnight and trough in the afternoon. However, variation in TSH (and free T3) secretion is modest, meaning thyroid function can be assessed reliably from blood drawn at any time of day. T3 inhibits TRH and TSH production in the hypothalamus and pitu-itary; when plasma concentrations of T3 and T4 are raised in patients with thyrotoxicosis, TSH secretion should be suppressed. Conversely, in hypothyroidism due to thyroid gland dysfunction, low T3 and T4 should be associated with high circulating TSH levels. The relationship between TSH and T4 is classically described as inverse log-linear (Fig. 20.4), such that small changes in TSH levels reciprocate larger changes in free T4. For this reason, TSH is usually regarded as the most useful investigation of thyroid function, especially in the context of assessing replacement. Discrepant thyroid function tests, where TSH and thyroid hormones do not reciprocate as expected, most commonly occur due to problems with hormone measurement, but may indicate less common pathology. For example, in patients with pituitary disease, TSH may be inappropri-ately low or ‘normal’ in the context of low free T4 levels (see Box 20.5 and Box 20.51). Further, there can be a lag of several weeks in the thyrotroph response to changes to thyroid hormone levels; for example, levothyrox-ine therapy will raise T4 and T3 levels within approximately 2 weeks, but it can take 4–6 weeks for the TSH to reach a steady state. Heterophilic antibodies (host antibodies with affinity to the animal antibodies used in immunoassays) can interfere with the TSH assay and cause a spurious high or low measurement. Common patterns of abnormal thyroid func-tion test results and their interpretation are shown in Box 20.5. Other investigations of thyroid disease include the measurement of antibodies targeting the TSH receptor (TRAb) or other thyroid antigens (see Box 20.8), radioisotope imaging, fine needle aspiration biopsy and ultrasound. Their use is described below.

The most common presentations are hyperthyroidism (thyrotoxicosis), hypothyroidism and enlargement of the thyroid (goitre or thyroid nodule). Increasingly, thyroid dysfunction is identified in patients who are asymp-tomatic or who have relatively non-specific symptoms such as fatigue or changes to weight.
Thyrotoxicosis

Thyrotoxicosis describes a state in which the patient exhibits clinical features arising from elevated circulating levels of thyroid hormone. The most common causes are Graves disease, multinodular goitre, autonomously functioning thyroid nodules (toxic adenoma) and thy-roiditis (Box 20.6).
Clinical assessment

The clinical manifestations of thyrotoxicosis are shown in Box 20.7, and an approach to differential diagnosis is given in Figure 20.5. The most common symptoms are weight loss with a normal or increased appe-tite (although around 5% patients may exhibit weight gain), heat intoler-ance, palpitations, tremor and irritability. Tachycardia, palmar erythema and lid lag are common clinical signs. Not all patients have a palpable goitre, but experienced clinicians may discriminate the diffuse soft goi-tre of Graves disease from the irregular enlargement of a multinodular goitre. All causes of thyrotoxicosis can cause lid retraction and lid lag, due to potentiation of sympathetic innervation of the levator palpebrae muscles, but only Graves disease causes other features of ophthalmo-pathy, including periorbital oedema, conjunctival irritation, exophthalmos and diplopia. Pretibial myxoedema and the rare thyroid acropachy (a periosteal hypertrophy, indistinguishable from finger clubbing) are also specific to Graves disease (see p. 690).
Investigations

The first-line investigations are serum free T4 and TSH. If abnormal values are found, the tests should be repeated and the abnormality confirmed in view of the likely need for prolonged medical treatment or destructive therapy. In most patients, serum T3 and T4 are both elevated; elevation of only T3 (T3 toxicosis) is seen in about 5% of presentations. Therefore, free T3 should be assessed in cases with suppressed TSH and normal free T4 levels (T4 usually being at the upper end of the reference range). Serum TSH is undetectable in primary thyrotoxicosis, but values can be raised (or inappropriately normal) in the extremely rare syndrome of sec-ondary thyrotoxicosis caused by a TSH-producing pituitary adenoma, or where uncommon mutations in the thyroid hormone receptor cause thyroid hormone resistance. When biochemical thyrotoxicosis has been confirmed, measurement of TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb, elevated in Graves disease; Box 20.8) is recommended. Where TRAb assess-ment is not available, or is not detected, radioisotope scanning may help with diagnosis, as shown in Figure 20.5. Other non-specific laboratory abnormalities are common (Box 20.9). An electrocardiogram (ECG) may demonstrate sinus tachycardia and around 5%–10% patients may have atrial fibrillation. Radio-iodine uptake tests measure the proportion of isotope that is trapped in the whole gland, but have been largely superseded by tech-netium-99m (99m Tc) scintigraphy scans, which are quicker to perform with a lower dose of radioactivity and provide a higher-resolution image. In low-uptake thyrotoxicosis, the cause is usually a transient thyroiditis; an increase in global uptake is consistent with Graves disease, whilst local-ised uptake may be demonstrated in toxic nodular disease. Occasionally, patients induce ‘factitious thyrotoxicosis’ by consum-ing excessive amounts of a thyroid hormone preparation, most often levothyroxine. Exogenous levothyroxine suppresses pituitary TSH secretion and thus thyroid activity. Thyroglobulin production and release of endog-enous thyroid hormones are reduced. The T4:T3 ratio (typically 30:1 in conventional thyrotoxicosis) is increased to above 70:1 because circulat-ing T3 in factitious thyrotoxicosis is derived exclusively from the peripheral deiodination of T4. The combination of negligible iodine uptake, high T4:T3 ratio and a low or undetectable thyroglobulin is diagnostic.
Management

Definitive treatment of thyrotoxicosis depends on the underlying cause and may include antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine or surgery. A non-selective β-adrenoceptor antagonist (β-blocker), such as proprano-lol (80–16 mg in 4 divided doses), will alleviate but not abolish symptoms in most patients within 24–48 hours. Beta-blockers should not be used for long-term treatment of thyrotoxicosis, but are invaluable in the short term while patients are awaiting diagnosis and treatment. Verapamil may be used as an alternative to β-blockers, e.g. in patients with asthma, but usually is only effective in improving tachycardia and is less helpful managing other systemic symptoms of thyrotoxicosis.
Atrial fibrillation in thyrotoxicosis

Atrial fibrillation occurs in about 5%–10% of patients with thyrotoxicosis. The incidence is higher in men and increases with age, such that almost half of all males with thyrotoxicosis over the age of 60 are affected. Moreover, subclinical thyrotoxicosis (see p. 701) is a risk factor for atrial fibrillation. Characteristically, the ventricular rate is little influenced by digoxin (likely due to increased clearance) but responds to the addition of a β-blocker. Thromboembolic vascular complications are particularly common in thyro-toxic atrial fibrillation, so anticoagulation is required unless contraindicated. Once thyroid hormone and TSH concentrations have returned to normal, atrial fibrillation will spontaneously revert to sinus rhythm in about 50% of patients; cardioversion should be considered in the remainder.
Thyrotoxic crisis (‘thyroid storm’)

This is a rare but life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis with mortal-ity rates of 8%–25%. The most prominent signs are fever, agitation, delir-ium, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation and, in the older patient, cardiac failure. Thyrotoxic crisis is a medical emergency. It is precipitated most commonly by infection in a patient with unrecognised or inadequately treated thyro-toxicosis. It may also develop in patients with uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis shortly after thyroid manipulation during thyroidectomy or within a few days of iodine-131 (131 I) therapy, when acute radiation damage may lead to a tran-sient rise in serum thyroid hormone levels. Urgent specialist endocrine input should be sought in cases of suspected ‘thyroid storm’, both to confirm the diagnosis and provide advice on appropriate treatment. Patients should be rehydrated. Beta-blockade using propranolol, either orally (40–80 mg 4 times daily) or intravenously (0.5–2 mg, slow bolus) should be initiated; close monitoring may be needed for patients with congestive heart failure. Oral propylthiouracil (PTU) (200–250 mg every 4 hours) should be given to inhibit the synthesis of new thyroid hormone. PTU is preferred to carbimazole (20 mg every 6 hours) as it also inhibits the conversion of T4 to T3. PTU and propranolol can be administered by nasogastric tube if necessary; however, IV treatment may be necessary due to reduced gastrointestinal absorption. Both glucocorticoids (hydro-cortisone 100 mg IV every 8 hours) and iodine reduce the conversion of T4 to active T3. Iodine (saturated potassium iodide solution/Lugol’s solution) 0.25 mL every 6 hours orally or sodium ipodate, a radiographic contrast medium (500 mg per day orally), should restore serum T3 levels to normal in 48–72 hours. Administration 1 hour after PTU or carbimazole should limit the risk of stimulating thyroid hormone release (p. 706). After 10–14 days the patient can usually be maintained on carbimazole alone.
Hyperthyroidism in old age
Some of the diagnostic and management challenges of hyperthyroidism in older people are highlighted in Box 20.12.
Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism has a prevalence of 0.5%–5% in populations replete in iodine and may approach 10% in populations with endemic iodine deficiency. Autoimmune disease (Hashimoto thyroiditis), thyroid failure following 131 I or surgical treatment of thyrotoxicosis account for over 90% of cases, except in areas where iodine deficiency is endemic (Box 20.10). Women are affected approximately six times more fre-quently than men.
Clinical assessment

The clinical presentation depends on the duration and severity of the hypothyroidism. Those in whom complete thyroid failure has developed insidiously over months or years may present with many of the clinical features listed in Box 20.7. A consequence of prolonged hypothyroidism is the infiltration of many body tissues by the mucopolysaccharides hya-luronic acid and chondroitin sulphate, resulting in a low-pitched voice, poor hearing, slurred speech due to a large tongue, and compression of the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome). Infiltration of the dermis gives rise to non-pitting oedema (myxoedema), predomi-nantly in the skin of the hands, feet and eyelids. The resultant perior-bital puffiness is often striking and may be combined with facial pallor due to vasoconstriction and anaemia, or a lemon-yellow tint to the skin caused by carotenaemia, along with purplish lips and malar flush. Most cases of hypothyroidism are not clinically obvious and thyroid function testing should be considered in individuals complaining of non-specific symptoms such as tiredness, weight gain, depression or carpal tunnel syndrome. The key discriminatory features in the history and examination are highlighted in Figure 20.6. Care must be taken to identify patients with transient hypothyroidism, in whom life-long levothyroxine therapy is inap-propriate. This may occur during the first 6 months after 131 I treatment of Graves disease, in the post-thyrotoxic phase of subacute thyroiditis and in post-partum thyroiditis. In these conditions, levothyroxine treatment is not always necessary, as the patient may be asymptomatic during the short period of thyroid failure.
Investigations

In the majority of cases, hypothyroidism results from an intrinsic dis-order of the thyroid gland (primary hypothyroidism). In this situation, serum T4 is low and TSH is elevated, usually in excess of 20 mIU/L. Measurements of serum T3 are unhelpful since they do not discrimi-nate reliably between euthyroidism and hypothyroidism. Measurement of thyroid peroxidase antibodies is helpful but further investigations are rarely required (see Fig. 20.6). Secondary hypothyroidism (where both TSH and free T4 levels are low) is rare and is caused by failure of TSH secretion in an individual with hypothalamic or anterior pituitary dis-ease. Other non-specific laboratory abnormalities are shown in Box 20.9. In severe, prolonged hypothyroidism, the ECG classically demon-strates sinus bradycardia with low-voltage complexes and may show prolongation of the QRS complex and T-wave flattening or inversion.

Management

Treatment is with levothyroxine replacement. The average replacement dose of levothyroxine is 1.6 μg/kg (100 μg in a 70 kg adult). In healthy younger adults, it is safe to commence an estimated full dose. In older individuals, and those with a history of cardiovascular disease, it is cus-tomary to start with a low dose of 25–50 μg per day for 3 weeks before increasing to the estimated full dose. Levothyroxine has a half-life of 7 days and should be taken as a single daily dose. Ten weeks should pass before repeating thyroid function tests and adjusting the dose as TSH takes several weeks to reach a steady state. Symptomatic improvement usually takes 2–3 weeks. Reduction in weight and periorbital puffiness occurs quickly, but the restoration of skin and hair texture and resolution of any effusions may take 3–6 months. As illustrated in Figure 20.6, most patients do not require specialist review but will need life-long levothy-roxine therapy. The dose of levothyroxine should be adjusted to maintain serum TSH within the reference range. To achieve this, serum T4 often needs to be in the upper part of the reference range because the T3 required for receptor activation is derived exclusively from conversion of T4 within the target tissues, without the usual contribution from thyroid secretion. Some physicians advocate combined replacement with T4 (levothyrox-ine) and T3 (liothyronine) or preparations of animal thyroid extract, but these approaches remain controversial and are not supported by robust evidence. Some patients remain symptomatic despite normalisation of TSH and may wish to take extra levothyroxine, suppressing their TSH. However, a suppressed TSH is a risk factor for osteoporosis and atrial fibrillation (see below; subclinical thyrotoxicosis), so this approach cannot be recommended. It is important to measure thyroid function every 1–2 years once the dose of levothyroxine is stabilised to assess adherence and allow adjust-ment for changes in levothyroxine requirements (Box 20.11). Some patients have a persistent elevation of serum TSH despite an ostensibly adequate replacement dose of levothyroxine; most commonly, this is a consequence of suboptimal adherence to therapy. There may be dif-ferences in bioavailability between the numerous generic preparations of levothyroxine, and if an individual is experiencing marked changes in serum TSH despite optimal adherence, the prescription of a branded preparation of levothyroxine could be considered. There is some limited evidence that suggests levothyroxine absorption may be better when the drug is taken before bed. In some individuals with variable adherence, levothyroxine is taken diligently or even in excess for a few days prior to a clinic visit, resulting in the seemingly anomalous combination of a high serum T4 and high TSH (see Box 20.5).

Levothyroxine replacement in ischaemic heart disease

Hypothyroidism and ischaemic heart disease are common comorbidi-ties. Although angina may remain unchanged in severity or paradoxically disappear with restoration of metabolic rate, exacerbation of myocardial ischaemia, infarction and sudden death are recognised complications of levothyroxine replacement, even using doses as low as 25 μg per day. In patients with known ischaemic heart disease, thyroid hormone replace-ment should be introduced at low dose and increased very slowly under specialist supervision. Coronary intervention may be required if angina is exacerbated by levothyroxine replacement therapy.
Hypothyroidism in old age
Box 20.12 illustrates some of the diagnostic and management chal-lenges of hypothyroidism in older people.
Hypothyroidism in pregnancy

Women with hypothyroidism usually require an increased dose of lev-othyroxine in pregnancy; inadequately treated hypothyroidism in preg-nancy has been associated with impaired neurodevelopment in the fetus. This is discussed in more detail on page 1308 (see also Box 20.13).
Myxoedema coma

This is a very rare presentation of hypothyroidism in which there is a depressed level of consciousness (not always coma), usually in an older patient who appears myxoedematous. Body temperature may be as low as 25°C, convulsions are not uncommon and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure and protein content are raised. The mortality rate is 50% and survival depends on early recognition and treatment of hypothyroidism and other factors contributing to the altered consciousness level, such as medication, cardiac failure, infection, hyponatraemia and respiratory failure. Myxoedema coma is a medical emergency and treatment must begin before biochemical confirmation of the diagnosis. Suspected cases should be treated with 200–400 μg levothyroxine followed by 1.6 μg/kg/ day (with the dose reduced by 25% if the IV route is required). Liothyronine 2.5–10 μg every 8 hours may be needed alongside levothyroxine as there may be impaired deiodination in the context of myxoedema. Liothyronine 20 μg every 8 hours could be considered where IV levothyroxine is not available. In survivors, there is a rise in body temperature within 24 hours and, after 48–72 hours, it is usually possible to switch patients to oral levothyroxine in a dose of 1.6 μg/kg daily, with lower doses considered in patients vulnerable to coronary artery disease. Unless it is apparent that the patient has primary hypothyroidism, the thyroid failure should also be assumed to be secondary to hypothalamic or pituitary disease. Empirical treatment with hydrocortisone, pending the results of fT4, TSH and cor-tisol measurement is recommended (100 mg as intravenous bolus and then 200 mg/day, either as a continuous infusion or in 4 divided doses). Symptoms of hypothyroidism with normal thyroid function tests

The classic symptoms of hypothyroidism are, by their very nature, non-specific (see Box 20.3). There is a wide differential diagnosis for symptoms such as fatigue, weight gain and low mood. As has been noted, outside the context of pituitary and hypothalamic disease, serum TSH is an excellent measure of an individual’s thyroid hormone status. However, some individuals believe that they have hypothyroidism despite normal serum TSH concentrations. They require reassurance that their symptoms are being taken seriously and that organic disease has been carefully considered; if their symptoms persist, referral to a team special-ising in medically unexplained symptoms should be considered.
Asymptomatic abnormal thyroid function tests

One of the most common problems in medical practice is how to manage patients with abnormal thyroid function tests who have no obvious signs or symptoms of thyroid disease. These can be divided into three categories.
Subclinical thyrotoxicosis

Serum TSH is undetectable and serum T3 and T4 are at the upper end of the reference range. This combination is most often found in older patients with multinodular goitre. These patients are at increased risk of atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis; therapy, either with 131 I or low-dose thionamide should be considered. Otherwise, annual review is essential, as the conversion rate to overt thyrotoxicosis is 5% each year.
Subclinical hypothyroidism

Serum TSH is raised and serum T3 and T4 concentrations are at the lower end of the reference range. This may persist for many years, although there is a risk of progression to overt thyroid failure, particularly if antibodies to thyroid peroxidase are present or if the TSH rises above 10 mIU/L. In patients with non-specific symptoms, a trial of levothyroxine therapy may be appropriate. In those with positive autoantibodies or a TSH greater than 10 mIU/L, it is better to treat the thyroid failure early rather than risk loss to follow-up and subsequent presentation with pro-found hypothyroidism. Levothyroxine should be initiated and titrated as for hypothyroidism.
Non-thyroidal illness (‘sick euthyroidism’)

This typically presents with a low serum TSH, raised T4 and normal or low T3 in a patient with systemic illness who does not have clinical evi-dence of thyroid disease. These abnormalities are caused by decreased peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 (with conversion instead to reverse T3), altered levels of binding proteins and their affinity for thyroid hormones, and often reduced secretion of TSH. During convalescence, serum TSH concentrations may increase to levels found in primary hypothyroidism. Treatment is generally not required. As thyroid function tests are difficult to interpret in patients with non-thyroidal illness, it is wise to avoid per-forming thyroid function tests unless there is clinical evidence of concom-itant thyroid disease. If an abnormal result is found, treatment should only be initiated with specialist advice and the diagnosis should be re-evalu-ated after recovery.
Thyroid lump or swelling

A lump or swelling in the thyroid gland can be a source of considerable anxiety for patients. There are numerous causes but, broadly speaking, a thyroid swelling is either a solitary nodule, a multinodular goitre or a diffuse goitre (Box 20.14; see p. 690). Nodular thyroid disease is more common in women and occurs in approximately 30% of the adult female population. Most thyroid nodules are impalpable, but may be identified when imaging of the neck is per-formed for another reason. Palpable thyroid nodules occur in 4%–8% of adult women and 1%–2% of adult men, and classically present when the individual (or their friend or relative) notices a lump in the neck. Multinodular goitre and solitary nodules sometimes present with acute painful enlargement due to haemorrhage into a nodule. Patients with thyroid nodules often worry that they have cancer, but only 5%–10% of thyroid nodules are malignant. A nodule presenting in child-hood or adolescence, particularly if there is a history of head and neck irradiation, or presentation in an older patient should heighten suspicion of a primary thyroid malignancy. The presence of cervical lymphadenopathy also increases the likelihood of malignancy.
