text: Globally, colorectal cancer is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer in males and second in females. High-income countries have the high-est incidence of colorectal cancer, while Africa and South Asia have the lowest incidence. The incidence is continuing to increase on a worldwide basis, with the fastest rise in incidence occurring in younger populations, although incidence rates have stabilised in high-income countries. In the UK, the incidence is around 70 per 100 000 of the population. The con-dition becomes increasingly common over the age of 50 years.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Pathophysiology
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Both environmental and genetic factors are important in colorectal carcino-genesis, as outlined in Figure 22.45. More than 200 loci that predispose to colorectal cancer have been identified by genome-wide association studies, but the effect size of the individual genetic variants is small. While the vast majority of colorectal cancers are sporadic, occurring in people without a family history of the disorder, about 3%–5% of individuals have hereditary colorectal cancer due to pathogenic variants in a single gene.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Genetics
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: The key pathophysiological factors are outlined in Figure 22.46. The development of colorectal cancer results from the accumulation of multi-ple somatic genetic pathogenic variants, accompanied by chromosomal instability, microsatellite instability and widespread hypermethylation of genes across the genome resulting in silencing of tumour suppressor genes. There are three main pathways of genetic instability and each is asso-ciated with distinct histological, clinical and prognostic features.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Chromosomal instability. Mutations or deletions of portions of chro-mosomes arise, with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) and inactivation of specific tumour suppressor genes. In LOH, one allele of a gene is deleted, but gene inactivation occurs only when a subsequent path-ogenic variant affects the other allele. Chromosomal instability (CIN) occurs in around 85% of colorectal cancers.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Microsatellite instability. This involves germline mutations in one of six genes encoding enzymes involved in repairing errors that occur normally during DNA replication (DNA mismatch repair); these genes are designated hMSH2, hMSH6, hMLH1, hMLH3, hPMS1 and hPMS2. Replication errors accumulate and can be detected in ‘microsatellites’ of repetitive DNA sequences. They also occur in important regulatory genes, resulting in a genetically unstable phe-notype and accumulation of multiple somatic mutations throughout the genome that eventually lead to cancer. Around 15% of sporadic cancers develop this way, as do most cases of hereditary non-poly-posis colon cancer (HNPCC).
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). This phenotype is found in approximately 20%–30% of colorectal cancers and results in widespread gene hypermethylation. The result is functional loss of tumour suppressor genes.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: There are two distinct pathways of carcinogenesis: the classical ade-noma–carcinoma pathway and the serrated neoplasia pathway. In the classical adenoma–carcinoma pathway, an adenoma is the precursor lesion. Adenomas progress to form carcinomas through the sequential acquisition of mutations, as the result of chromosomal and microsatellite instability (see Fig. 22.46). It is thought to take between 5 and 10 years for an adenoma to develop into a carcinoma. The serrated neoplasia path-way is characterised by a serrated polyp as a precursor lesion. Serrated polyps (hyperplastic, sessile serrated lesions, and traditional serrated adenomas) were previously thought to be non-neoplastic. However, it is now thought that sessile serrated lesions and traditional serrated ade-nomas are precursor lesions for malignancy. While hyperplastic polyps are generally still viewed as non-neoplastic, some subtypes are thought to be precursors of sessile serrated lesions. There are two pathways of carcinoma formation via the serrated neoplasia pathway, through the traditional serrated and sessile routes, with genetic instability through microsatellite instability and CIMP (Fig. 22.47), although molecular path-ways are still not well understood. The serrated neoplasia pathway is associated with faster carcinoma development in comparison to the classical adenoma–carcinoma pathway.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Environment
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: The majority of colorectal cancers are sporadic, and the development of carcinoma is dependent upon genetic predisposition and environmental triggers. In keeping with this, it is thought that up to 50% of cases of colorectal cancer may potentially be preventable by lifestyle modifica-tions. Several risks factors increase the risk of colorectal cancer, such as smoking, alcohol and type 2 diabetes. In addition, dietary factors are also key in the pathophysiology of colorectal cancer, such as low fruit and vegetable intake (see Fig. 22.45).
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Clinical features
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Symptoms vary, depending on the site of the carcinoma. However, the disease is often asymptomatic until at an advanced stage. In tumours of the left colon, fresh rectal bleeding is common and obstruction occurs early. Tumours of the right colon present with anaemia from occult bleeding or with altered bowel habit, but obstruction is a late feature. Colicky lower abdominal pain is present in two-thirds of patients and rectal bleeding occurs in 50%. A minority present with features of either obstruction or perforation, leading to peritonitis, localised abscess or fis-tula formation. Carcinoma of the rectum usually causes early bleeding, mucus discharge or a feeling of incomplete emptying. Between 10% and 20% of patients present with iron deficiency anaemia or weight loss. On examination, there may be a palpable mass, signs of anaemia or hepatomegaly from metastases. Low rectal tumours may be palpable on digital examination.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Investigations
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice because it is more sensitive and specific than barium enema. Furthermore, lesions can be biopsied and polyps removed. Patients in whom colonoscopy is incomplete and those who are at high risk of complications can be investigated by CT colonography (virtual colonoscopy). This is a sensitive and non-invasive technique for diagnosing tumours and polyps of more than 6 mm diame-ter. When the diagnosis of colon cancer has been made, CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis should be performed as a staging investigation, par-ticularly to detect hepatic metastases, with an increasing role of MRI for further characterisation of liver lesions. Pelvic MRI or endoanal ultrasound should be used for local staging of rectal cancer. Measurement of serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels is of limited value in diagnosis, since values are normal in many patients, but CEA testing can be helpful during follow-up to monitor for recurrence. FDG PET-CT has a role in the staging of patients with metastatic disease being considered for treatment with curative intent, as well as in patients with previously treated colorectal cancer with rising CEA and negative investigations to look for occult dis-ease. Tumour stage (TNM) at diagnosis (Fig. 22.48) is the most important determinant of prognosis, determining the overall stage of the cancer.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Management
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Endoscopy
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Early colorectal cancers may be amenable to endoscopic treatment, using techniques such as endoscopic mucosal resection, endoscopic submucosal dissection and endoscopic full-thickness resection. Endoscopic submucosal dissection and endoscopic full-thickness resection tend to be used when there is suspicion of superficial sub-mucosal invasion. In addition to such a procedure, surgical mesenteric lymphadenectomy may be required.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Curative therapy
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: In the absence of metastases, or when metastases are limited to the liver, surgery remains the cornerstone of curative treatment. Outcomes are improved by the judicious use of chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy in addition to surgery and all patients should be discussed in a multi-disciplinary team meeting. Rectal cancers can be complex to operate on due to the anatomy of the pelvis and positive margins result in poor outcomes for patients. Neoadjuvant radiotherapy, chemoradiotherapy or chemotherapy should be offered to individuals with high-risk rectal cancers to increase the subsequent chance of a complete (R0) surgical resection and to reduce risk of future recurrence. Perioperative or adju-vant post-operative chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil (or capecitabine) +/− oxaliplatin is indicated for T3–4 N0–2 M0 colon cancers to reduce risk of recurrence in those fit enough for it. There is increasing inter-est in the use of immunotherapy/checkpoint inhibitor treatment for the 15% of patients who have mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) cancers, where a high rate of complete responses can be seen with neoadju-vant immunotherapy treatment. Some patients with metastatic colorectal cancer can also be cured or have prolonged survival and should be dis-cussed in appropriate multidisciplinary meetings. When metastatic dis-ease is confined to the liver, hepatic surgery and/or ablative techniques should be considered, with a chance of cure. Patients with a small number of metastases limited to the lung can be considered for surgical resection, radiofrequency ablation or radiotherapy. Some individuals with non-aggressive metastatic disease limited to the peritoneum can benefit from cytoreductive surgery and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemother-apy. Post-operatively, patients should undergo colonoscopy after 1 year and then 3 years later to search for local recurrence or development of new lesions.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Palliative management
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Surgical resection, laser therapy or expandable metal stenting of the pri-mary tumour is appropriate for some patients with metastases to treat bleeding, pain or obstruction. Palliative radiotherapy is sometimes useful for pain or bleeding from pelvic disease or bone or lung metastases. Palliative chemotherapy can improve symptoms, quality of life and sur-vival in patients who are fit enough to benefit. Colorectal cancers should be tested for dMMR and pathogenic variants in NRAS, KRAS or BRAF V600E. This molecular stratification helps in assessment of prognosis for patients with inoperable metastatic disease (median < 1 year for BRAF mutated cancers to median 3 years with RAS/BRAF wild type cancers) and predicts the response to targeted treatments. Initial palli-ative chemotherapy includes combinations of 5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and/or irinotecan. Chemotherapy is often given with monoclonal antibody therapies bevacizumab (vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor) or panitumumab/cetuximab (epidermal growth factor inhibitors for RAS and BRAF wild type cancers). For patients with dMMR tumours, checkpoint inhibitor therapy can result in impressive responses.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Prevention and screening
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Secondary prevention aims to detect and remove lesions at an early or pre-malignant stage by screening the asymptomatic general population. Several potential methods exist:
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Population-based screening of people between the age of 50 and 74 years by regular faecal immunochemical testing (FIT) reduces colorectal cancer mortality and increases the proportion of early cancers detected. Serial stool testing with or without subsequent colonoscopy is the screening method of choice in the UK.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Colonoscopy remains the gold standard and allows preventative polypectomy, but is expensive, requires bowel preparation and car-ries risks (perforation approximately 1:1000). Many countries lack the resources to offer this form of screening.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • CT colonography is fast and low-risk, and offers equivalent sensi-tivity to colonoscopy. Disadvantages include reduced sensitivity to detect polyps of less than 6 mm, the requirement for bowel prepara-tion, exposure to ionising radiation and its inability to offer therapeu-tic intent.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Hereditary syndromes predisposing to colorectal cancer
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Whilst hereditary syndromes are rare, collectively accounting for 3%–5% of colorectal carcinomas, they are important to identify, as the risk of colorectal carcinoma is high in these individuals.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Non-polyposis syndromes
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC), also known as Lynch syndrome, has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance, with a positive family history of colon cancer occurring at a young age. It is the commonest hereditary cancer syndrome, accounting for 1%–3% of all colorectal cancer cases. The lifetime risk in affected individuals is 80%, with a mean age at cancer development of 45 years. In contrast to spo-radic colon cancer, two-thirds of tumours occur proximally. The clinical diagnostic criteria are listed in Box 22.54. However, over recent years, the diagnosis has shifted from clinical criteria to genetic testing for path-ogenic variants in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2 and EPCAM genes, and testing of tumour material for microsatellite instability by polymerase chain reaction and by immunohistochemistry for mismatch repair proteins. In a subset of patients, there is also an increased incidence of cancers of the endometrium, ovary, urinary tract, stomach, pancreas, small intestine and
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: CNS, related to inheritance of different mismatch repair gene mutations. Those who fulfil the criteria for HNPCC should be referred for pedigree assessment, genetic testing (see above) and colonoscopy. These should begin at either 25 years or 35 years (dependent upon the specific genetic abnormalities detected). Colonoscopy needs to be repeated every 2 years, but despite this, interval cancers can still occur. Regular daily use of aspirin is thought to reduce colorectal cancer risk.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Polyposis syndromes
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: A summary of the clinical features of polyposis syndromes is shown in Box 22.55. It is important to note that, while the hamartomatous polyps in Peutz–Jeghers syndrome and juvenile polyposis are not themselves neoplastic, both disorders are associated with an increased risk of malig-nancy of the breast, colon, ovary and thyroid.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Familial adenomatous polyposis
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a rare autosomal dominant dis-order affecting about 1 in 14 000 of the population and accounting for 0.07% of colorectal cancers. It results from germline pathogenic variant of the tumour suppressor APC gene, followed by acquired pathogenic variant of the remaining allele (Ch. 3). The APC gene is large and over 1400 different pathogenic variants have been reported, but most are loss-of-function variants resulting in a truncated APC protein. This pro-tein normally binds to and sequesters β-catenin, but is unable to do so when truncated, allowing β-catenin to translocate to the nucleus, where it up-regulates the expression of many genes. Pathogenic variants are detected in around 95% of FAP cases. Around 25% of cases arise as new mutations and have no family history. Hundreds to thousands of adenomatous colonic polyps develop in 80% of patients by age 15 (Fig. 22.49), with symptoms such as 22.54 Modified Amsterdam criteria* for hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Three or more relatives with colon cancer (with at least one affected first-degree relative)
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Colorectal cancer in two or more generations
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • At least one member affected under 50 years of age
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Familial adenomatous polyposis excluded * These criteria are strict and may miss some families with hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer. The diagnosis should also be considered in individuals with colorectal or endometrial cancer under 45 years of age.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: rectal bleeding beginning a few years later. In those affected, cancer will develop within 10–15 years of the appearance of adenomas and 90% of patients will develop colorectal cancer by the age of 50 years. Despite surveillance, approximately 1 in 4 patients with FAP have cancer by the time they undergo colectomy. There appears to be phenotypic variability in FAP, with an attenuated form resulting in fewer than 100 adenomatous polyps and later onset of polyposis and cancer. A second gene involved in base excision repair (MutY homolog, MUTYH) has been identified and may give rise to colonic polyposis. MUTYH displays autosomal recessive inheritance and leads to tens to hundreds of polyps and proximal colon cancer. This variant is referred to as MUTYH-associated polyposis (MAP). In FAP, non-neoplastic cystic fundic gland polyps occur in the stom-ach, but adenomatous polyps also arise uncommonly. Duodenal adeno-mas are found in over 90% and are most common around the ampulla of Vater. Malignant transformation to adenocarcinoma takes place in 10% and is the leading cause of death in those who have had prophylactic colectomy. Many extra-intestinal features are also seen (Box 22.56). Desmoid tumours occur in up to one-third of patients and usually arise in the mesentery or abdominal wall. Although benign, they may become very large, causing compression of adjacent organs, intestinal obstruction or vascular compromise and are difficult to remove. They sometimes respond to hormonal therapy with tamoxifen, and the NSAID sulindac may bring about regression in some, by unknown mechanisms.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: 22.56 Extra-intestinal features of familial adenomatous polyposis
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE, 70%–80%)
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Epidermoid cysts (extremities, face, scalp) * (50%)
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Benign osteomas, especially skull and angle of mandible* (50%–90%)
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Dental abnormalities (15%–25%)*
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Desmoid tumours (10%–15%)
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Other malignancies (brain, thyroid, liver, adrenal; 1%–3%) *Gardner syndrome.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE) occurs in some cases and is seen as dark, round, pigmented retinal lesions. When present in an at-risk individual, these are 100% predictive of the presence of FAP. A variant, Turcot syndrome, is characterised by FAP with primary CNS tumours (astrocytoma or medulloblastoma). Early identification of affected individuals before symptoms develop is essential. The diagnosis can be excluded if sigmoidoscopy is normal. In newly diagnosed cases, genetic testing should be carried out to confirm the diagnosis and identify the causal pathogenic variant. Subsequently, all first-degree relatives should undergo genetic testing (Ch. 3). In families with known FAP, adolescents should undergo genetic testing at 13–14 years of age and patients who are found to have the pathogenic variant should be offered colectomy after school or college education has been completed. The operation of choice is total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch–anal anastomosis. Ileoanal pouch construction may be associ-ated with reduced fertility in women, which may be due to Fallopian tube scarring post-surgery. Therefore, colectomy with ileorectal anastomo-sis can be used, but is associated with a risk of cancer in the retained rectum. Periodic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy every 1–3 years is recommended to detect and monitor duodenal and periampullary ade-nomas. If large, these may be amenable to endoscopic resection.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Peutz–Jeghers syndrome occurs in around 1 in 120 000 of the popula-tion, accounting for less than 0.01% of colorectal cancer cases. Multiple hamartomatous polyps occur in the small intestine and colon, as well as melanin pigmentation of the lips, mouth and digits (Fig. 22.50). Most cases are asymptomatic, although chronic bleeding, anaemia or intus-susception can occur. There is a significant risk of small bowel or colonic adenocarcinoma and of cancer of the pancreas, lung, testis, ovary, breast and endometrium. Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder with high penetrance, most commonly resulting from truncating pathogenic variants in a serine–threonine kinase gene on chromosome 19p (STK11). The diagnosis requires two of the three following features:
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • small bowel polyposis
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • mucocutaneous pigmentation
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • a family history suggesting autosomal dominant inheritance.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: The diagnosis can be made by genetic testing, but this may be incon-clusive, since pathogenic variants in genes other than STK11 can cause the disorder. Affected people should undergo regular upper endoscopy, colonoscopy and small bowel and pancreatic imaging. Polyps greater than 1 cm in size should be removed. Testicular examination is essential for men, while women should undergo pelvic examination, cervical smears and reg-ular mammography (lifetime risk of breast cancer of 50%). Asymptomatic relatives of affected patients should also undergo screening.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Juvenile polyposis
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: In juvenile polyposis, tens to hundreds of mucus-filled hamartomatous polyps are found in the colorectum. One-third of cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and up to one-fifth develop colorectal cancer before the age of 40. The criteria for diagnosis are:
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • ten or more colonic juvenile polyps
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • juvenile polyps elsewhere in the gut, or
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • any polyps in those with a family history.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Germline pathogenic variants in the SMAD4 gene are often found, as well as pathogenic variants in the BMPR1A gene. SMAD4 variants may have a more aggressive clinical phenotype, while BMPR1A is particularly impli-cated in European populations. Colonoscopy with polypectomy should be performed every 1–2 years and colectomy considered for extensive involve-ment. Periodic upper gastrointestinal endoscopy should be performed every 1–2 years, in view of the risk of gastric and duodenal cancer.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Cronkhite–Canada syndrome
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Cronkhite–Canada syndrome is a rare non-hereditary polyposis syn-drome characterised by cystic polyps in the gastrointestinal tract, alo-pecia, nail dystrophy, and skin hyperpigmentation. Symptoms include abdominal pain and diarrhoea. It is thought to have an inflammatory basis but the pathogenesis is poorly understood. It may respond to cor-ticosteroid therapy.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Cowden syndrome
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Cowden syndrome is characterised by the occurrence of benign hamar-tomas in the gastrointestinal tract along with other congenital anomalies. It is caused by loss-of-function pathogenic variants in the PTEN tumour suppressor gene. The risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer and thy-roid cancer is increased.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Diverticula are acquired and are most common in the sigmoid and descending colon of middle-aged people. Asymptomatic diverticula (diverticulosis) are present in over 50% of people above the age of 70 years. Symptomatic diverticular disease supervenes in 10%–25% of cases, while complicated diverticulosis (acute diverticulitis, pericolic abscess, bleeding, perforation or stricture) is uncommon.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Pathophysiology
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: A life-long refined diet with a relative deficiency of fibre is thought to be responsible, and the condition is rare in populations with a high dietary fibre intake, such as in Asia, where it more often affects the right side of the colon. It is postulated that small-volume stools require high intra-colonic pressures for propulsion and this leads to herniation of mucosa between the taeniae coli (Fig. 22.51). Whilst the pathophysiology of diverticular disease is thought to be mainly due to environmental risk factors, recent evidence suggests the involvement of predisposing genetic factors. Diverticula consist of protrusions of mucosa covered by peritoneum. There is commonly hypertrophy of the circular muscle coat. Inflammation is thought to result from impaction of diverticula with faecoliths. This may resolve spontaneously or progress to cause haem-orrhage, perforation, local abscess formation, fistula and peritonitis. Repeated attacks of inflammation lead to thickening of the bowel wall, narrowing of the lumen and eventual obstruction.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Clinical features
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Symptoms are usually the result of associated constipation or spasm. Colicky pain is suprapubic or felt in the left iliac fossa. The sigmoid colon may be palpable and, in attacks of diverticulitis, there is local tenderness, guarding, rigidity (‘left-sided appendicitis’) and sometimes a palpable mass. During these episodes, there may be diarrhoea, rectal bleeding or fever. The differential diagnosis includes colorectal cancer, ischae-mic colitis, IBD and infection. Diverticular disease may be complicated by perforation, pericolic abscess, fistula formation (usually colovesical), acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding and obstruction. These complica-tions are more common in patients who take NSAIDs or aspirin. After one attack of diverticulitis, the recurrence rate is around 3% per year. Over 10–30 years, perforation, obstruction or bleeding may occur, each affecting 5% of patients.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Investigations
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Investigations are usually performed to exclude colorectal neoplasia. Diverticula can be seen during colonoscopy or on imaging modalities such as CT scan, CT colonography or barium enema (see Fig. 22.12C). In severe diverticulosis, colonoscopy requires expertise and carries a risk of perforation. CT is used to assess complications, such as perforation or pericolic abscess.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Management
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Diverticular disease that is asymptomatic and discovered coinciden-tally requires no treatment. Constipation can be relieved by a high-fibre diet, with or without a bulking laxative (ispaghula husk, 1–2 sachets daily), taken with plenty of fluids. Stimulant laxatives (Box 22.57) should be avoided. Antispasmodics may sometimes help. Acute attacks of diverticulitis may require the use of antibiotics active against gram-neg-ative and anaerobic organisms. Severe cases require intravenous flu-ids, intravenous antibiotics, analgesia and nasogastric suction, but randomised trials show no benefit from acute resection compared to conservative management. Emergency surgery is reserved for severe haemorrhage or perforation. Percutaneous drainage of acute paracolic abscesses can be effective and avoids the need for emergency surgery. Patients who have repeated attacks of obstruction should undergo elective surgery once the acute episode has settled, in order to resect the affected segment of bowel with restoration of continuity by primary anastomosis.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: 22.58 Constipation in old age
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Evaluation: particular attention should be paid to immobility, dietary fluid and fibre intake, drugs and depression.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Immobility: predisposes to constipation by increasing the colonic transit time; the longer this is, the greater the fluid absorption and the harder the stool.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Bulking agents: can make matters worse in patients with slow transit times and should be avoided.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: • Overflow diarrhoea: if faecal impaction develops, paradoxical overflow diarrhoea may occur. If antidiarrhoeal agents are given, the underlying impaction may worsen and result in serious complications, such as stercoral ulceration and bleeding.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: The clinical approach to patients with constipation and its aetiology have been described on page 821.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Simple constipation
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Simple constipation is extremely common and does not signify underly-ing organic disease. It usually responds to increased dietary fibre or the use of bulking agents; an adequate fluid intake is also essential. Many types of laxative are available, and these are listed in Box 22.57.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Severe idiopathic constipation
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This occurs almost exclusively in young women and often begins in childhood or adolescence. The cause is unknown, but some have ‘slow transit’ with reduced motor activity in the colon. Others have ‘dyssyner-gic defaecation’, resulting from inappropriate contraction of the external anal sphincter and puborectalis muscle (anismus). The condition is often resistant to treatment. Bulking agents may exacerbate symptoms, but prokinetic agents or balanced solutions of polyethylene glycol 3350 ben-efit some patients with slow transit. Glycerol suppositories and biofeed-back techniques are used for those with dyssynergic defaecation. Others benefit from agents such as prucalopride or linaclotide. Rarely, subtotal colectomy may be necessary as a last resort.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Faecal impaction
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: In faecal impaction, a large, hard mass of stool fills the rectum. This tends to occur in disabled, immobile or institutionalised patients, espe-cially frail older adults or those with dementia (Box 22.58). Constipating drugs, autonomic neuropathy and painful anal conditions also contrib-ute. Megacolon, intestinal obstruction and urinary tract infections may supervene. Perforation and bleeding from pressure-induced ulceration are occasionally seen. Overflow diarrhoea may also be a presenting fea-ture, sometimes leading to worsening of symptoms with the incorrect use of antidiarrhoeal medication. Treatment should involve adequate hydration and careful digital disimpaction after softening the impacted stool with arachis oil enemas. Stimulant laxatives should be avoided.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Melanosis coli and laxative misuse syndromes
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Long-term consumption of stimulant laxatives leads to accumulation of lipofuscin pigment in macrophages in the lamina propria. This imparts a brown discoloration to the colonic mucosa, often described as resem-bling ‘tiger skin’. The condition is benign and resolves when the laxatives are stopped. Prolonged laxative use may rarely result in megacolon or ‘cathartic colon’, in which barium enema demonstrates a featureless mucosa, loss of haustra and shortening of the bowel. Surreptitious laxative misuse is a psychiatric condition seen in young women, some of whom have a history of bulimia or anorexia nervosa (Ch. 29). They complain of refractory watery diarrhoea. Laxative use is usually denied and may continue, even when patients are undergoing investigation. Screening of urine for laxatives may reveal the diagnosis.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Hirschsprung disease
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This disease is characterised by constipation and colonic dilatation (meg-acolon) due to congenital absence of ganglion cells in the large intestine. Incidence is approximately 1:5000. About one-third of patients have a positive family history and, in these families, the disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance. About 50% of familial cases and 15% of sporadic cases have pathogenic variants affect-ing the RET proto-oncogene, which is also implicated in multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) types 2a and 2b (p. 742). Unlike MEN 2a and 2b, which are caused by activating RET variants, Hirschsprung disease is caused by loss-of-function variants. In some kindreds, Hirschsprung disease and MEN can actually co-segregate and this presumably represents both ‘switch off’ and ‘switch on’ of RET in different tissues. Although RET is the most important susceptibility gene, some patients with RET variants do not develop clinical Hirschsprung disease and pathogenic variants in other genes have been identified that interact to cause the disease. All of the genes implicated in Hirschsprung disease are involved in the regula-tion of enteric neurogenesis and the mutations cause failure of migration of neuroblasts into the gut wall during embryogenesis. Ganglion cells are absent from nerve plexuses, most commonly in a short segment of the rectum and/or sigmoid colon. As a result, the internal anal sphincter fails to relax. Constipation, abdominal distension and vomiting usually develop immediately after birth, but a few cases do not present until childhood or adolescence. The rectum is empty on digital examination. A plain abdominal X-ray or barium enema shows a small rectum and colonic dilatation above the narrowed segment. Full-thickness biopsies are required to demonstrate nerve plexuses and confirm the absence of ganglion cells. Histochemical stains for acetylcholinesterase are also used. Anorectal manometry demonstrates failure of the internal sphincter to relax with bal-loon distension. Treatment involves resection of the affected segment.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Acquired megacolon
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This may develop in childhood as a result of voluntary withholding of stool during toilet training and can present with faecal impaction and soiling. In such cases, it presents after the first year of life and is distin-guished from Hirschsprung disease by the urge to defaecate and the presence of stool in the rectum. It usually responds to osmotic laxatives. In adults, acquired megacolon has several causes. It is seen in patients with depression or dementia, either as part of the condition or as a side-effect of antidepressant drugs. Prolonged misuse of stimulant laxa-tives may cause degeneration of the myenteric plexus, while interruption of sensory or motor innervation may be responsible in a number of neu-rological disorders. Patients taking large doses of opioid analgesics can develop a megacolon: so-called ‘narcotic bowel syndrome’. Systemic sclerosis and hypothyroidism are other recognised causes.

text: Most patients can be managed conservatively by treatment of the underlying cause, high-residue diets, laxatives and the judicious use of enemas. Prokinetics are helpful in a minority of patients. Opioid-induced constipation can be treated with the specific peripheral opioid recep-tor antagonists, such as naloxegol, methylnaltrexone and naldeme-dine. Subtotal colectomy is a last resort for the most severely affected patients.

text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) has many causes (Box 22.59) and is characterised by sudden onset of painless, massive enlargement of the proximal colon; there are no features of mechani-cal obstruction. Bowel sounds are normal or high-pitched, rather than absent. Left untreated, it may progress to perforation, peritonitis and death. Abdominal X-rays show colonic dilatation with air extending to the rec-tum. Caecal diameter greater than 10 cm is associated with a high risk of perforation. CT with contrast demonstrates the absence of mechanical obstruction. Management consists of treating the underlying disorder and cor-recting any biochemical abnormalities. The anticholinesterase neostig-mine is effective in enhancing parasympathetic activity and gut motility. Decompression, with either a rectal tube or colonoscope, may be effec-tive but needs to be repeated until the condition resolves. In severe cases, surgical or fluoroscopic defunctioning caecostomy is necessary.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Haemorrhoids
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Haemorrhoids (commonly known as piles) arise from congestion of the internal and/or external venous plexuses around the anal canal. They are extremely common in adults. The aetiology is unknown, although they are associated with constipation and straining, and may develop for the first time during pregnancy. First-degree piles bleed, while second-de-gree piles prolapse but retract spontaneously. Third-degree piles are those that require manual replacement after prolapsing. Bright red rectal bleeding occurs after defaecation. Other symptoms include pain, pruri-tus ani and mucus discharge; thrombosis can occur in prolapsed piles, which can be very painful (Fig. 22.52). Treatment involves measures to prevent constipation and straining. Band ligation is effective for many, but a minority of patients require haemorrhoidectomy, which is usually curative. Alternatively, Doppler-guided haemorrhoidal artery ligation and mucopexy may be required.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Pruritus ani
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This is common and can stem from many causes (Box 22.60), most of which result in contamination of the perianal skin with faecal contents. Itching may be severe and results in an itch–scratch–itch cycle that exacerbates the problem. When no underlying cause is found, all local barrier ointments and creams must be stopped. Good personal hygiene is essential, with careful washing after defaecation. The perineal area must be kept dry and clean. Bulk-forming laxatives may reduce faecal soiling.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This is most common in young adults and occurs on the anterior rectal wall. It is thought to result from localised chronic trauma and/or ischaemia associated with disordered puborectalis function and mucosal prolapse. The ulcer is seen at sigmoidoscopy, and biopsies show a characteristic accumulation of collagen. Symptoms include minor bleeding and mucus per rectum, tenesmus and perineal pain. Treatment is often difficult, but avoidance of strain-ing at defaecation is important and treatment of constipation may help. Marked mucosal prolapse is treated surgically.
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Anal fissure
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: In this common problem, traumatic or ischaemic damage to the anal mucosa results in a superficial mucosal tear, most commonly in the mid-line posteriorly. Spasm of the internal anal sphincter exacerbates the condition. Severe pain occurs on defaecation and there may be minor bleeding, mucus discharge and pruritus. The skin may be indurated and an oedematous skin tag, or ‘sentinel pile’, adjacent to the fissure is common. Avoidance of constipation with bulk-forming laxatives and increased fluid intake is important. Relaxation of the internal sphincter is normally mediated by nitric oxide and 0.2% glyceryl trinitrate, which donates nitric oxide and improves mucosal blood flow, is effective in 60%–80% of patients. Diltiazem cream (2%) can be used as an alternative. Resistant 22.61 Causes of faecal incontinence

text: Anorectal abscesses and fistulae
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: Perianal abscesses develop between the internal and external anal sphincters and may point at the perianal skin. Ischiorectal abscesses occur lateral to the sphincters in the ischiorectal fossa. They usually result from infection of anal glands by normal intestinal bacteria. Crohn disease (see below) is sometimes responsible. Patients complain of extreme perianal pain, fever and/or discharge of pus. Spontaneous rupture may lead to the development of fistulae. These may be superficial or track through the anal sphincters to reach the rectum. Abscesses are drained surgically and fistulae are carefully managed according to their anatomy.

text: Faecal incontinence
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: The normal control of anal continence is described on page 806. Common causes of faecal incontinence are listed in Box 22.61. High-risk patients include frail older people, women after childbirth and those with severe neurological/spinal disorders, learning disabilities or cognitive impairment. Patients are often embarrassed to admit to incontinence and may complain only of ‘diarrhoea’. A careful history and examination, espe-cially of the anorectum and perineum, may help to establish the under-lying cause. Endoanal ultrasound is valuable for defining the integrity of the anal sphincters, while anorectal physiology and MR proctography are also useful investigations.

text: Management
section_path: Disorders of the colon and rectum

text: This is often very difficult. Underlying disorders should be treated and diarrhoea managed with loperamide, diphenoxylate or codeine phos-phate. Attention must be paid to a proper diet and adequate fluid intake. Pelvic floor exercises, biofeedback and bowel retraining techniques help some patients, and those with confirmed anal sphincter defects may benefit from sphincter repair operations. Where sphincter repair is not appropriate, a trial of sacral nerve stimulation is undertaken with a view to insertion of a permanent stimulator but, if unsuccessful, creation of a neo-sphincter may be possible, by graciloplasty or by an artificial anal sphincter.
