text: Ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease are chronic inflammatory bowel dis-eases that pursue a protracted relapsing and remitting course, usually extending over many years. The diseases have many similarities and it is sometimes impossible to differentiate between them. One crucial dis-tinction is that ulcerative colitis involves only the colonic mucosa, while Crohn disease can involve any part of the gastrointestinal tract from mouth to anus. A comparison of the main features of ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease is provided in Box 22.62.

The incidence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) varies widely between populations. The highest incidence is in North America, Europe and Oceania. A rapid increase in incidence in the 21st century has been seen in newly industrialised countries in Asia, Africa and South America, with the adoption of an increasingly Westernised lifestyle. Both diseases most commonly start in the second and third decades of life, with a second smaller incidence peak in the seventh decade. The number of people with IBD over the age of 65 years, however, is increas-ing, and it is becoming more common in younger children. Approximately 620 000 people are affected by IBD in the UK, with a population prev-alence of 0.5%–1%. Life expectancy in patients with IBD is similar to that of the general population. Although many patients require surgery and admission to hospital for other reasons, with substantial associated morbidity, the majority have an excellent work record and pursue a nor-mal life.
Pathophysiology

Both environmental and genetic factors contribute to the pathogenesis of IBD (Box 22.63), and evidence from genome-wide association studies suggests that genetic variants that predispose to Crohn disease may have undergone positive selection by protecting against infectious dis-eases, including tuberculosis. It is thought that IBD develops because these genetically susceptible individuals mount an abnormal inflammatory response to environmental triggers, such as intestinal bacteria. This leads to inflammation of the intestine with involvement of a wide array of innate and adaptive immune cell responses, with release of inflammatory medi-ators, including tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α), interleukin (IL)-12 and IL-23, which cause tissue damage (Fig. 22.53). There appears to be an association between microbial dysbiosis and IBD. For example, there is a reduced diversity, primarily of Firmicutes and Bacteroides, and a rel-ative increase in Enterobacteriaceae. Functional changes in the bacteria are important and include a reduction of anti-inflammatory metabolites, such as butyrate and other short-chain fatty acids. While microbial dysbi-osis has been recognised in IBD, a causal role has yet to be established. There is emerging evidence that the virome and mycobiome (fungal spe-cies) may be important in the development of IBD. In both diseases, the intestinal wall is infiltrated with acute and chronic inflammatory cells, but there are important differences between the conditions in the distribution of lesions and in histological features (Fig. 22.54).
22.63 Factors associated with the development of inflammatory bowel disease
Genetic
• Both CD and UC are common in Ashkenazi Jews
• 10% have first-degree relative/one or more close relative with IBD
• High concordance in identical twins (40%–50% CD; 20%–25% UC)

• Multiple susceptibility loci identified at genome-wide levels of significance; most confer susceptibility to both CD and UC; many are also susceptibility loci for other inflammatory conditions (especially ankylosing spondylosis and psoriasis)
• UC and CD are both associated with polymorphic variants at HLA locus, and with multiple genes involved with immune signalling (especially IL-23 and IL-10 pathways)
• CD is associated with polymorphic variants close to genes involved in innate immunity and autophagy (NOD2, ATG16L1 and IRGM)
• UC is associated with genetic defects in barrier function
• Variants at NOD2 locus associated with ileal and stricturing disease, and hence a need for resectional surgery
• HLA-DR*103 is associated with severe UC
Environmental
• UC is more common in non-smokers and ex-smokers
• CD is more common in smokers (relative risk = 3)
• CD is associated with a low-residue, high-refined-sugar diet
• Commensal gut microbiota are altered (dysbiosis) in CD and UC
• Appendicectomy protects against UC (CD = Crohn disease; HLA = human leucocyte antigen; IBD = inflammatory bowel disease; IL = interleukin; UC = ulcerative colitis)
Ulcerative colitis

Inflammation invariably involves the rectum (proctitis) and spreads prox-imally in a continuous manner to involve the entire colon in some cases (pancolitis). In long-standing pancolitis, the bowel can become short-ened and post-inflammatory ‘pseudopolyps’ develop; these are normal or hypertrophied residual mucosa within areas of atrophy (Fig. 22.55). The inflammatory process is limited to the mucosa and spares the deeper layers of the bowel wall (Fig. 22.56). Both acute and chronic inflammatory cells infiltrate the lamina propria and the crypts (‘crypti-tis’). Crypt abscesses are typical. Goblet cells lose their mucus and, in long-standing cases, glands become distorted. Dysplasia, characterised by heaping of cells within crypts, nuclear atypia and increased mitotic rate, may herald the development of colon cancer.
Crohn disease

The sites most commonly involved, in order of frequency, are the terminal ileum and right side of the colon, the small intestine, the colon alone, and the perianal region (see Fig. 22.54). The entire wall of the bowel is oedematous and thickened, and there are deep ulcers that often appear as linear fissures; because of this, the mucosa between them is described as ‘cobblestone’. These ulcers may penetrate through the bowel wall to initiate abscesses or fistulae involving the bowel, bladder, uterus, vagina and skin of the perineum. The mesenteric lymph nodes are enlarged and the mesentery is thickened. Crohn disease has a patchy distribution and the inflammatory process is interrupted by islands of normal mucosa, resulting in ‘skip lesions’. On histological examination, the bowel wall is thickened with a chronic inflammatory infiltrate throughout all layers (Fig. 22.57).
Clinical features
Ulcerative colitis

The cardinal symptoms are rectal bleeding with passage of mucus and bloody diarrhoea. The presentation varies, depending on the site and severity of the disease (see Fig. 22.54), as well as the presence of extra-intestinal manifestations. The first attack is usually the most severe and is followed by relapses and remissions. Emotional stress, intercur-rent infection, gastroenteritis, antibiotics or NSAID therapy may all pro-voke a relapse. Proctitis causes rectal bleeding and mucus discharge, accompanied by tenesmus. Some patients pass frequent, small-vol-ume fluid stools, while others pass pellety stools due to constipation upstream of the inflamed rectum. Left-sided and extensive colitis causes bloody diarrhoea with mucus, often with abdominal cramps. In severe cases, anorexia, malaise, weight loss and abdominal pain occur and the patient is toxic, with fever, tachycardia and signs of peritoneal inflamma-tion (Box 22.64).
Crohn disease

The major symptoms are abdominal pain, diarrhoea and weight loss. Ileal Crohn disease (Figs. 22.58 and 22.59) may cause subacute or even acute intestinal obstruction. Occasionally, the presentation is with a perforated abscess. Abdominal pain is often associated with diarrhoea, which is usually watery and does not contain blood or mucus. Patients may lose weight because they avoid food, since eating provokes pain. Weight loss may also be due to malabsorption and some patients pre-sent with features of fat, protein or vitamin deficiencies. Crohn colitis pre-sents in an identical manner to ulcerative colitis, but rectal sparing and the presence of perianal disease favour a diagnosis of Crohn disease. Many present with symptoms of both small bowel and colonic disease. A few present with isolated perianal disease, vomiting from jejunal stric-tures or severe oral ulceration. Physical examination often reveals evidence of weight loss and anaemia with the inflamed area. An abdominal mass may be palpable and is due to matted loops of thickened bowel or an intra-abdominal abscess. Perianal skin tags, fissures or fistulae are found in at least 50% of those affected.
Differential diagnosis

Conditions that can mimic UC or CD are summarised in Box 22.65. The most important issue is to distinguish the first attack of UC from infection. In general, diarrhoea lasting longer than 10 days in Western countries is unlikely to be the result of infection, whereas a history of foreign travel, antibiotic exposure (Clostridioides difficile/pseudomem-branous colitis) or homosexual contact increases the possibility of infec-tion, which should be excluded by the appropriate investigations (see below). The diagnosis of Crohn disease is usually more straightforward based on imaging findings and clinical presentation, but terminal ileal disease can be mistaken for an appendix abscess, colonic carcinoma, pelvic inflammatory disease, lymphoma, tuberculosis, Yersinia enteroco-litica infection, actinomycosis or mesenteric adenitis. In atypical cases, biopsy or surgical resection may be necessary to confirm or exclude the diagnosis of CD.
Complications
Life-threatening colonic inflammation

This can occur in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn colitis. In the most extreme cases, the colon dilates (toxic megacolon) and bacterial toxins pass freely across the diseased mucosa into the portal and then sys-temic circulation. This complication arises most commonly during the first attack of colitis and is recognised by the features described in Box 22.64. An abdominal X-ray should be taken daily because, when the transverse colon is dilated to more than 6 cm (Fig. 22.60), there is a high risk of colonic perforation, although this complication can also occur in the absence of toxic megacolon. Severe colonic inflammation with toxic dilatation is a surgical emergency and often requires colectomy.
Haemorrhage
Haemorrhage due to erosion of a major artery is rare but can occur in both conditions. This is more common in Crohn disease, where deep ulceration can erode into larger vessels.
Fistulae

These are specific to Crohn disease. Enteroenteric fistulae can cause diarrhoea and malabsorption due to blind loop syndrome. Enterovesical fistulation causes recurrent urinary infections and pneumaturia. An enter-ovaginal fistula causes a faeculent vaginal discharge. Fistulation from the bowel may also cause perianal or ischiorectal abscesses, fissures and fistulae.
Cancer

The risk of dysplasia and colorectal cancer increases with the duration and extent of uncontrolled colonic inflammation in colitis. Patients who have long-standing, extensive colitis are at highest risk. There is evidence that 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA) therapy may reduce the risk of dyspla-sia and neoplasia in ulcerative colitis. Thiopurines also seem to reduce the risk of colorectal cancer in ulcerative colitis, but not Crohn disease. However, these benefits must be weighed against the very small increase in lymphoma, especially in older patients and with long duration of use. The cumulative incidence for IBD-associated colorectal cancer has been reported at 1% at 10 years after diagnosis, which increases to 7% after 30 years. For unknown reasons, the risk is particularly high in patients who have concomitant primary sclerosing cholangitis. Tumours develop in areas of dysplasia and may be multiple. Patients with long-standing colitis are therefore entered into surveillance programmes beginning 8 years after diagnosis, with patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis having annual surveillance colonoscopy from diagnosis. Targeted biop-sies of areas that show abnormalities on staining with indigo carmine or methylene blue increase the chance of detecting dysplasia (termed pancolonic chromo-endoscopy) or, if not performed, colonoscopy with random biopsies taken every 10 cm can be performed in screening for malignancy. The procedure allows patients to be stratified into high-, medium- or low-risk groups to determine the interval between surveil-lance procedures. Family history of colorectal cancer is also an important factor to consider. If high-grade dysplasia is found, panproctocolectomy is usually recommended because of the high risk of colorectal cancer.
Extra-intestinal complications

Extra-intestinal complications are common in IBD and may dominate the clinical picture (Fig. 22.61). Some of these occur during relapse of intes-tinal disease, whereas others are unrelated to current activity of intestinal disease.
Investigations

Investigations are necessary to confirm the diagnosis, define disease distribution and activity, and identify complications. Full blood count may show anaemia resulting from bleeding or malabsorption of iron, folic acid or vitamin B 12. Platelet count can also be high as a marker of chronic inflammation. Serum albumin concentration falls as a consequence of protein-losing enteropathy, inflammatory disease or poor nutrition. The ESR and CRP are elevated in exacerbations and in response to abscess formation. Faecal calprotectin has a high sensitivity for detecting gas-trointestinal inflammation and may be elevated, even when the CRP is normal. It is particularly useful for distinguishing inflammatory bowel dis-ease from irritable bowel syndrome at diagnosis, and for subsequent monitoring of disease activity.
Bacteriology

At initial presentation, stool microscopy, culture and examination for Clostridioides difficile toxin or for ova and cysts, blood cultures and serological tests should be performed. These investigations should be repeated in established disease to exclude superimposed enteric infec-tion in patients who present with exacerbations of IBD. During acute flares necessitating hospital admission, three separate stool samples should be sent for bacteriology to maximise sensitivity. In addition, biop-sies for cytomegalovirus should be considered at time of endoscopy in patients with refractory colitis.
Endoscopy

Patients who present with diarrhoea plus raised inflammatory markers or alarm features, such as weight loss, rectal bleeding and anaemia, should undergo ileocolonoscopy. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is occasionally performed to make a diagnosis, especially during acute severe pres-entations when ileocolonoscopy may confer an unacceptable risk; ileo-colonoscopy should still be performed at a later date, however, in order to evaluate disease extent. In ulcerative colitis, there is loss of vascular pattern, granularity, friability and contact bleeding, with or without ulcer-ation (Fig. 22.62). In Crohn disease, patchy inflammation, with discrete, deep ulcers, strictures and perianal disease (fissures, fistulae and skin tags), is typically observed, often with rectal sparing. In established dis-ease, colonoscopy may show active inflammation with pseudopolyps or a complicating carcinoma. Biopsies should be taken from each anatom-ical segment (terminal ileum, right colon, transverse colon, left colon and rectum) to confirm the diagnosis and define disease extent, and also to seek dysplasia in patients with long-standing colitis guided by panco-lonic chromo-endoscopy. In Crohn disease, wireless capsule endoscopy has a greater sensitivity for detecting small bowel disease in comparison to radiological techniques and is useful when there is a high suspicion of Crohn disease despite normal imaging. A dissolvable patency capsule should be performed prior if there are concerns for small bowel stric-tures. Enteroscopy may be required to make a histological diagnosis of small bowel Crohn disease, when the inflamed segment is out of reach of standard endoscopes, or for a therapeutic indication, such as dilata-tion of strictures. In individuals with upper gastrointestinal symptoms, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy may be useful. However, this is not routinely performed in adults with suspected or proven Crohn disease.
Radiology

Where colonoscopy is incomplete, a CT colonography is preferred. Small bowel imaging is essential to complete staging of Crohn disease. Imaging with MRI may reveal thickening of the bowel wall and stricture (see Fig. 22.58) as well as providing information on pelvic and perineal involvement. These MRI studies use an orally administered small bowel– distending agent and intravenous contrast to provide transmural imaging that can usefully distinguish between predominantly inflammatory stric-tures (that should respond to anti-inflammatory medical strategies) and fibrotic strictures (that require a mechanical solution, such as surgical resection, stricturoplasty or endoscopic balloon dilatation). Traditional X-rays using barium follow-through may also be used (see Fig. 22.59), but these have largely been superseded by MRI imaging. A plain abdominal

X-ray is essential in the management of patients who present with severe active disease. Dilatation of the colon (see Fig. 22.60), mucosal oedema (thumb-printing) or evidence of perforation may be found. Patients with proctitis may have features of proximal faecal loading. In small bowel Crohn disease, there may be evidence of intestinal obstruction or dis-placement of bowel loops by a mass. Ultrasound is a very powerful tool to detect small bowel inflammation and stricture formation, but it is oper-ator-dependent. The role of CT is limited to screening for complications, such as perforation or abscess formation, in the acutely unwell.
Management

Medical therapy plays an important role in the management of IBD. However, optimal management depends on establishing a multidiscipli-nary team-based approach involving physicians, surgeons, radiologists, nurse specialists, pharmacists and dietitians. Both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease are life-long conditions and have important psychosocial implications; specialist nurses, counsellors and patient support groups have key roles in education, reassurance and coping. The key aims of medical therapy are to:
• treat acute attacks (induce remission)
• prevent relapses (maintain remission)
• prevent bowel damage
• detect dysplasia and prevent carcinoma
• select appropriate patients for surgery.
Medical therapy

Several medical treatment options exist in the management for IBD. Whilst traditional management for IBD has been through the use of conventional immunosuppressives, there has been a rapid expansion in the use of advanced medical therapies, with common treatments described below.
Conventional immunosuppressive therapies
Conventional immunosuppressives used in IBD are summarised in Box 22.66.

Aminosalicylates (5-ASA) 5-ASAs are more commonly used in ulcera-tive colitis than in Crohn disease. 5-ASAs are thought to have multiple anti-inflammatory effects, including inhibition of mediators of lipoxygen-ase and cyclooxygenase, modulating cytokine release from the mucosa. Several types are available, with different means of delivery to the colon; pH-dependent (Asacol, Salofalk), time-dependent (Pentasa) or bacte-rial breakdown by colonic bacteria from a carrier molecule (sulfasala-zine, balsalazide). While sulfasalazine was the first 5-ASA to be used in IBD, side-effects are common, such as headache, nausea, diarrhoea and blood dyscrasias. Other 5-ASAs are better tolerated. 5-ASAs can be administered orally or topically (suppositories or enema). Patients commencing a 5-ASA should have their urea and electrolytes checked at baseline, after 2–3 months and then annually, as nephrotoxicity can rarely occur (1 in 4000 patient years).

Glucocorticoids Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone, hydrocortisone, budesonide and beclomethasone can be used to induce clinical remission in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease but have no role in preventing relapse. They can be administered orally, topically (suppositories or enema) or intravenously and have powerful anti-inflammatory effects. When admin-istered, it is important to have high vigilance for complications, such as osteoporosis, diabetes and weight gain. Simultaneous calcium and vita-min D supplementation should be given for bone protection. Budesonide is a potent glucocorticoid, which is efficiently cleared from circulation by the liver, thereby minimising adrenocortical suppression and side-effects. It is commonly used in the treatment of active ileitis and ileocolitis.

Thiopurines Thiopurines used in IBD are azathioprine and mercap-topurine. They are immunomodulators that induce T-cell apoptosis. Azathioprine and mercaptopurine are administered orally and metabo-lised to thioguanine nucleotides (TGNs). Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) methylates thiopurine metabolites away from TGNs and affects drug levels. Leucopenia can occur in 3%, particularly in those with genetic variants in TPMT that are associated with reduced TPMT activity. Because of this, TPMT genotyping is generally performed prior to starting treatment, and thiopurines are often avoided if this reveals variants with reduced TMPT activity due to the risk of myelosuppression. Genetic vari-ations in NUDT15 similarly influence thiopurine metabolism and variations in this gene can also be tested where available. Thiopurines take around 6 weeks after starting treatment to be effective. Around 20% of patients will have complications leading to drug withdrawal. Complications include influenza-like syndrome with myalgia, nausea and vomiting. Other adverse effects include hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis. Patients should be counselled on the increased lymphoma (approximately two-to threefold) and non-melanoma skin cancer (life-long sun protection advised) risk. Caution should be exercised in prescribing thiopurines in patients presenting over the age of 60 years due to the increased risk of malignancy.

Methotrexate Methotrexate can be used for maintenance therapy in Crohn disease but has no role in ulcerative colitis. It is commonly used in individu-als who have failed to respond with thiopurines. It is a folic acid antagonist, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, preventing DNA synthesis. The bio-availability of oral methotrexate is variable when compared to parenteral administration, with the subcutaneous route being preferred. Nausea, sto-matitis, diarrhoea, hepatotoxicity and pneumonitis can occur with metho-trexate. Folic acid should be given concurrently to reduce gastrointestinal and liver toxicity. Women of child-bearing potential must use a robust con-traceptive method and should be counselled to plan pregnancy with a 3-month methotrexate-free period prior to conception as it is teratogenic.

Ciclosporin Ciclosporin is a calcineurin inhibitor, which inhibits T-cell signal-ling and prevents lymphocyte activation. It is used in ulcerative colitis that has responded poorly to glucocorticoids but has no role in Crohn disease. Major adverse effects include nephrotoxicity, infections and neurotoxicity (including seizures). Others include tremor, paraesthesiae, abnormal liver function tests and hirsutism. In severe UC, ciclosporin is usually adminis-tered intravenously, and responders to treatment are subsequently con-verted to oral administration. This may be continued for several months as a bridging therapy before starting a thiopurine for longer-term control of disease activity.

Antibiotics Antibiotics are useful in perianal Crohn disease and pou-chitis. There is little evidence comparing different antibiotics for acute pouchitis, although ciprofloxacin is better tolerated with fewer adverse effects than metronidazole. The major concern is peripheral neuropathy with long-term metronidazole, with tendon inflammation and damage potentially occurring with ciprofloxacin. Combination antibiotics may be needed for chronic pouchitis. Antibiotics tend to be used in combination with thiopurines and anti-TNF therapy in perianal disease.
Biologics and other targeted immunosuppressives

Several classes of targeted immunosuppressive are used in the manage-ment of IBD, as summarised in Box 22.67. In general, these medicines are used in patients with moderate to severe IBD that has not responded adequately to conventional therapy, although the precise licensed indi-cation for individual drugs varies. At present, sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor (S1PR) modulators, ozanimod and etrasimod are only approved for use in UC whereas the other drugs can be used in either UC or CD. Their sites of action are shown in Figure 22.63. Before commencing these therapies, screening for active and latent infection is important, with screening including a chest X-ray and interferon gamma release assay (IGRA) for tuberculosis; serology for hepatitis B, C and HIV is also necessary. Some centres also screen for infection with cytomegalovirus (CMV), varicella zoster virus (VZV) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and delay treatment in those with evidence of recent infection. Live vaccines should be avoided during treatment with all of these agents, but immunisation to protect against VZV, COVID-19 and influenza are all recommended for people on these medications.

Anti-TNF antibodies These include infliximab, adalimumab, golimumab and certolizumab. They are monoclonal antibodies typically given by sub-cutaneous injection, which bind to and neutralise TNF-α, reducing inflam-mation in the gut. Etanercept, a decoy receptor for TNF-α, is not effective in IBD. They are generally well tolerated but acute (anaphylactic) and delayed (serum sickness) infusion reactions can occur after multiple infu-sions of infliximab. Anti-drug antibody titres and drug levels can also be measured to assess efficacy. Anti-TNF antibodies are contraindicated in active infection and in patients with pre-existing moderate to severe heart failure. There is a possible increased risk of malignancy, and demyelinat-ing disease is a rare adverse effect. Treatment should continue so long as efficacy is maintained with reassessment of response every 12 months.

Anti-α4β7 integrin Vedolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks α4β7 integrin expressed on leucocytes and inhibits leucocyte interaction with a gut-specific receptor on endothelium, reducing leucocyte migration into gut mucosa. It is a gut-selective biologic used in both ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease. Side-effects include nasopharyngitis, arthralgia and headache. Treatment should be discontinued if there is no improvement after 14 weeks but otherwise should be continued so long as efficacy is maintained with reassessment of response every 12 months.

Janus kinase inhibitors These include tofacitinib, upadacitinib and fil-gotinib. These Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors selectively inhibit different isoforms of Janus kinases. Tofacitinib has greater selectivity for JAK1 and JAK3, whereas upadacitinib and filgotinib have greater selectively for JAK1. They have the advantage of oral administration. High doses should be avoided in patients at risk of venous thrombo-embolism and treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy. In addition, caution should be used in individuals with cardiovascular disease and risk factors for malignancy, as well as in individuals above the age of 65 years. Herpes zoster infection is a relatively common adverse event. Because of this, zoster vaccination is currently recommended for all patients on these medicines. Treatment should continue so long as efficacy is maintained, with reassessment of response every 12 months.

Interleukin 12 and interleukin 23 inhibitors Ustekinumab, risankizumab and mirikizumab are monoclonal antibodies used in IBD. Ustekinumab binds to the p40 subunit of both IL-12 and IL-23, thereby inhibiting the actions of both cytokines, whereas risankizumab and mirikizumab are specific IL-23 inhibitors binding to the p19 subunit of this cytokine. All of these drugs inhibit T-cell activation, thereby exerting an anti-inflammatory effect. Adverse effects include nasopharyngitis, headache and arthralgia. Treatment should continue so long as efficacy is maintained, with reas-sessment of response every 12 months.

Sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulators Ozanimod and etrasimod bind to sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors (S1PRs), preventing their activation by sphigosine-1-phosphate (S1P). Ozanimod specifically binds to S1P receptors 1 and 5, whereas etrasimod binds to S1P recep-tors 1, 4 and 5. This prevents the movement of T lymphocytes from lymph nodes into the circulation, thereby reducing inflammation. Like Janus kinase inhibitors, they have the advantage of oral administration. Side-effects include nasopharyngitis, lymphopenia, headache, bradycar-dia, blurred vision and hypertension. In addition, S1PR modulators may increase the risk of skin cancer, with adequate skin care protection being advised. Treatment should continue so long as efficacy is maintained, with reassessment of response every 12 months.
Therapeutic drug monitoring

Up to one-third of patients do not respond to targeted immunosuppres-sives (primary non-response), and up to half discontinue after an initial positive response due to secondary loss of response or adverse effects. There is evidence that the outcomes are most favourable when drug con-centrations are within the therapeutic range, whereas suboptimal drug concentrations may be due to inadequate dosing or the development of anti-drug antibodies, leading to treatment failure. Therapeutic drug monitoring is used most often in patients on anti-TNF therapy, to ensure that patients have adequate drug levels, pre-emptively preventing flares.

Combination treatment of anti-TNF therapy with thiopurines or metho-trexate can be used to reduce the risk of anti-drug antibodies develop-ing. Therapeutic drug monitoring can also be performed with thiopurines, by measurement of thiopurine metabolites measured to tailor dosing.
Ulcerative colitis

Active ulcerative colitis Patients with active ulcerative colitis can be ini-tially treated with topical or oral 5-aminosalicylate acid (5-ASA) therapy. Patients with left-sided or extensive ulcerative colitis should continue oral 5-ASA in the long term to prevent relapse and minimise the risk of dys-plasia. Individuals with an incomplete response to 5-ASA treatment may require treatment with systemic glucocorticoids, conventional or targeted immunosuppressive therapy. Glucocorticoids should never be used for maintenance therapy. An algorithm for the management of active ulcera-tive colitis is shown in Figure 22.64.

Severe ulcerative colitis Patients who present with acute severe colitis (meeting the Truelove–Witts criteria, see Box 22.64) are best managed in hospital and should be monitored jointly by a physician and surgeon:
• clinically: for the presence of abdominal pain, temperature, pulse rate, stool blood and frequency
• by laboratory testing: haemoglobin, white cell count, albumin, elec-trolytes, ESR and CRP, stool culture, including Clostridioides difficile toxin assay
• radiologically: for colonic dilatation on plain abdominal X-rays.

All patients should be given supportive treatment with intravenous flu-ids to correct dehydration and enteral nutritional support should be pro-vided for malnourished patients (Box 22.68). Intravenous glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 60 mg every 24 hours or hydrocortisone 100 mg four times daily) should be given by infusion or bolus injection. Patients should receive prophylactic low-molecular weight heparin, as the risk of venous thromboembolism is significantly increased. Topical and oral ami-nosalicylates have no role to play in the acute severe attack. Response to therapy is judged over the first 3 days. Patients who do not respond promptly to glucocorticoids should be considered for medical rescue therapy with infliximab (5 mg/kg) or ciclosporin (2 mg/kg daily by intrave-nous infusion followed by 5 mg/kg daily, then orally after 7 days), which can avoid the need for urgent colectomy in approximately 60% of cases. Patients who develop colonic dilatation (> 6 cm), those whose clinical and laboratory measurements deteriorate and those who do not respond after 7–10 days’ maximal medical treatment usually require urgent sur-gery. Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is the operation of choice and can be performed open or laparoscopically, dependent upon local expertise. The surgical and medical teams should liaise early in the dis-ease course and, if possible, the patient should have the opportunity to speak with the stoma nurse prior to colectomy.

Maintenance of remission Life-long maintenance therapy is recom-mended for all patients with left-sided or extensive disease but may not be necessary in those with proctitis, although up to 20% of these patients may develop a proximal extension of disease over their lifetime. Once-daily oral 5-aminosalicylates are the preferred first-line agents. Sulfasalazine has a higher incidence of side-effects but is equally effec-tive and can be considered in patients with coexistent arthropathy. Patients who frequently relapse despite aminosalicylate drugs have in the past always been offered thiopurines (azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine). While thiopurines still have a role for treatment, other immunosuppres-sive drugs should also be considered early. Targeted immunosuppressive therapy with anti-TNF antibodies (infliximab, adalimumab or golimumab) can be considered for maintenance treatment in patients with moderate to severe ulcerative colitis. Combination therapy with infliximab and a thiopurine should be used where possible, as it is more effective than monotherapy with infliximab. In patients where anti-TNF treatment has failed, anti-α4β7 integrin antibodies (vedolizumab), Janus kinase inhib-itors (tofacitinib, filgotinib, upadacitinib), IL-12/IL-23 inhibitors (usteki-numab, risankizumab, mirikizumab) and S1PR modulators (ozanimod, etrasimod) can all be used to maintain remission.
Crohn disease

Principles of management Crohn disease is a progressive condition that may result in stricture or fistula formation if suboptimally treated. It is therefore important to agree long-term treatment goals with the patient; these are to induce remission and then maintain glucocorticoid-free remission with a normal quality of life. Treatment should focus on monitoring the patient carefully for evidence of disease activity and com-plications (Box 22.69) and ensuring that mucosal healing is achieved.

Induction of remission in mild to moderate disease Glucocorticoids can be used as treatment for active Crohn disease. The drug of first choice in patients with ileal disease is budesonide, since it undergoes 90% first-pass metabolism in the liver and has very little systemic toxicity. A typical regimen is 9 mg once daily for 4 weeks, with a stepwise reduction of 3 mg every 4 weeks until therapy is stopped. If there is no response to budesonide within 2 weeks, the patient should be switched to predniso-lone, which has greater efficacy. This is typically given in a dose of 40 mg daily, reducing by 5 mg/week over 8 weeks, at which point treatment is stopped. Oral prednisolone in the dose regimen described above is the treatment of choice for inducing remission in colonic Crohn disease. As an alternative to glucocorticoid therapy, enteral nutrition with either an elemental (constituent amino acids) or polymeric (liquid protein) diet may induce remission. Both types of diet are equally effective, but the polymeric one is more palatable when taken by mouth, and this improves adherence. It is particularly effective in children, in whom equal efficacy to glucocorticoids has been demonstrated, and in extensive ileal disease in adults. As well as resting the gut and providing excellent nutritional sup-port, it also has a direct anti-inflammatory effect. It is an effective bridge to urgent staging investigations at first presentation and can be given by mouth or by nasogastric tube. With sufficient explanation, encourage-ment and motivation, most patients will tolerate it well.

Induction and maintenance of remission in severe disease Patients with severe disease can be treated with systemic glucocorticoids short term, but early introduction of targeted immunosuppressives should be considered in these individuals providing that complications, such as perforation or abscess, have been excluded. Anti-TNF, anti-α4β7 inte-grin, anti-IL-12/23 and JAK inhibitors can all be considered to maintain remission in such patients. Combination therapy of infliximab with a thi-opurine is more effective than monotherapy with infliximab. Combination therapy of infliximab with methotrexate may also be used to reduce the risk of anti-drug antibodies developing. In patients who still require gluco-corticoids despite optimising treatment with targeted immunosuppres-sives, other options must be considered, including surgery. Cigarette smokers with Crohn disease should be strongly advised to stop. Those that do not stop smoking fare much worse, with increased rates of relapse and surgical intervention. The adverse effects of smok-ing are more pronounced in women than in men. Careful monitoring of disease activity (see Box 22.69) is the key to maintaining sustained 22.70 Indications for surgery in ulcerative colitis
