Newer treatments may also be beneficial after ESA failure, includ-ing imetelstat (a telomerase inhibitor), which has been approved by the

FDA. Some patients with low-risk MDS on long-term red cell transfusion programmes may benefit from iron chelation, most conveniently oral deferasirox. Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G–CSF) is recom-mended for short-term use in neutropenic patients with active infection. A rare subtype called MDS with isolated del(5q) responds well to lenalid-omide (an immunomodulatory drug), with two-thirds of anaemic patients becoming transfusion-independent for up to 2 years.

Allogeneic HSCT may afford a cure in patients with a good performance status and high-risk disease (IPSS-R high and very high) and some inter-mediate- and low-risk patients, especially younger patients with marked cytopenias or transfusion dependence. Some 50% of transplanted patients are long-term survivors, though relapse of MDS remains the biggest problem. Azacitidine (a hypomethylating agent) has improved survival by a median of 9 months compared to supportive care or low-in-tensity chemotherapy for high-risk patients and remains a recommended standard of care for those not eligible for transplantation. Whether or not the addition of venetoclax to azacitidine is beneficial in high-risk MDS, as it has been in AML, remains to be seen.

Lymphomas are neoplasms arising from cells of the lymphocyte lineage and a majority involve a more mature stage of lymphocyte development than seen in ALL. They are diagnosed from the pathological findings on lymph node or tissue biopsy as Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The vast majority are of B-cell origin with approximately 10% of cases being of T-cell origin in Western data sets. Higher rates of T-cell lympho-mas are reported in other parts of the world, though selection bias has confounded some studies. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are classified as low- or high-grade tumours based on their proliferation rate. The normal architecture of the lymph node is outlined in Fig. 24.35.
• High-grade lymphomas divide rapidly, are typically present for a matter of weeks before diagnosis and often progress rapidly. They may be life-threatening with high risk of extranodal involvement.

• Low-grade lymphomas divide slowly, may be present for many months before diagnosis, and typically behave in an indolent fash-ion. They are frequently widely disseminated in lymph node groups and other tissues of the lymphoreticular system.

The histological hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is the presence of Reed–Sternberg cells: large, malignant lymphoid cells of B-cell origin (Fig. 24.36). They are often present only in small numbers, but are sur-rounded by large numbers of reactive non-malignant T cells, plasma cells and granulocytes, including eosinophils. The epidemiology of HL is shown in Box 24.56 and its histological WHO classification in Box 24.57. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL is slow-growing, localised and rarely fatal. It has biological features such as CD20-positive malignant cells, and in some patients, the feature of a relapsing and remitting clinical course that makes it more akin to a low-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lym-phoma. As such, this entity has been re-classified as nodular lymphocyte predominant B-cell lymphoma in ICC, though remains unchanged in WHO 5th edition. Classical HL is divided into four histological subtypes from the appearance of the Reed–Sternberg cells and surrounding reactive cells. The nodular sclerosing type is more common in young patients and in women. Mixed cellularity is more common in older patients. Lymphocyte-rich HL usually presents in men. Lymphocyte-depleted HL is rare.

The peak age of presentation in high-income countries is 18 to 35 years of age. There is painless, rubbery, lymphadenopathy usually in the neck, supraclavicular fossae and mediastinum, i.e. presenting in the upper body. The lymph nodes may fluctuate in size. Young patients with nod-ular sclerosing disease may have large mediastinal masses that are surprisingly asymptomatic, but may cause dry cough and some breath-lessness. Spread is contiguous from one lymph node to the next along lymphatic chains and progressing from the upper body to below the dia-phragm. Isolated subdiaphragmatic nodes occur in fewer than 10% at diagnosis. Hepatosplenomegaly may be present but does not always indicate disease in those organs and can be reactive. Extranodal dis-ease, such as bone, brain or skin involvement, is rare. Systemic symp-toms include so-called ‘B symptoms’ of drenching night sweats, fever and loss of 10% body weight. Other symptoms can include pruritus and rarely, but dramatically, alcohol-induced pain within lymph nodes.
24.56 Epidemiology and aetiology of Hodgkin lymphoma
Incidence
• Approximately 4 new cases/100 000 population/year
Sex ratio
• Slight male excess (1.5:1) except nodular sclerosing subtype, with a female excess
Age
• Median age 31 years; first peak at 20–35 years and second at 50–70 years
Aetiology
• Unknown
• More common in patients from well-educated backgrounds and small families
• Three times more likely with a history of infectious mononucleosis but no definitive causal link to Epstein–Barr virus infection proven
Treatment of HL depends on the stage at presentation; investigations therefore aim not only to diagnose lymphoma, but also to determine the extent of disease (Box 24.58).

• FBC may be normal. If a normochromic, normocytic anaemia or lymphopenia is present, this is a poor prognostic factor, particularly in advanced disease. Eosinophilia, neutrophilia or thrombocytosis may be present.
• ESR may be raised and is an adverse prognostic factor.
• Renal function tests are required to ensure function is normal prior to treatment.
• Liver function may be abnormal in the absence of disease or may reflect hepatic infiltration. An obstructive pattern may be caused by nodes at the porta hepatis.
• LDH may be raised and is an adverse prognostic factor.
• Chest X-ray may show a mediastinal mass.

• CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis permits staging. Bulky dis-ease (> 10 cm in a single nodal mass or a mediastinal mass > one third the maximum diameter of thorax on chest X-ray) is an adverse prognostic feature.
• Lymph node biopsy is crucial for diagnosis and may be undertaken surgically or by percutaneous needle biopsy under radiological guid-ance (Fig. 24.37).

• Positron emission tomography–CT (PET-CT) scanning has become standard of care. This identifies nodes involved with HL that are F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid and this allows more accurate 18 staging and monitoring of early and end-of-treatment responses, which increasingly dictate therapeutic strategy (Fig. 24.38).

Given the high cure rate and excellent prognosis of a majority of young and middle-aged patients with HL, the aim is to maintain maximum cure rates while minimising long-term treatment-related toxicity. Treatment approaches involve defining patients as early-stage disease (stages IA/ IB and IIA) or advanced stage disease (IIB, III and IV). The ABVD regi-men (doxorubicin (Adriamycin), bleomycin, vinblastine and dacarbazine) continues to be used in the UK, while the more intensive BEACOPP or BEACOPDAC regimens (bleomycin, etoposide, doxorubicin (Adriamycin), cyclophosphamide, vincristine (oncovin), prednisolone, procarbazine or dacarbazine) is a more effective and increasingly favoured alternative, though with an increased risk of side-effects including infertility and treat-ment-related MDS and AML. Radiotherapy is a very effective modality of treatment in combination with chemotherapy, However, long-term toxic-ity has led to more judicious use in recent times.

Standard therapy for early-stage patients without additional risk factors, such as bulk disease or high ESR, is two cycles of ABVD combined with 20 Gy radiotherapy to the involved sites of disease. Standard therapy for early-stage patients with additional risk factors is four cycles of ABVD combined with 30 Gy radiotherapy. Careful planning of radiotherapy is required to limit the doses delivered to normal tissues, and new planning techniques continue to improve targeting of radiotherapy. Nevertheless, the long-term risks of second cancers and heart and lung disease within the radiation fields remain a concern, especially for young people with a high cure rate and potentially decades of life ahead of them. Early-stage patients who have a negative FDG PET-CT scan after two to four cycles of combination chemotherapy can safely omit radiotherapy. For example, the UK RAPID trial showed that three cycles of ABVD leading to a negative PET produced an overall survival rate of greater than 90% without radiotherapy, though the relapse rate requiring additional therapy was about 7% higher than in patients who received radiotherapy. The German HD17 trial in early-stage patients with additional unfavourable risk factors similarly had a > 90% progression-free and overall survival rate with two cycles of BEACOPP and two cycles of ABVD without radi-otherapy in patients with a negative PET scan at the end of treatment. Such PET-adapted therapy can spare a large majority of young patients from the long-term effects of radiotherapy, though at the cost of a slightly increased relapse risk in some studies.

Patients with advanced-stage disease are commonly managed with chemotherapy alone. Standard treatment in the UK has been 6–8 cycles of ABVD, followed by an assessment of response. A negative FDG PET-CT after two cycles of ABVD (interim PET-2 response) pre-dicts a very good outcome from continuing with up to six cycles of ABVD. Indeed, the same outcome is achieved by omitting the bleomy-cin from the last four cycles and using AVD alone, thus reducing the risk of lung toxicity (RATHL trial). Even more impressive results of > 90% 5-year progression-free survival can be achieved with just four cycles of BEACOPP if the interim PET-2 scan is negative (German HD18 trial). Patients who have a positive FDG PET-CT after two cycles of ABVD, however, have a high relapse risk if they continue with ABVD, with only 13% being relapse-free at 2 years. Switching to BEACOPP/DAC from ABVD or continuing with BEACOPP/DAC for six cycles in these patients improves the relapse-free survival to approximately 65%–90%. Adding the immunochemotherapy drug brentuximab vedotin (see below) to AVD (A 2 VD) also produces better overall survival compared to ABVD, though this has not been widely adopted in the UK to date. Elderly, frail patients tolerate ABVD poorly and are at high risk of pul-monary toxicity with bleomycin. BEACOPP/DAC is not readily deliverable to patients over the age of 60 years or with comorbidities. Lower-intensity chemotherapies, such as AVD omitting bleomycin, or anthracycline and bleomycin free regimens, can produce prolonged remissions in some patients. Patients with relapsed disease that respond to salvage chemotherapy and ideally become FDG PET-CT-negative are considered for autologous HSCT (p. 966). Those with resistant disease might ben-efit from an allogeneic HSCT. Brentuximab vedotin is an antibody–drug conjugate directed against CD30 on the Reed–Sternberg cell surface. This antibody delivers the antimitotic toxin monomethyl auristatin E to the Hodgkin cells and, as a single agent, can produce good responses in patients who have failed, or are not suitable for an autologous transplant and can be a ‘bridge’ to an allogeneic transplant. Reed–Sternberg cells over-express the cell surface protein programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1). This engages with programmed death protein 1 (PD-1) on T cells and leads to T-cell ‘exhaustion’. This ‘immune checkpoint’ is an impor-tant survival mechanism for Reed–Sternberg cells. The immunotherapy drugs pembrolizumab and nivolumab can inhibit this ‘checkpoint’ in the immune response and allow T-cell killing of Reed–Sternberg cells. Both drugs are available for patients who have failed multiple lines of treatment and can produce further remissions. This class of drugs has recently been shown to be very effective in first-line treatment in combination with chemotherapy (e.g. nivolumab-AVD) and may become future treatments of choice.

Over 90% of patients with early-stage HL achieve complete remission when treated with chemotherapy followed by involved field radiother-apy, with the great majority cured. The major challenge is how to reduce treatment intensity, and hence long-term toxicity, without reducing the excellent cure rates in this group. Omitting radiotherapy in most FDG PET-CT-negative patients is one major step forward in this regard. Historically, between 50% and 70% of those with advanced-stage HL were cured. The Hasenclever index (Box 24.59) can be helpful in assigning approximate chances of cure when discussing treatment plans with advanced-stage patients. Recent data using FDG PET-CT to direct therapy suggest that long-term survival is improving to beyond 80%, especially in the context of BEACOPP/DAC therapy. Patients who fail to respond to initial chemotherapy or relapse within a year of initial therapy have a poor prognosis, but some may achieve long-term survival after autologous HSCT. Patients relapsing after 1 year may obtain long-term survival with further immunochemotherapy alone, but fit patients who respond frequently proceed to autologous HSCT.

Young women receiving breast irradiation during the treatment of chest disease have an increased risk of breast cancer and should participate in a breast-screening programme. Patients continuing to smoke after lung irradiation are at particular risk of future lung cancer. ABVD chemotherapy can cause cardiac and pulmonary toxicity, due to doxorubicin and bleomycin, respectively. Recommendations that patients attend survivorship clinics and have cardiac follow-up with echocardiography have generally been poorly implemented. The incidence of infertility and secondary myelodysplasia/AML is low with ABVD, but higher with BEACOPP. Recent UK data has demonstrated that replacing procarbazine with dacarbazine in the BEACOPP regimen (BEACOPDAC) is as effective in treating HL, improves female fertility and has less genotoxic effects on sperm. This has become a standard approach throughout the UK.

Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) represents a monoclonal proliferation of lymphoid cells of B-cell (90%) or T-cell (10%) origin. The incidence of these tumours increases with age, to 62.8/million population per annum at age 75 years, and the overall rate is recorded as increasing at about 3% per year since the 1970s, though some of these data suffer from ascertainment bias. The epidemiology of NHL is shown in Box 24.60. Previous classifica-tions were based principally on histological appearances. The current WHO and ICC classifications stratify according to cell lineage (T or B cells) and incorporate clinical features, histology, genetic abnormalities and concepts related to the biology of the lymphoma. Clinically, the most important factor is grade, which reflects proliferation rate. High-grade NHL has high proliferation rates, rapidly produces symptoms, is fatal if untreated, but is potentially curable. Low-grade NHL has low prolifera-tion rates, may be asymptomatic for many months or even years before presentation, runs an indolent course, but is frequently disseminated at diagnosis and not commonly curable by conventional therapy. Of all cases of NHL in the developed world, over 50% are either diffuse large B-cell NHL (high-grade) or follicular NHL (low-grade) (Fig. 24.39). Other forms of NHL, including Burkitt lymphoma, mantle cell lymphoma, mar-ginal zone lymphomas including mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas and T-cell lymphomas are individually less common.

Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL is often widely disseminated at pres-entation, including in extranodal sites. Patients present with lymph node enlargement (Fig. 24.40), which may be associated with systemic upset: weight loss, sweat, fever and itching. Hepatosplenomegaly may be present. Sites of extranodal involvement are protean and include the bone marrow, gut, thyroid, lung, skin, testis, breast, brain and, more rarely, bone and adrenal glands. Bone marrow involvement is more com-mon in low-grade (50%–60%) than high-grade (10%) disease. Other extranodal sites tend to be more common in high-grade disease, par-ticularly CNS involvement. Compression syndromes may occur, includ-ing gut obstruction, ascites, superior vena cava obstruction and spinal cord compression. The same staging system (see Box 24.58) is used for both HL and NHL, but NHL is more likely to be stage III or IV at presentation.
These are as for HL, but in addition the following should be performed:
• Bone marrow aspiration and trephine to identify bone marrow involvement.
• Immunophenotyping of surface antigens to distinguish T-cell from B-cell tumours. This may be done on blood, marrow or nodal material.

• Cytogenetic analysis to detect chromosomal translocations, particu-larly rearrangements of the oncogene c-MYC and partners including BCL2 and molecular testing for T-cell receptor or immunoglobulin gene rearrangements. NGS lymphoid gene panels are available, but not routinely used in clinical practice.
• Immunoglobulin determination. Some lymphomas are associated with IgG or IgM paraproteins, which serve as markers for treatment response.

• Measurement of urate levels. Some very aggressive high-grade NHLs are associated with very high urate levels, which can precip-itate renal failure when treatment is started because of tumour lysis syndrome.
• HIV testing. HIV is a risk factor for some lymphomas and affects treatment decisions.
• Hepatitis B and C testing. This should be done prior to therapy with rituximab.

Most patients (80%) present with advanced stage disease and will run a relapsing and remitting course over several years. Overall survival has improved in recent years with more treatment options. Asymptomatic patients may not require therapy and are managed by ‘watching and waiting’. Indications for treatment include marked systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy causing discomfort or disfigurement, bone marrow fail-ure or compression syndromes. In follicular lymphoma the indications for treatment are covered in the Groupe d’Etude des Lymphomes Folliculaires (GELF) criteria. The treatment options for follicular lymphoma are:
• Radiotherapy. This can be used for localised stage I disease, which is rare. FDG PET-CT-confirmed stage I disease has a 70% cure rate with radiotherapy.
• Chemotherapy. Immunochemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment for patients with advanced stage disease requiring therapy.

• Monoclonal antibody therapy. Humanised monoclonal antibodies (‘biologic therapy’; p. 963) can be used to target surface antigens on tumour cells and to induce tumour cell apoptosis directly. The anti-CD20 antibody rituximab has been shown to induce durable clinical responses in up to 60% of patients when given alone and acts synergistically when given with chemotherapy. The UK Watch and Wait trial showed that single agent rituximab (R) given over two years delayed the time to requiring chemotherapy by more than ten years on average and this is an option for some patients with asymptomatic advanced stage follicular lymphoma who would rather not watch and wait. Rituximab or a second-generation anti-CD20 antibody, obinutuzumab, in combination with cyclophos-phamide, vincristine and prednisolone (R-CVP), cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin), vincristine (oncovin), predniso-lone (R-CHOP) or bendamustine (R-bendamustine) are commonly used as first-line therapy. There is no clear advantage of one regi-men over another, though R-CHOP and R-bendamustine are most used. Obinutuzumab combined with chemotherapy showed longer progression-free survival compared to similar chemotherapy with rituximab. Two years of maintenance therapy with single-agent rituximab, following achievement of first or second response, especially if this is only a partial response, delays the time to next treatment. However, rituximab maintenance has not shown a survival benefit.

• Targeted therapy. The PI3 kinase inhibitor idelalisib is approved for relapsed follicular lymphoma, but rarely used nowadays because of toxicity. Ibrutinib (see Fig. 24.33) is approved for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma (a poor-prognosis lymphoma with low-grade histol-ogy, but aggressive clinical behaviour). Ibrutinib and zanubrutinib are used in Waldenström macroglobulinaemia (also known as lym-phoplasmacytic lymphoma, see below). Newer therapies are likely to become more widely used in low-grade lymphomas soon. These include bispecific antibodies and CAR-T cell therapy.

• Transplantation. High-dose chemotherapy and autologous HSCT can produce long remissions in patients with relapsed disease. Decisions on the timing of such treatment are complex in the context of rituximab maintenance and newer therapies. However, younger patients with short first remissions (progression of disease within 24 months, POD24) or second remissions or who relapse during rituximab maintenance should be considered. Some 25% of patients undergo high-grade transformation to DLBCL, and this is difficult to treat. R-CHOP or alternative salvage therapy followed by autologous HSCT is considered in fit patients. CAR-T is an option for some patients as outlined below.
Patients with diffuse large B-cell NHL need treatment at initial presentation:

• Chemotherapy. The majority (> 90%) are treated with intravenous combination chemotherapy, typically with the CHOP regimen (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (hydroxydaunorubicin), vincristine (oncovin) and prednisolone).

• Monoclonal antibody therapy. When combined with CHOP chemotherapy, rituximab (R) increases the complete response rates and improves overall survival. R-CHOP, 4–6 cycles, is rec-ommended as first-line therapy for all relatively fit patients with an International Prognostic Index (IPI) of 0–1 (Box 24.61). Younger patients with stage I disease and a negative PET scan after four cycles of R-CHOP can avoid radiotherapy, though most older patients with stage I disease will receive dual modality therapy with R-CHOP 4–6 cycles and radiotherapy. For all patients beyond stage I, the treatment is based on 6 cycles of R-CHOP. The addition of a second antibody–drug conjugate against CD79 (polatuzumab vedotin) and removal of vincristine because of the combined neurotoxicity (R-Pola-CHP) demonstrated better pro-gression-free survival than R-CHOP in patients with IPI > 1 (see Box 24.61). This is now the treatment of choice in many centres. More intensive chemotherapy combinations are considered for 24.61 The International Prognostic Index (IPI) for high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma
One point for each of:
• Age > 60 years
• ECOG PS > 1
• Ann Arbour stage III or IV
• > 1 extra nodal site

• LDH > normal (ECOG PS = Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status [see Box 8.6]; LDH = lactate dehydrogenase) aggressive lymphomas including Burkitt lymphoma, double hit large B-cell lymphoma (MYC and BCL-2 rearrangements) and by some centres treating young patients with DLBCL with high IPI. Dose reduction (R-mini-CHOP) is preferable in those over 80 years of age and replacement of doxorubicin with gemcitabine (R-GCVP) in those with impaired cardiac function. Fit patients with a high risk of CNS relapse based on a CNS IPI ≥ 5, or certain involved sites such as adrenal glands or testicles, may benefit from CNS prophylaxis during treatment. The preferred approach is two doses of high-dose methotrexate at the end of R-CHOP, though more intensive regimens have this built in. Radiotherapy. Stage I patients without bulky disease are treated with four cycles of R-CHOP, followed by involved site radiother-apy, unless PET negative when radiotherapy can be avoided for younger patients as discussed above. Radiotherapy is also con-sidered for a residual localised site of bulk disease after chemo-therapy, especially in the elderly with limited further treatment options if they relapse, and for spinal cord and other compression syndromes. HSCT. Autologous HSCT (p. 966) benefits patients with relapsed disease that is sensitive to salvage immunochemotherapy. As with HL, achieving a negative FDG PET scan prior to autologous trans-plantation is desirable. CAR-T therapy (see Fig. 24.17 and p. 967) is licensed for cer-tain patients with relapsed DLBCL or high-grade transformation of f ­ ollicular and other low-grade lymphomas and can salvage patients from a desperate situation. Specifically, CAR-T therapy is available in second-line therapy of DLBCL for patients who relapse within 12 months of initial therapy following randomised trials demonstrating superiority over autologous HSCT in this situation. CAR-T in third line of DLBCL therapy, after failure of autologous HSCT or in patients not fit for autograft, remains the commonest use at the present time. Two licensed BiTE antibodies (see Fig. 24.18 and p. 968), glofitamab and epcoritamab, are available as monotherapy after two or more failed lines of systemic therapy in DLBCL and have been effective in some patients following failed CAR-T.
• Radiotherapy. Stage I patients without bulky disease are treated
• HSCT. Autologous HSCT (p. 966) benefits patients with relapsed
• CAR-T therapy (see Fig. 24.17 and p. 967) is licensed for cer-
• Two licensed BiTE antibodies (see Fig. 24.18 and p. 968), glofitamab

A small proportion of stage I patients with low-grade NHL are cured by involved field radiotherapy. Advanced stage low-grade lymphomas are generally considered incurable and run a remitting and relapsing course, with an overall median survival of 12 years. Transformation to a high-grade NHL occurs at approximately 3% per annum and is associated with poor survival. In diffuse large B-cell NHL treated with R-CHOP, some 75% of patients overall respond initially to therapy and 50% will have dis-ease-free survival at 5 years. The prognosis for patients with high-grade NHL is further refined according to the IPI (see Box 24.61) For high-grade NHL, 5-year survival ranges from over 75% in those with low-risk scores (age < 60 years, stage I or II, one or fewer extranodal sites, normal LDH and good performance status) to 25% in those with high-risk scores (increasing age, advanced stage, concomitant disease and a raised LDH). Rearrangements of the c-MYC oncogene, either alone (more com-monly seen in Burkitt lymphoma) or with rearrangements of BCL2 and/ or BCL6 in high grade lymphomas are recognised entities. In the most recent WHO 5th edition classification, double hit MYC and BCL-2 r ­ earrangements are distinguished as carrying a poor prognosis and are increasingly treated more aggressively as outlined above, whilst c-MYC rearrangements alone or with BCL-6 are not distinguished as separate entities with additional prognostic significance. Relapse is associated with a poor response to further chemotherapy (< 10% 5-year survival). In fit patients, largely under 70 years, autologous HSCT improves sur-vival in chemosensitive cases producing long-term remissions/cures of ~20%–30%, while CAR-T therapy is associated with ~40% cure within the licensed indications.

Gammopathy refers to over-production of one or more classes of immu-noglobulin. It may be polyclonal in association with acute or chronic inflammation, such as infection including HIV, sarcoidosis, autoimmune disorders or some malignancies. Alternatively, a monoclonal increase in a single immunoglobulin class may occur in association with normal or reduced levels of the other immunoglobulins (immunoparesis). Such monoclonal proteins (also called M-proteins, paraproteins or monoclonal gammopathies) occur as a feature of myeloma, solitary plasmacytomas, lymphoma, amyloidosis and occasionally solid tumours. They also occur in benign conditions including connective tissue diseases such as rheu-matoid arthritis or polymyalgia rheumatica and infections such as HIV. In addition, they may be present with no underlying disease (monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance). Gammopathies are detected by plasma immunoelectrophoresis.

In monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS, also known as benign monoclonal gammopathy), a paraprotein is present in the blood, but there are no other features of myeloma, Waldenström macroglobuli-naemia (see below), lymphoma, amyloidosis or related disease. It is a com-mon condition associated with increasing age; a paraprotein is present in 1% of the population aged over 50 years, increasing to 5% over 80 years.

Patients are usually asymptomatic and the paraprotein is found on blood testing for other reasons. The routine blood count and biochemistry are normal, the paraprotein is usually present in small amounts (< 15 g/L) with no associated immunoparesis and there are no lytic bone lesions. The bone marrow may have increased plasma cells, but these constitute less than 10% of nucleated cells.

After follow-up of 20 years, only one-quarter of cases will progress to myeloma or a related disorder (i.e. around 1% per annum). There is no certain way of predicting progression in an individual patient. There have been several attempts to define high risk MGUS by identifying risk factors. The best known is the Mayo Clinic study identifying serum paraprotein > 15 g/L, non-IgG paraprotein isotype (IgA predominantly) and abnormal serum free light chain ratio (SFLR). An abnormal SFLR increases the risk of progression and patients with an abnormal ratio should be monitored for progression on an annual basis.

This is a low-grade lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma associated with an IgM paraprotein, sometimes causing clinical features of hyperviscosity syndrome. It is a rare tumour occurring in old age and more commonly affects males. It is important to remember that IgM paraproteins are associated with lymphoma, most commonly lymphoplasmacytic lym-phoma, rather than myeloma. True IgM myeloma is very rare. Patients classically present with features of hyperviscosity, such as headache, nosebleeds, bruising, delirium and visual disturbance. However, presentation is commonly with anaemia, systemic symptoms, splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy, or may be asymptomatic with an IgM paraprotein detected on routine screening. On investigation, patients have an IgM paraprotein associated with a raised plasma viscosity. The bone marrow has a characteristic appearance, with infiltration of lym-phoid cells, plasma cells and sometimes prominent mast cells. A high proportion of patients have a mutation in the MYD88 gene.
If patients show symptoms of hyperviscosity and anaemia, plasmapher-esis is required to remove IgM and make blood transfusion possible.

Chemotherapy with alkylating agents, such as chlorambucil, has histor-ically been the mainstay of treatment, controlling disease in over 50%. Fludarabine may be more effective in this disease but has more side-ef-fects. Rituximab in combination with chemotherapy, e.g. bendamustine (R-bendamustine) or cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone (RCD), is commonly used. BTK inhibitors, ibrutinib and zanubrutinib, are very effective and approved for use in second line and more recently first line for less fit patients. Rituximab alone can cause a rapid release of IgM and increase in viscosity, and rituximab is best avoided at the very start of treatment if the IgM paraprotein level is high. The improvement in treat-ments have led to four out of five patients living longer than 5 years.

This is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells (derived from B cells), which is associated with paraproteinaemia. In most cases an excess of light chain is produced, and, in some cases, only light chain is produced (light-chain myeloma); this appears in the urine as Bence Jones pro-teinuria and can be measured in the urine or serum as free light chains. The frequency of different isotypes of monoclonal protein in myeloma is shown in Box 24.62. Some clinical features of myeloma, including renal impairment, infections and rarely hyperviscosity, relate to the effects of the paraproteins and associated immunoparesis. Although a small number of malignant plasma cells are present in the circulation, the majority are present in the bone marrow. The malignant plasma cells produce a complex network of cytokines, which activate osteoclasts and result in net bone reabsorption. The resulting lytic lesions cause bone pain, fractures and hypercalcaemia. Marrow involvement can result in anaemia or pancytopenia.

The incidence of myeloma is 4/100 000 new cases per annum, with a male-to-female ratio of 2:1. The median age at diagnosis is 60–70 years and the disease is more common in people of African Caribbean origin. The clinical features are demonstrated in Figure 24.41. Diagnosis of myeloma requires two of the following criteria to be fulfilled:
• increased malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow (> 10%)
• serum and/or urinary paraprotein
• skeletal lytic lesions or other end-organ damage, e.g. renal failure.

Bone marrow aspiration, plasma and urine electrophoresis, and a skeletal survey are thus required; the latter is classically a series of plain X-rays, but frequently nowadays low-dose CT scan or whole-body MRI is performed. Normal immunoglobulin levels, i.e. the absence of immu-noparesis, should cast doubt on the diagnosis. Paraproteinaemia can cause an elevated ESR, but this is a non-specific test; only approximately 5% of patients with a persistently elevated ESR above 100 mm/hr have underlying myeloma. Serum albumin and β 2 -microglobulin are prognos-tic, along with a cytogenetic analysis of the tumour cells.

If patients are asymptomatic with no evidence of end-organ damage (e.g. to kidneys, bone marrow or bone), treatment may not be required. So-called asymptomatic myeloma is traditionally managed by close monitoring for the development of end-organ damage (symptomatic myeloma). High-risk features for progression in asymptomatic patients are generally defined as one or more of:
• Bone marrow plasma cells: more than 20% of bone marrow plasma cells
• Serum monoclonal protein: more than 2 g/dL
• Serum free light chain ratio: more than 20
• International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) International Scoring System (ISS; Box 24.63): a high-risk score (III)

Such high-risk patients have been shown to benefit from treatment with the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab. In a recent trial, progression-free survival at 5 years was 63.1% with daratumumab and 40.8% with active monitoring. For all symptomatic myeloma patients, initial therapy involves support-ive care.
• High fluid intake to treat renal impairment and hypercalcaemia (p. 171)
• Analgesia for bone pain
• Bisphosphonates for hypercalcaemia and to delay other skeletal-related events (p. 171)
• Allopurinol to prevent urate nephropathy
• Plasmapheresis, if necessary, for hyperviscosity
• Antibiotic prophylaxis with levofloxacin during the first 3 months of therapy.

Myeloma remains incurable and follows a relapsing and remitting disease course over several years. Patients will receive multiple lines of therapy interspersed with periods of remission or stable disease off therapy. Patients are initially assessed for their fitness and eligibility for autolo-gous HSCT, and treatment pathways vary accordingly. Autologous HSCT remains a treatment goal for fit patients, despite newer therapies. Myeloma therapy has improved with the use of novel agents, which now provide the backbone of therapy and have led to a complex array of treatment regi-mens and sequence in which they are used. The availability of these drugs and regimens varies considerably in different health-care environments. The key classes of drugs include immunomodulatory drugs (thalidomide, lenalidomide and pomalidomide), proteosome inhibitors (bortezomib, carfilzomib and ixazomib) and anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies (daratu-mumab and isatuximab) (Fig. 24.42). Chemotherapy, e.g. cyclophospha-mide, is combined with these drugs in some regimens. The most recently introduced therapies include the BiTE antibodies teclistamab (anti-BCMA) and talquetamab (anti-GPRC5D) and CAR-T therapy directed at the BCMA antigen. The combination of drugs and the sequencing varies by centre based on availability and clinicians’ preferences and has changed frequently in recent years with the growth of available novel agents. Patient preferences based on the considerable side-effect profiles of novel therapies and the need to travel long distances for certain treatments are important considerations, especially in frail elderly patients. Myeloma remains incurable. The aim of treatment for all patients is to maximise the depth and duration of response to improve symptoms and limit further end-organ damage, while minimising toxicity to lengthen survival and improve quality of life. For first-line therapy in older patients who are unsuitable for autolo-gous HSCT (transplant ineligible), the following regimens are commonly used in the UK:
• Bortezomib (Velcade), thalidomide or lenalidomide, and dexametha-sone (VTD or VRD); or with the addition of daratumumab (Dara-VTD and Dara-VRD)
• Lenalidomide–dexamethasone, followed by lenalidomide alone
• Thalidomide in combination with an alkylating agent (melphalan) and a glucocorticoid (MPT)

Thalidomide and lenalidomide both have anti-angiogenic effects against tumour blood vessels and immunomodulatory effects. Both can cause somnolence, constipation, peripheral neuropathy and thrombo-sis, though lenalidomide has a better side-effect profile. It is vital that females of child-bearing age use adequate contraception, as thalido-mide and lenalidomide are teratogenic. Bortezomib is associated with significant neuropathy, including autonomic neuropathy and constipa-tion. Treatment is administered until paraprotein levels have stopped falling. This is termed ‘plateau phase’ and can last for weeks or years. Lenalidomide maintenance can prolong the plateau phase. In younger, fitter patients considered eligible for transplant, standard treatments include first-line therapies, such as cyclophosphamide, tha-lidomide and dexamethasone (CTD), VTD or VRD as above, to maximum response followed by autologous HSCT. More recently, a fourth drug, the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody daratumumab, added to these reg-imens to produce Dara-VTD, and Dara-VRD followed with autologous HSCT, has extended remission and survival by 50% and is the standard approach in many centres. In all patients who have achieved maximal response, lenalidomide maintenance prolongs the response. When myeloma progresses, treatment is given to induce a further pla-teau phase. The increasing movement of novel agents to first-line use has led to re-evaluation of second and subsequent lines of therapies. Pomalidomide, carfilzomib, ixazomib, daratumumab and the BiTE anti-bodies, teclistamab and talquetamab, are options in relapsed/refractory disease, depending on which agents have been used previously. Patients who respond may benefit from a second autologous HSCT. CAR-T ther-apy is likely to play an increasing role in coming years.

This is effective for localised bone pain not responding to simple anal-gesia and for pathological fractures. It is also useful for the emer-gency treatment of spinal cord compression complicating extradural plasmacytomas.

Long-term bisphosphonate therapy reduces bone pain and skeletal events. These drugs protect bone and may cause apoptosis of malig-nant plasma cells. There is evidence that intravenous zoledronate in combination with anti-myeloma therapy confers a survival advantage over oral bisphosphonates. Osteonecrosis of the jaw may be associated with long-term use or poor oral hygiene and gum sepsis; regular dental review, including a check before starting therapy, is therefore important.

The IMWG ISS (see Box 24.63) identifies poor prognostic features, including a high β 2 -microglobulin and low albumin at diagnosis (ISS stage III, median survival 29 months). Those with a normal albumin and a low β 2 -microglobulin (ISS stage I) have a median survival of 62 months. Increasingly, cytogenetic analysis is used to identify poor-risk patients, e.g. t(4;14), del(17/17p), t(14;16), t(14;20), non-hyperdiploidy and gain(1q). Use of autologous HSCT and advances in drug therapy with the newer agents have increased survival. Over one-third of patients are now surviving for 5 years, compared with only one-quarter 10 years ago. The outlook may improve further with new immune effector cell therapies and combinations of treatments.

These are rare presentations of plasma cell malignancy in which an iso-lated tumour occurs in soft tissues or bone. Two-thirds of cases occur in soft tissues and are commonly centred around the upper aerodigestive tract, but can occur anywhere. Others present as bone tumours, com-monly in long bones and vertebrae. Patients present with pain, palpable lumps or compression symptoms, such as difficulty swallowing, short-ness of breath or cord compression. Diagnosis involves tissue biopsy, which demonstrates a solid tumour of monoclonal plasma cells, and staging to exclude disseminated multiple myeloma. Some cases are associated with a low-level paraprotein, but other features of myeloma are absent. Primary treatment is usually with radiotherapy. This can be curative, especially in soft tissue plasmacytomas, which less frequently progress to myeloma. Plasmacytomas of bone have a high rate of progression to myeloma and must be monitored carefully or treated as myeloma from the outset. Rarely myeloma presents as multiple plasmacytomas of bone.

These are a group of rare tissue-infiltrating conditions affecting children and less commonly adults. Histiocytes are immune cells found in vari-ous tissues throughout the body, whose functions include phagocytosis (tissue macrophages), activation of the immune system and promot-ing immune tolerance via antigen presentation to T cells (Fig. 24.43). Disorders resulting from pathological infiltration of tissues by histocytes are shown in Box 24.64. Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is the commonest type and is caused by mutations in cell signalling known as the MAP kinase path-way. Key genes mutated in this pathway include BRAF (65%–70%) and MAP2K (20%). LCH can present with isolated painless lumps, e.g. of bone (eosinophilic granuloma) or with symptoms of disseminated tissue involvement including bone, lung, skin (e.g. persistent nappy rash), lym-phadenopathy, splenomegaly and periodontal disease. Diagnosis can be difficult because of the rarity and multiple symptoms at presentation. Management includes surgical excision or radiotherapy of an isolated lesion or topical or systemic chemotherapy drugs, including methotrex-ate, etoposide and cladribine in disseminated LCH. The BRAF inhibitors, e.g. vemurafenib, have shown promising activity in relapsed LCH. Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) results from mutations in immune genes, e.g. PRF-1. Presentation is predominantly in children with tissue infiltration by histiocytes and macrophages. Abnormal cytokine production, e.g. interferon-gamma and activation of complement, leads to hyperinflammation and associated haemophagocytosis of blood cells producing pancytopenia. Treatment is based around immunosuppres-sion with glucocorticoids, chemotherapy or ciclosporin, all with the aim of proceeding to allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Newer treatments aimed at inhibiting cytokines or complement activation are being studied. An acquired form of reactive haemophagocytosis called macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) or secondary HLH is associated with a range of conditions including rheumatological conditions, e.g. juvenile idiopathic arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and Kawasaki disease, acute viral infections, e.g. EBV, CMV, HHV-6, SARS-CoV-2 and T-cell lymphomas. These diverse conditions generate a cytokine storm, which drives the MAS. Patients present very unwell with fever, 24.64 Histiocytic disorders
• Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH)
• Cutaneous and mucocutaneous histiocytosis (C)
• Malignant histiocytosis (M)
• Rosai–Dorfman disease (RD)

• Haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) severe pancytopenia, deranged coagulation tests, hepatomegaly and a very high ferritin level (often measured in the tens of thousands μg/L). Management includes supportive care, glucocorticoids or other immu-nosuppression, inhibition of IL-1 with anakinra and, if possible, treatment of the underlying condition.

This is a rare disorder in Europe and North America, with 2–4 new cases per million population per annum. The disease is much more common in certain other parts of the world, e.g. east Asia. The basic problem is fail-ure of the pluripotent stem cells because of an autoimmune attack, pro-ducing hypoplasia of the bone marrow with pancytopenia in the blood. As such, this is an autoimmune disease, but the trigger is unknown in primary acquired aplastic anaemia (AA). The diagnosis rests on exclusion of other causes of secondary aplastic anaemia (see below) and rare con-genital causes, such as Fanconi anaemia.

Patients present with symptoms of bone marrow failure, usually anae-mia or bleeding, and less commonly, infections. A FBC demonstrates pancytopenia, low reticulocytes and often macrocytosis. A proportion of patients have abnormal LFTs as a manifestation of autoimmune hepatitis. A PNH clone (p. 961) is identified in some patients. Bone marrow aspira-tion and trephine reveal hypocellularity. The severity of aplastic anaemia is graded according to the Camitta criteria (Box 24.65).

Except some patients with non-severe AA, patients will require blood product support and aggressive management of infection. The progno-sis of severe AA managed with supportive therapy only is poor, and more than 50% of patients die, usually in the first year. The curative treatment for relatively young and fit patients (traditionally < 35 years) with severe idiopathic AA is allogeneic HSCT (p. 966). Older patients aged approx-imately up to 50 years may be candidates if they have no comorbidi-ties. Those with a compatible sibling, or increasingly matched unrelated donor, should proceed to transplantation as soon as possible; they have a 75%–90% chance of long-term cure. In older and less fit patients and those without a suitable donor, immunosuppressive therapy (IST) with horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) and ciclosporin is the treatment of choice and gives 5-year survival rates of 75%. Unrelated donor allografts have been reserved for suitable patients who fail IST, but are increasingly used first line. The thrombopoietin receptor agonist eltrombopag has pro-duced trilineage responses in patients who fail IST and is licensed for this indication. More recently, the addition of eltrombopag to ATG and ciclo-sporin A (CsA) has been shown beneficial in improving responses and this is standard of care in many centres. During the COVID pandemic, older and frailer patients were treated with single agent eltrombopag as first-line therapy, to avoid the high risk from COVID of immunosuppres-sion with ATG and CsA. This proved effective in a proportion of patients and continues to be used off licence in some centres. Non-transplanted patients may relapse, or other clonal disorders of haematopoiesis may evolve, such as paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (p. 961), myel-odysplastic syndrome (p. 993) and AML (p. 986). Patients with aplastic anaemia are followed up long-term.

Causes of this condition are listed in Box 24.66. It is not practical to list all the drugs that have been suspected of causing aplasia. It is important to check the reported side-effects of all drugs taken over the preceding months. In some instances, the cytopenia is more selective and affects only one cell line, most often the neutrophils. Frequently, this is an inci-dental finding, with no ill-health. It probably has an immune basis, but this is difficult to prove. The clinical features and methods of diagnosis are the same as for pri-mary idiopathic aplastic anaemia. An underlying cause should be treated or removed, but otherwise management is as for the idiopathic form.

These are a group of chronic conditions characterised by clonal prolifer-ation of marrow stem/precursor cells. Polycythaemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythaemia (ET) and primary myelofibrosis (PMF) are the non-leu-kaemic myeloproliferative neoplasms. Although most patients are classi-fiable as having one of these disorders, some have overlapping features, and there is often progression from one to another, e.g. PV to myelofibro-sis. A mutation in the gene on chromosome 9 encoding the signal trans-duction molecule JAK-2 (JAK-2 V617F) has been found in more than 90% of PV cases and 50% of those with essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis; less frequently, mutations may be identified in exon 12 of JAK-2. Mutations in the calreticulin gene (CALR), which produces a chaperone protein that protects proteins moving from the endoplasmic reticulin to the cytoplasm, have been found in a further 25% of patients with essential thrombocythaemia. Less commonly, mutations can be detected in the thrombopoietin receptor gene MPL.

In myelofibrosis, the marrow is initially hypercellular, with an excess of abnormal megakaryocytes that release growth factors, such as plate-let-derived growth factor, to the marrow microenvironment, resulting in a reactive proliferation of fibroblasts. As the disease progresses, the mar-row becomes fibrosed. Most patients present over the age of 50 years, with lassitude, weight loss and night sweats. The spleen can be massively enlarged due to extramedullary haematopoiesis (blood cell formation outside the bone marrow), and painful splenic infarcts may occur. The characteristic blood picture is leucoerythroblastic anaemia, with cir-culating immature red blood cells (increased reticulocytes and nucleated red blood cells) and granulocyte precursors (myelocytes). The red cells are shaped like teardrops (teardrop poikilocytes), and giant platelets may be seen in the blood. The white count varies from low to moderately high and the platelet count may be high, normal or low. Urate levels may be high due to increased cell breakdown, and folate deficiency is common. The marrow is often difficult to aspirate and a trephine biopsy shows an excess of megakaryocytes, increased reticulin and fibrous tissue replacement. The presence of a pathological JAK-2 mutation supports the diagnosis.

Median survival is 4 years from diagnosis, but ranges from 1 year to over 20 years. Treatment is directed at control of symptoms, e.g. red cell trans-fusions for anaemia. Folic acid should be given to prevent deficiency. Cytotoxic therapy with hydroxycarbamide may help control spleen size, the white cell counts or systemic symptoms. Splenectomy may be required for a grossly enlarged spleen or symptomatic pancytopenia secondary to splenic pooling of cells and hypersplenism. Allogeneic HSCT may be con-sidered for younger patients. Ruxolitinib, an inhibitor of JAK-1 and JAK-2, is effective at reducing systemic symptoms and splenomegaly and may improve life expectancy with longer-term use. Momelotinib is an inhibitor of JAK and activin A receptor type 1 (ACVR1), which has been shown to improve anaemia and reduce transfusion requirements. Fedratinib, a JAK-2 inhibitor, also reduces splenomegaly and improves symptom burden and has demonstrated efficacy in those refractory to, or intolerant of, ruxolitinib.

Uncontrolled proliferation of megakaryocytes results in a raised level of circulating platelets that are often dysfunctional. Prior to a diagnosis of essential thrombocythaemia being made, reactive causes of thrombo-cytosis must be excluded (see Box 24.15). The presence of pathogenic JAK-2 V617F, CALR or, rarely, MPL mutations supports the diagno-sis, but is not universal. Patients present at a median age of 60 years with vascular occlusion, acrocyanosis (painful discoloured fingertips) or bleeding, or with an asymptomatic isolated raised platelet count. A small percentage (around 5%) will transform to acute leukaemia and others to myelofibrosis. It is likely that most patients with essential thrombocythaemia benefit from low-dose aspirin to reduce the risk of occlusive vascular events. Low-risk patients (age < 40 years, platelet count < 1500 × 10 9 /L and no bleeding or thrombosis) may not require treatment to reduce the platelet count. For those with a platelet count above 1500 × 10 9 /L, with symptoms, or with other risk factors for thrombosis such as diabetes or hypertension, treatment to control platelet counts should be given. Agents include oral hydroxycarbamide or anagrelide, an inhibitor of meg-akaryocyte maturation. Intravenous radioactive phosphorus (32 P) may be useful in old age, but is rarely available nowadays, and interferon-alfa has a role in younger patients, including pregnant women and women planning to conceive.

PV occurs mainly in patients over the age of 40 years and presents either as an incidental finding of a high haemoglobin, or with symptoms of hyperviscosity, such as lassitude, loss of concentration, headaches, dizziness, blackouts, pruritus and epistaxis. Some patients present with manifestations of peripheral arterial or cerebrovascular disease. Venous thromboembolism may also occur. Peptic ulceration is common, some-times complicated by bleeding. Patients are often plethoric, and many have a palpable spleen at diagnosis. Investigation of polycythaemia is discussed on page 953. The diag-nosis of PV now rests on the demonstration of a high haematocrit and the presence of a pathogenic JAK-2 mutation (positive in 95% of cases). In the occasional JAK-2-negative cases, a raised red cell mass and absence of causes of secondary erythrocytosis must be established. The spleen may be enlarged and neutrophil and platelet counts are frequently raised, an abnormal karyotype may be found in the marrow and in vitro culture of the marrow can be used to demonstrate autonomous growth in the absence of added growth factors.

Aspirin reduces the risk of thrombosis. Venesection gives prompt relief of hyperviscosity symptoms. Between 400 and 500 mL of blood (less if the patient is in old age) are removed and the venesection is repeated every 5–7 days until the haematocrit is reduced to below 45%. Less frequent, regular venesection will maintain this level until the haemoglobin remains reduced because of iron deficiency. Suppression of marrow proliferation with hydroxycarbamide or inter-feron-alfa may reduce the risk of vascular occlusion, control spleen size and reduce transformation to myelofibrosis. The JAK-2 inhibitor ruxol-itinib is licensed for patients whose disease is not controlled by hydrox-ycarbamide. Median survival after diagnosis in treated patients exceeds 10 years. Some patients survive more than 20 years; however, cerebro-vascular or coronary events occur in up to 60% of patients. The dis-ease may convert to another myeloproliferative disorder, with about 15% developing acute leukaemia or myelofibrosis.

The initial formation of the platelet plug (see Fig. 24.6A; also known as ‘primary haemostasis’) may fail in thrombocytopenia (p. 958), von Willebrand disease (p. 1009), and also in platelet function disorders and diseases affecting the vessel wall.
Vessel wall abnormalities may be:
• congenital, such as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
• acquired, as in vasculitis (Ch. 25) or scurvy.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is a dominantly inherited condition caused by pathogenic variants in the genes encoding endoglin and activin receptor-like kinase, which are endothelial cell receptors for transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), a potent angiogenic cytokine. Telangiectasia and small aneurysms are found on the fingertips, face and tongue, and in the nasal passages, lung and gastrointestinal tract. A sig-nificant proportion of these patients develop larger pulmonary arterio-venous malformations (PAVMs) that cause arterial hypoxaemia due to a right-to-left shunt. These predispose to paradoxical embolism, resulting in stroke or cerebral abscess. All patients with HHT should be screened for PAVMs and cerebral AVMs; if these are found, ablation by embolisa-tion should be considered. Patients present either with recurrent bleeds, particularly epistaxis, or with iron deficiency due to occult gastrointestinal bleeding. Treatment can be difficult because of the multiple bleeding points, but regular iron therapy often allows the marrow to compensate for blood loss. Local cautery or laser therapy may prevent single lesions from bleeding. A vari-ety of medical therapies have been tried, but none has been found to be universally effective.

Vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (type 4) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder (1/100 000) caused by a defect in type 3 collagen that results in fragile blood vessels and organ membranes, leading to bleeding and organ rupture. Classical joint hypermobility (Ch. 25) is often limited in this form of the disease, but skin changes and facial appearance are typical. The diagnosis should be considered when there is a history of bleeding with normal laboratory tests.

Vitamin C deficiency affects the normal synthesis of collagen and results in a bleeding disorder characterised by perifollicular and petechial haem-orrhage, bruising and subperiosteal bleeding. The key to diagnosis is the dietary history (Ch. 5).

Bleeding may result from thrombocytopenia (see Box 24.14) or from congenital or acquired abnormalities of platelet function. The most com-monly acquired disorders are iatrogenic, resulting from the use of aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor, dipyridamole and the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors to prevent arterial thrombosis (see Box 24.27). Inherited platelet function abnormalities are relatively rare. Congenital abnormalities may be due to deficiency of the membrane glycoproteins, e.g. Glanzmann thrombas-thenia (IIb/IIIa) or Bernard–Soulier syndrome (Ib), or due to the presence of defective platelet granules, e.g. a deficiency of dense (delta) gran-ules (see Fig. 24.7) giving rise to storage pool disorders. The congen-ital macrothrombocytopathies that are due to mutations in the myosin heavy chain gene MYH-9 are characterised by large platelets, inclusion bodies in the neutrophils (Döhle bodies) and a variety of other features, including sensorineural deafness and renal abnormalities. Other famil-ial thrombocytopathies are important, as they can be associated with somatic features (thrombocytopenia with absent radii, TAR), and some are associated with a propensity for development of bone marrow failure or dysplasia (e.g. mutations in RUNX-1 and ANKRD 26). Apart from Glanzmann thrombasthenia, these conditions are mild dis-orders, with bleeding typically occurring after trauma or surgery, but rarely spontaneously. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive con-dition associated with a variable, but often severe bleeding disorder. These conditions are usually managed by local mechanical measures, but antifi-brinolytics, such as tranexamic acid, may be useful and, in severe bleed-ing, platelet transfusion may be required. Recombinant VIIa is licensed for the treatment of resistant bleeding in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
Thrombocytopenia occurs in many disease processes, as listed in Box 24.14, many of which are discussed elsewhere in this chapter.

Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is immune-mediated with involvement of autoantibodies, most often directed against the platelet membrane glycoprotein IIb/IIIa, which sensitise the platelet, resulting in premature removal from the circulation by cells of the reticulo-endothelial system. It is not a single disorder; some cases occur in isolation while others are associated with underlying immune dysregulation in condi-tions such as connective tissue diseases, HIV infection, B-cell malignan-cies, pregnancy and certain drug therapies. The clinical presentation and pathogenesis are similar, whatever the cause of ITP.

The presentation depends on the degree of thrombocytopenia. Spontaneous bleeding typically occurs only when the platelet count is below 20 × 10 9 /L. At higher counts, the patient may complain of easy bruising or sometimes epistaxis or menorrhagia. Many cases with counts of more than 50 × 10 9 /L are discovered by chance. In adults, ITP more commonly affects females and may have an insid-ious onset. Unlike ITP in children, it is unusual for there to be a history of a preceding viral infection. The development of ITP in the context of COVID-19 infection has been documented. Symptoms or signs of a connective tissue disease may be apparent at presentation or emerge several years later. Patients aged over 65 years should be considered for a bone marrow examination to look for an accompanying B-cell malig-nancy and appropriate autoantibody testing performed if a diagnosis of connective tissue disease is suspected. HIV testing should be consid-ered because a positive result will have major implications for appro-priate therapy. The peripheral blood film is normal, apart from a greatly reduced platelet number, while the bone marrow typically demonstrates an increase in megakaryocytes.

Many patients with stable compensated ITP and a platelet count of more than 30 × 10 9 /L do not require treatment to raise the platelet count, except at times of increased bleeding risk, such as surgery and biopsy. First-line therapy for patients with spontaneous bleeding is with high doses of glu-cocorticoids, either prednisolone (1 mg/kg daily) or dexamethasone (40 mg daily for 4 days), to suppress antibody production and inhibit phagocytosis of sensitised platelets by reticulo-endothelial cells. Administration of intra-venous immunoglobulin can raise the platelet count by blocking antibody receptors on reticulo-endothelial cells and is combined with glucocorticoid therapy if there is severe haemostatic failure, especially with evidence of significant mucosal bleeding or a slow response to glucocorticoids alone. Persistent or potentially life-threatening bleeding should be treated with platelet transfusion in addition to the other therapies. The condition may become chronic, with remissions and relapses. Relapses should be treated either with further glucocorticoids or sec-ond-line therapies. The options for second-line therapy include the throm-bopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RA) eltrombopag, avatrombopag and romiplostim (which stimulate new platelet formation), the splenic tyro­ sine kinase inhibitor fostamatinib, splenectomy and immunosuppression. Where splenectomy is considered, the precautions shown in Box 24.40 need to be in place. Splenectomy produces complete remission in about 70% of patients and improvement in a further 20%–25% in favourable cases. The TPO-RAs induce response in around 75% of cases, usually within 10–14 days. Low-dose glucocorticoid therapy and immunosup-pressants such as rituximab, ciclosporin, mycophenolate and tacrolimus may also produce remissions. The order in which therapies should be used is not entirely clear, although the TPO-RAs and fostamatinib are licensed for this indication, while the immunosuppressive agents are not.

Normal coagulation is explained in Figure 24.6 and the effects of age are discussed in Box 24.67. Coagulation factor deficiency may be congen-ital or acquired and may affect one or several of the coagulation factors (Box 24.68). Inherited disorders are almost uniformly related to decreased synthesis, as a result of mutation in the gene encoding a key protein in coagulation. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Haemophilia A and B are the most common sin-gle coagulation factor deficiencies, but inherited deficiencies of all the other coagulation factors are seen. Acquired disorders may be due to under-production (e.g. in liver failure), increased consumption (e.g. in DIC) or inhibition of function of coagulation factors (such as heparin ther-apy or immune inhibitors of coagulation, e.g. acquired haemophilia A).
Factor VIII deficiency resulting in haemophilia A affects 1/10 000 indi-viduals. It is the most common congenital coagulation factor deficiency.
24.67 Haemostasis and thrombosis in old age
• Thrombocytopenia: reasonably common because of the rising prevalence of disorders in which it may be a secondary feature and also because of the greater use of drugs that can cause it.
• ‘Senile’ purpura: presumed to be due to an age-associated loss of subcutaneous fat and the collagenous support of small blood vessels, making them more prone to damage from minor trauma.

• Thrombosis: incidence of thromboembolic disease rises with increasing age. This may be due to stasis and concurrent illness, to which older people are prone. Some studies show increased platelet aggregation with age and others age-associated hyperactivity of the haemostatic system, which could contribute to a prothrombotic state.

• Thromboprophylaxis: should be considered in all older patients who are immobile as a result of acute illness. Prophylaxis is not required in chronic immobility without a medical cause, as there is no associated increase in thromboembolism.

• Anticoagulation: older patients are more sensitive to the anticoagulant effects of warfarin, partly due to the concurrent use of other drugs and the presence of other pathology. Life-threatening or fatal bleeds on warfarin are significantly more common in those over 80 years.
