text: Osteomalacia and rickets
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Severe and prolonged vitamin D deficiency can result in the occur-rence of osteomalacia in adults and rickets in children. Improvements in nutrition mean that these are now relatively uncommon conditions in high-income countries, but they remain prevalent in older housebound individuals, who may have a poor diet and limited sunlight exposure, in women who wear facial coverings such as the niqab or burka, and in people with malabsorption.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Pathogenesis
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Osteomalacia and rickets occur as the result of chronic secondary hyper-parathyroidism, which invariably accompanies severe and long-standing vitamin D deficiency. The sustained elevation in PTH levels maintains nor-mal levels of serum calcium by increasing bone resorption, which even-tually causes progressive demineralisation of the skeleton. Phosphate released during the process of bone resorption is lost through increased renal excretion, resulting in hypophosphataemia. The raised levels of PTH stimulate osteoblast activity and cause new bone formation, but the matrix is not mineralised properly because of deficiency of calcium and phosphate. The under-mineralised bone is soft, mechanically weak and subject to fractures, particularly stress fractures. Normal levels of serum calcium tend to be maintained until a very advanced stage, when hypocalcaemia may occur.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Clinical features
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Vitamin D deficiency in children causes delayed development, muscle hypotonia, craniotabes (small unossified areas in membranous bones of the skull that yield to finger pressure with a cracking feeling), bossing of the frontal and parietal bones and delayed anterior fontanelle closure, enlargement of epiphyses at the lower end of the radius and swelling of the rib costochondral junctions (‘rickety rosary’). Osteomalacia in adults can present with fractures and low BMD, mimicking osteoporosis. Other symptoms include bone pain and general malaise. Proximal muscle weakness is prominent, and the patient may walk with a waddling gait and struggle to climb stairs or stand up from a chair. There may be bone and muscle tenderness on pressure, and focal bone pain can be due to fissure fractures of the ribs and pelvis.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Investigations
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: The diagnosis can usually be made by measurement of serum 25(OH)D, PTH, calcium, phosphate and ALP. Typically, serum ALP levels are raised, 25(OH)D levels are undetectable and PTH is markedly elevated. Serum phosphate levels tend to be low, but serum calcium is usually normal, unless the disease is advanced. X-rays often show osteopenia or verte-bral crush fractures and, with more advanced disease, focal radiolucent areas (pseudofractures or Looser zones) may be seen in ribs, pelvis and long bones (Fig. 25.61). In children, there is thickening and widening of the epiphyseal plate. A radionuclide bone scan may show multiple hot spots in the ribs and pelvis at the site of fractures and the appearance may be mistaken for metastases. Where there is doubt, the diagnosis can be confirmed by bone biopsy, which shows the pathognomonic increased thickness and extent of osteoid seams (see Fig. 25.61).
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Management
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Osteomalacia and rickets respond promptly to treatment with vitamin D. A wide variety of doses can be used. Treatment with between 10 000 and 25 000 IU daily for 2–4 weeks is associated with rapid clinical improve-ment, an elevation in serum 25(OH)D and a reduction in PTH. Serum ALP levels sometimes rise initially as mineralisation of bone increases, but eventually fall to within the reference range as the bone disease heals. Subsequently, the dose of vitamin D can usually be reduced to a main-tenance level of 800–1600 IU daily (10–20 μg), except in patients with malabsorption, who may require higher maintenance doses.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Vitamin D-resistant rickets
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: This is a genetically determined condition that presents in childhood with rickets that is resistant to therapy with vitamin D in standard dosages.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Pathogenesis
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Type I vitamin D-resistant rickets (VDRR) is caused by loss-of-function pathogenic variants in the 25(OH)D-1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) enzyme, which converts 25(OH)D to the active metabolite 1,25(OH) 2 D 3. Type II
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: VDRR is caused by loss-of-function pathogenic variants in the vitamin D receptor, which impair its ability to activate gene transcription. Both are recessive disorders and consanguinity is common.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Clinical features
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: These are as described above for infantile rickets. The diagnosis is usually first suspected when the patient fails to respond to vitamin D supplementation.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Investigations
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: The biochemical features of type I VDRR are like those of ordinary vitamin D deficiency, except that levels of 25(OH)D are normal, but 1,25(OH) 2 D is low. In type II VDRR, 25(OH)D is normal, but PTH and 1,25(OH) 2 D 3 values are raised. The diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic testing.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Management
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Type I VDRR responds fully to treatment with the active vitamin D metab-olites 1α-hydroxy-vitamin D (1–2 μg daily, orally) or 1,25-dihydroxy-vita-min D (0.25–1.5 μg daily, orally). Calcium supplements are not necessary unless there is dietary deficiency. Type II VDRR sometimes responds partially to very high doses of active vitamin D metabolites, which can activate the mutant receptor, although additional calcium and phosphate supplements are also necessary.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: This group of disorders are caused by inherited defects in renal tubular phosphate reabsorption. The most common is X-linked hypophospha-taemic rickets (XLH), but autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms also occur (see Box 25.74).
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Pathophysiology
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Most forms of hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets are associated with raised circulating concentrations of the phosphate-regulating hormone fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). This hormone is produced by oste-ocytes (see Fig. 25.2) and enters the circulation, where it is normally inactivated by proteolytic cleavage. Production of FGF23 by osteocytes is under tonic inhibition by DMP1 and PHEX. In XLH, the inhibitory effect on FGF23 production is lost due to pathogenic loss-of-function variants in PHEX and a similar situation occurs in autosomal recessive hypophos-phataemic rickets (ARHR1) due to pathogenic loss-of-function variants in DMP1. In autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (ADHR), there are pathogenic variants in FGF23, which result in the protein being degraded, thereby causing accumulation of intact FGF23 hormone in the circulation. In all three diseases, the elevation in FGF23 results in osteomalacia and rickets by causing phosphaturia by down-regulation of sodium-dependent phosphate transporters in the renal tubules, and by inhibiting conversion of 25(OH)D to 1,25(OH) 2 D by the kidney, which in turn causes reduced calcium and phosphate absorption from the gut.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Clinical features
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: The presentation is with symptoms and signs of rickets during childhood that do not respond to vitamin D supplementation. In adults, hypophos-phataemic rickets may be accompanied by dental abscesses, and by bone and joint pain due to the development of an enthesopathy or stress fractures.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Investigations
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: The diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic testing. Routine biochemistry shows a low serum phosphate and a reduction in tubular reabsorption of phosphate. Serum concentrations of FGF23 are markedly elevated. Serum levels of 25(OH)D are variable and PTH is normal or elevated.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Management
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: The aim of treatment is to ameliorate symptoms, restore normal growth and maintain serum phosphate levels within the reference range. Burosumab, a neutralising antibody to FGF23, is now the treatment of choice for XLH in both children and adults as it reverses the metabolic abnormalities that are typical of the disorder. If for any reason burosumab cannot be given, XLH can be treated with phos-phate supplements (1–4 g daily) and alfacalcidol (1–2 μg daily) or cal-citriol (0.5–1.5 μg daily), with the aim of promoting intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. Levels of calcium and phosphate, as well as renal function, should be monitored regularly during treatment and renal ultrasound examination is recommended periodically to check for evidence of nephrocalcinosis. The therapeutic goal is to main-tain serum phosphate concentrations within the normal range, but to avoid hypercalcaemia.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Tumour-induced osteomalacia
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: This is a rare syndrome caused by over-production of FGF23 by mes-enchymal tumours. The presentation is with severe osteomalacia and hypophosphataemia in an adult patient with no obvious predisposing risk factor for vitamin D deficiency. Biochemical findings are as described for hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets. The underlying tumour can be difficult to find and multiple modality imaging with whole-body MRI, CT and somatostatin or gallium-68 (68 Ga)-DOTATATE PET-CT scintigraphy is often needed. Options for medical management include phosphate supplements and active vitamin D metabolites or burosumab, but the treatment of choice is surgical resection of the primary tumour, which is curative.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Hypophosphatasia
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Hypophosphatasia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function pathogenic variants in the TNALP gene, which results in accumulation of pyrophosphate and inhibition of bone mineralisation. The typical presentation is with severe intractable rickets during infancy, sometimes in association with seizures. Investigations show low or unde-tectable levels of serum ALP, but normal levels of calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D metabolites. Urine excretion of pyridoxal 5′ phos-phate and phosphoethanolamine (substrates for ALP) is increased. In severely affected patients, remarkable therapeutic responses have been obtained with recombinant ALP therapy (asfotase alfa), which is curative. Heterozygous carriers of these variants in TNALP are often asympto-matic and picked up as the result of a low ALP. There is some evidence that they may be at increased risk of osteoporosis. If present, osteoporo-sis can be treated with standard therapy. Enzyme replacement is seldom used in heterozygotes due to the high cost but can be considered on a case-by-case basis.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Other causes of osteomalacia
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: These are summarised in Box 25.74. Osteomalacia may occur as a component of renal osteodystrophy in patients with chronic kidney dis-ease. The mechanism is reduced conversion of 25(OH)D into the active metabolite 1,25(OH) 2 D by the failing kidney. Aluminium intoxication is now rare due to reduced use of aluminium-containing phosphate bind-ers and removal of aluminium from the water supplies used in dialysis. If aluminium intoxication is suspected, the diagnosis can be confirmed by demonstration of aluminium at the calcification front in a bone biopsy. Osteomalacia due to bisphosphonates has mostly been described in patients with Paget disease who are receiving etidronate and high-dose pamidronate. It is usually asymptomatic, and healing occurs when treatment is stopped. Excessive fluoride intake causes osteoma-lacia due to direct inhibition of mineralisation and is common in parts of the world where there is a high fluoride content in drinking water. The condition reverses when fluoride intake is reduced. Also, repeated IV iron preparations have been linked to causing (FGF23-mediated renal phosphate-wasting) hypophosphataemic osteomalacia. Data suggests ferric carboxymaltose is most commonly implicated. The mechanism is still to be determined. The condition resolves on cessation of the relevant IV iron.
section_path: Osteomalacia, rickets and vitamin D deficiency

text: Paget disease of bone (PDB) is characterised by focal areas of increased and disorganised bone remodelling involving one or more skeletal sites. The disease is common in the UK, affecting about 0.2% of those aged above 60. It is less common in other countries in Europe and is rare in Asia. The prevalence doubles each decade from the age of 50 onwards and affects up to 7% of the UK population by the age of 85.
Pathophysiology

The primary abnormality is increased osteoclastic bone resorption, accom-panied by marrow fibrosis, increased vascularity of bone and increased, but disorganised, bone formation. Osteoclasts in PDB are greater in num-ber and unusually large, containing characteristic nuclear inclusion bodies. Genetic factors are important and pathogenic variants in the SQSTM1 gene are a common cause of classical PDB. The presence of nuclear inclusion bodies in osteoclasts has fuelled speculation that PDB might be caused by a slow virus infection, but this remains unproven, and recent evidence suggests they may be aggregates of undegraded proteins. Biomechanical factors may influence which bones are affected, as PDB often starts at sites of muscle insertions into bone and, in some cases, localises to bones or limbs that have been subjected to repetitive trauma or overuse. Involvement of subchondral bone can compromise the joint and predispose to OA. The prevalence of PDB has fallen in many countries over recent decades, indicat-ing that environmental factors play a role, but their identity remains unclear.
Clinical features

The axial skeleton is predominantly affected, and commonly affected sites are the pelvis, femur, tibia, lumbar spine, skull and scapula. The most com-mon presentation is with musculoskeletal pain. This can either be due to increased metabolic activity of the disease, deformity or stress fractures. More commonly it is due to a coexisting problem, particularly osteoarthritis. Paget disease can occasionally present with bone deformity, deafness and pathological fractures. Sometimes no symptoms are present, and in about 20% the diagnosis is made by imaging or finding a raised ALP on a blood test performed for another reason. Clinical signs include bone deformity and expansion, and increased warmth over an affected bone. Neurological problems, such as deafness, cranial nerve defects, nerve root pain, spinal cord compression and spinal stenosis, may occur due to enlargement of affected bones and encroachment on the spinal cord and nerve foramina. Surprisingly, deafness is seldom due to compression of the auditory nerve, but instead is conductive in nature due to osteosclerosis of the temporal bone. The increased vascularity of Pagetic bone can very rarely precipitate high-output cardiac failure in older patients with limited cardiac reserve. Osteosarcoma is an unusual but serious complication that presents with increasing pain and swelling of an affected site.
Investigations

The characteristic features are an isolated elevation in ALP and bone expansion on X-rays, with alternating areas of radiolucency and osteo-sclerosis (Fig. 25.62). Levels of ALP can be normal if only a single bone is affected. The best way of identifying affected sites is a radionuclide bone scan, which shows increased uptake in affected bones (see Fig. 25.62). If the bone scan is positive, X-rays should be taken to con-firm the diagnosis. Bone biopsy is not usually required but may help to exclude osteosclerotic metastases in cases of diagnostic uncertainty.
Management

The main indication for treatment with inhibitors of bone resorption is bone pain, localised to an affected site, which is thought to be due to increased metabolic activity. Patients should be carefully assessed to determine the cause of the pain since it can be difficult to differentiate the pain caused by increased metabolic activity of PDB from that caused by complications such as bone deformity, nerve compression symp-toms and OA. Various agents can be used (Box 25.75), but zoledronic acid is considered the treatment of choice since it is highly effective at suppressing elevated bone turnover in PDB and is most likely to give a favourable pain response. Intravenous pamidronate and oral risedronate can also be effective. Calcitonin may also help symptoms but is sel-dom used unless there is a contraindication to bisphosphonate therapy. If there is doubt about whether the pain is due to PDB, it can be worth-while giving a therapeutic trial of bisphosphonate to determine whether the symptoms improve. A positive response usually indicates that the pain was due to increased metabolic activity. Repeated courses of bis-phosphonates can be given if symptoms recur. Recent studies have shown that prophylactic zoledronic acid can reverse or arrest early PDB in asymptomatic carriers of pathogenic SQSTM1 variants.
Complex regional pain syndrome type 1

Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) type 1 is characterised by gradual onset of pain, swelling and local tenderness, usually affecting a limb extremity. It may be triggered by fracture but can also occur in association with soft tissue injury, pregnancy and intercurrent illness or can develop spontaneously. The cause is unknown, but abnormalities of the sympathetic nervous system are thought to play a pathogenic role. The affected limb is swollen and tender, and there may be evidence of regional autonomic dysfunction with abnormal sweating and changes in skin colour and temperature. The diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the features shown in Box 25.76. Support for the diagnosis can be obtained with MRI, which shows bone marrow oedema, or radionuclide bone scan, which shows a local increase in tracer uptake. X-rays typ-ically show localised patchy osteoporosis. Haematology, biochemistry and immunology are normal. The aims of treatment are to control pain and encourage mobilisation. Analgesics, NSAIDs, antineuropathic agents, calcitonin, glucocorticoids, β-adrenoceptor antagonists (β-blockers), sympathectomy and bisphos-phonates have all been tried with variable efficacy. Pain can resolve in some patients with time, but many have persistent symptoms and fail to regain normal function.
Osteonecrosis

Osteonecrosis is the term used to describe death of bone due to impair-ment of its blood supply. Frequently affected sites are the femoral head, humeral head, navicular and scaphoid. In some cases, the condition occurs as the result of direct trauma that interrupts the blood supply to the affected bone. This is the reason for osteonecrosis of the femoral head following fractures of the femoral neck and in patients with throm-bophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, Gaucher disease and haemoglo-binopathies, such as sickle-cell disorder. Other important predisposing factors include high-dose glucocorticoid treatment, alcohol excess, SLE, HIV and radiotherapy, but in many of these conditions pathophysiology is poorly understood. The presentation is with pain localised to the affected site, which is exacerbated by weight-bearing. The diagnosis can be con-firmed by MRI, which shows evidence of subchondral necrotic bone and bone marrow oedema. X-rays are normal in the early stages, but later may show evidence of osteosclerosis and deformity of the affected bone. There is no specific treatment. Management should focus on controlling pain and encouraging mobilisation. Symptoms often improve spontane-ously with time, but joint replacement may be required in patients who have persisting pain in association with significant structural damage to the affected joint.
Scheuermann osteochondritis

This disorder predominantly affects adolescent boys, who develop a dorsal kyphosis in association with irregular radiographic ossification of the vertebral end plates. It has a strong genetic component and may sometimes be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Most patients are asymptomatic, but back pain aggravated by exercise and relieved by rest may occur. Excessive exercise and heavy manual labour before epiphyseal fusion has occurred may aggravate symptoms. Management consists of advice to avoid excessive activity and provision of protective postural exercises. Rarely, corrective surgery may be required if there is severe deformity. Scheuermann disease can sometimes present for the first time in adulthood, when it can be confused with osteoporo-tic vertebral fractures. It can be differentiated from osteoporosis by the characteristic X-ray changes, which show mild wedge deformity of 3–4 adjacent vertebrae, irregularity of the vertebral end plates, and normal BMD on DXA examination.
Fibrous dysplasia

This is an acquired systemic disorder that mainly affects the skeleton and is caused by somatic gain-of-function pathogenic variants in the GNAS1 gene. The characteristic presentation is with bone pain and pathological fractures. Associated features include endocrine dysfunction, especially precocious puberty, and café-au-lait skin pigmentation (McCune–Albright syndrome). The diagnosis can usually be made by imaging, which shows focal, predominantly osteolytic lesions with bone expansion on X-rays (Fig. 25.63), and focal increased uptake on bone scan. The condition may cause a single (monostotic) or multiple (polyostotic) lesions. The condition can superficially resemble Paget disease of bone, but the ear-lier age of onset and pattern of involvement are usually distinctive. Very rarely, malignant change can occur and should be suspected if there is a sudden increase in pain and swelling. Management is symptomatic. Intravenous bisphosphonates are often used in an attempt to control pain, but the evidence base for their efficacy is weak. Orthopaedic sur-gery may be required for treatment of fracture and deformity or to prevent a pathological fracture in a weight-bearing bone. Endocrine manifesta-tions, such as precocious puberty, may require specific treatment.
Osteogenesis imperfecta

Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is the name given to a group of disorders characterised by severe osteoporosis and multiple fractures in infancy and childhood. In about 80% of cases the disease is caused by pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the COL1A1 and COL1A2 genes, which encode proteins that make type I collagen. These result in reduced collagen produc-tion (in mild OI) or in formation of abnormal collagen chains that are rapidly degraded (in severe OI). Pathogenic variants in several other genes have been described that can cause OI, some of which affect post-translational modification of collagen and others that affect bone formation. Many patients have no family history. Some of these have new variants whereas others may have recessive forms of the disease. The Sillence classification is commonly used to grade severity in people with pathogenic COL1A1 or COL1A2 variants. This varies from neonatal lethal OI (type II), through very severe OI with multiple fractures in infancy and childhood (types III and IV), to mild (type I), in which affected patients typically have blue sclerae. The typical presentation of OI is with low trauma fractures during infancy, but the high fracture rate persists throughout life. However, OI is a systemic disease with effects on the cardiopulmonary and gastrointestinal system, soft tis-sues, tendons, muscle, and joints, hearing, eyesight, and dental health. The diagnosis is often made clinically but increasingly is confirmed by genetic testing. The disease can be mistaken for non-accidental injury in childhood and for osteoporosis in adulthood; in such cases, genetic testing is of par-ticular value. Treatment is multidisciplinary, involving surgical reduction and fixation of fractures and correction of limb deformities, with physiotherapy and occupational therapy for rehabilitation of patients with bone deform-ity. Bisphosphonates are widely used in the treatment of children and ado-lescents with OI, especially intravenous pamidronate and zoledronic acid, but there is limited evidence for efficacy in fracture prevention. Adults are also prescribed bisphosphonates but with no evidence for efficacy in frac-ture prevention. A recent trial of TPTD followed by ZA similarly showed no anti-fracture efficacy in OI, illustrating the importance of reduced bone quality rather than reduced bone density in the pathogenesis of fractures.
Osteopetrosis

Osteopetrosis is the collective name given to a rare group of inherited diseases caused by failure of osteoclast function. Presentation is highly variable, ranging from a lethal disorder that presents with bone marrow failure in infancy to a milder and sometimes asymptomatic form that presents in adulthood. Severe osteopetrosis is inherited in an auto-somal recessive manner and presents with failure to thrive, delayed dentition, cranial nerve palsies (due to absent cranial foramina), blind-ness, anaemia and recurrent infections due to bone marrow failure. The adult-onset type (Albers–Schönberg disease) shows autosomal dominant inheritance and presents with bone pain, cranial nerve pal-sies, osteomyelitis, OA or fracture; it is sometimes detected as an inci-dental radiographic finding. The pathogenic loss-of-function variants responsible for ‘osteoclast-poor’ osteopetrosis affect TNFRSF11A or TNFRSF11, which encode RANK and RANKL, respectively. Both pro-teins are critical for osteoclast differentiation. Pathogenic variants in genes involved in bone resorption cause ‘osteoclast-rich’ osteopetro-sis. These include variants in TCIRG1, which encodes a component of the osteoclast proton pump, and variants in CLCN7, which encodes the osteoclast chloride pump. The most effective treatment is bone marrow transplantation that can provide a source of osteoclasts that resorb bone normally, but this is not effective in patients with patho-genic variants in RANKL. Medical management has limited efficacy, but IFN-γ treatment may improve blood counts and reduce the frequency of infections.
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva

Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a rare inherited disor-der caused by heterozygous gain-of-function pathogenic variants in ACVR1, which encodes the activin A receptor type 1, a bone mor-phogenetic protein (BMP) type 1 receptor. It is characterised by wide-spread foci of heterotopic ossification (HO) affecting muscle and soft tissues, which cause severe pain, deformity, disability and early mor-tality. Intermittent inflammatory flare ups triggered by injury, injections or surgery can occur. Corticosteroids (prednisolone 40 mg daily) are indicated to treat flare ups, and many patients are on low-dose pred-nisolone long term. Until recently there had been no disease-modifying therapy. Palovarotene, a retinoid receptor agonist, has recently been approved by the FDA to prevent new bone lesions in FOP but was rejected by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for this indication due to concerns about efficacy. Garetosmab, an antibody to activin A, has shown promising results in blocking the development of new lesions and reducing the number of flare ups.
Sclerosing bone dysplasias

These are rare diseases characterised by osteosclerosis and increased bone formation. Van Buchem disease and sclerosteosis are recessive disorders caused by pathogenic loss-of-function variants in the SOST gene, which encodes sclerostin, a protein which suppresses bone forma-tion and increases bone resorption (see Fig. 25.2). The resulting lack of functional sclerostin increases bone formation and reduces bone resorp-tion causing bone overgrowth, with enlargement of the cranium and jaw, tall stature and cranial nerve palsies. There is no effective treatment. High bone mass syndrome is a benign disorder caused by pathogenic vari-ants in LRP4 or LRP5. It is characterised by unusually high bone density. The variants render the LRP receptors resistant to the inhibitory effects of sclerostin. Most patients are asymptomatic, but bone overgrowth in the palate (torus palatinus) and enlargement of the mandible can occur in later life. Treatment is not usually required. Camurati–Engelmann dis-ease is an autosomal dominant condition caused by gain-of-function pathogenic variants in TGFB1. It presents with bone pain, muscle weak-ness and osteosclerosis mainly affecting the diaphysis of long bones. Glucocorticoids can help the bone pain, although usually analgesics are also required.
Achondroplasia

Achondroplasia is a rare genetic disorder characterised by short stat-ure, limb shortening, foramen magnum stenosis and hearing impair-ment caused by gain-of-function pathogenic variants in FGFR3, which encodes the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3. It is inherited in an auto-somal dominant fashion. The diagnosis can usually be made clinically and confirmed by genetic testing. Kyphoscoliosis and spinal stenosis are common complications in adulthood. Vosoritide, a C-type natriuretic peptide analogue, has been found to increase linear growth in children with achondroplasia, but the effect on health-related quality of life in the long term remains to be determined. Surgical decompression of the fora-men magnum and corrective orthopaedic surgery for limb deformity and kyphoscoliosis may be required.

Primary tumours of bones and joints are rare, have a peak incidence in childhood and adolescence, and can be benign or malignant (Box 25.77). Paget disease of bone accounts for most cases of osteo-sarcoma occurring above the age of 40.
Osteosarcoma

This is a rare tumour with an incidence of 0.6–0.85 per 100 000 popula-tion. It is the most common primary bone tumour. Most patients present under the age of 30, but osteosarcoma also occurs in old age in associ-ation with Paget disease. The presentation is with local pain and swell-ing. X-rays show expansion of the bone with a surrounding soft tissue mass, often containing islands of calcification. If the diagnosis is being considered, MRI or CT should be performed to determine the extent of tumour. Patients suspected of having osteosarcoma should be referred to a specialist oncology team for management. Treatment depends on histological type, but generally involves surgical removal of the tumour, followed by chemotherapy and radiotherapy. The prognosis is normally good in cases that present in childhood and adolescence, but poor in older patients.
Chondrosarcoma

This is the second most common primary bone tumour. Presentation is as described for osteosarcoma. The treatment of choice is surgical resection since chondrosarcomas are relatively resistant to chemother-apy and radiotherapy. The prognosis is good for low-grade tumours, but poor for anaplastic tumours.
Ewing sarcoma

This is the third most common sarcoma, which presents almost exclu-sively under the age of 40. Presentation is as described for osteosarcoma. Treatment is by local excision and surgical resection. The prognosis is excellent for patients who present before metastasis has occurred.
Metastatic bone disease

Metastatic bone disease may present in a variety of ways: with localised or generalised progressive bone pain, generalised regional pain, symptoms of spinal cord compression, or acute pain due to pathological fracture.

Systemic features, such as weight loss and anorexia, and symptoms refer-able to the primary tumour are often present. The tumours that most com-monly metastasise to bone are myeloma and those of bronchus, breast, prostate, kidney and thyroid. Management is discussed in Chapter 8.
Many systemic diseases can affect the locomotor system, and many drugs may cause adverse musculoskeletal effects (Box 25.78). The most common examples are described here.
Malignant disease

Malignant disease can cause a variety of non-metastatic musculo-skeletal problems (Box 25.79). One of the most striking is hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy (HPOA), characterised by clubbing and painful swelling of the limbs, periosteal new bone formation and arthralgia/arthritis. The most common causes are bronchial carci-noma and mesothelioma. Bone scintigraphy shows increased per-iosteal uptake before new bone is apparent on X-ray. The course follows that of the underlying malignancy, and HPOA resolves if malignancy is cured.
25.79 Rheumatological manifestations of malignancy
• Polyarthritis
• Dermatomyositis and polymyositis
• Hypophosphataemic osteomalacia
• Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy
• Vasculitis
• Autoimmune connective tissue disease
• Raynaud syndrome
• Polymyalgia rheumatica-like syndrome
Endocrine disease

Hypothyroidism may present with carpal tunnel syndrome or, rarely, with painful, symmetrical proximal myopathy and muscle hypertro-phy. Both resolve with levothyroxine replacement. Primary hyperpara-thyroidism is associated with osteoporosis and also predisposes to CPPD disease and to calcific periarthritis, especially in patients with renal disease. Diabetes mellitus commonly causes diabetic cheiroarthropathy, characterised by tightening of skin and periarticular structures, causing flexion deformities of the fingers that may be painful. Diabetic oste-opathy presents as forefoot pain with radiographic progression from osteopenia to complete osteolysis of the phalanges and metatarsals. Diabetes also predisposes to osteoporosis, fragility fractures, adhesive capsulitis, Dupuytren contracture, osteomyelitis, septic arthritis and Charcot joints. Acromegaly can be associated with mechanical back pain, with normal or excessive movement; carpal tunnel syndrome; Raynaud syndrome and an arthropathy (50%). This arthropathy mainly affects the large joints and has clinical similarities to OA, but with a normal or increased range of movement. X-rays may show widening of joint spaces, squaring of bone ends, generalised osteopenia and tufting of terminal phalanges. It does not improve with treatment of the acromegaly and is an important cause of reduced quality of life in affected individuals.
Haematological disease

Haemochromatosis is complicated by arthropathy in about 50% of cases. It typically presents between the ages of 40 and 50 and may predate other features of the disease. The small joints of the hands and wrists are typically affected, but the hips, shoulders and knees may also be involved. The X-ray changes resemble OA, but cysts are often multiple and prominent with little osteophyte formation. Involvement of the radiocarpal and MCP joints may occur, which is unusual in primary OA, and about 30% have CPPD. Treatment of the haemochromatosis does not influence the arthropathy, though methotrexate and colchi-cine are options for polyarticular chronic CPPD disease; otherwise, management is as described for OA. Haemophilia can be complicated by haemarthrosis, which, if recurrent, can result in the development of secondary OA. Sickle-cell disorder may be associated with bone pain, osteonecrosis and osteomyelitis. Thalassaemia may be complicated by bone deformity, especially affecting the craniofacial bones, and by osteoporosis.
Neurological disease

Neurological disease may result in rapidly destructive arthritis of joints, first described by Charcot in association with syphilis. The cause of Charcot arthropathy is incompletely understood but may involve repeti-tive trauma as the result of sensory loss and altered blood flow secondary to impaired sympathetic nervous system control. The main predisposing diseases and sites of involvement are:
• diabetic neuropathy (hindfoot)
• syringomyelia (shoulder, elbow, wrist)
• leprosy (hands, feet)
• tabes dorsalis (knees, spine).

The presentation is with subacute or chronic monoarthritis. Pain can occur, especially at the onset, but once the joint is severely deranged, pain is often minimal, and signs become disproportionately greater than symptoms. The joint is often grossly swollen, with effusion, crepitus, marked instability and deformity, but usually no increased warmth. X-rays show disorganisation of normal joint architecture and often multiple loose bodies (Fig. 25.64), and either no (atrophic) or gross (hypertrophic) new bone formation. Management principally involves orthoses and occa-sionally arthrodesis.
Anterior tibial compartment syndrome

This is characterised by severe pain in the front of the lower leg, aggra-vated by exercise and relieved by rest. Symptoms result from fascial compression of the muscles in the anterior tibial compartment and may be associated with foot drop. Treatment is by surgical decompression.
Carpal tunnel syndrome

This is a common nerve entrapment syndrome caused by compression of the median nerve at the wrist. It presents with numbness, tingling and pain in a median nerve distribution. Severe nerve compression can cause thumb weakness and thenar eminence muscle wasting. The differential diagnosis includes C6 radicu-lopathy. The most common non-mechanical, systemic causes are hypo-thyroidism, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis, obesity and pregnancy (especially in the third trimester). In some patients, no underlying cause can be identified. Carpal tunnel syndrome often responds to treatment of the underlying condition, but other options include local glucocorticoid injections and surgical decompression.
Ulnar nerve neuropathy

The ulna nerve can be irritated or compressed at the elbow or wrist to cause symptoms and weakness in the hand. The distribution of sen-sory symptoms is in the lateral three fingers. Severe nerve compression can result in small hand (intrinsic) muscle wasting. Differential diagno-sis includes C7–T1 radiculopathy and inclusion body myositis (IBM) (p. 1070). Causes include RA at the elbow and injuries/trauma at the wrist. Splinting, steroid injections at the site of nerve compression and surgery are therapy options.
Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis

Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) is a common disorder, affecting 10% of men and 8% of women over the age of 65, but its prevalence increases further with age and is associated with obesity, hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is characterised by syndes-mophytes and florid new bone formation along the anterolateral aspect of contiguous vertebral bodies (Fig. 25.65). DISH is distinguished from lumbar spondylosis by the absence of disc space narrowing and mar-ginal vertebral body sclerosis, and from ankylosing spondylitis by the absence of sacroiliitis or apophyseal joint fusion. It is usually an asymp-tomatic radiographic finding but can induce back pain through causing degenerative back disease, or pain at peripheral sites, such as the heel, in association with enthesophyte formation.
Dupuytren contracture

Dupuytren contracture is characterised by fibrosis and contracture of the superficial palmar fascia of the hands. The patient is unable to extend the fingers fully and there is puckering of the skin with palpable nodules. The ring and little fingers are usually the first and worst affected. Dupuytren contrac-ture is usually painless but causes problems due to limitation of hand func-tion and snagging of the curled fingers in pockets. It is age-related, usually bilateral and more common in men. There is a strong genetic component and it sometimes may be familial, with dominant inheritance. The condi-tion can be associated with plantar fibromatosis, Peyronie disease, alcohol misuse and chronic vibration injury. It is very slowly progressive. Often no treatment is required, but it can be treated medically by local injections of collagenase or surgically by fasciotomy if symptoms are troublesome.
Hereditary diseases of connective tissue

Hereditary diseases of connective tissue (HDCT) are typically and promi-nently characterised by connective tissue laxity, a range of musculoskel-etal, skin and internal organ dysfunction features and joint hypermobility. The main conditions are:
• Marfan syndrome
• Ehlers–Danlos syndromes (EDS)
• Osteogenesis imperfecta (p. 1086).

Marfan syndrome (1:5000) is caused by pathogenic variants in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin, an extracellular matrix protein. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Clinical features include long limbs, tall stature, scoliosis, high-arched palate, pes planus, joint hypermobility, skin striae and cutis laxa, aortic dilatation, aortic and mitral valve lesions, myopia and eye lens dislocation, pneumothoraces and myotonia. Loeys– Dietz syndrome is similar but is differentiated by the typical presence of aneurysms and arterial tortuosity.

Classical EDS can be caused by pathogenic loss-of-function variants in COL5A1 or COL5A2, which encode the alpha 1 and alpha 2 chains of type 5 collagen, or loss-of-function variants in COL1A1, which encodes the alpha 1 chain of type 1 collagen. Classical EDS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Clinical features include joint hypermobility combined with skin fragility and velvety or lax skin with extensive scarring. Vascular EDS (vEDS) is caused by pathogenic loss-of-function variants in COL3A1, which encodes type III collagen. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. The most important complications are blood vessel dissection and rupture as well as hollow organ rupture, which are poten-tially fatal. Easy bruising and thin skin are common features. Generalised hypermobility is present in about one-third of patients. Treatment is with angiotensin receptor blockers or β-blockers to try to reduce the risk of vascular events. Hypermobile Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (hEDS), which is also known as EDS type 3, is used to describe a polygenic form of joint hypermobility. Typical features are recurrent dislocations, easy bruising, gastrointestinal symptoms, pelvic and bladder symptoms and postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS), in which there is dizziness, hypotension and an increased heart rate on standing. Patients with hEDS who come to specialist care with widespread pains are often noted to have neurodiversity (autism, ADHD) with interoception and sensory processing risk factors. The Beighton score is useful to characterise the degree of joint hypermobility in all EDS types (Box 25.80) and is a key part of diagnosing hEDS (Box 25.81). In the EDS Society 2017 nosology, the term hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD) can be assigned as a diagnosis where some features of hEDS are present but where there is no generalised joint hypermobility (see Box 25.81).

Pigmented villonodular synovitis is an uncommon proliferative disorder of synovium, which typically affects young adults. It is caused by a somatic chromosomal translocation in synovial cells that places the CSF1 gene downstream of the COL6A3 gene promoter. The result is local over-production of M-CSF, which causes accumulation of macrophages in the joint. The presentation is with joint swelling, limitation of movement and local discomfort. The diagnosis can be confirmed by MRI or synovial biopsy. Treatment is by surgical or radiation synovectomy.
Scoliosis

Scoliosis is characterised by an abnormal lateral curvature of the spine of greater than 10 degrees. Scoliosis may be secondary to known dis-orders or idiopathic. In about 20% of cases, scoliosis is secondary to a neuromuscular disorder, such as muscular dystrophy, cerebral palsy or neurofibromatosis. It may also occur in association with hereditary connective tissue diseases, such as Marfan syndrome. Scoliosis may also develop in later life, usually because of structural changes in the spine from degenerative change. The term idiopathic scoliosis is used to describe the remaining cases where there is no obvious cause. In fact, there is strong evidence from twin studies that idiopathic scoliosis is genetically mediated, in keeping with the finding that it is evident during childhood or adolescence. It is often asymptomatic, but it can persist into adulthood and may become symptomatic, associated with evolving degenerative changes. The diagnosis of scoliosis can be made clinically by physical examina-tion and confirmed by X-ray. External bracing and/or surgical interven-tion may be considered in adolescents with severe deformities to correct deformity or prevent progression, but the evidence base is poor. In adult-hood, treatment is symptomatic in nature with analgesics, NSAIDs or antineuropathic medications.
Spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis

Spondylolysis describes a break in the integrity of the vertebral neural arch. The principal cause is an acquired defect in the pars interarticula-ris due to a fracture, mainly seen in gymnasts, dancers and runners, in whom it is an important cause of back pain. Spondylolisthesis describes the condition in which a defect causes slippage of a vertebra on the one below. This may be congenital, post-traumatic or degenerative. Rarely, it can result from metastatic destruction of the posterior ele-ments. Uncomplicated spondylolysis does not cause symptoms, but spondylolisthesis can lead to low back pain aggravated by standing and walking. Occasionally, symptoms of nerve root or spinal compression may occur. The diagnosis can be made on oblique X-rays of the lum-bar spine, but MRI may be required if there is neurological involvement. Advice on posture and muscle-strengthening exercises is required in mild cases. Surgical fusion is indicated for severe and recurrent low back pain. Surgical decompression is mandatory prior to fusion in patients with significant lumbar stenosis or symptoms of cauda equina compression.
Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis and SAPHO syndrome

Chronic non-bacterial osteomyelitis (CNO) typically occurs in children, adolescents and young adults, and is characterised by pain, osteitis and osteosclerosis of affected bones. It may target a single bone or multiple bones. CNO can occur in the absence of other features or be part of the synovitis–acne–pustulosis–hyperostosis–osteitis (SAPHO) syndrome. These disorders often target the clavicles and bones of the anterior chest wall, but other bones may be affected, including the mandible, spine, pelvis and lower limb bones. CNO-SAPHO syndrome may be part of a spectrum of autoinflammatory bone disease that includes psoriatic arthritis. Other features of CNO-SAPHO include a pustular rash affecting the palms and soles of the feet, enthesitis, spondylodiscitis, sacroiliitis and synovitis of peripheral joints. The diagnosis can be confirmed with imaging: whole-body MRI is recommended in children, whereas in adults recommended options include MRI, NaF PET-CT or bone scintigraphy combined with CT scanning (SPECT). Regional imaging with X-rays and CT show osteosclerosis and hyperostosis in chronic cases. Various treatments have been used, including glucocorticoids, csDMARDs, bis-phosphonates, anakinra, anti-TNF-α, and anti-IL-17, with most success arising from bDMARD use. The cause is unknown but has been sug-gested to be an autoinflammatory process triggered by a microorganism.

25.1 Which of the following statements about classical synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (csDMARDs) is true? A. Leflunomide has a short half-life and clears from the body quickly when it is stopped B. Sulfasalazine can stain contact lenses yellow C. It is recommended that the genotype for polymorphisms in the thiopurine S-methyltransferase (TPMT) gene should be checked D. Abnormalities of liver function tests and full blood count are common adverse effects of hydroxychloroquine therapy for rheumatoid arthritis E. Methotrexate is safe to take throughout pregnancy
Answer: B.

A is False – leflunomide has a long half-life and takes many months to clear from the body when stopped. Excretion of leflunomide can be expedited by a short course of cholestyramine. B is True – urine can be yellow-stained also. C is False – TPMT is checked before azathioprine is prescribed. 1 in 300 people have a homozygous TPMT allele genotype which leads to very slow drug metabolism, which increases the risk of azathioprine toxicity markedly. D is False – abnormal LFT and FBC are not common adverse effects of hydroxychloroquine. E is False – metho-trexate needs to be stopped 3 months before conception.

25.2 Which of the following statements about biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs/‘biologics’) is true? A. Biologics are carcinogenic B. Monoclonal antibodies to IL-17 are an effective treatment for rheumatoid arthritis C. Like all anti-TNF-α therapies, etanercept can be used in axial spondyloarthritis patients to also control associated Crohn disease D. All anti-TNF-α bDMARDs should be stopped in the third trimester of pregnancy since they cross the placenta and can cause immunosuppression in the neonate E. In ANCA-positive vasculitis, a commonly used regimen to induce remission is rituximab 1 g by infusion 2 weeks apart coupled with reducing doses of glucocorticoids followed by further infusions of 500–1000 mg once every 6 months
Answer: E.

A is False – biologics are not carcinogenic, but patients who develop cancer while on treatment may exhibit accelerated progression of the tumour due to suppression of the immune response. B is False – anti IL-17 therapy is effective in psoriatic arthritis and axial spondyloarthri-tis but not in rheumatoid arthritis. C is False – anti-TNF-α monoclonal antibodies generally are effective in enteropathic arthritis, but etaner-cept should be avoided as it not effective in the treatment of inflam-matory bowel disease. D is False – it is customary for most anti-TNF-α cDMARDs to be stopped because they cross the placenta, but an exception is certolizumab, which is a pegylated antibody that does not cross the placenta and can be used safely throughout pregnancy. E is True – various regimens of rituximab have been used in ANCA-positive vasculitis, but induction with rituximab 1000 mg 2 weeks apart followed by 500–1000 mg every 6 months is in common use.

25.3 Infections that affect the musculoskeletal system are not common but their effects can be severe. Which of the following statements about infections is true? A. The mortality of septic arthritis is about 1% B. Gonococcal septic arthritis is a symmetrical polyarthritis similar to rheumatoid arthritis

C. Diabetes is a particularly important risk factor for osteomyelitis, accounting for about 30% of cases D. Where TB of a joint is suspected, fluid should be drawn and analysed by microscopy, culture and PCR E. Tuberculosis may be accompanied by a reactive arthritis (Poncet disease), but unlike other forms of reactive arthritis, there is direct infection of the affected joints by tubercle bacilli
Answer: C.

A is False – overall, septic arthritis still has a mortality of about 10% despite advances in antimicrobial therapy. B is False – gonococcal infec-tion can present with a migratory arthralgia, low-grade fever and tenosyn-ovitis, which may precede the development of an oligo- or monoarthritis. Painful pustular skin lesions may also be present. C is True. D is False – culture of synovial fluid is positive in between 20% and 40% of cases, but examination of synovial fluid or synovial tissue by PCR can yield the diag-nosis more rapidly, with positive results in more than 95% of culture-posi-tive cases and 50%–60% of culture-negative cases. E is False – in Poncet disease the affected joints are not directly infected.

25.4 Which of the following statements about osteoarthritis (OA) is true? A. Across different ethnicities the prevalence of hip (10%) and knee (20%) OA has been found to be approximately the same B. Generalised erosive osteoarthritis should be treated with csDMARDs C. Unexplained early-onset OA requires additional investigation, as the condition can be caused by acromegaly, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, some skeletal dysplasias, Stickler syndrome and haemochromatosis amongst other conditions, for example D. The thoracic spine facet joints and intervertebral disc– vertebral end plates are the sites in the spine most often affected by an OA process E. Arthroplasty is an effective treatment for severe hip or knee OA. However, in over 50% of cases, joint replacements fail after 10 years
Answer: C.

A is False – the prevalence of OA rises progressively with age, and it has been estimated that 45% of all people develop knee OA and 25% hip OA at some point during life. Although some are asymptomatic, the lifetime risk of having a total hip or knee replacement for OA in someone aged 50 is about 11% for women and 8% for men in the UK. There are major ethnic differences in susceptibility: the prevalence of hip OA is lower in Africa, China, Japan and South Asia than in European countries, while that of knee OA is higher. B is False – in general, erosive OA does not respond to csDMARDs, though clinicians may in selected cases trial a csDMARD for a limited period of time. C is True – other conditions include X-linked hypophosphataemia and rare genetic conditions of car-tilage and connective tissue matrix. D is False – the cervical and lumbar spine facet joints and intervertebral disc–vertebral end plates are the sites most often affected by an OA process, where the disease complex is referred to as cervical and lumbar spondylosis, respectively. E is False – over 95% of joint replacements completed for hip or knee OA continue to function well into the second decade after surgery, and most provide life-long, pain-free function.

25.5 In the investigation and management of ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV), which of the following is true? A. The most common presentation of granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is with skin rash and renal involvement

B. Imaging of the lungs is not necessary if the diagnosis of GPA has been made otherwise C. Initial management of organ-threatening AAV is with mycophenolate or methotrexate plus glucocorticoids D. In eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), once the condition is in remission, treatment can be stopped and patients can be reassured and discharged from follow-up care E. Once remission of AAV is attained, rituximab is generally considered the most appropriate ongoing treatment to maintain remission
Answer: E.

A is False – the most common presentation of GPA is with epistaxis, nasal crusting and sinusitis, but haemoptysis and mucosal ulceration may also occur. Other head and neck features of GPA are deafness from inner ear involvement and proptosis from inflammation of the retro-orbital tissue. Skin rash and renal inflammatory involvement, though, are fea-tures of GPA. B is False – imaging of the upper airways, chest and nasal passages with MRI should always be considered, as airways involvement is common in GPA and defining the extent of GPA before treatment is started is advisable. C is False – initial management of organ-threatening AAV is with high-dose glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive therapy, such as pulse intravenous methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for 3 days coupled with intravenous rituximab 1 g given twice 2 weeks apart. Oral cyclophosphamide up to 2 mg/kg/day for 3 months, or pulsed IV cyclophosphamide 15 mg/kg (IV) every 2–3 weeks for 6–10 doses, can be used as an alternative to rituximab. D is False – whatever the subtype, patients with AAV must be followed on a regular and long-term basis since the condition tends to relapse, monitoring urinalysis for blood and protein, plasma creatinine, FBC, ESR, CRP, lung function and PR3 or MPO antibody titres. E is True – azathioprine, MTX or MMF can be used as an alternative to rituximab to maintain remission but are less effective.

25.6 Which of the following statements is true about X-linked hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets (XLH)? A. Women are more severely affected than men B. The main underlying mechanism of hypophosphataemia is an elevation in circulating parathyroid hormone levels which promote urinary excretion of phosphate C. Typical features on routine biochemical testing are an elevation in serum calcium and a reduction in serum phosphate with normal serum 25(OH)D concentrations D. Circulating concentrations of FGF23 are significantly elevated E. The condition is typically transmitted from affected fathers to their sons
Answer: D.

A is False – men are affected more severely than women as only one of the X-chromosomes carries a pathogenic variant in PHEX, the causal gene. B is False – although serum PTH can be elevated in XLH and high levels of PTH promote phosphate excretion, this is not the main cause of hypophosphataemia. C is False – although phosphate is low, serum calcium is normal or low in XLH. D is True – serum FGF23 is raised in XLH and this is the main cause of the hypophosphataemia, although the causal gene is PHEX, which is thought to regulate FGF23 production by mechanisms that are still poorly understood. E is False – the condition is X-linked, which means that father-to-son transmission is never observed. It is transmitted from mothers who are carriers of pathogenic variants in PHEX to their sons.

25.7 A 75-year-old woman presents with pain and stiffness in her shoulders of 8 weeks’ duration. Examination is unremarkable and muscle power is normal. Investigations reveal a normal full blood count and normal routine biochemistry with CK 125 U/mL. The erythrocyte sedimentation rare is 55 mm/hr (normal < 30) and CRP is 25 mg/L (normal < 5). Immunology screen is negative. Testing for rheumatoid factor is positive, with a value of 8 units/ mL (normal < 5.1). What is the most likely diagnosis? A. Rheumatoid arthritis B. Fibromyalgia C. Polymyositis D. Polymyalgia rheumatica E. Calcific tendinitis rotator cuff
Answer: D.

A is False – the clinical picture is not consistent with rheumatoid arthri-tis, which typically presents with swelling and stiffness of the small joints of the hands and feet. Although rheumatoid factor is slightly raised, this is almost certainly a false positive, as low concentrations of rheumatoid factor are common above the age of 70. B is False – fibromyalgia is asso-ciated with generalised pain and local tender spots. The symptoms are not localised to the shoulder girdle and inflammatory markers are normal in fibromyalgia. C is False – the predominant symptom in polymyositis is muscle weakness rather than pain, and CK is almost always raised. D is True – the clinical features of proximal muscle pain and stiffness affecting the shoulder girdle in a woman of this age in the absence of muscle weakness is typical of polymyalgia rheumatica. E is False – although calcific tendinitis can cause shoulder pain, it is not associated with an increase in inflammatory markers like CRP and ESR.
