Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is a heterogeneous group of immune-mediated conditions of acute peripheral nerve inflammation, with an incidence of 1–2/100 000/year. In Europe and North America, the most common variant is an acute inflammatory demyelinating poly-neuropathy (AIDP). Axonal variants, either motor (acute motor axonal neuropathy, AMAN) or sensorimotor, are more common in China and Japan, and account for 10% of GBS in Western countries, often asso-ciated with Campylobacter jejuni. The hallmark is an acute paralysis evolving over days or weeks, with loss of tendon reflexes. About two-thirds of those with AIDP have a prior history of infection, and an auto-immune response triggered by the preceding infection is thought to cause peripheral nerve inflammation. A number of GBS variants have been described, associated with specific anti-ganglioside antibodies; the best recognised is Miller Fisher syndrome, which involves anti-GQ1b antibodies.
Clinical features

Distal paraesthesia and pain precede muscle weakness that ascends rapidly from lower to upper limbs and is more marked proximally than distally. Facial and bulbar weakness commonly develops, and respira-tory weakness requiring ventilatory support occurs in 20% of cases. Weakness progresses over a maximum of 4 weeks (usually less). Rapid deterioration to respiratory failure can develop within hours. Examination shows diffuse weakness with loss of reflexes. Miller Fisher syndrome presents with internal and external ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia.
Investigations

The CSF protein is raised, but may be normal in the first 10 days. There is usually no increase in CSF white cell count (> 50×10 6 cells/L suggests an alternative diagnosis; though the cell count may be considerably higher in HIV infection). Electrophysiological changes may emerge after a week or so, with conduction block and multifocal motor slowing, sometimes most evident proximally as delayed F waves. Antibodies to the ganglio-side GM1 are found in about 25%, usually the motor axonal form. Other causes of an acute neuromuscular paralysis should be considered (e.g. poliomyelitis, botulism, acute intermittent porphyria, diphtheria, spinal cord syndromes or myasthenia), via the history and examination. Nerve roots are an important site of inflammation, and contrast uptake is some-times seen here in contrast-enhanced MRI spinal cord imaging.
Management

Active treatment with plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobu-lin therapy shortens the duration of ventilation and improves progno-sis. In severe GBS, both intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and plasma exchange started within 2 weeks of onset hasten recovery, with similar rates of adverse effects but IVIg treatment is significantly more likely to be completed than plasma exchange. The choice of treatment often depends on logistical considerations. Overall, 80% of patients recover completely within 3–6 months, 4% die and the remainder suffer resid-ual neurological disability, which can be severe. Regular monitoring of respiratory function (vital capacity) is needed in the acute phase, as res-piratory failure may develop with little warning. Adverse prognostic fea-tures include older age, rapid deterioration to ventilation and evidence of axonal loss on EMG. Supportive measures to prevent pressure sores and deep venous thrombosis are essential.

The most common axonal and demyelinating causes of polyneuropathy are shown in Box 27.97. A chronic symmetrical axonal polyneuropathy, evolving over months or years, is the most common form of chronic neuropathy. Diabetes mellitus is the most common cause but in about 25%–50% no cause can be found.
Hereditary neuropathy

Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease (CMT) is an umbrella term for the inherited neuropathies. The members of this group of syndromes have different clinical and genetic features. The most common CMT is the autosomal dominantly inherited CMT type 1, usually caused by a duplication in the PMP-22 gene. Common signs are distal wasting (‘inverted champagne bottle’ legs), often with pes cavus, and predominantly motor involve-ment. X-linked and recessively inherited forms of CMT, causing demyeli-nating or axonal neuropathies, also occur.
Chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy

The acquired chronic demyelinating neuropathies include chronic inflam-matory demyelinating peripheral neuropathy (CIDP), multifocal motor neuropathy (see above) and paraprotein-associated demyelinating neu-ropathy. CIDP typically presents with relapsing or progressive motor and sensory changes, evolving over more than 8 weeks (in distinction to the more acute GBS). It is important to recognise, as it usually responds to intravenous immunoglobulin and other immunotherapies such as gluco-corticoids or plasma exchange. Some 10% of patients with acquired demyelinating polyneuropathy have an abnormal serum paraprotein, sometimes associated with a monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance (MGUS) or lymphop-roliferative malignancy. Those with distal sensory involvement and prom-inent neuropathic tremor may also demonstrate positive antibodies to myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG antibodies).

Trauma usually damages either the upper or the lower parts of the brachial plexus, according to the mechanics of the injury. The clinical features depend on the anatomical site of the damage (Box 27.101). Lower parts of the brachial plexus are vulnerable to infiltration from breast or apical lung tumours (Pancoast tumour) or damage by ther-apeutic irradiation. The lower plexus may also be compressed by a cervical rib or fibrous band between C7 and the first rib at the thoracic outlet. Neuralgic amyotrophy (also known as brachial neuritis) presents as an acute brachial plexopathy of probable inflammatory origin. Severe shoul-der pain precedes the appearance of a patchy upper brachial plexus lesion, with motor and/or sensory involvement. There is no specific treat-ment and recovery is often incomplete; it may recur in about 25% and there is a rare autosomal dominant hereditary form. The appearance of vesicles should indicate the alternative diagnosis of motor zoster.

Lumbosacral plexus lesions may be caused by neoplastic infiltration or compression by retroperitoneal haematomas. A small-vessel vasculopa-thy can produce a unilateral or bilateral lumbar plexopathy in association with diabetes mellitus (‘diabetic amyotrophy’) or an idiopathic form in non-diabetic patients. This presents with painful wasting of the quadri-ceps with weakness of knee extension and an absent knee reflex.

Spinal root lesions (radiculopathy) are described above. Clinical features include muscle weakness and wasting and dermatomal sensory and reflex loss, which reflect the pattern of the roots involved. Pain in the muscles innervated by the affected roots may be prominent.
This is the most common cause of acutely evolving, fatigable weakness and preferentially affects ocular, facial and bulbar muscles.
Pathophysiology

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease, most commonly (80% of cases) caused by antibodies to acetylcholine receptors in the post-junc-tional membrane of the neuromuscular junction. The resultant blockage of neuromuscular transmission and complement-mediated inflammatory response reduces the number of acetylcholine receptors and damages the end plate (Fig. 27.65). Other antibodies can produce a similar clinical pic-ture, most notably autoantibodies to muscle-specific kinase (MuSK), which is involved in the regulation and maintenance of acetylcholine receptors. About 15% of patients (mainly those with late onset) have a thy-moma, most of the remainder displaying thymic follicular hyperplasia. Myasthenic patients are more likely to have associated organ-specific autoimmune diseases. Triggers are not always evident but some drugs (e.g. penicillamine) can precipitate an antibody-mediated myasthenic syndrome that may persist after drug withdrawal. Other drugs, especially aminoglycosides and quinolones, may exacerbate the neuromuscular blockade and should be avoided in patients with myasthenia.
Clinical features

Myasthenia gravis usually presents between the ages of 15 and 50 years and there is a female preponderance in younger patients. In older patients, males are more commonly affected. It tends to run a relapsing and remitting course. The most evident symptom is fatigable muscle weakness; move-ment is initially strong but rapidly weakens as muscle use continues. Worsening of symptoms towards the end of the day or following exer-cise is characteristic. There are no sensory signs or signs of involve-ment of the CNS, although weakness of the oculomotor muscles may mimic a central eye movement disorder. The first symptoms are usu-ally intermittent ptosis or diplopia but weakness of chewing, swallow-ing, speaking or limb movement also occurs. Resting of the eyelids (looking downwards) may be followed by increased reflex elevation with up-gaze (so-called Cogan lid twitch sign). Any limb muscle may be affected, most commonly those of the shoulder girdle; the patient is unable to undertake tasks above shoulder level, such as combing the hair, without frequent rests. Respiratory muscles may be involved and respiratory failure is an avoidable cause of death. Aspiration may occur if the cough is ineffectual. Ventilatory support is required where weakness is severe or of abrupt onset. Subtypes of myasthenia gravis include ocular myasthenia, where disease is often confined to eye muscles, and generalised myasthenia, where more widespread muscle involvement is seen which can include bulbar and respiratory muscles. There is often overlap between these subtypes. Congenital (genetic) forms of myasthenia also exist and do not have an autoimmune basis.
Investigations

Serological investigations play an important role in the diagnosis of myas-thenia gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are highly specific, but seronegative cases also exist and further serological testing, e.g. for MuSK antibodies, should be performed if AChR antibodies are negative. Anti-MuSK antibodies are associated with prominent bulbar involvement.

Neurophysiological assessment is important in establishing the diag-nosis. Repetitive stimulation during nerve conduction studies may show a characteristic decremental response if the muscle has been clinically affected. Specialised single fibre EMG changes such as ‘jitter’ may also be seen. All patients should have a thoracic CT or MRI to exclude thy-moma, especially those without anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Screening for associated autoimmune disorders, particularly thyroid dis-ease, is important. Intravenous injection of the short-acting anticholinesterase edropho-nium bromide (the Tensilon test) is less widely used than before and requires specialist involvement in cases where there is diagnostic doubt. Structural imaging (e.g. MRI of brainstem) may be needed to exclude alternative diagnoses that can cause ocular–bulbar weakness.
Management

The goals of treatment are to maximise the activity of acetylcholine at remaining receptors in the neuromuscular junctions and to limit or abolish the immunological attack on motor end plates. The duration of action of acetylcholine is prolonged by inhibiting ace-tylcholinesterase. The most commonly used anticholinesterase drug is pyridostigmine. Muscarinic side-effects, including diarrhoea and colic, may be controlled by propantheline. Myasthenia gravis can cause life-threatening disease, often referred to as ‘myasthenic crisis’, when bulbar and respiratory failure occurs. Prompt acute immunotherapy, often using intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, is required, together with a longer-term immuno-suppressive approach. Supportive respiratory care, and early involve-ment of intensive care teams, is important during these periods. Immunological treatment of myasthenia is outlined in Box 27.102. Thymoma should be managed with joint oncology and thoracic surgery input. Prognosis is variable and remissions may occur spontaneously. When myasthenia is entirely ocular, prognosis is excellent and disability slight. Younger seropositive patients with generalised disease may bene-fit from thymectomy in the absence of thymoma, while older patients are less likely to have a remission despite treatment. Rapid progression of the disease more than 5 years after onset is uncommon. Some medications, such as aminoglycoside antibiotics, can worsen myasthenia gravis (myaware.org provides a list of drugs to avoid).
27.102 Immunological treatment of myasthenia
Acute treatments
Intravenous immunoglobulin
• Lowers production of antibodies and rapidly reduces weakness
Plasma exchange
• Removing antibody from the blood may produce marked improvement; this is usually brief, so is normally reserved for myasthenic crisis or for pre-operative preparation
Long-term treatments
Glucocorticoid treatment

• Improvement can be preceded by marked exacerbation of myasthenic symptoms, so treatment should be initiated cautiously in an environment where deterioration can be managed. In an outpatient setting many neurologists start corticosteroids at a low dose and increase gradually. If urgent high-dose steroids are needed this may require hospital admission
• Usually necessary to continue for months or years, risking adverse effects
Pharmacological immunosuppression treatment
• Azathioprine 2.5 mg/kg daily reduces the necessary dosage of glucocorticoids and may allow withdrawal. Effect on clinical features may be delayed for months
• Mycophenolate mofetil lacking
• Antibody based biologic therapies, e.g. Efgartigimod alfa
Thymectomy
• Likely to be required for thymoma
• Should be considered in any antibody-positive patient under 45 years with symptoms not confined to extraocular muscles, unless the disease has been established for more than 7 years

Other rarer conditions can present with muscle weakness due to impaired transmission across the neuromuscular junction. The most common of these is the Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), which can occur as an inflammatory or paraneoplastic phenome-non. Antibodies to pre-synaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (see Fig. 27.65) impair transmitter release. Patients may have autonomic dysfunction (e.g. dry mouth) in addition to muscle weakness but the cardinal clinical sign is absence of tendon reflexes, which return after sustained contraction of the relevant muscle. The condition is asso-ciated with underlying malignancy in a high percentage of cases and investigation must be directed towards identifying any neoplasm. Diagnosis is made electrophysiologically on the presence of post-te-tanic potentiation of motor response to nerve stimulation at a frequency of 20–50/sec. Treatment is with 3,4-diaminopyridine, or pyridostigmine and immunosuppression.

Muscle disease, either hereditary or acquired, is rare. Most typically, it presents with a proximal symmetrical weakness. Diagnosis is depend-ent on recognition of clinical clues, such as cardiorespiratory involve-ment, evolution, family history, exposure to drugs, the presence of contractures, myotonia and other systemic features, and on investi-gation findings, most importantly EMG and muscle biopsy. Hereditary syndromes include the muscular dystrophies, muscle channelopathies, metabolic myopathies (including mitochondrial diseases) and congen-ital myopathies.

These are inherited disorders with progressive muscle destruction and may be associated with cardiac and/or respiratory involvement and sometimes non-myopathic features (Box 27.103). Myotonic dystrophy is the most common, with a prevalence of about 12/100 000.
Clinical features

The pattern of the clinical features is defined by the specific syn-dromes. Onset is often in childhood, although some patients, espe-cially those with myotonic dystrophy, may present as adults. Wasting and weakness are usually symmetrical, without fasciculation or sen-sory loss, and tendon reflexes are usually preserved until a late stage. Weakness is usually proximal, except in myotonic dystrophy type 1, when it is distal.
Investigations

The diagnosis can be confirmed by specific molecular genetic testing, supplemented with EMG and muscle biopsy if necessary. Creatine kinase is markedly elevated in the dystrophinopathies (Duchenne and Becker) but is normal or moderately elevated in the other dystrophies. Screening for an associated cardiac abnormality (cardiomyopathy or dysrhythmia) is important.
Management

There is no specific therapy for most of these conditions but physio-therapy and occupational therapy help patients cope with their disabil-ity. Glucocorticoids can be used in Duchenne muscular dystrophy but side-effects should be anticipated and avoided by dose modification. Treatment of associated cardiac failure or arrhythmia (with pacemaker insertion if necessary) may be required; similarly, management of res-piratory complications (including nocturnal hypoventilation) can improve quality of life. Improvements in non-invasive ventilation have led to sig-nificant improvements in survival for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Genetic counselling is important.
27.104 Inherited disorders of muscle metabolism

There are a large number of rare inherited disorders that interfere with the biochemical pathways that maintain the energy supply (adenosine triphosphate, ATP) to muscles. These are mostly recessively inherited deficiencies in the enzymes necessary for glycogen or fatty acid (β-ox-idation) metabolism (Box 27.104). They typically present with muscle weakness and pain.
Mitochondrial disorders

Mitochondrial diseases are discussed on page 47. Mitochondria are pres-ent in all tissues and dysfunction causes widespread effects on vision (optic atrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, cataracts), hearing (sensorineural deafness) and the endocrine, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and renal systems. Any combination of these should raise the suspicion of a mitochondrial disor-der, especially if there is evidence of maternal transmission.
27.105 Mitochondrial syndromes

Mitochondrial dysfunction can be caused by alterations in either mitochondrial DNA or genes encoding for oxidative processes. Genetic abnormalities or pathogenic variants in mitochondrial DNA may affect single individuals and single tissues (most commonly muscle). Thus, patients with exercise intolerance, myalgia and sometimes recurrent myoglobinuria may have isolated pathogenic variants in genes encoding for oxidation pathways. Inherited disorders of the oxidative pathways of the respiratory chain in mitochondria cause a group of disorders, either restricted to the muscle or associated with non-myopathic features (Box 27.105). Many of these mitochondrial disorders are inherited via the mitochondrial genome, down the maternal line. Diagnosis is based on clinical appearances, supported by muscle biopsy appearance (usually with ‘ragged red’ and/ or cytochrome oxidase-negative fibres), and specific pathogenic variants either on blood or, more reliably, muscle testing. Pathogenic variants may be due either to point pathogenic variants or to deletions of mitochon-drial DNA.

A disorder called Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is char-acterised by acute or subacute loss of vision, most frequently in males, due to bilateral optic atrophy. Three point pathogenic variants account for more than 90% of LHON cases.
Channelopathies

Inherited abnormalities of the sodium, calcium and chloride ion chan-nels in striated muscle produce various syndromes of familial periodic paralysis, myotonia and malignant hyperthermia, which may be rec-ognised by their clinical characteristics and potassium abnormalities (Box 27.106). Genetic testing is available.
These include the inflammatory myopathies, or myopathy associated with a range of metabolic and endocrine disorders or drug and toxin exposure (Fig. 27.66).

27.1. A patient describes a two-day history of progressive tingling and numbness, starting in both feet but now including both arms. She has difficulty walking today. Examination shows mildly reduced sensation in arms and legs and mild weakness, with reduced reflexes. Where is the most likely location of the lesion?
A. B. C. D. E.
Cerebral hemispheres Spinal cord Nerve roots and peripheral nerve Neuromuscular junction Muscle
Answer: C.

The symmetrical involvement of both sensory and motor modalities, together with reduced reflexes, is consistent with a peripheral nerve localisation. Evolution of symptoms over this time course suggests an inflammatory cause, such as Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS). Prompt recognition is important since bulbar and respiratory weakness can develop, and supportive care, including respiratory support, can be required. GBS responds to treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange. Neuromuscular disease and muscle disease do not cause sensory disturbance, and lesions in the spinal cord or cerebral hemispheres are usually associated with brisk reflexes.
27.2. Which of the following statements about neuroimaging is true?

A. Computed tomography should always be performed before lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis B. Computed tomography is the investigation of choice for a thunderclap headache C. Accurate imaging of cerebral blood vessels requires invasive angiography D. A diagnosis of multiple sclerosis (MS) always requires magnetic resonance (MR) imaging E. Parkinson disease should only be diagnosed following a positive dopamine active transporter (DAT) scan
Answer: B.

Thunderclap headache (a very severe headache of abrupt onset, reaching maximum intensity within 60 seconds) should always raise the possibility of a serious underlying cause and is a medical emergency. An important cause is subarachnoid haemorrhage. Computed tomography is a rapid and widely available imaging modality for detection of acute bleeding. Modern neuroimaging allows blood vessels to be visualised without the need for invasive angiography. MR imaging plays an impor-tant role in the diagnosis of MS by helping to demonstrate dissemination of lesions in time and space, and excluding alterative diagnoses; how-ever, MS can also be diagnosed in settings where MR imaging is not available.

27.3. A 65-year-old man from the UK presents with a three-day history of bilateral leg weakness and numbness. Last year he had an episode of left optic neuritis, which did not fully resolve. On examination he is afebrile, with severe bilateral leg weakness (MRC power grade 1/5 throughout) and has brisk lower limb reflexes with a sensory level at T4. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows an inflammatory lesion in the thoracic spinal cord stretching from T3 to T7. What is the most specific diagnostic investigation to be performed next?
A. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis for oligoclonal bands B. CSF analysis for schistosomiasis
C. Blood test for aquaporin-4 antibodies D. MRI of the head E. Whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)
Answer: C.

The clinical syndrome is severe optic nerve and spinal cord inflamma-tion, with imaging evidence of longitudinally extensive transverse myeli-tis (LETM). While optico-spinal inflammation is most commonly seen in multiple sclerosis (MS), the severe nature of both lesions and the long spinal cord lesion (over 3 vertebral segments in length) are not typical for MS. While infections, including schistosomiasis, can cause long spinal cord lesions, the most likely cause for this clinical picture is neuromyeli-tis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), and aquaporin-4 antibodies are highly specific for this diagnosis. NMOSD can also occur with myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies, as well as seronegative cases.
27.4. Which of the following statements about cryptococcal meningitis is true?

A. Only immunosuppressed individuals develop cryptococcal meningitis B. Cryptococcal meningitis is a cause of high cerebrospinal fluid protein and glucose C. Cerebrospinal fluid India ink test is the investigation of choice for cryptococcal meningitis D. High cerebrospinal fluid pressure in cryptococcal meningitis is treated with frequent, often daily, lumbar punctures E. Cryptococcal antigen may be present in cerebrospinal fluid, but not in the serum
Answer: D.

Although cryptococcal meningitis (CM) usually occurs in the immuno-suppressed, it can occur in the immunocompetent. CM results in a high cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) protein and low CSF glucose. Cryptococcal antigen is present in the CSF and sometimes the serum. The India ink test is still used in some regions but sensitivity is limited, particularly in non-HIV-related CM. High CSF pressure in CM is treated with frequent, sometimes daily, lumbar punctures.
27.5. Which of the following statements about seizures is true?

A. All patients who have had a confirmed seizure should be told not to drive B. The electroencephalogram (EEG) is always abnormal in people with epilepsy C. Neuroimaging should be performed on all individuals who have had a generalised seizure D. Neuroimaging is not required for individuals who have had a focal seizure E. Anticonvulsants should be started after a first seizure
Answer: A.

It is the physician’s prime duty to ensure that the patient is aware of the legal obligation to stop driving and inform the relevant driving authority after having a single seizure. In the UK, patients are usually eligible to drive a motor vehicle six months after a single seizure provided there are no factors that would increase the risk of further seizure. There are far more stringent criteria for heavy goods and public service vehicle drivers. EEG can be normal in people with epilepsy, and neuroimaging is particu-larly important in individuals who have focal-onset seizures.

27.6. A 75-year-old woman presents with a transient episode of right facial weakness, right hand weakness and dysarthria, witnessed by her daughter. At her clinic appointment she has a blood pressure of 175/95 mmHg. Which area of the brain is likely to have been involved in her symptoms?
A. B. C. D. E.
Right parietal lobe Left occipital lobe Brainstem Left frontal lobe All of the above
Answer: D.
The right face and hand weakness makes involvement of the con-tralateral motor cortex, in the precentral gyrus of frontal lobe, most likely.
27.7. In the same patient, stenosis of a cervical artery is found on a CT angiogram of her neck vessels. Which stenosis or stenoses would be an indication for surgical intervention?
A. B. C. D. E.
Left internal carotid stenosis Right carotid stenosis Left vertebral artery stenosis Left subclavian stenosis Left external carotid stenosis
Answer: A.
Left internal carotid stenosis: stenoses of the other arteries indicate large vessel atheroma, but none would be expected to lead to a left hemisphere transient ischaemic attack.
27.8. For the same patient, a left carotid endarterectomy is planned. Which of the following treatments should be considered (choose all that apply)?
A. B. C. D. E.
Carotid endarterectomy only Blood pressure lowering LDL cholesterol lowering Antiplatelet agent Anticoagulant
Answer: B, C, D.

Blood pressure lowering, LDL cholesterol lowering and an antiplatelet are all indicated here in addition to carotid endarterectomy. An anticoag-ulant is only indicated if atrial fibrillation is identified.

27.9. A 54-year-old man has a sudden onset of a severe left hemiparesis and left facial weakness. He has no pain. He is inattentive to his left side. He has atrial fibrillation. He arrives at the emergency department 1 hour after the onset of the symptoms. Which are the best differential diagnoses (choose all that apply)?
A. B. C. D. E.
Ischaemic stroke Intracerebral haemorrhage Subarachnoid haemorrhage Transient ischaemic attack Brain tumour
Answer: A, B.

This man has presented with an acute focal neurological deficit that is severe at 3 hours. This is unlikely to be due to a TIA, and a subarachnoid haemorrhage usually presents with headache or, when severe, coma. Rarely a bleed from a ruptured aneurysm can be predominantly paren-chymal with little subarachnoid blood. The sudden onset of symptoms makes a brain tumour unlikely. Both an intracerebral haemorrhage and an ischaemic stroke present with a stroke syndrome.

27.10. In the same patient, a CT of the brain is performed within 30 minutes of his arrival to the emergency department, and this CT head is normal at first review. Which of the following statements best describes the situation?

A. An ischaemic stroke is the likeliest diagnosis and thrombolysis is appropriate B. An ischaemic stroke is the likeliest diagnosis and thrombolysis is not appropriate C. Multiple sclerosis is the likeliest diagnosis and steroids are most appropriate D. Immediate thrombectomy is the next best step E. Intravenous heparin is appropriate
Answer: A.

A normal CT scan does not preclude a diagnosis of ischaemic stroke, which is the most likely diagnosis here. Because this is the case, throm-bolysis is the most important action; thrombectomy is also likely to be indicated, but would need the identification of an occluded artery with an angiogram. A sudden onset of severe cortical symptoms is not a common presentation of multiple sclerosis. Intravenous heparins do not improve recovery in acute ischaemic stroke, even with atrial fibrillation.

The ability to see is an important aspect of everyday life. Although rarely a cause of mortality, visual impairment can have a profoundly negative impact on socioeconomic status, and the prevalence of blindness is dis-proportionately increased in less affluent parts of the world. Examination of the eye should be an integral part of clinical assessment. Abnormalities of the eye can be due to intrinsic ocular abnormalities or can be manifestations of systemic disease. Globally, although refrac-tive errors and cataract remain the main causes of visual impairment, significant progress has occurred in prevention and treatment. Public health measures have reduced diseases of poor hygiene and unclean water, such as trachoma and onchocerciasis, and greater access to surgery has reduced the burden of untreated cataract and glaucoma. However, inherited retinal dystrophies, the leading cause of blindness in working-age people, remains untreatable, and with longevity comes age-related macular degeneration, the leading cause of sight loss in ageing.
Visual pathways, innervation of the eye and the control of eye movement are discussed in Chapter 27.

The eyelids serve essential protective and functional roles, including shielding the eye, distributing the tear film and maintaining ocular surface integrity. Structurally, they consist of tarsal plates containing meibomian glands, the orbicularis oculi muscle (responsible for eyelid closure and innervated by the facial nerve), the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (which elevates the upper eyelid, innervated by the oculomotor nerve), and the Müller muscle (sympathetically innervated, assisting in eyelid elevation). Sensory innervation is provided by the trigeminal nerve, with the ophthalmic (V 1) and maxillary (V 2) divisions innervating the upper and lower eyelids, respectively.

The eye comprises three principal layers (Fig. 28.1): the outer fibrous tunic (sclera/cornea), the middle vascular tunic (uvea), and the inner neu-ral tunic (retina), each playing distinct roles in maintaining ocular function.

• Fibrous tunic. The sclera is a dense, avascular connective tissue providing structural integrity and serves as the attachment site for the extraocular muscles. The cornea is a transparent, avascular structure composed of six layers: the epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Dua layer, Descemet membrane and endothelium. It serves as the primary refractive element of the eye, contributing approxi-mately 40 dioptres of the total refractive power.

• Vascular tunic (uvea). The uvea includes the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The choroid is a highly vascularised tissue rich in mel-anocytes, which absorb stray light and supply nutrients to the outer retinal layers. The ciliary body comprises the ciliary muscle, responsible for lens accommodation, and the ciliary processes, which secrete aqueous humour into the anterior chamber. The iris contains smooth muscle fibres (sphincter pupillae and dilator pupil-lae) that modulate pupil size, thus controlling the amount of light reaching the retina.

• Neural tunic (retina). The retina is a complex, multi-layered struc-ture where phototransduction occurs. It contains photoreceptors (rods and cones), bipolar cells, ganglion cells, horizontal cells and amacrine cells. The rods are responsible for scotopic (low-light) vision, while cones mediate photopic (daylight) and colour vision, with subtypes sensitive to short (S), medium (M) and long (L) wavelengths of light. The macula, particularly the fovea centralis, contains a high density of cones and is critical for high-resolution central vision.

The orbit is a bony cavity that houses and protects the eye, along with its associated structures, including the extraocular muscles, optic nerve, blood vessels and fat. The orbital walls are formed by seven bones: the frontal, sphenoid, zygomatic, maxillary, palatine, lacrimal and ethmoid bones. The orbit’s primary function is to protect the eye from trauma and to provide a stable and functional environment for ocular movements.
• Orbital fat. Orbital fat cushions the eye within the orbit, allowing for smooth movement and acting as a shock absorber.

• Orbital blood supply. The ophthalmic artery, a branch of the internal carotid artery, provides the primary blood supply to the orbit and eye, branching into the central retinal artery, ciliary arteries, and other branches that nourish the ocular structures.

• Venous drainage. Venous blood is drained from the orbit via the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, which empty into the cavern-ous sinus. This venous network is essential for maintaining proper intraorbital pressure and function.

The lacrimal system plays a vital role in the production, distribution, and drainage of tears, which are essential for ocular surface health and vision. Tears provide lubrication, remove debris and contain antimicrobial pro-teins such as lysozyme.

• Lacrimal gland. Located in the superolateral aspect of the orbit, the lacrimal gland produces the aqueous layer of the tear film. Stimulation of the lacrimal gland is primarily mediated by the para-sympathetic nervous system via the facial nerve (7th cranial nerve).

• Tear film. The tear film comprises three layers: the lipid layer (pro-duced by the meibomian glands), the aqueous layer (from the lacri-mal gland), and the mucin layer (from goblet cells in the conjunctiva). This multi-layered structure stabilises the tear film and prevents rapid evaporation.

• Tear drainage. Tears drain through the puncta located at the medial canthus of the eyelids into the canaliculi, then into the lacrimal sac, and finally through the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal cavity. Proper functioning of this system is crucial to prevent conditions such as dry eye syndrome or epiphora (excessive tearing).

The eye’s movement is controlled by six extraocular muscles: the supe-rior, inferior, medial and lateral rectus muscles, and the superior and infe-rior oblique muscles (Fig. 28.2). These muscles are innervated by three cranial nerves:
• Oculomotor nerve (3rd cranial nerve). Innervates the superior, inferior and medial rectus muscles, as well as the inferior oblique and leva-tor palpebrae superioris muscles.
• Trochlear nerve (4th cranial nerve). Innervates the superior oblique muscle, which intorts and depresses the eye.
• Abducens nerve (6th cranial nerve). Innervates the lateral rectus muscle, responsible for abducting the eye.

Coordination of these muscles ensures smooth, precise and con-jugate eye movements, allowing for proper alignment of the eyes and enabling binocular vision. Dysfunction in any of these muscles or their innervating nerves can lead to strabismus or diplopia.
Ophthalmic investigations encompass a wide range of diagnostic tests and imaging techniques that are essential for the evaluation, diagnosis and management of eye disorders (Fig. 28.3).

Slit-lamp biomicroscopy is a fundamental technique that allows for a detailed examination of the anterior segment of the eye, including the cornea, iris, lens and anterior chamber. To visualise the posterior seg-ment, a fundus lens is used. This allows for a non-contact stereoscopic view of the retina.

Intraocular pressure (IOP) refers to the fluid pressure inside the eye, which is regulated by the balance between the production and drain-age of aqueous humour in the anterior chamber of the eye. Normal IOP ranges from 10 to 21 mmHg. Elevated IOP is a significant risk factor for glaucoma, a group of eye diseases that can lead to optic nerve damage and vision loss. The gold standard for measuring IOP is Goldmann Applanation Tonometry. This device is commonly attached on an ophthalmic slit lamp but requires a degree of clinical experience to use. Alternative methods designed for the non-ophthalmologist such as rebound tonometry (e.g. iCare) or non-contract tonometry (the ‘air puff test’) are useful screening tools. If specialised equip-ment is not available, a rough IOP estimation can be made by gently palpating the eyeball through the upper eyelid with the index fingers, applying alternating pressure. This technique may help differentiate between a very hard eye with increased IOP, as seen in acute angle closure, and a very soft eye. However, caution should be exercised in cases of suspected ocular injury, especially if perforation is possible.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging modality that provides high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina, optic nerve and macula. It plays a critical role in diagnosing and monitoring retinal conditions such as age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular oedema and glaucoma.

Fundus photography captures detailed images of the retina, optic disc, macula and posterior pole, allowing for documentation and longitudinal comparison of retinal changes over time. Advances in wide-field imaging technology now enable up to 200 degrees of the retina to be photo-graphed in a single image through an undilated pupil.

Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) involves the intravenous injec-tion of fluorescein dye to visualise the retinal and choroidal vasculature. Indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) uses indocyanine green dye to provide enhanced imaging of the choroidal circulation, making it particu-larly useful in diagnosing conditions like polypoidal choroidal vasculopa-thy and uveitis disorders of the choriocapillaris.

OCT angiography (OCTA) is a form of OCT that provides detailed images of the blood flow in the retina and choroid without requiring dye injection. It is particularly useful for assessing macular diseases, such as wet age-related macular degeneration. Because it is non-invasive, OCTA is increasingly being used as an alternative to FFA.

Visual field testing, such as the Humphrey automated visual field test, is used to assess both peripheral and central vision. Automated perimetry is generally superior to confrontational visual field test-ing and is considered the gold standard, as it provides a quantita-tive assessment that allows for tracking changes over time. Visual field defects are often associated with conditions like glaucoma, optic neuropathies and neurological disorders affecting the visual pathway.
B-scan ultrasound allows visualisation of the posterior segment of the eye when conditions like dense cataracts or vitreous haemorrhages obstruct a direct view.

Electrophysiological tests, such as electroretinography (ERG) and visual evoked potentials (VEP), assess the electrical responses of the retina and visual pathway to light stimuli, providing valuable insights into retinal and optic nerve function, especially in cases of unexplained vision loss.

Headache (pp. 222 and 1167), diplopia (p. 1176) and ptosis (p. 1177) are important and common presenting symptoms of ophthalmic dis-ease, although clearly they have a wide differential diagnosis, which is discussed in the indicated chapters.

Common causes of acute red eye are summarised in Box 28.1. Differentiating the causes of acute red eye is best achieved through a slit-lamp examination, which allows for the identification of intraocular inflammation and the assessment of IOP. In the absence of a slit lamp, serious pathology can typically be identified by screening for reduced visual acuity, elevated IOP, abnormal pupil response to light and corneal pathology. Fluorescein eye drops or fluorets should be used to evaluate the integrity of the ocular surface under cobalt blue light, to detect any epithelial defects or ulcers.

Sudden loss of vision is an ophthalmic emergency and should prompt urgent referral to ophthalmology for evaluation. Clinical fundus and optic nerve appearance usually enable the diagnosis to be determined. Common causes are summarised in Box 28.2.
Gradual loss in vision can be attributed to any ocular structure along the visual pathway, and common causes are summarised in Box 28.3.

Flashes usually result from retinal traction, such as vitreoretinal traction or proliferative retinopathies like diabetic retinopathy or sickle-cell retin-opathy. However, flashes can also have neurological causes, including migraine auras or occipital lobe disturbances, which should be consid-ered if retinal pathology is not identified. Floaters are common and often arise from degenerative changes in the vitreous, like vitreous condensations. They may also occur due to vitreous haemorrhage, which can happen with or without retinal tears. This can be linked to retinal neovascularisation, especially in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, or can be caused by vitritis associated with inter-mediate or posterior uveitis. Rarely, floaters can indicate more serious conditions, such as lymphoma or amyloidosis. Flashes and floaters together are most often caused by a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD). A retinal examination should be conducted to exclude any concurrent retinal tears or breaks, which, if untreated, can potentially lead to retinal detachment.

Epiphora, or excessive tearing, can result from three main mecha-nisms: increased tear production, impaired lacrimal pump function, or decreased tear drainage. These mechanisms can have various causes:
• Increased tear production:
• Reflex tearing: triggered by local irritation or inflammation, com-mon causes include foreign bodies, conjunctivitis, keratitis or blepharitis.
• Systemic conditions: diseases like thyroid eye disease (Graves ophthalmopathy) can cause ocular surface irritation and increased tear production.
• Lacrimal pump failure:
• Dysfunction in the eyelids or orbicularis oculi muscle impairs tear drainage.
• Lid laxity: age-related changes can affect eyelid fit, reducing the pump’s effectiveness.
• Orbicularis muscle weakness: often caused by facial nerve palsy, this weakens the lacrimal pump.
• Decreased tear drainage:
• Obstruction in the tear drainage system reduces outflow.
• Punctal stenosis: due to ageing, inflammation or eversion of the punctum.
• Canalicular obstruction: caused by infections, chronic inflamma-tion or trauma.
• Nasolacrimal duct obstruction: can result from congenital issues, trauma, tumours or chronic inflammation.

The appearance of a white pupil (leucocoria) in a child, which may sometimes be identified as the lack of a red reflex in photography, requires urgent assessment for the exclusion of retinoblastoma. It typically affects children under 5 years old and can occur in one or both eyes. If left untreated retinoblastoma can be life-threatening. Congenital cataract can also cause leucocoria and may be seen in isolation or associated with a systemic condition, e.g. congeni-tal infections (TORCH – toxoplasmosis, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex) or metabolic disorders, e.g. galactosaemia. Other causes include Coats disease, retinal detachment, persistent fetal vasculature or retinal toxocariasis and require evaluation by an ophthalmologist.

Anisocoria is a condition characterised by unequal pupil sizes, which can be a normal physiological variation or indicate an underlying neurological, ocular or systemic disorder, requiring careful evaluation to determine the cause. Figure 28.4 outlines an approach to determine the underlying cause.
Clinical features

Viral conjunctivitis, frequently caused by adenoviruses, presents with watery discharge, conjunctival injection and often pre-auricular lymphadenopathy. Bacterial conjunctivitis is more commonly associated with purulent dis-charge, enabling differentiation from viral causes. Bacterial conjunctivitis is commonly secondary to pathogens such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Allergic conjunctivitis presents with intense itching, tearing and bilateral involvement, often accompanied by chemosis and papillary hypertrophy of the conjunctiva.
Investigations

Diagnosis is typically clinical; however, in cases where the diagnosis is uncertain or if the condition is severe or refractory, additional investiga-tions may be warranted. Conjunctival swabs for Gram staining and cul-ture can aid in identifying bacterial pathogens. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing may be employed for viral identification, particularly in epi-demic keratoconjunctivitis. Allergy testing may be considered in cases of chronic or recurrent allergic conjunctivitis.
Management

Management is guided by the underlying cause. Viral conjunctivitis is self-limiting, with treatment focused on symptomatic relief using lubri-cating eye drops and cool compresses. Bacterial conjunctivitis requires topical antibiotics, such as chloramphenicol to reduce the duration of symptoms and transmission. Allergic conjunctivitis is managed with topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilisers or glucocorticoids in severe cases. Preventive measures include strict hand hygiene and avoidance of eye rubbing to reduce transmission and exacerbation of symptoms.
Pathogenesis

Microbial keratitis is a serious and potentially blinding condition result-ing from infection of the cornea caused by bacteria, fungi, viruses or parasites, leading to corneal ulceration and inflammation. Pathogenesis typically involves a breach in the corneal epithelium, which allows microorganisms to invade and colonise the stroma. Common risk fac-tors include contact lens wear, trauma, ocular surface disease and immunosuppression.
Clinical features

Patients with microbial keratitis often present with acute onset of eye pain, redness, photophobia, blurred vision and discharge. Central/paracentral ulceration is always more serious than peripheral ulcers due to the involvement of the visual axis and implications for vision. The use of topical fluorescein visualised under cobalt blue light as part of the examination is useful to delineate the extent of corneal epithelial loss. Bacterial or fungal causes typically have a visible corneal infiltrate or ulcer, accompanied by stromal oedema and anterior chamber inflam-mation. Severe cases can lead to hypopyon formation (the accumula-tion of inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber forming a visible layer) and corneal perforation. Differentiation may be challenging clinically. Preceding corneal trauma and contact with soil or plant matter or immu-nosuppression should raise suspicion of fungal involvement. Rarely, the free-living amoeba Acanthamoeba castellanii can be a cause of contact lens–associated keratitis, presenting subacutely with pain out of pro-portion to clinical signs. It can also lead to corneal nerve infiltration and scleritis, in addition to keratitis. Herpes simplex keratitis is a common cause of infective keratitis which can involve corneal epithelium, stroma or endothelium. The pathogno-monic appearance of a dendritic ulcer and loss of corneal sensation are characteristic of epithelial disease (see p. 1247, image L). In advanced disease, larger ‘geographic’ ulcers may be visible.
Investigations

Diagnosis is primarily clinical. Differentiation between bacterial and fun-gal causes requires investigation in the form of corneal scrapings for microscopy, culture and sensitivity testing before empirical treatment is commenced to identify the causative organism, enabling a tailored thera-peutic approach. In suspected herpetic disease, corneal swabs for PCR for viral pathogens are useful to confirm the diagnosis. PCR and confo-cal microscopy are useful in identifying Acanthamoeba keratitis. Contact lenses, solutions and cases can also be cultured to aid organism detec-tion if implication is suspected.
Management

For herpetic disease, epithelial involvement can be treated with top-ical aciclovir 3% ointment/ganciclovir 0.15% gel 5 times daily for 14 days. Topical glucocorticoid use in active epithelial involvement can significantly worsen the disease. Stromal and endothelial involvement require topical glucocorticoids, in addition to antiviral treatment, follow-ing the resolution of any epithelial involvement. Long-term oral aciclovir (400 mg twice daily) provides prophylaxis to reduce the frequency of recurrent disease. Prompt initiation of broad-spectrum empirical topical antibiotics should be commenced for suspected bacterial keratitis. Monotherapy with fluo-roquinolones (e.g. ofloxacin, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin) or combined therapy with a cephalosporin (cefuroxime 5%) and fluoroquinolone are common first-line therapies. Treatment is divided into the sterilisation phase – hourly drops for 48 hours – followed by a healing phase where the frequency is reduced. Severe cases or inability to self-administer treatment may require hospitalisation. Regular follow-up is essential to monitor response and prevent complications, which may include corneal perforation.

For fungal keratitis, topical broad-spectrum antifungal agents such as preservative-free clotrimazole 1%, voriconazole 1% or natamycin 5% are initiated hourly for 72 hours. Systemic antifungal treatment should be considered for severe disease. For Acanthamoeba, chlorhexidine 0.02% drops and propamidine 0.1% every 2 hours is initial therapy.

Ocular chemical injuries are serious emergencies that occur when harm-ful substances come into contact with the eye. These injuries are classi-fied into alkali and acid burns, with alkali burns being more severe due to their ability to penetrate deeper into ocular tissues. Common causative agents include alkalis such as household cleaners (sodium hydroxide, pH 14), plaster (calcium hydroxide, pH 14) and acids such as battery fluid (sulphuric acid, pH 1) and bleach (sodium hypochlorite, pH 1).
Clinical features

Acute symptoms of chemical eye injuries include intense pain, red-ness, tearing, blurred vision and a sensation of a foreign body in the eye. Clinically, there may be an epithelial defect involving the cornea and affected conjunctiva/sclera. Alkaline burns can lead to increased ocu-lar pressure. Late clinical features include corneal scarring, cicatricial changes, symblepharon formation, dry eye and limbal stem cell defi-ciency if severe.
Management

The pH of the affected surface should be measured and then topi-cal anaesthetic instilled. If available, a speculum can be inserted and the affected area immediately irrigated with at least 2 litres of water or saline, until the pH is neutralised (normal tears can be slightly alkaline (up to pH 7.4)). The eyelids should be everted to ensure any residual matter is removed. pH testing must be undertaken post-irrigation and again 5 minutes later to ensure stability, and irrigation repeated if the pH is abnormal. Ophthalmology assessment is paramount to assess the extent of the injury. Treatment depends on severity, but topical antibiotics, cycloplegia (therapeutic pupillary dilatation), topical lubricants and oral analgesia are the mainstay treatment for mild cases. More severe cases may require systemic tetracyclines to prevent tissue necrosis and, in alkali injuries, ascorbic acid may be of additional benefit.
Clinical features

Episcleritis and scleritis are inflammatory conditions of the eye, with epi-scleritis involving the episclera (the outermost layer) and scleritis affecting the deeper scleral tissues. Episcleritis is typically benign, presenting with mild discomfort, localised redness and no vision loss. It often affects young adults and may be idiopathic or associated with mild systemic conditions. Scleritis is more severe, characterised by intense, deep eye pain, redness with a bluish hue, photophobia and potential vision impair-ment. Scleritis is commonly associated with systemic autoimmune dis-eases such as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, or granulomatosis with polyangiitis. It can be either anterior or posterior, and diffuse, nodular or necrotising (with necrotising being the most severe and potentially leading to vision loss).
Investigations

Diagnosis of episcleritis and scleritis is primarily clinical. Episcleritis usu-ally requires no further testing, but recurrent cases may prompt a workup for systemic associations. Blood tests, including full blood count (FBC), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP) and spe-cific tests for autoimmune markers (e.g. rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies) may be performed to identify underlying systemic conditions. B-scan ultrasound is useful in cases of posterior scleritis to identify a characteristic thickened choroid and fluid within the episcleral space, extending around the optic nerve (‘T sign’).
Management

Episcleritis is generally self-limiting, with management focused on symp-tomatic relief using lubricants or topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Treatment of scleritis depends on the severity and underlying cause. Initial management includes systemic NSAIDs or glucocorticoids. In severe cases, immunosuppressive agents such as methotrexate, cyclo-phosphamide or biologics may be required. Treating the underlying sys-temic condition is crucial to prevent recurrence and complications.
Clinical features

Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is a severe and potentially sight-threat-ening type of keratitis that involves inflammation and ulceration of the peripheral cornea. It is believed to result from immune complex deposi-tion at the limbus (the border area between the cornea and the sclera), leading to obliterative vasculitis with subsequent corneal thinning and stromal melt. It is commonly associated with systemic autoimmune dis-eases (see Ch. 25) including rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa, relaps-ing polychondritis and microscopic polyangiitis. Clinically, patients pre-sent with symptoms including eye pain, redness, tearing and decreased vision. On examination, there may be conjunctival injection, corneal thin-ning, ulceration and a crescent-shaped lesion near the limbus. In severe cases, corneal perforation can occur, posing a risk of vision loss.
Investigations

Corneal scraping may be performed to rule out infectious causes. Systemic evaluation is crucial, including blood tests for autoimmune markers (e.g. antinuclear antibodies (ANA), rheumatoid factor, myeloper-oxidase (MPO), proteinase 3 (PR3)). Collaboration with a rheumatologist is often necessary for comprehensive evaluation.
Management

Management of PUK involves addressing both the local ocular disease and any underlying systemic condition. Systemic immunosuppressive therapy, such as methotrexate or cyclophosphamide, may be required for underlying autoimmune conditions. In severe cases, surgical interven-tion like corneal transplantation or amniotic membrane grafting may be necessary to restore corneal integrity.

Cataract refers to the opacification of the crystalline lens of the eye, lead-ing to impaired vision. Cataracts are the leading cause of blindness worldwide, with preva-lence increasing significantly with age. The burden of cataract-related visual impairment is particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income countries, where access to surgical intervention may be limited. Age-related cataracts account for the majority of cases, although congen-ital and secondary cataracts contribute to the overall disease burden. Modifiable risk factors include glucocorticoid use, ocular trauma, ultravi-olet (UV) radiation exposure, diabetes and smoking.
Clinical features

Patients with cataracts commonly present with a gradual, painless decline in vision. Symptoms include glare, especially in bright light or while driving at night, diminished visual acuity, halos around lights and difficulty distinguishing colours. The severity and type of visual distur-bance depend on the cataract’s location and density within the lens. Nuclear sclerotic cataracts often cause myopic shifts, while cortical cat-aracts may lead to glare and contrast sensitivity issues. Certain systemic conditions are associated with characteristic cataract types, such as ‘oil drop’ cataracts in galactosaemia, ‘sunflower’ cataracts in Wilson disease due to copper deposition, and ‘Christmas tree’ cataracts in myotonic dystrophy (characterised by multi-coloured needle-like inclusions within the lens).
Diagnosis

The diagnosis of cataract may be visual without equipment in severe cases; however, a dilated slit-lamp examination allows for the detailed visualisation of any lens opacity while ruling out other posterior segment pathology that might be contributing to the visual impairment, providing visual prognostic information post-surgery. Additional imaging modali-ties, such as OCT and B-scan ultrasound, may be employed to further evaluate the posterior chamber in cases where the fundus is not clearly visible.
Management

The definitive management of cataracts is surgical extraction, which is indicated when the cataract impairs daily activities or quality of life. The most common surgical technique is phacoemulsification with intraocular lens (IOL) implantation, which is highly effective but requires expensive, advanced technology and consumables. In resource-limited settings, manual small incision cataract surgery (MSICS) is often utilised, which is less dependent on sophisticated equipment and offers a cost-effective alternative, with outcomes comparable to phacoemulsification in terms of visual rehabilitation.
Epidemiology

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is an acquired, degenerative disorder affecting the macula, primarily in adults over 50 years old. Its prevalence increases with age, making it a significant cause of vision impairment in the elderly population.
Pathogenesis

AMD can be categorised into two main forms: dry (atrophic) AMD and wet (neovascular) AMD. Dry AMD, the more common form, is charac-terised by subretinal drusen deposition, which may lead to blurring and metamorphopsia. As the disease progresses, it can result in loss of the retinal pigment epithelium (geographic atrophy), causing scotomas that may involve the central vision. Neovascular AMD involves choroidal neo-vascularisation, where abnormal blood vessels grow under the retina, leading to leakage, bleeding and scar formation, resulting in rapid vision loss.
Clinical features

Dry AMD typically presents with gradual visual changes such as blurring and distorted vision (metamorphopsia). Geographic atrophy can lead to central scotomas. In contrast, neovascular AMD often presents with a sudden onset of central distortion and visual loss, progressing rapidly over weeks.
Diagnosis and investigations

Dry AMD is diagnosed through clinical examination and imaging tech-niques like OCT to assess drusen and retinal changes. Neovascular AMD has traditionally been diagnosed with FFA to identify areas of choroidal neovascularisation. However, OCT and OCTA are increasingly used, ena-bling non-invasive cross-sectional imaging of the macula, helping differ-entiate AMD from other retinal pathologies and monitoring the response to therapy.
Management

The management of dry AMD is primarily supportive, focusing on visual aids such as magnifiers, appropriate lighting and specialised adaptations for daily living, along with addressing modifiable risk factors like smoking cessation. Emerging therapies, including intravitreal complement inhib-itors, like pegcetacoplan, aim to slow the progression of geographic atrophy but are not yet widely adopted. An Amsler grid can be used for self-monitoring to detect changes that may indicate progression to neovascular AMD. Neovascular AMD is managed with intravitreal injections of anti-vas-cular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents such as bevacizumab (off-label), ranibizumab, aflibercept and faricimab. These treatments inhibit abnormal blood vessel growth and limit scar formation, sig-nificantly improving visual outcomes. However, intravitreal therapy is resource-intensive, requiring regular injections and monitoring to prevent irreversible visual loss due to delayed treatment.
Epidemiology

Diabetic eye disease, particularly diabetic retinopathy, is one of the most common microvascular complications of diabetes and a leading cause of blindness globally. It affects approximately one-third of indi-viduals with diabetes, with prevalence rates correlating strongly with the duration of the disease and glycaemic control. In patients with type 1 diabetes, nearly all will develop some degree of retinopathy after 20 years, while up to 60% of those with type 2 diabetes may be affected. Key risk factors include poor glycaemic control, hypertension, hyperlip-idaemia and nephropathy. Diabetic retinopathy is also more prevalent among certain ethnic groups, including Hispanic and African American populations. Prevention of diabetic eye disease hinges on meticulous control of diabetes and associated risk factors. Maintaining HbA1c levels below 53 mmol/mol, controlling blood pressure and managing dyslipidaemia significantly reduce the risk of retinopathy progression. The increasing use of advanced technology in type 1 diabetes, such as artificial pan-creas systems, may in the future reduce the incidence and severity of diabetic retinopathy, as these systems can significantly improve glycae-mic control. Systematic screening for asymptomatic proliferative retin-opathy is cost-effective and has led to population-based programmes in many countries. The inclusion of universal OCT scanning has high sensitivity and specificity for detecting diabetic macular oedema. While annual screening is standard, evidence suggests that patients with consistently normal results, especially those with type 2 diabetes, can be screened every two years. Pregnant women should be screened each trimester as increased angiogenic factors and rapid improvement in glycaemic control can lead to a substantial worsening of diabetic retinopathy.
Clinical features

Diabetic retinopathy progresses through stages, beginning with non-pro-liferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), characterised by microaneurysms, retinal haemorrhages, cotton wool spots and hard exudates. As the disease advances to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), neovascu-larisation occurs due to retinal ischaemia, leading to fragile new blood vessels that can bleed, causing vitreous haemorrhage and tractional reti-nal detachment. Diabetic macular oedema (DMO) can occur at any stage and involves the accumulation of fluid in the macula, leading to central vision loss. The pathophysiology involves chronic hyperglycaemia-in-duced damage to retinal blood vessels, increased vascular permeability and capillary occlusion.
Diagnosis and investigations

Screening programmes for diabetic retinopathy have been estab-lished in many countries. Annual or biannual assessment of retinal photographs from non-mydriatic retinal cameras is used to identify possible retinopathy and DMO at an early stage. Formal diagnosis of diabetic eye disease requires a dilated fundoscopic examination to visualise the characteristic retinal vascular changes. Optical coher-ence tomography (OCT) provides detailed cross-sectional images of the retina, allowing for the detection of macular oedema and its response to treatment. FFA helps to identify areas of retinal non-per-fusion and neovascularisation.
Management

Management strategies focus on slowing disease progression and preserving vision. In proliferative diabetic retinopathy, panretinal laser photocoagulation therapy is extremely effective at preserving vision by inducing regression of neovascularisation (Fig. 28.5). Centre-involving diabetic macular oedema is predominantly treated with intravitreal injec-tions of anti-VEGF agents, such as bevacizumab, ranibizumab and aflibercept, which reduce vascular permeability and inhibit abnormal blood vessel growth. In advanced cases, vitrectomy may be necessary to remove non-resolving vitreous haemorrhage or repair tractional retinal detachments.

Retinal vein occlusion (RVO) is a common retinal vascular disorder and a significant cause of visual impairment. It occurs due to the blockage of retinal veins, leading to increased venous pressure, haemorrhage and retinal oedema. RVO is classified into two main types: central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), where the main retinal vein is blocked, and branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), affecting one of its smaller branches. Both types can cause vision loss, depending on the extent and location of the occlusion.
Epidemiology

RVO is the second most common retinal vascular disease after diabetic retinopathy, affecting approximately 16 million people worldwide. The incidence increases with age, and it is more common in individuals over 50 years. BRVO is more prevalent than CRVO, accounting for about 80% of cases. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidae-mia and smoking. There is no significant gender predilection, although some studies suggest a slightly higher incidence in males.
Clinical features

Patients with RVO typically present with sudden, painless vision loss or blurring in one eye. CRVO usually results in more severe visual impair-ment compared to BRVO. Clinical examination may reveal retinal haem-orrhages, cotton wool spots, macular oedema and dilated tortuous veins. Neovascularisation and macular oedema are common complica-tions that can further deteriorate vision.
Diagnosis and investigations

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by fundoscopic findings (Fig. 28.6A). Additional imaging, such as fluorescein angiography, is used to assess the extent of retinal ischaemia and leakage, while OCT helps evaluate macular oedema. In younger patients with RVO, further investi-gations are warranted to rule out underlying systemic conditions such as hypercoagulable states, vasculitis or thrombophilia.
Management

Management of RVO includes intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF agents or glucocorticoids to reduce macular oedema and laser photocoagula-tion if neovascularisation occurs. Systemic risk factors such as hyper-tension, diabetes and hyperlipidaemia should be optimally controlled to prevent recurrence or progression.

Retinal artery occlusion is a sight-threatening condition caused by the obstruction of the central retinal artery or one of its branches, leading to sudden and severe vision loss. Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) affects the entire retina, while branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO) affects a specific sector of the retina corresponding to the blocked branch. These occlusions are typically due to emboli or thrombi and are associated with cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension, ath-erosclerosis and cardiac diseases. Retinal artery occlusion is an ocular emergency, as the retina’s limited tolerance to ischaemia can lead to irreversible damage within a short period.
Clinical features

Patients with CRAO typically present with sudden, painless and profound vision loss in one eye, while those with BRAO experience a sudden visual field defect in one eye corresponding to the affected retinal area. On examination, the retina appears pale and swollen, with a characteristic cherry-red spot at the fovea in CRAO (Fig. 28.6B). In BRAO, the pallor and swelling are confined to the specific area supplied by the occluded branch artery (Fig. 28.6C).
Diagnosis and investigations

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by fundoscopic findings. OCT may show retinal oedema. It is crucial to measure ESR and CRP to exclude giant cell arteritis as a cause, especially in patients over 50 years old, given the risk of second eye involvement if missed. Additional inves-tigations include carotid Doppler ultrasound and cardiac evaluation to identify embolic sources.
Management

Management aims to restore retinal perfusion as quickly as possible, as there is a critical window of opportunity – typically 6 hours of onset during which time intervention may improve outcomes. Immediate measures include reducing intraocular pressure through ocular mas-sage, anterior chamber paracentesis or intravenous medications like acetazolamide. While the prognosis for BRAO is generally better than CRAO, rapid intervention remains crucial. Systemic management involves controlling cardiovascular risk factors and considering anti-coagulation therapy if indicated. Long-term management focuses on preventing recurrence by addressing underlying systemic conditions and modifying risk factors. If giant cell arteritis is suspected, initiate high-dose glucocorticoids promptly to prevent further vision loss and systemic complications.
Epidemiology

Retinal detachment affects approximately 1 in 10 000 people per year. It is more common in individuals over 40, with a higher prevalence in males, those with high myopia, a history of eye surgery (such as cata-ract removal) or trauma. It is also associated with conditions like lattice degeneration (an abnormally thin retina) and family history.
Pathogenesis

Retinal detachment occurs when the retina separates from the underly-ing retinal pigment epithelium. This can be due to a tear or hole (rheg-matogenous), traction from scar tissue (tractional) or fluid accumulation beneath the retina (exudative).
Clinical features

Patients typically present with sudden onset of floaters, flashes of light (photopsia) and a shadow or curtain-like effect in their visual field. Vision loss progresses if not treated promptly. Pain is usually absent unless associated with trauma.
Diagnosis

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, confirmed by fundoscopic examination showing an elevated retina with or without tears. B-scan ultrasonography can assist when the view is obscured, such as by vitreous haemorrhage.
Management

Immediate referral to an ophthalmologist is critical. Treatment involves reattaching the retina, typically via procedures like pars planar vitrec-tomy or scleral buckling. The choice depends on the type and extent of detachment. Intervention prior to macular involvement improves the prognosis for visual recovery.

text: Sickle-cell retinopathy is a common ocular manifestation in patients with sickle-cell disorder (p. 981), particularly those with haemoglobin SC dis-order (HbSC) or HbSβ + (sickle–beta plus thalassaemia). The condition can present with asymptomatic peripheral retinal changes or progress to vision-threatening complications. Non-proliferative changes include ‘salmon patch’ haemorrhages, refractile deposits, and ‘black sunburst’ lesions. Proliferative sickle-cell retinopathy (PSR) is characterised by neo-vascularisation, which may lead to complications such as vitreous haem-orrhage, retinal detachment or neovascular glaucoma. The hallmark of PSR is the ‘sea fan’ neovascularisation, typically located in the peripheral retina.

text: Management
section_path: Miscellaneous retinal manifestations of multisystem disorders

text: Management of sickle-cell retinopathy focuses on early detection and prevention of complications. Regular ophthalmologic evaluations are essential, especially in high-risk patients. For proliferative retinopathy, treatment options include laser photocoagulation to regress neovascular-isation, anti-VEGF injections and vitreoretinal surgery in advanced cases with retinal detachment or persistent vitreous hemorrhage. Optimising systemic management of sickle-cell disorder is also crucial in reducing overall disease burden.

text: Ocular manifestations of von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease
section_path: Miscellaneous retinal manifestations of multisystem disorders

text: Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) disease (p. 1230) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the VHL gene, leading to abnor-mal blood vessel growth and tumour formation in various organs. Retinal hemangioblastomas are the most common ocular finding in VHL, appearing as well-defined, orange–red vascular tumours in the ret-ina. They can lead to visual disturbances, including floaters, visual field loss and, if untreated, vision loss due to retinal detachment or macular oedema. Management includes laser photocoagulation, cryotherapy or, in advanced cases, vitreoretinal surgery to preserve vision and prevent complications. Periodic ophthalmic monitoring is crucial.

text: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), also known as Bourneville disease (p. 1144), is a genetic disorder characterised by the development of benign tumours in multiple organs, including the eyes. Ocular manifestations in TSC primarily include retinal hamartomas, which are non-cancerous growths that appear as greyish, elevated lesions in the retina. These hamartomas are typically asymptomatic, but can occasionally lead to visual disturbances if they affect the macula or optic nerve. Management is generally conservative, as most retinal hamartomas do not require treatment unless they cause significant visual impairment.
