text: Uveitis is an umbrella term for inflammation anywhere in the uveal tract, retina, choroid or vitreous. The inflammation can be classified based on the location within the eye: anterior, intermediate, posterior or panuveitis. It may result from autoimmune disorders, infections, trauma or exposure to toxins, and it can lead to complications like glaucoma, cataracts, or vision loss if not properly treated.

Anterior uveitis is the most common form of uveitis, characterised by inflammation of the anterior segment of the uveal tract, including the iris and ciliary body. Causes may be idiopathic, autoimmune or infective. Approximately 50%–70% of patients with anterior uveitis are positive for

HLA-B27. This association is particularly strong in individuals with certain seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis, reac-tive arthritis and psoriatic arthritis (Ch. 25). While less common, infective causes may be viral-related (herpes simplex (HSV), varicella zoster (VZV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV)) or bacterial (tuberculosis and syphilis).
Clinical features

Anterior uveitis typically presents with eye pain, redness, photophobia and blurred vision. There may be conjunctival injection, keratic precipi-tates (small circular deposits on the corneal endothelium composed of inflammatory cells), pupil distortion (secondary to posterior synechiae) and inflammatory cells and flare visible in the anterior chamber on slit-lamp examination. In severe cases, a hypopyon (fluid level of inflamma-tory cells) may be visible.
Investigations

Diagnosis is primarily clinical, using slit-lamp examination to identify cells and flare. A dilated fundus examination is warranted to ensure the absence of posterior uveitis in all cases. In patients with a history of back pain greater than 3 months, with an age of onset less than 45 years old or joint pains requiring visits to health-care professionals, HLA-B27 testing is warranted, with referral to a rheumatologist if positive. Where clinical features suggest a viral infective cause, anterior chamber para-centesis can be performed for PCR analysis.
Management

Treatment involves glucocorticoid eye drops to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents to relieve pain from iris spasm and break posterior synechiae. Specific treatment for infective aetiology is given if identified.

Intermediate uveitis is a disease entity where the majority of the ocular inflammation is isolated to the vitreous cavity. While approximately a third of cases are idiopathic, multiple sclerosis and sarcoidosis are common systemic associations.

Posterior uveitis refers to inflammation involving the retina, choroid and optic nerve. It is the least common, but most sight-threatening form of uveitis, often resulting in significant visual impairment if not promptly identified and treated. This condition can be associated with various infectious, autoimmune or systemic diseases, and requires a thorough clinical evaluation to determine the underlying cause and guide man-agement. A comprehensive review of the forms of posterior uveitis are beyond the scope of this chapter, but notable causes are outlined below.
Ocular tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB) is covered in detail in Chapter 17. Ocular extrapul-monary manifestations can occur in approximately 1%–2% of patients; however, in endemic regions and among immunocompromised individ-uals, the prevalence can be higher. Ocular TB can affect any part of the eye with a varied presentation. Anteriorly, scleritis or anterior uveitis, clas-sically with ‘mutton-fat’ keratic precipitates, can occur. Posterior uveitis manifestations include tuberous choroidal granulomas, retinal vasculitis, multifocal retinitis or serpiginous choroiditis. Management is often in con-junction with respiratory physicians and includes anti-tuberculosis ther-apy (ATT) for at least 6 to 9 months, with glucocorticoids to control ocular inflammation. Latent tuberculosis is a particular concern in cases of non-infectious uveitis treated with biologics, which may induce active systemic infection.
Ocular syphilis

Syphilis is covered in detail in Chapter 15. Ocular manifestations of syphilis occur in 1%–5% of syphilis infections and can present at any stage of the disease. Often referred to as ‘the great masquerader’ due to the ability to mimic the signs and symptoms of other diseases, the spectrum of ophthalmic involvement is broad, requiring a high index of suspicion and low threshold for screening, particularly in any cases of bilateral uveitis. Several pathognomonic retinal appearances, termed acute syphilitic posterior placoid chorioretinitis (ASPCC) and syph-ilitic retinitis, are increasingly well recognised. Other manifestations may include optic neuritis, interstitial keratitis, cranial nerve palsies or light-near dissociation pupil involvement (Argyll Robertson pupil). Co-infection with HIV occurs in around one-third of cases. Ocular involvement should be treated with a neurosyphilis regime as outlined in Chapter 15, which is highly effective.
Ocular toxoplasmosis

Toxoplasmosis is covered in detail in Chapter 14. Ocular toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of posterior uveitis worldwide. Symptoms vary depending on the severity of the activation and the location of the lesion, but commonly include floaters, blurred vision, photophobia and pain. On examination patients may show character-istic white focal lesions on the retina with overlying vitreous inflamma-tion giving a ‘headlight in the fog’ appearance (Fig. 28.7C). Recurrences commonly occur adjacent to previous pigmented lesions. In the immu-nocompromised, appearances can vary and mimic acute retinal necrosis in some cases. Diagnosis is largely clinical. Lesions adjacent to the optic nerve, within the macular or adjacent to the retinal arcades, should be treated in all cases. Due to the toxicity profile of the drugs used, the risks versus ben-efits of treating peripheral lesions are debatable, but may reduce the risk of recurrence. Treatment typically involves a combination of antiparasitic medication like pyrimethamine and sulfadiazine, along with glucocorti-coids to reduce inflammation. There is good evidence that prophylaxis following an activation reduces the risk of further episodes.
Acute retinal necrosis

Acute retinal necrosis (ARN) is a severe viral infection of the retina, typi-cally caused by herpes viruses, herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV). It is a rare but potentially blinding condition that pri-marily affects immunocompetent individuals. Patients with ARN usually present with symptoms of acute onset of blurred vision, floaters, redness and eye pain. Vision loss can pro-gress quickly. On examination, ARN is characterised by peripheral retinal necrosis, vasculitis and moderate to severe vitritis (see Fig. 28.7A). There may also be involvement of the optic nerve and macula in advanced cases. Delayed retinal detachment can also occur fol-lowing resolution. Lymphoma, syphilis and toxoplasmosis in the immunocompromised may mimic the appearance in some cases. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of aqueous fluid samples enables the identification of the spe-cific viral pathogen. Intravitreal foscarnet is often undertaken at the time of aqueous sampling, together with oral valaciclovir or intravenous (IV) aciclovir. Early intervention improves the prognosis, but visual outcomes can vary depending on the extent of retinal involvement.
Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is covered in detail in Chapter 17. Ocular manifestations occur in between 25% and 50% of patients with systemic disease. It can involve any part of the eye, with anterior uveitis being the most common form. Other ocular manifestations include conjunctival gran-ulomas, lacrimal gland enlargement, intermediate or posterior uveitis, and retinal vasculitis characterised by periphlebitis with ‘candle-wax drippings’. Optic nerve involvement, scleritis and orbital inflammation are also seen. Diagnosis is supported by biopsy showing non-caseating granulo-mas, chest imaging and elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) levels. Treatment involves glucocorticoids and immunosuppressive agents to manage inflammation.
Clinical features

Endophthalmitis is an ocular emergency characterised by marked inflammation of the intraocular cavities, typically secondary to infection. Common clinical features include severe ocular pain, significant reduc-tion in visual acuity, redness and photophobia. On examination, there is often a marked conjunctival injection, corneal oedema and a visible hypopyon in the anterior chamber. The posterior segment may exhibit vitreous opacities, and the red reflex is usually reduced or absent. The condition most frequently arises following intraocular surgery or pene-trating trauma (exogenous endophthalmitis), or less commonly from haematogenous spread of systemic infection (endogenous endoph-thalmitis). The causes of endogenous endophthalmitis are therefore the causes of blood-stream infection (Ch. 14). Gram-positive bacteria are most common, followed by gram-negative bacteria and then fungi, mainly Candida, which characteristically causes creamy-white retinal or chorioretinal lesions (see Fig. 28.7B).
Investigations

Diagnostic samples, ideally from both the aqueous and vitreous, should be obtained for Gram stain, culture and sensitivity testing. B-scan ultra-sonography serves as an adjunctive tool when direct visualisation of the posterior segment is compromised, identifying features such as dense vitritis or retinal detachment.
Management

Immediate treatment is critical and includes intravitreal administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, commonly vancomycin and ceftazidime, at the time of diagnostic samples being taken. Pars plana vitrectomy is considered in severe or refractory cases, particularly when the visual prognosis is poor or the infection is unresponsive. Systemic antibiotics may be indicated in cases of endogenous endophthalmitis. The visual prognosis varies significantly and is influenced by the rapidity of diagno-sis and intervention, as well as the virulence of the causative organism.

Optic disc swelling can be a developmental variant of normal (pseudo-papilloedema), a manifestation of optic nerve pathology or a reflection of more widespread nerve-fibre oedema, as with retinal vein occlusion. Unilateral optic disc swelling can result from various ocular, neuro-logical and systemic conditions. Key differential diagnoses are shown in Box 28.4.
Clinical features

Papilloedema is the swelling of the optic disc secondary to raised intra-cranial pressure as outlined in Figure 28.8. The extent of papilloedema can be graded on the Frisén scale from 0 to 5 (Box 28.5). Patients may present with symptoms such as headaches, transient visual obscura-tions, nausea, vomiting and diplopia due to 6th nerve palsy. Visual acu-ity is typically preserved in the early stages, but prolonged or severe papilloedema can lead to progressive visual field loss and permanent vision impairment. Fundoscopic examination reveals hyperaemia of the optic disc, blurred disc margins, venous engorgement, haemorrhages and cotton wool spots. Chronic papilloedema may lead to optic atrophy characterised by a pale, shrunken disc.
Investigations

Diagnosis begins with fundoscopy to confirm optic disc swelling. OCT provides detailed imaging of the optic nerve head and retinal nerve fibre layer, aiding in the assessment and monitoring of disc oedema. Optic disc autofluorescence imaging or B-scan ultrasound is useful in exclud-ing optic disc drusen, which may mimic mild papilloedema. Baseline visual field testing helps monitor disease progression. Blood pressure (to exclude hypertensive papillopathy) and calculation of body mass index (as a risk factor for idiopathic intracranial hypertension; p. 1231) should be undertaken. Urgent computed tomography (CT) head and CT venogram are essen-tial to exclude mass lesions, hydrocephalus or other structural causes of raised intracranial pressure and to exclude venous sinus thrombosis (Ch. 27). A lumbar puncture, performed after imaging, enables the open-ing pressure to be measured and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid to exclude infection or inflammation.
Management

Treatment targets the underlying cause of raised intracranial pressure. In idiopathic intracranial hypertension, management includes weight reduc-tion, acetazolamide and diuretics. Refractory cases may require surgical intervention, such as optic nerve sheath fenestration or cerebrospinal fluid shunting. Regular monitoring of visual fields and optic disc appear-ance is necessary to guide treatment and prevent vision loss.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, is a chronic vasculitis primarily affecting large and medium-sized arteries, particularly the temporal arteries. Clinical features, diagnosis and management are discussed in Chapter 25. Ocular manifestations include:

• Visual loss. Sudden, painless monocular vision loss is a common presentation and is often due to arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy (AAION), which results from occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries. Visual loss in GCA is typically severe and can be permanent if the diagnosis is delayed and treatment is not promptly instituted. Vision loss can also occur secondary to central retinal artery occlusion.
• Amaurosis fugax. Some patients may experience transient visual obscurations or episodes of temporary vision loss, known as amau-rosis fugax, before permanent visual loss occurs.
• Diplopia. Double vision may occur due to ischaemia of the extraocu-lar muscles or their nerve supply, particularly the 3rd cranial nerve.

The vision loss in one eye often precedes similar events in the con-tralateral eye if the condition remains untreated. The primary goal in treating GCA is to prevent vision loss and other ischaemic complications. The mainstay of treatment is high-dose glucocorticoids, which should be initiated as soon as GCA is sus-pected, before a confirmatory temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy is performed. Steroid-sparing agents like tocilizumab (an IL-6 receptor antagonist) are sometimes used in patients requiring prolonged treat-ment. With prompt diagnosis and treatment, the prognosis for GCA has improved significantly, especially regarding the prevention of vision loss. However, relapses are common, and long-term follow-up is necessary. Approximately 15%–20% of patients may experience permanent visual impairment.
Clinical features

Non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy (NAION) typically presents in adults over 50 years old with sudden, painless, monocular vision loss. This vision loss often occurs upon waking and can range from mild to severe. Visual field defects are common, most notably altitudinal defects, although other patterns can occur. Patients may report blurred vision or a dark spot in their central or peripheral vision. On fundoscopic examination, optic disc oedema is often observed, along with splinter haemorrhages at the disc margin. The affected disc is usually pale and swollen, and the condition is more likely in patients with a ‘crowded’ optic disc appearance.
Investigations

The diagnosis of NAION is primarily clinical, based on history and fundo-scopic findings and the exclusion of GCA given the risk of second eye involvement if missed. Visual field testing typically shows characteristic defects and OCT can be used to assess optic nerve head swelling and ret-inal nerve fibre layer thickness. Blood tests, including FBC, ESR, CRP (to exclude GCA), HbA1c and lipid profile, with assessment of cardiovascular risk factors, are essential to identify and manage systemic contributors.
Management

There is no definitive treatment for NAION. Management focuses on con-trolling systemic risk factors such as hypertension, diabetes and hyper-lipidaemia to reduce the risk of fellow eye involvement, which occurs in 15%–25% of cases. Although various treatments, including glucocorti-coids and antiplatelet therapy, have been studied, none have demon-strated consistent efficacy in altering disease progression.
Clinical features

Optic neuritis is an inflammation of the optic nerve that often presents with acute vision loss, usually in one eye. Patients typically experience eye pain, especially with eye movement, and vision loss that progresses over hours to days. Other common symptoms include colour vision defi-cits, such as difficulty distinguishing reds, and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) (see p. 691). Visual field defects, such as central scoto-mas, are also common. Some patients report a history of preceding viral illness, and optic neuritis can be the first presentation of multiple sclerosis (MS; p. 1205).
Investigations

The diagnosis of optic neuritis is primarily clinical, but investigations are important to confirm and assess underlying causes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain and orbits with gadolinium contrast is the most useful test, showing enhancement of the optic nerve in acute cases. An MRI can also assess for other lesions suggestive of MS.
Management

Mild cases of optic neuritis may be observed for spontaneous recovery. Glucocorticoids may speed up recovery but do not affect the final visual outcome. Intravenous methylprednisolone is typically used for severe cases. If no demyelinating lesions are observed on MRI, approximately 25% of patients with idiopathic optic neuritis develop MS over 15 years. The risk increases to 75% over the same time period if lesions are pres-ent on MRI imaging.
Clinical features

Ocular myasthenia gravis (OMG) is a subtype of myasthenia gravis (Ch. 27) that primarily affects the muscles controlling eye movements and eye-lids. It commonly presents with ptosis (drooping of one or both eyelids) and diplopia (double vision) due to weakness of the extraocular mus-cles. Symptoms may fluctuate in severity and often worsen with fatigue or sustained activity. The condition is usually asymmetrical and patients may notice symptoms more prominently on one side. Despite affecting eye muscles, OMG can potentially progress to generalised myasthenia gravis, involving other muscle groups.
Investigations

Diagnosis of OMG involves clinical evaluation and several diagnos-tic tests. Ice pack test and rest test are quick bedside tests that can help confirm the diagnosis. Acetylcholine receptor antibody (AChR-Ab) testing is positive in between 50% and 70%. Anti-MuSk antibodies are more common in generalised myasthenia gravis (MG), but if positive in OMG may indicate a higher likelihood of progression to generalised MG. Single-fibre electromyography (SFEMG) is highly sensitive for detecting neuromuscular transmission defects. Repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) may also be used but is less sensitive for ocular muscles.
Management

Treatment of OMG focuses on improving symptoms and preventing progression. Pyridostigmine, an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, is often the first-line treatment. Glucocorticoids and other immunosuppressive agents, such as azathioprine, may be used for more severe or refrac-tory cases. Thymectomy is generally reserved for those with thymoma or generalised disease. Eyelid crutches or prisms can be used, respectively, for symptomatic relief of ptosis and diplopia.

Optic atrophy refers to the degeneration of optic nerve, leading to optic disc pallor visible on fundoscopy. There are many causes of optic atrophy (Box 28.6). History, examination and specific investigations may help to identify the cause.
Clinical features

Optic neuropathy refers to damage to the optic nerve, leading to visual impairment. Clinical features include sudden or gradual vision loss, often affecting one eye, and may present as central, peripheral or altitudinal visual field defects. Patients might experience decreased colour vision (dyschromatopsia) and a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) in unilateral or asymmetric cases. Pain, especially with eye movement, is commonly associated with optic neuritis, but not with other types like ischaemic optic neuropathy.
Investigations

Evaluation involves a detailed ophthalmic examination, including visual acuity, colour vision testing and fundoscopy to assess the optic disc. Visual field testing helps identify specific patterns of vision loss. OCT measures retinal nerve fibre layer thickness, aiding in detecting optic nerve damage. Imaging studies like MRI of the brain and orbits are cru-cial for identifying inflammatory, demyelinating or compressive lesions. Blood tests, including inflammatory markers and specific antibodies, can help diagnose underlying causes like giant cell arteritis or autoimmune conditions.
Management

Treatment depends on the underlying cause. For optic neuritis, high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids may accelerate recovery. Ischaemic optic neuropathy management includes addressing cardiovascular risk factors. In compressive optic neuropathy, surgical intervention may be necessary to relieve pressure on the optic nerve. Long-term management focuses on monitoring vision changes and prevent-ing further damage through the treatment of associated systemic conditions.

Glaucoma is the second leading cause of blindness worldwide after cat-aracts. It is a group of eye disorders characterised by progressive optic nerve damage, often associated with elevated IOP. The primary types of glaucoma include primary open-angle glaucoma, angle-closure glau-coma and secondary glaucomas, each with distinct pathophysiological mechanisms.

Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is the most common form of glaucoma and a leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. It predominantly affects adults over 40 years of age, with increasing prev-alence in older populations. The condition shows a higher prevalence in African and Hispanic populations compared to White Europeans, with African ancestry associated with earlier onset and more rapid progression. A family history of glaucoma, elevated IOP, myopia and systemic conditions such as hypertension and diabetes are recognised risk factors. POAG affects both genders, but there is a slightly higher risk in males.
Clinical features

POAG is characterised by an open anterior chamber angle, optic nerve head changes and visual field loss. It is often asymptomatic in the early stages, with no pain or redness, and vision loss typically begins periph-erally, progressing slowly towards central vision. Patients may not notice vision changes until significant optic nerve damage has occurred.
Investigations

Diagnosis of POAG involves a comprehensive eye examination, includ-ing IOP measurement using tonometry, pachymetry to measure corneal thickness (which influences IOP readings), gonioscopy to confirm an open angle and optic nerve head evaluation via slit-lamp biomicroscopy or OCT. Automated visual field testing enables a quantifiable comparison of disease progression over time.
Management

Management aims to lower IOP to slow disease progression. Initial treatment with 360° selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) can delay the need for topical treatment. Where SLT is unavailable or declined, topical treatment with a prostaglandin analogue is the first-line treat-ment. Beta-adrenoceptor antagonists (β-blockers), alpha agonists, sympathomimetic and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are additional options where intraocular pressure is insufficiently controlled. The range of topical glaucoma medication is outlined in Box 28.7. Surgical options are reserved for cases refractory to medical and laser thera-pies. In mild or moderate glaucoma, minimally invasive glaucoma sur-gery (MIGS) may be considered. Where greater intraocular pressure reductions are required, trabeculectomy or drainage implants may be considered. Regular monitoring including IOP checks, visual field analysis and optic nerve evaluation is required to adjust treatment as needed.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma is an ophthalmic emergency charac-terised by a sudden increase in IOP due to impaired outflow of aque-ous humour through a closed or narrowed anterior chamber angle. Epidemiologically, it predominantly affects older adults, with a higher incidence in females and individuals of Asian and Inuit descent. Risk fac-tors include advancing age, hyperopia, a shallow anterior chamber and a family history of the condition.
Clinical features

Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with rapid onset of severe ocu-lar pain, headache and decreased visual acuity, often accompanied by halos around lights. Associated systemic symptoms such as nausea and vomiting are common due to the abrupt elevation in IOP. Examination reveals a red eye, corneal oedema leading to a hazy appearance, a mid-dilated and fixed pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber. IOP is mark-edly elevated, frequently exceeding 40–50 mmHg.
Management

Immediate IOP reduction is required to prevent optic nerve damage and irreversible vision loss. This is initially achieved with intravenous aceta-zolamide in combination with topical pressure-lowering medication and pilocarpine to induce miosis. Definitive management involves laser peripheral iridotomy to create an alternative aqueous humour outflow pathway, preventing recurrence. In refractory cases, surgical lens extrac-tion may be indicated.

Secondary glaucomas are a group of eye conditions where increased IOP results from underlying ocular or systemic disorders, leading to optic nerve damage and vision loss. These glaucomas can arise due to various causes, including eye trauma, inflammation (like uveitis), vascular disor-ders (such as central retinal vein occlusion), medications (like glucocorti-coids) or intraocular tumours.

Recognition of a tense orbit (orbital compartment syndrome) and the need for immediate intervention can be vision-saving. Orbital injuries resulting in soft tissue oedema and retrobulbar haemorrhage within the confined bony orbit can increase intraorbital pressure, restricting blood flow and causing irreversible optic nerve injury and sight loss.
Clinical features
Visual acuity will be reduced, but to assess this may require the opening of tense eyelids. Proptosis is often painful, with resistance to retropulsion.

Eye pressure is elevated and a relative afferent pupillary defect is present. The diagnosis is largely clinical, as while CT orbital imaging may demon-strate the presence of a retrobulbar haemorrhage, this should not delay performing a lateral canthotomy.
Management

If suspected, lateral canthotomy (incision of the lateral canthal tendon) and cantholysis (disinsertion of the lateral canthal tendon) should be per-formed. If no improvement, IV acetazolamide and IV mannitol can be used.

Orbital cellulitis is a serious infection of the tissues surrounding the eye within the orbit. It is often caused by bacterial spread from adjacent structures such as the sinuses. It is an ophthalmic and medical emer-gency with the potential to cause loss of vision and rarely loss of life if there is extension into adjacent intracranial structures.
Pathogenesis

The infection typically spreads from the paranasal sinuses, most commonly the ethmoid sinus. The most common pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus species and anaerobes; in chil-dren, Haemophilus influenzae type B was historically common, but has decreased due to vaccination.
Clinical features

The distinction between orbital cellulitis and, more commonly, preseptal cellulitis is critical in guiding management. Features to aid differentiation are outlined in Box 28.8. For cases of preseptal cellulitis, investigations are not usually necessary. For all suspected orbital cellulitis, undertake temperature measurement, FBC, blood cultures and CT orbits and sinuses (pre- and post-contrast).
Management

Children less than 2 years old should be treated as orbital cellulitis due to their orbital septum having not fully developed and the associated greater risk of progression. Admit patients suspected of having orbital celluli-tis for IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + metronidazole). Early ophthalmology assessment should be obtained. Ear, nose and throat (ENT) assessment should be arranged to assess for sinus drainage.
Skin malignancies are discussed in detail in Chapter 26.

Representing approximately 85%–90% of all eyelid cancers, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most prevalent eyelid malignancy. It typically presents as a slow-growing, pearly nodule with rolled edges, often accompanied by ulceration. While BCC rarely metastasises, it can cause extensive local tissue destruction if not treated promptly (see Fig. 26.12).

Accounting for about 5%–10% of eyelid malignancies, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is more aggressive than BCC. It presents as a scaly, erythematous lesion with irregular borders and may ulcerate. Unlike BCC, SCC has a higher risk of metastasis to regional lymph nodes and distant organs.

A rare but highly aggressive eyelid malignancy, sebaceous carcinoma arises from the sebaceous glands, commonly in the upper eyelid. It may mimic benign lesions, such as chalazia or blepharitis, causing diagnostic delays. Sebaceous carcinoma has a high recurrence rate and potential for both local invasion and distant metastasis.

Though rare, melanoma of the eyelid is a highly aggressive cancer with a significant risk of metastasis. It often presents as a pigmented lesion with irregular borders and rapid growth, requiring prompt diagnosis and management (Fig. 28.9B). Common risk factors for these malignancies include prolonged ultra-violet (UV) exposure, fair skin, advanced age and a history of previous skin cancers.

Malignancies of the ocular surface are rare but serious conditions that can affect the conjunctiva, cornea and surrounding tissues. The most common types include squamous cell carcinoma, conjunctival mela-noma and lymphoma. Squamous cell carcinoma typically arises from the limbal region and is associated with risk factors such as ultraviolet (UV) radiation, human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and immunosuppression (Fig. 28.9C). Conjunctival melanoma originates from melanocytes and presents as a pigmented lesion, often associated with primary acquired melanosis (PAM). Ocular surface lymphomas, commonly of the muco-sa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) type, may present as painless, salmon-pink lesions.

Choroidal melanomas are primary ocular malignancies originating from melanocytes. Choroidal melanoma, the most common intraocular mela-noma in adults, often presents asymptomatically but may cause blurred vision, floaters, or flashes. It appears as a pigmented or non-pigmented, dome- or mushroom-shaped lesion with possible subretinal fluid and ret-inal detachment. The diagnosis is mainly clinical through examination combined with ret-inal imaging and ultrasonography to assess the internal characteristics. The goal of treatment is to preserve life and, where possible, vision. Management depends on tumour size, location and presence of metas-tases. Options include brachytherapy (radioactive plaques surgically placed on the sclera), external beam radiation therapy and surgical enu-cleation. Systemic therapy (see p. 1115) may be required for metastatic disease (usually liver).

Ocular metastasis refers to the spread of cancer cells to the eye from a primary tumour located elsewhere in the body, most commonly originating from the breast or lung. The choroid is the most frequent site of metastasis within the eye due to its rich vascular supply. Metastasis to the orbit can also occur (Fig. 28.10). Symptoms vary depending on location. Retro-orbital locations may cause proptosis and restricted eye movements. Choroidal lesions may cause blurred vision, visual field defects or pain, although some cases are asymptomatic. Diagnosis is typically made through clinical examination, imaging techniques like ultrasound and MRI and sometimes biopsy. Treatment options depend on location but include excision, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and tar-geted therapies, aiming to preserve vision and control the underlying systemic disease.

Retinoblastoma is the most common malignant intraocular tumour in chil-dren, originating from the retinal cells of the eye. It is primarily caused by mutations in the RB1 gene, either inherited or occurring spontaneously.

The disease often presents in children under 5 years of age, with symp-toms including leucocoria (white pupillary reflex), strabismus, vision loss, or eye redness and swelling. Early diagnosis is critical and is typically made through fundoscopy, ultrasound and MRI. Treatment options vary based on the extent of the disease and may include enucleation, chemo-therapy, radiation therapy, laser therapy or cryotherapy, aiming to pre-serve vision and prevent metastasis (Fig. 28.11).

28.1. A 28-year-old man has been referred to eye casualty complaining of a red, watering, painful and photophobic eye for the last 6 days. He is not a contact lens wearer and has been using chloramphenicol ointment from the chemist, which is not improving the symptoms. He has no significant medical history. Examination is challenging due to the degree of photophobia. His eye is very injected with ciliary flush and the pupil reacts sluggishly. What is the most common cause of this condition?
A. B. C. D. E.
Microbial keratitis Episcleritis Angle-closure glaucoma Blepharitis Acute anterior uveitis
Answer: E.

This is a typical presentation of anterior uveitis. Idiopathic anterior uve-itis is the most common form. The aetiology is unknown but could be related to cross-reactivity with particular microbial antigens. Systemic associations of anterior uveitis include HLA-B27 spondyloarthropa-thies, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and reactive arthritis as well as Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis. Infective causes include Herpesviridae herpes simplex and varicella zoster, syphilis, tubercu-losis and, rarely, Lyme disease. Other associated systemic conditions include sarcoidosis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Behçet disease and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Less common causes include drug-induced, especially anti-cancer drugs, haematological malignancy and even recent tattoos. It is therefore important to take a full systemic history, social and drug history to look for these associations. Microbial keratitis is less likely given the absence of trauma or contact lens use and no corneal infiltrates. Acute angle-closure glaucoma can cause a fixed mid-dilated pupil but is unlikely in this age group. Blepharitis and episcleritis are not typically associated with significant photophobia and would not cause pupillary changes.

28.2. A 35-year-old woman has noticed a change in the appearance of her right eye for the past 5–6 weeks. She describes a slight deterioration in vision and the eye has been aching, which is exacerbated with eye movement. Past medical history includes one spontaneous vaginal delivery and diet-controlled gestational diabetes. She takes the oral contraceptive pill. On examination, visual acuity is 6/12 in the right eye, 6/6 in the left. She has a full range of eye movements but complains of a tugging sensation on upgaze. Her colour vision, visual field testing and pupillary responses are normal. Externally her eyelids are not swollen or red, the eyes are both white. She has 2 mm of proptosis on the right side, and you can see 1 mm of sclera above the cornea. Her basic observations are all within range. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. B. C. D. E.
Orbital cellulitis Thyroid eye disease Cavernous sinus thrombosis Idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome Optic neuritis
Answer: B.

Thyroid eye disease is the most common cause of both unilateral and bilateral proptosis in adults. Typical features include ocular pain at rest, which is exacerbated with eye movements (gaze-evoked pain), swelling and redness of the lids, conjunctiva, plica and caruncle, double vision and proptosis. Sight-threatening complications of thyroid eye disease occur secondary to the increased orbital pressure. If this damages the optic nerve it is termed dysthyroid optic neuropathy, or if orbital swelling causes proptosis so severe that the eyelids cannot close this may result in corneal exposure keratopathy, a potentially sight- and eye-threaten-ing condition. It is always important to consider orbital cellulitis in cases of proptosis, but this would present more acutely with severe lid swell-ing, oedema, pain and usually with systemic manifestations including pyrexia. The differential diagnosis of proptosis is extensive, including trauma, vascular lesions such as carotid cavernous fistulas or cavern-ous sinus thrombosis, neoplastic lesions and inflammatory conditions. Optic neuritis can present with reduced visual acuity and retrobulbar pain classically exacerbated with eye movement. However, optic neuritis is not associated with proptosis; additionally, optic nerve function, which includes colour vision, visual field testing and pupillary responses, would be abnormal.

28.3. A 73-year-old man attends his optician. He was hospitalised following a stroke a few months ago, causing weakness in his left face, arm and leg. Although his mobility has improved, he reports his vision on the left is not any better. He wears spectacles for both near and distance and wanted these updating to improve his vision. His past medical history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), hypercholesterolaemia and benign prostatic hyperplasia. The optician performs visual field testing. What is the most likely pattern of visual field loss?
A. B. C. D. E.
Left monocular loss Right homonymous hemianopia Left homonymous hemianopia Bitemporal hemianopia Left superior altitudinal visual field defect
Answer: C.

The left-sided hemiparesis described would be caused by a stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere. The same pathology would affect the right optic radiation. Fibres representing the left temporal hemifield and the right nasal hemifield travel in the right optic radiation. Damage in this area would therefore cause a left homonymous hemianopia. This can be preferentially superior or inferior depending on the particular location of the stroke. Patients may interpret these symptoms and describe it as visual loss from one eye, which is why confrontational visual fields are an important part of a cranial nerve exam. Bitemporal hemianopia is classically caused by pituitary or other chiasmal pathology. Monocular altitudinal visual field defects are caused by pathology affecting the optic nerve or retina.

28.4. A 23-year-old man presents with a two-day history of a red, painful, photophobic left eye. He describes a burning sensation. He has no past ocular history, does not wear contact lenses and is usually fit and well. A drop of fluorescein is instilled into his eye and on examination with blue light a branching dendritic lesion is seen. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
A. B. C. D. E.
Topical aciclovir Oral aciclovir Topical steroid Topical antibiotics Topical lubricants
Answer: A.

A dendritic lesion in the absence of a history of contact lens wear is typical of herpes simplex keratitis. Débridement of the area with a viral swab has a twofold benefit: firstly, it reduces the viral load; and sec-ondly, if it is a first presentation of herpetic eye disease, it is important to establish a formal diagnosis. This is followed by treatment with topical aciclovir until the lesion is resolved. Some types of herpetic eye disease including recurrent presentations benefit from treatment with oral aci-clovir. Topical steroid is absolutely contraindicated in the absence of antiviral cover. Topical antibiotics or lubricants will not help because the aetiology is viral.

28.5. A 63-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of left-sided headache and blurring of vision in his left eye for the past 12 hours. He has also noticed pain on chewing and aching in his shoulders. Snellen visual acuities are 6/6 right eye and 6/60 left eye. There is a left afferent pupillary defect, and the left optic disc is swollen. What is the most appropriate first-line investigation for the most likely diagnosis in this presentation?
A. B. C. D. E.
Blood pressure Inflammatory blood markers MRI of the brain Temporal artery biopsy CT head scan
Answer: B.

The diagnosis of highest clinical concern is arteritic anterior ischae-mia optic neuropathy secondary to giant cell arteritis (GCA) in this sce-nario. This diagnosis would be supported by elevated ESR, CRP and a reactive thrombocytosis. Given the end-organ damage, intravenous methylprednisolone should be commenced while awaiting diagnostic confirmation with a temporal artery ultrasound or biopsy. Hypertension is associated with non-arteritic anterior ischaemia optic neuropathy. While high-resolution MRI can detect luminal stenosis or enhancement of the superficial temporal arteries to support a diagnosis of GCA, temporal artery ultrasound, where available, and temporal artery biopsy remain the gold standard of diagnosis.

28.6. A 78-year-old man presents with a decline in his left eye central vision over the past week, making it difficult for him to read and recognise faces. He reports that straight lines appear wavy. He is on medication for hypertension, but this is well controlled. On examination, his vision is 6/9 in his left eye and 6/24 in his right eye. There is no RAPD. He has bilateral nuclear sclerotic cataracts and a cup:disc ratio of 0.6. There are yellow drusen deposits bilaterally but a small haemorrhage at the left macular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A. B. C. D. E.
Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Central retinal vein occlusion Wet age-related macular degeneration Cataracts
Answer: D.

Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is characterised by the gradual loss of central vision, distortion of straight lines and difficulty with tasks requiring detailed vision, such as reading. The presence of drusen and pigmentary changes in the macula are hallmark signs of AMD. The presence of a haemorrhage suggests a choroidal neovascular mem-brane (wet AMD) which is likely causing disruption of his macula and associated visual changes. Urgent referral to ophthalmology services should be arranged to confirm the diagnosis with OCT and OCTA or fluorescein angiography. Treatment is a course of intravitreal anti-VEGF medication.

text: Psychiatric disorders have traditionally been considered as ‘mental’ rather than as ‘physical’ illnesses. This is because they manifest with disordered functioning in the areas of emotion, perception, thinking and memory, and formerly had no clearly biological basis. However, as biochemical and structural abnormalities of the brain are identified in an increasing number of psychiatric disorders, and psychological and behavioural factors are identified in many medical illnesses, the distinc-tion between mental and physical illness has become questionable. The World Health Organization (WHO) periodically publishes its International Classification of Diseases (ICD), which provides defini-tions for every recognised clinical condition. The 11th Revision (ICD-11, released in 2022) comprises 26 chapters. The diagnoses listed in Chapter 6, ‘Mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders’ (Box 29.1), are used by psychiatrists around the world in everyday clinical practice, and it is these conditions that provide the focus for this chapter. Psychiatric disorders are among the most common of all human illnesses. The WHO’s Global Burden of Disease study found ‘mental, neurological and substance misuse disorders’ to be the leading cause of ‘years lost to disability’ (YLDs), accounting for almost 20% of global YLDs, with anxiety and mood disorders alone accounting for over 10%. As with most clinical conditions, the prevalence of mental disorders var-ies with the setting. In the general population, depression, anxiety disor-ders and adjustment disorders are most common (> 10%) and psychosis is rare (< 2%); in acute medical wards of general hospitals, organic disor-ders such as delirium are very common, with prevalence highest among sick, older patients; in specialist general psychiatric services, psychoses are the most common disorders (Box 29.2).
section_path: Screening for cognitive impairment – the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA)

text: As in other areas of medicine, the psychiatric assessment comprises a structured clinical history and examination followed by appropriate inves-tigations. However, psychiatric assessment differs from a standard med-ical assessment in the following ways:
• There is greater emphasis on the history and relatively less reliance on investigations.
• A large part of the clinical examination component is conducted as the history is being taken rather than as a discrete set of procedures afterwards.
• It commonly includes the interviewing of an informant, usually a relative or friend who knows the patient, especially when the illness affects the patient’s ability to give an accurate history.

A full psychiatric history (Box 29.3) incorporating a detailed mental state examination may take an hour or more because of its complexity. A brief mental state examination, usually taking no more than a few min-utes, should be part of the assessment of all patients, not merely those deemed to have psychiatric illnesses.
The aims of the interview are to:
• establish a therapeutic relationship with the patient
• elicit the symptoms, history and background information (see Box 29.3)
• examine the mental state
• provide information, reassurance and advice.

The mental state examination (MSE) is a systematic examination of the patient’s thinking, emotion and behaviour. As with the clinical examina-tion in other areas of medicine, the aim is to elicit objective clinical signs. While many aspects of the patient’s mental state may be observed as the 29.3 How to structure a psychiatric interview
Presenting problem
Reason for referral
• Why the patient has been referred and by whom
Presenting complaints
• The patient should be asked to describe the main problems for which help is requested and what they want the doctor to do
History of present illness
• The patient should be asked to describe the course of the illness from when symptoms were first noticed
• The interviewer asks direct questions to determine the nature, duration and severity of symptoms, and any associated factors
Background
Family history
• Description of parents and siblings, and a record of any mental illness in relatives
Personal history
• Birth and early developmental history, major events in childhood, education, occupational history, relationship(s), marriage, children, current social circumstances
Previous medical and psychiatric history
• Previous health, accidents and operations
• Use of alcohol, tobacco and other drugs

• Direct questions may be needed concerning previous psychiatric history since this may not be volunteered: ‘Have you ever been treated for depression or nerves?’ or ‘Have you ever suffered a nervous breakdown?’
Previous personality

• The patterns of behaviour and thinking that characterise a person, including their relationships with other people and reactions to stress (useful information may be obtained from an informant who has known the patient well for many years) history is being taken, specific enquiries about important features should always be made.

Any abnormalities of alertness or motor behaviour, such as restless-ness or retardation, should be noted. The level of consciousness should be determined, especially in the assessment of possible delirium.
Speed and fluency should be observed, including slow (retarded) speech and word-finding difficulty. ‘Pressure of speech’ describes rapid speech that is difficult to interrupt.

This can be judged by facial expression, posture and movements. Patients should also be asked if they feel sad or depressed and if they lack ability to experience pleasure (anhedonia). Are they anxious, worried or tense? Is mood elevated with excess energy and a reduced need for sleep, as in (hypo)mania?

The content of thought can be elicited by asking ‘What are your main concerns?’ Is thinking negative, guilty or hopeless, suggesting depres-sion? Are there thoughts of self-harm? If so, enquiry should be made about plans. Are patients excessively worried about many things, sug-gesting anxiety? Do they think that they are especially powerful, impor-tant or gifted (grandiose thoughts), suggesting mania? The form of thinking may also be abnormal. In schizophrenia, patients may display loosened associations between ideas, making it difficult to follow their train of thought. There may also be abnormalities of thought possession, when patients experience the intrusion of alien thoughts into their mind or the broadcasting of their own thoughts to other people.
A delusion is a false belief, out of keeping with a patient’s cultural back-ground, which is held with conviction despite evidence to the contrary.
Illusions are misperceptions of real stimuli. Hallucinations are sensory perceptions that occur in the absence of external stimuli, such as hearing voices when no one is present.

Cognitive function has many components: memory, concentration, visuospatial abilities, executive function and so on. In most cases, a brief assessment of orientation (person, place and time – the patient is asked their name, age, date of birth, what building they are in, the current date and day of the week) and attention (‘serial 7 s’ – the patient is asked to subtract 7 from 100 and then 7 from the answer, and so on) is suffi-cient to exclude clinically significant cognitive impairment. Where there is reason to suspect cognitive impairment, a standardised screening tool should be used. In delirium, cognitive impairment typically fluctuates over time so may be missed by a single assessment. The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) is a useful screen-ing questionnaire that covers all the main domains of cognitive function (see p. 1269). It is designed to be easy to use and is freely available online in many different languages. Another widely used screening test is the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), although this is subject to copyright. The Addenbrooke’s Cognitive Examination, 3rd edition (ACE-III) offers a more comprehensive assessment and brief training courses for clinicians wishing to use it. These resources are available online (see ‘Further information’).

Patients should be asked what they think their symptoms are due to and whether they warrant treatment. The failure of a patient to understand their own symptoms is referred to as ‘lack of insight’. Psychotic patients characteristically have lack of insight and fail to accept that they are in need of treatment.

In many areas of medicine, laboratory or radiological tests play a cen-tral role in diagnosis. Such tests are often performed in psychiatry but are typically used to exclude non-psychiatric illness rather than to con-firm a psychiatric diagnosis. For example, in a patient presenting with symptoms of anxiety, it may be appropriate to check thyroid function to exclude thyrotoxicosis as a cause of their symptoms. Specific inves-tigations are recommended in certain psychiatric conditions, such as dementia, delirium, substance misuse and eating disorders, as shown in Box 29.4. Further details of each of these disorders are discussed later in the chapter.

Most psychiatric disorders result from a complex interplay between psy-chological, social, environmental and genetic factors. Each of these fac-tors may play a role in predisposing to, precipitating or perpetuating a disorder (Box 29.5).

Genetic factors play a predisposing role in many psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. However, while some dis-orders, such as Huntington disease, are due to mutations in a single gene, the genetic contribution to most psychiatric disorders is polygenic in nature and mediated by the combined effects of several genetic vari-ants, each with modest effects and modulated by environmental factors.

Brain structure is grossly normal in most psychiatric disorders, although abnormalities may be observed in some conditions, such as general-ised cerebral atrophy in Alzheimer disease and enlarged ventricles with a slightly decreased brain size in schizophrenia. Functioning of the brain, however, is commonly altered due to changes in neurotransmitters such as dopamine, noradrenaline (norepinephrine) and 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT, serotonin). Functional differences in specific areas of the brain are increasingly being recognised using advanced imaging techniques. For example, positron emission tomography (PET) studies of dopa-mine ligand binding in schizophrenia have consistently demonstrated increased dopamine synthesis in the striatum, even in untreated patients, while a smaller body of PET evidence points towards reductions in 5-HT transporter binding in the mid-brain and amygdala in depression. Pattern classification approaches to structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data can accurately predict the development of schizo-phrenia in at-risk populations, while generalised grey matter loss over time is a marker of poor prognosis. Increased anterior cingulate activity in depression is a consistent predictor of good response to both antide-pressants and cognitive behaviour therapy. While these and other imag-ing techniques show potential as diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic aids, they remain research tools at the present time.

It is also increasingly clear that psychiatric disorders are associated with disruptions in neuronal systems rather than single sites. These can be char-acterised using diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) of white-matter projection fibres and resting-state/task-based functional MRI (fMRI) studies of inter-re-gional connectivity. For example, DTI has shown reduced white-matter den-sity in limbic (‘emotional’) system tracts, such as the fornix and cingulum, in many disorders. Resting-state fMRI studies consistently identify ‘default mode’, salience and executive control networks of interconnected neuronal populations for certain mental activities. These pathways are implicated in several psychiatric disorders but, as yet, in non-specific ways.
Early childhood adversity, such as emotional deprivation or abuse, pre-disposes to most psychiatric disorders, such as depression, eating dis-orders and personality disorders in adulthood.

The relationship between personality and psychiatric disorder can be difficult to assess because the development of psychiatric disorder can impact on a person’s personality. Some personality types do predispose to the development of a psychiatric disorder, for example, an obsessional (‘anankastic’) personality increases the risk of obsessive–compulsive dis-order. A disordered personality may also perpetuate a psychiatric disor-der once it is established, leading to a poorer prognosis.

A person’s behaviour may predispose to the development or perpetu-ation of a disorder. Examples include excess alcohol intake leading to dependence, dieting in anorexia or persistent avoidance of the feared situation in phobia.

The lack of a close, confiding relationship predisposes to some psychi-atric disorders, such as depression, and this may be particularly relevant in older adults where social isolation is common (Box 29.6). As well as predisposing to psychiatric disorders, the reduced social support that results from having a psychiatric disorder may also act to perpetuate it.

Social and environmental stressors often play an important role in pre-cipitating psychiatric disorder in those who are predisposed, such as trauma in post-traumatic stress disorder, losses (such as bereavement) in depression, and events perceived as threatening (such as potential loss of employment) in anxiety.
29.6 Medical psychiatry in old age
• Organic psychiatric disorders: especially common, so cognitive function should always be assessed; if impaired, an associated medical condition or adverse drug effect should be suspected.
• Disturbed behaviour: delirium is the most common cause.
• Depression: common. Just because a person is old and frail does not mean that depression is ‘to be expected’ and that it should not be treated.
• Self-harm: associated with an increased risk of completed suicide.
• Medically unexplained symptoms: common and often associated with depressive disorder.
• Loneliness, poverty and lack of social support: must be taken into consideration in management decisions.

Delirium is a medical disorder that is common in older adults and in patients in high-dependency and intensive care units. The causes, assessment and management of delirium are described in Chapter 32.

Misuse of alcohol is a major problem worldwide. It presents in a multitude of ways, which are discussed later on in this chapter and summarised in Box 29.31 below. In many cases, the link to alcohol is obvious; in others, it may not be, since denial and concealment of alcohol intake are common.

The patient should be asked to describe a typical week’s drinking, quan-tified in terms of units of alcohol (1 unit contains approximately 8 g alco-hol and is the equivalent of half a pint of beer (284 mL), a single measure of spirits or a small glass of wine). The history from the patient may need corroboration by the general practitioner (GP), earlier medical records and family members.

Abnormalities in routine biochemistry and haematology can support the diagnosis of alcohol excess (such as the finding of a raised mean cell volume (MCV) and/or raised γ-glutamyl transferase (GGT)), but such tests are abnormal in only half of problem drinkers; consequently, normal results on these tests do not exclude an alcohol problem. When abnor-mal, these measures may be helpful in challenging denial and monitoring treatment response. Transient elastography (also known as FibroScan) is an ultrasound-based technique that measures fibrosis and steatosis. It is used in specialist services to complement information derived from tests of MCV and GGT.
The prevention and management of alcohol-related problems are dis-cussed later in this chapter.

The misuse of drugs of all kinds is also widespread. As well as the gen-eral headings listed for alcohol problems in Box 29.31 below, additional problems may occur in association with substance misuse (Box 29.7). These can be broken down into two broad categories:
• problems linked with the route of administration, such as intrave-nous injection
• problems arising from pressure applied to doctors to prescribe the misused substances.
Assessment and management are described later in this chapter in the section on substance misuse.
29.7 Substance misuse
Complications arising from the route of use
Intravenous
• Local: abscesses, cellulitis, thrombosis
• Systemic: bacterial (endocarditis), viral (hepatitis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV))
Nasal ingestion
• Erosion of nasal septum, epistaxis
Smoking
• Oral, laryngeal and lung cancer
Inhalation
• Burns, chemical pneumonitis, rashes
Pressure to prescribe misused substance
• Manipulation, deceit and threats
• Factitious description of illness
• Malingering

Delusions and hallucinations are abnormal beliefs and perceptions that have no rational basis. They are often due to psychiatric illness, but can be secondary to substance misuse, physical illness or neurological dis-orders, such as epilepsy.

A delusion is a false belief, out of keeping with a patient’s cultural back-ground, which is held with conviction despite evidence to the contrary. It is common to classify delusions on the basis of their content. They may be:
• persecutory – such as a conviction that others are out to harm one
• hypochondriacal – such as an unfounded conviction that one has cancer
• grandiose – such as a belief that one has special powers or status
• nihilistic – such as ‘My head is missing’, ‘I have no body’ or ‘I am dead’.

Hallucinations are defined as sensory perceptions occurring without external stimuli. They can occur in any sensory modality, but most com-monly are visual or auditory. Typical examples are hearing voices when no one else is present, or seeing ‘visions’. Hallucinations have the quality of ordinary perceptions and are perceived as originating in the external world, not in the patient’s own mind (when they are termed ‘pseudo-hal-lucinations’). Those occurring when falling asleep (‘hypnagogic’) and on waking (‘hypnopompic’) are a normal phenomenon and not pathological. Hallucinations should be distinguished from illusions, which are misper-ceptions of real external stimuli (such as mistaking a shrub for a person in poor light).

Careful and tactful enquiry is required because agitation, terror or the fear of being thought ‘mad’ may make patients unable or unwilling to volunteer or describe their abnormal beliefs or perceptions. The nature of hallucinations can be important diagnostically; for example, ‘running commentary’ voices that discuss the patient are strongly associated with schizophrenia. In general, auditory hallucinations suggest schizophrenia, while hallucinations in other sensory modalities (especially vision but also taste and smell) suggest an organic cause, such as substance misuse, delirium or temporal lobe epilepsy. Hallucinations and delusions often co-occur. If their content is consistent with coexisting emotional symptoms, they are described as ‘mood-congru-ent’. Thus, patients with severely depressed mood may believe themselves responsible for all the evils in the world, and hear voices saying, ‘You are worthless. Go and kill yourself’. In this case, the diagnosis of depressive psychosis is made on the basis of the congruence of different phenomena (mood, delusion and hallucination). Incongruence between hallucinations, delusions and mood suggests schizophrenia.

The presence of hallucinations and/or delusions should not automatically trigger a round of investigations. Rather, a careful clinical assessment of the nature, extent and time course of the person’s symptoms will gener-ate a list of likely diagnoses, and investigations can then be deployed to differentiate between these. When hallucinations and/or delusions arise in the context of disturbed consciousness and impaired cognition, the diagnosis is usually an organic disorder, most commonly delirium and/or dementia, and should be investigated accordingly.

The management of hallucinations and/or delusions is primarily the man-agement of the underlying condition (such as delirium, schizophrenia, mania or psychotic depression). However, certain principles apply what-ever the underlying cause. Hallucinations and delusions can be very real to, and often frightening for, the person who is experiencing them. They will often seek reassurance from the doctor. The doctor should acknowledge that these experiences are real for the patient while avoiding being drawn into colluding with the patient’s false beliefs or perceptions. Statements such as ‘Sometimes when we are unwell our brain plays tricks on us’ can help to reassure a patient. Where the patient lacks insight, however, a more neutral ‘We will have to agree to disagree’ may be necessary to avoid conflict. Antipsychotic medication can reduce psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusion, and is often used in combination with other sedating medication (such as a benzodiazepine) to alleviate acute dis-tress and reduce behavioural disturbance.

It is not uncommon for general hospital patients to report low mood. It is important to differentiate an understandable, self-limiting reaction to adversity (such as physical illness or bad news), which is normal and requires support rather than ‘treatment’, from a depressive disorder, which is characterised by a more severe and persistent disturbance of mood and requires specific treatment.

Depression is a relatively common illness, with a prevalence of approxi-mately 5% in the general population and 10%–20% in medical patients. It is important to note that depression has physical as well as mental symptoms (Box 29.8). The diagnosis of depression in the medically ill, who may have physical symptoms of disease such as weight loss, fatigue, disturbed sleep, reduced appetite and so on that overlap with the physical symptoms of depression, relies on detection of the core psychological symptoms of ‘anhedonia’ (inability to experience pleasure) and the negative cognitive triad (see Box 29.18). In some cases, depression may occur as a result of a direct effect of a medical condition or its treatment on the brain, when it is referred to as an ‘organic mood disorder’ (Box 29.9).

When a patient appears to be low in mood, it is good practice to ask them specifically about their mood. Do they feel low (nausea, over-sedation, par-kinsonism and so on can all cause a patient to appear low in mood). If so, how long have they been feeling low? Are they still able to enjoy things? To what do they attribute their low mood? If the low mood is persistent, not adequately explained by circumstances and/or associated with anhedonia, the patient should be investigated for depression. Where a patient’s mood is extremely low, the clinician should ask about suicide. Asking about suicide does not increase the risk of it occurring, whereas failure to enquire denies the opportunity to prevent it. The assessment of suicide risk is described in the self-harm section later in this chapter.

Where a patient’s low mood is an understandable reaction to adversity, the clinical team can support the patient by minimising uncertainty through open and effective clinical communication and by addressing isolation (allowing access to visitors, telephone and so on). More details of the strategies avail-able for management of depression are provided later in this chapter.

Elevated mood is much less common than depressed mood, and in med-ical settings is often secondary to drug or alcohol misuse, an organic dis-order or medical treatment. Where none of these applies, the patient may be experiencing a manic (or, if less severe, ‘hypomanic’) episode as part of a bipolar affective disorder. Mania is the converse of depression. It may manifest as infectious joviality, over-activity, lack of sleep and appetite, undue optimism, over-talkativeness, irritability, and recklessness in spending and sexual behaviour. When elated mood is severe, psychotic symptoms are often evident, like delusions of grandeur such as believing erroneously that one is royalty.

The first investigation for any medical patient presenting with persistent and inexplicable elevated mood in the absence of a history of bipolar affective disorder is a medication review. Mania is a relatively common side-effect of certain classes of drug, such as glucocorticoids, and is a rare side-effect of many other drugs. Recreational, herbal and over-the-counter prepara-tions should also be considered. Second-line investigations include tests for Cushing syndrome, thyrotoxicosis, syphilis and encephalitis.

The management of bipolar disorder and disturbed or aggressive behaviour are discussed in the relevant sections later in this chapter. The management of organic mania involves identifying and addressing the underlying cause.

Anxiety may be transient, persistent, episodic or limited to specific situa-tions. The symptoms of anxiety are both psychological and physical (Box 29.10). The differential diagnosis of anxiety is shown in Box 29.11. Most anxiety is part of a transient adjustment to stressful events: adjustment disorders. Other more persistent forms of anxiety are described in detail on page 1284.

Anxiety may occasionally be a manifestation of a medical condition such as thyrotoxicosis (see Box 29.11). Tests to exclude or confirm these con-ditions should be considered, particularly if anxiety is a new symptom that has arisen in the absence of an obvious stressor.

The management of specific anxiety disorders is discussed later in this chapter. Benzodiazepines and related drugs, while extremely effective in the short term, cause tolerance and unpleasant or even dangerous withdrawal syndromes if used for more than a few weeks.

• Adjustment disorder
